learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly set up the trigonometric ratio but is stuck on a basic algebraic step, incorrectly guessing that they should divide by $L$ to isolate the numerator. They need to recognize that because the horizontal distance is currently being divided by $L$, they must use the inverse operation (multiplication) to isolate it.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to identify the inverse operation of division, or ask them to evaluate what would happen to the fraction if they actually divided by $L$.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Algebraic Step
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to identify the inverse operation of division, or ask them to evaluate what would happen to the right side of the equation if they followed their guess and divided by $L$.

rubric_items.title: Defer Physics Context
rubric_items.description: Keep the immediate focus strictly on resolving the algebraic isolation of the horizontal distance, deferring any return to the physics concept of torque until this math step is correct.

rubric_items.title: Validate Variable Choice
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner correctly identified $L$ as the term that needs to be moved to the other side of the equation.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner to multiply by $L$ or provide the final isolated expression ($L \cos(\theta)$).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the learner's guess (e.g., 'No, try again') without directing their attention to the mathematical operations currently present in the equation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused by the abstract statement that a triangle is half a rectangle and cannot yet see how this modifies their familiar 'length times width' formula. They need a concrete way to visualize this geometric relationship before they can deduce the triangle area formula and eventually apply it to the hexagonal base.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to visualize or draw a rectangle and cut it in half diagonally, then ask how that physical action would affect the 'length times width' area.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Visualization of Halving
rubric_items.description: The response must guide the learner to visualize or draw cutting a rectangle in half (e.g., drawing a diagonal line from one corner to the opposite corner) to clearly see the two resulting triangles.

rubric_items.title: Elicit the Mathematical Effect
rubric_items.description: The response should ask the learner to deduce what happens to the total area (or the 'length times width' calculation) when the rectangle is split into those two equal triangles.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Formula
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly state the triangle area formula (e.g., '1/2 * base * height') or directly tell the learner to 'divide length times width by 2'.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Returning to the Hexagon or Volume
rubric_items.description: The response should not move back to discussing the six triangles, the hexagonal garden bed, or its 3D volume before the area formula for a single triangle is resolved.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely repeat that a triangle is half a rectangle without providing a concrete, step-by-step way to visualize or construct that relationship.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that physical injuries ('boo-boos') are not inherited, but they maintain the misconception that environmental exposure ('dirt') permanently alters a biological trait (fur color) that is then passed down. They need scaffolding to realize that getting dirty, exactly like getting an injury, is an acquired external change that does not affect the traits passed to offspring.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should create cognitive conflict by asking the learner to explain why a 'boo-boo' wouldn't be passed down to babies, but dirt would be, forcing them to compare these two acquired traits.

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirms the learner's correct realization that the babies would not be born missing a patch of fur.

rubric_items.title: Compare Acquired Traits
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to compare the 'boo-boo' directly to the dirt (e.g., 'Why wouldn't the boo-boo pass down, but the dirt would?') to create cognitive conflict about why they treat these two external changes differently.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Offspring Transmission
rubric_items.description: Directs the cognitive focus specifically to how the parent's external change (dirt) transfers to the babies, rather than just arguing about whether the parent can get clean (since the learner already rejected the bath analogy).

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for directly explaining that dirt is only a temporary surface coating or explicitly stating that acquired traits cannot be inherited.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for introducing formal genetic terms (DNA, genes, alleles) or moving to a new topic before resolving the learner's specific claim that 'dirt changes your fur.'

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is overgeneralizing the algebraic substitution, wondering if the height (h) is also squared or changed just like the radius. They need to understand that because the premise only specified doubling the radius, the independent variable h remains constant.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that asks the learner to reflect on the original premise (doubling the radius) to deduce for themselves whether the height of the cylinder has changed.

rubric_items.title: Addresses the Status of h
rubric_items.description: The response must directly address the learner's question by establishing, or prompting the learner to establish, whether the height (h) changes.

rubric_items.title: Prompts for the Underlying Reason
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to explain why h stays the same by referencing the original premise (e.g., 'Did we change the height?' or 'What does the problem say we are doubling?').

rubric_items.title: Physical Grounding
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connects the variable h to the physical height of the cylinder to help the learner visualize why it is independent of the radius.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply tell the learner the answer ('h stays the same because we only doubled the radius') without asking a follow-up question that requires the learner to do some cognitive work.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Evasion
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ignore the learner's specific question about h and prematurely force them back to calculating the final volume or writing the final formula.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has lost track of the skip-counting pattern (+4 wheels per truck) and reverted to counting by ones, guessing 'nine' as the next number after eight. They need a cue to distinguish between sequential counting and the +4 pattern they successfully used earlier in the dialogue.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should redirect the learner to the +4 pattern or their previous calculations to help them determine the next total after eight, without giving away the answer.

rubric_items.title: Cue the +4 Rule or Truck Context
rubric_items.description: The tutor must provide a conceptual cue to help the learner correct their mistake, such as reminding them that each truck adds 4 wheels or asking them to recall their previous answer for three trucks.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Next Total
rubric_items.description: The tutor's response should culminate in a prompt that asks the learner to identify the specific number that comes after 8 in the sequence.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Counting by Ones
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly acknowledges why the learner said 'nine' (e.g., noting that 9 comes next when counting normally) before redirecting them to the skip-counting pattern.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Sequence)
rubric_items.description: The tutor provides the next number (12) or the rest of the sequence (12, 16, 20) instead of requiring the learner to retrieve or calculate it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: The tutor rejects 'nine' or simply asks the learner to try again without providing a conceptual cue (like the +4 rule, the trucks, or previous answers) to help them find the right number.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the environment triggers the trait but is confused by the fact that the DNA doesn't change, leading them to falsely conclude the gene isn't involved at all. They need to realize that the gene is still necessary because it provides the instructions to build the temperature-sensitive enzyme in the first place.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should ask a guiding question that prompts the learner to think about where the enzyme comes from, bridging the gap between the unchanging gene and the environment-sensitive enzyme.

rubric_items.title: Targeting the Gene-Enzyme Connection
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to consider the origin of the enzyme or what provides the instructions to make it, guiding them to connect the gene to the enzyme.

rubric_items.title: Validating the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges the learner's logic, validating that it makes sense to question the gene's role since the tutor just stated the DNA sequence doesn't change.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Blueprint
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tells the learner that the gene makes, codes for, or provides the blueprint for the enzyme, doing the reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Missing the Enzyme Link
rubric_items.description: Responds to the learner's question without mentioning the 'enzyme', leaving them stranded without the necessary biological stepping stone to understand the gene's role.

rubric_items.title: Reverting to the Environment
rubric_items.description: Focuses the prompt on how the cold temperature affects the rabbit, a concept the learner has already successfully grasped.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly calculated that 8 alpha decays would result in a loss of 16 protons. Their immediate bottleneck is recognizing that this expected loss of 16 protons does not match the actual change in atomic number from Uranium (92) to Lead (82), which is the necessary stepping stone to discovering the role of beta decays.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the learner's calculation of 16 and prompt them to calculate the actual difference in atomic number between Uranium (92) and Lead (82) to expose the numerical discrepancy.

rubric_items.title: Validate Calculation
rubric_items.description: Confirms that the learner's calculation of 16 protons lost from the alpha decays is correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Actual Difference
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to determine the actual change in protons (atomic number) between the starting Uranium (92) and the ending Lead (82).

rubric_items.title: Frame as Discrepancy
rubric_items.description: Explicitly asks the learner to compare their calculated loss (16) with the actual change, setting up a cognitive conflict.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Briefly praises or acknowledges the learner's underlying logic (e.g., recognizing that 8 alphas times 2 protons equals 16).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Give Away the Difference
rubric_items.description: Provides the result of the subtraction (10 protons) instead of requiring the learner to calculate the actual difference themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Beta Decay Introduction
rubric_items.description: Mentions 'beta decays' or explains how the discrepancy is resolved before the learner has explicitly identified the numerical mismatch in protons.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Confirms the answer '16' but fails to provide a specific follow-up prompt directing the learner to look at the actual atomic numbers.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is expressing surprise and seeking confirmation that multiple low-energy photons cannot pool their energy to break a single chemical bond. They need to understand the strictly one-to-one, instantaneous nature of photon absorption to resolve why total energy does not dictate the breaking of individual bonds.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm that photon energies do not combine and provide a conceptual reason or analogy explaining why absorption is a strictly one-to-one, instantaneous event.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Non-Combining
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's realization by confirming that photon energies do not combine or pool together.

rubric_items.title: Explain One-to-One Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Help the learner visualize why the energies cannot pool, either by explaining the instantaneous nature of the absorption or by using an analogy of a single, all-or-nothing event.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Analogy Continuity
rubric_items.description: Re-use the established ping-pong ball or bullet analogy to explain why multiple impacts don't add up (e.g., the target recovers instantly before the next ball hits).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unhelpful Dismissal
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely say 'No, they don't' without offering any conceptual scaffolding to help the learner make sense of this counterintuitive rule.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Quantum Jargon
rubric_items.description: Penalize the introduction of complex quantum mechanical terms (like wave-function collapse or the photoelectric work function) that overcomplicate the basic one-to-one concept.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully applied the binary mapping rule to the first three pixels of the row but remains slightly tentative, seeking validation. Having demonstrated they understand the mechanics, they are now ready to have the step-by-step scaffolding removed so they can complete the rest of the sequence independently.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct answer and prompt them to translate the remainder of the row on their own.

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Mapping
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner is correct that the shaded square translates to a 1.

rubric_items.title: Fade Scaffolding
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to write out the 1s and 0s for the rest of the row independently.

rubric_items.title: Build Confidence
rubric_items.description: Provide brief positive reinforcement to address the learner's tentativeness (indicated by their question '... right?').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Tedious Over-scaffolding
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to identify the very next single pixel (e.g., 'What is the fourth square?'), failing to release the step-by-step guidance now that the pattern is grasped.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Doing the Work
rubric_items.description: Provide the binary sequence for the rest of the row instead of requiring the learner to generate it.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly applied the negative sign for a rightward horizontal shift based on the tutor's hint, but mistakenly swapped in the target peak day (172) instead of the shift distance (81) they had just calculated.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct use of 'minus' while prompting them to reuse the actual shift distance (81 days) rather than the target day.

rubric_items.title: Redirect to Shift Distance
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to use the shift distance they already calculated (81) instead of the target peak day (172).

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Sign
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or validates that the learner correctly chose subtraction ('minus') to represent the rightward shift.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly provides the correct combined answer (e.g., 'It should be minus 81' or 'x - 81') instead of letting the learner assemble it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's answer vaguely (e.g., 'Not quite' or 'Try again') without specifically directing their attention back to the 81-day shift amount.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Number Meanings
rubric_items.description: Explicitly contrasts the meaning of the two numbers (explaining that 172 is the destination, while 81 is the distance traveled) to resolve the conceptual conflation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified the necessary algebraic operation (dividing by v^2) to isolate the drag coefficient k from the equation kv^2 = mg, but is seeking validation before finalizing the step. They are at the very end of a procedural bottleneck and just need confirmation to complete the algebraic manipulation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm that dividing by v^2 is the correct step and prompt the learner to state the final, isolated equation for k.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Division Step
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's proposal to divide both sides by v^2.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Final Equation
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to write out or state the final resulting equation for k.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Final Equation
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final isolated equation (e.g., k = mg/v^2) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a vague counter-question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that leaves the learner stranded without validating their correct algebraic intuition.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Algebraic Success
rubric_items.description: Praise the learner for successfully figuring out the mathematical steps to isolate the variable.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully calculated the individual mass-position products (50 and 100) but is stuck on the next procedural step of the weighted average formula. They need targeted guidance to compute the necessary sums (either the sum of the products or the total mass) before dividing.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct products and prompt the learner to perform the next intermediate step—either adding the products together or calculating the total mass—without giving away the final division step.

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Products
rubric_items.description: Confirm that the learner correctly calculated the mass-height products of 50 and 100.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Next Procedural Step
rubric_items.description: Guide the learner to compute the next required sum—either by adding the two products together (50 + 100) or by finding the total mass (10 + 100).

rubric_items.title: Connect to Average Concept
rubric_items.description: Relate the current step back to the general concept of calculating an average, where finding a total sum is a necessary intermediate step.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not perform the addition for the learner (e.g., stating the sum is 150 or the total mass is 110) and do not prematurely give away the final division step.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unguided Prompting
rubric_items.description: Do not merely ask 'What's next?' or 'What do you think?' without providing scaffolding for how to combine the numbers.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is tentatively guessing that the sides meet at the top vertex, but lacks confidence and is relying on a vague visual impression rather than confirming the specific intersection of the labeled sides.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to look specifically at the blueprint to confirm whether the sides labeled 4 and 5 intersect exactly at the 40-degree angle, encouraging them to ground their guess in the provided visual evidence.

rubric_items.title: Direct Visual Verification
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to verify their guess by checking the blueprint to see if the sides labeled 4 and 5 actually connect at the 40-degree angle.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Tentative Guess
rubric_items.description: The response should acknowledge the learner's tentative answer ('at the top') to validate their participation before asking them to verify it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The response must not confirm or deny whether the sides meet at the top or whether the 40-degree angle is the included angle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response must not ask a generic question (e.g., 'Are you sure?' or 'Why do you think that?') without directing the learner back to the concrete visual evidence of the sides and angle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature SAS Conclusion
rubric_items.description: The response must not jump to asking if the triangles are congruent or if SAS applies before the learner has confidently established the included angle.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is blocked because they believe they need a numerical value for mass to proceed, which is preventing them from following the tutor's previous instruction to set up the equation. They need to realize that they can use the variable 'm' as a placeholder to discover its algebraic behavior.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly instruct the learner to use the letter 'm' as a placeholder and prompt them to write out the full equation so they can visually recognize the cancellation themselves.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Equation Formulation
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to write out or state the full equation (e.g., ma = m * g * sin(25°)) keeping mass in the expression.

rubric_items.title: Address the Missing Value Block
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly clarify that the learner does not need a numerical value for mass right now and can simply use the letter 'm' as a placeholder.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Hesitation
rubric_items.description: The tutor acknowledges that it is a good instinct to look for a numerical value or validates that it feels strange to write an equation with an unknown number.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Cancellation
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner that mass cancels out, divides away, or disappears from the equation, depriving them of the algebraic realization.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating the Previous Prompt
rubric_items.description: The tutor merely repeats the instruction to 'set them equal' or 'write the formula' without offering a new scaffold to help the learner past their fixation on the missing number.

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited that thermal energy consists of random molecular motion ('bouncing different ways'), but needs help connecting this randomness to why the energy is no longer 'useful' for macroscopic work. Additionally, they harbor a hidden belief that this dispersed heat will eventually cool down and disappear entirely, rather than just continuing to spread.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's excellent intuition about random motion and prompt them to contrast this chaotic bouncing with the coordinated, single-direction push needed to make the pendulum swing.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Random vs. Directional Motion
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to think about how molecules 'bouncing different ways' would interact with the pendulum, or ask what kind of molecular motion would be required to actually push the pendulum in one direction.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Microscopic Insight
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly affirm the learner's phrase 'bouncing different ways' as a highly accurate description of what heat or thermal energy actually is at the molecular level.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Disappearing' Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response includes a subtle check or reminder that these molecules will keep bouncing and transferring energy, addressing the learner's hidden belief that the heat will eventually 'cool down and disappear.'

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response introduces advanced vocabulary like 'entropy,' 'thermodynamics,' or 'dissipation' before the learner has fully reasoned through the physical mechanics of why random motion cannot do useful work.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner the conclusion (e.g., 'the molecules cancel each other out' or 'they would all need to hit it in the same direction') instead of asking the learner to deduce why the random bouncing fails to move the pendulum.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Continuations
rubric_items.description: The response merely asks a generic follow-up like 'Why does that matter?' or 'Tell me more' without specifically directing the learner's attention to the relationship between the bouncing molecules and the pendulum's movement.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is trapped in a cycle of guessing external environmental factors (sun, light, heat) to explain the spots, ignoring their own earlier, correct hypothesis about the parents. They need a prompt that breaks this cycle of environmental 'whack-a-mole' and redirects their attention back to internal, inherited causes.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should definitively close the door on environmental causes (e.g., by using a contrastive example of another breed in the heat) and redirect the learner to reconsider their earlier idea about the parents.

rubric_items.title: Prompting Internal Causes
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a question that directs the learner to think about internal factors, inheritance, or what the puppy is born with, shifting the focus away from the external environment.

rubric_items.title: Closing the Environmental Door
rubric_items.description: The tutor addresses the 'heat' guess in a way that definitively rules out the external surroundings (e.g., by using a contrastive example of another breed in the same heat, or by generalizing that no outside factor causes the spots).

rubric_items.title: Leveraging Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly reminds the learner of their earlier, overlooked guess ('From their parents?') to help them reconnect with the correct line of reasoning.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Whack-a-Mole
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply negates 'heat' and asks an open-ended 'what else?' question, which leaves the learner stranded and invites yet another environmental guess.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly states that the spots are caused by DNA, genes, or inheritance, giving away the answer instead of prompting the learner to articulate it.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is relying on a macroscopic mechanical analogy ('squeezing') to explain molecular transport, which stems from a hidden belief that the mitochondrion acts like a physical sponge storing molecules rather than a membrane packed with functional proteins. They need to transition from this 'storage and squeeze' model to a protein-mediated transport model.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should challenge the macroscopic 'squeezing' analogy by prompting the learner to recall what is actually packed into the inner membrane's folds (proteins) and asking how those structures might help ATP exit.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Membrane Crossing Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to propose a mechanism for how a molecule like ATP actually passes through a membrane, shifting their focus away from the macroscopic 'squeezing' analogy.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Membrane Proteins
rubric_items.description: Scaffolds the learner's thinking by referencing the proteins (or 'ATP maker things') already discussed, challenging the hidden belief that the folds are just empty storage space.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Directly names the exit mechanism (e.g., 'transport proteins,' 'channels,' or 'pores') instead of allowing the learner to connect the presence of membrane proteins to the concept of transport.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Simply rejects the 'squeezing' analogy (e.g., 'No, it doesn't squeeze') without providing a conceptual stepping stone, like the membrane proteins, to help the learner formulate a new idea.

rubric_items.title: Validate Boundary Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges the correct intuition behind the learner's question—that ATP faces a physical boundary (the membrane) that it must actively cross to reach the rest of the cell.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully overcome their misconception about including the imaginary unit 'i' in the distance formula and has proposed the correct expression for the magnitude of a complex number. They now need clear confirmation that their formula is correct so they can confidently apply it to their specific problem.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's correct formula and prompt them to apply it to their specific problem (e.g., calculating their force vector).

rubric_items.title: Validate the Formula
rubric_items.description: The tutor must clearly confirm that the learner's proposed formula, $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, is exactly right.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Application
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to take the next step by applying this correct formula to their specific numbers or problem context.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Re-teaching
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not launch into another explanation of why the 'i' is omitted, as the learner has already grasped this concept and needs to move forward.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Withholding Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not respond with a vague question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that withholds the direct validation the learner is seeking for their hard-won realization.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Formal Terminology
rubric_items.description: The tutor may optionally introduce the formal term 'magnitude' or 'absolute value' to label the distance formula the learner just deduced.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confusing revenue with profit, believing that the entire $15 selling price is kept and ignoring the $10 cost to acquire the shirt. They need a concrete, step-by-step breakdown of the transaction to see that the initial cost reduces the final amount kept.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a chronological or physical framing of the $15/$10 transaction (e.g., spending $10 out of pocket, then receiving $15) to prompt the learner to calculate the net gain.

rubric_items.title: Emphasize the Outgoing Cost
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly draw the learner's attention to the $10 that was spent to acquire the shirt, emphasizing that this money leaves their possession.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Net Amount
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to determine what remains of the $15 after the $10 cost is accounted for or paid back.

rubric_items.title: Chronological or Physical Framing
rubric_items.description: The tutor frames the scenario as a sequence of events (e.g., paying $10 first, then receiving $15) or a physical exchange to make the need for subtraction intuitive.

rubric_items.title: Giving Away the Answer or Operation
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly states the $5 profit or directly tells the learner to 'subtract 10 from 15', bypassing the learner's opportunity to deduce the relationship.

rubric_items.title: Reverting to Abstract Definitions
rubric_items.description: The tutor abandons the concrete $15/$10 example to re-explain the general definitions of revenue, cost, and profit, which would fail to address the learner's immediate confusion.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is bypassing the tutor's prompt to calculate the rate of change, instead guessing that the speed is 'constant' based on their persistent belief that a flat line means steady forward motion. They need to actually evaluate the change in height to mathematically prove to themselves that the vertical speed is zero.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should redirect the learner to perform the specific calculation requested in the previous turn, starting by asking them to identify the change in height during the flat section.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Height Change Calculation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to identify the specific change in height (or the numerator for the rate of change) during the flat section of the graph.

rubric_items.title: Refocus on Verticality
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner that the calculation is specifically for vertical speed, distinguishing it from their intuition about overall or forward motion.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Constant' Guess
rubric_items.description: Address the learner's question about 'constant speed' by framing the calculation as the way to test that hypothesis (e.g., 'Let's find the exact number first to see if that's true').

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful: Giving Away Zero
rubric_items.description: State that the vertical speed is zero or that the change in height is zero, doing the mathematical step for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful: Vague Formula Prompt
rubric_items.description: Tell the learner to 'use the formula' or 'calculate the rate of change' without breaking it down into the specific, manageable first step of finding the change in height.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has just experienced cognitive conflict, realizing through calculation that doubling the horizontal length of a right triangle does not halve its angle of inclination. They are stuck on the intuitive but incorrect assumption that angles scale linearly with side lengths and need scaffolding to visualize or test why this proportionality fails.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuitive guess and provide a concrete way to investigate the non-linear relationship, such as suggesting they draw the two triangles overlapping or test another length (like 5 feet) to see if the linear pattern holds.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Intuitive Guess
rubric_items.description: The tutor should acknowledge that the learner's expectation (that doubling the length would exactly halve the angle to 22.5 degrees) was a very logical and common intuitive assumption.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold an Investigation of the Relationship
rubric_items.description: The tutor must provide a concrete lens for the learner to explore why the angle didn't halve, such as suggesting they sketch the 10x10 and 20x10 triangles overlapping, or asking them to test the linear rule on a length of 5 feet (which would impossibly predict a 90-degree angle).

rubric_items.title: Highlight the Ratio vs. Angle Distinction
rubric_items.description: The tutor could explicitly draw the learner's attention to the fact that while the tangent ratio halved (from 1 to 0.5), the angle itself did not, helping to isolate the non-linear step in the calculation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Conceptual Reason
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not directly explain that trigonometric functions are non-linear or explicitly describe the geometric reason for the changing angle without letting the learner discover it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rebound
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not leave the learner stranded by simply asking a generic question like 'Why do you think it didn't halve?' without offering a visual or numerical tool to help them figure it out.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in their everyday visual experience; despite intellectually accepting that glass blocks infrared light, they cannot intuitively grasp that a camera looking at clear glass would see the glass itself rather than the person behind it.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that uses the previously established 'solid wall' analogy or traces the physical path of the light to help the learner deduce that the camera can only detect the glass itself.

rubric_items.title: Trace the Light Source
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to identify what physical object the light entering the camera lens is actually coming from if the person's light is stopped.

rubric_items.title: Re-invoke the Opaque Wall Analogy
rubric_items.description: Use the previously established concept of a solid wall (or another everyday opaque object) to help the learner bypass their visual bias about transparent glass.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Visual Bias
rubric_items.description: Validate the learner's persistent confusion by acknowledging that it is highly counterintuitive because our eyes easily see the person through the glass.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the camera sees the glass or detects the temperature of the glass.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repetitive Dead-Ends
rubric_items.description: Do not merely repeat the fact that the glass blocks the light, as the previous turn already did this without successfully shifting the learner's mental model.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that negative charges in the wood's atoms are repelled by the balloon, but lacks a mental model of the spatial boundaries of this movement within a solid insulator. They need a concrete spatial framework (like visualizing the atom as a bounded space) to deduce exactly where the charges shift without leaving the atom.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a spatial analogy for a single atom (e.g., a room or a sphere) and prompt the learner to deduce where the negative charges would go inside that space when the negative balloon approaches one side.

rubric_items.title: Provide Atomic Spatial Framework
rubric_items.description: The response establishes a concrete spatial boundary or analogy for a single atom (e.g., a tiny room, a bubble, or a sphere) to help the learner visualize the limited space the charges can move within.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Deduction of Position
rubric_items.description: The response asks the learner to use the concept of repulsion to predict where the negative charges will end up within that specific atomic space.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce the 'Trapped' Constraint
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly reminds the learner of the previously established fact that the charges remain trapped inside their specific atom while shifting.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response directly tells the learner the answer (e.g., 'they move to the back of the atom' or 'they move to the side furthest from the balloon') instead of letting them deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response simply asks the learner where the charges go (e.g., 'Where do you think?') without providing any spatial framework or analogy to constrain their guess, leaving them stranded.

rubric_items.title: Conductor Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response implies or states that the negative charges move into neighboring atoms or deep into the wall, which incorrectly describes a conductor rather than an insulator like wood.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully articulated the final step of the conversion process (multiplying by 7.48) and now understands the full sequence of operations. They need validation that this step completes the conversion to gallons, followed by a prompt to execute the calculation or synthesize the complete formula.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's final step and prompt them to execute the full calculation or write out the complete equation combining all three steps.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Final Step
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's question by confirming that multiplying by 7.48 is the correct final step to find the total volume in gallons.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Full Execution
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to execute the math using their specific numbers or to write out the complete equation that combines dividing by 12, multiplying by the area, and multiplying by 7.48.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Calculation Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not calculate the final numerical answer or write out the synthesized mathematical expression for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Affirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply say 'yes' or 'correct' without giving the learner a clear prompt to perform the calculation or write out the final equation.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or praise the learner for successfully breaking down and identifying all the steps of the multi-step conversion.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that heavy seeds survive in cracks while light seeds die on concrete, but they hold a teleological misconception, believing individual plants intentionally change their seed type to survive. They need to shift from thinking about individual intentional change to population-level change driven by the survival and reproduction of plants that already have heavy seeds.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A cognitive-conflict prompt that challenges the idea of intentional change (e.g., asking if a plant that dies on concrete can change its seeds, or if a plant can choose its traits) to guide the learner toward realizing that the population changes because only the heavy-seeded survivors reproduce.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Intentional Change
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to question the mechanism of change, specifically challenging the idea that an individual plant can actively choose or decide to alter its seeds.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Survivors' Offspring
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner's attention back to the plants that successfully survived in the cracks, prompting them to consider what kind of seeds those specific survivors will pass on.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Correct Outcome
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's underlying intuition that the overall group of plants does end up changing over time, before pivoting to correct the mechanism of how it happens.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Explanation of Natural Selection
rubric_items.description: Directly explains that the population changes because only heavy-seeded plants survive to reproduce, giving away the mechanism of natural selection instead of letting the learner deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Simply tells the learner 'no, plants don't change' or asks a generic 'how do you think it happens?' without grounding the prompt in the survival/death outcomes established in the previous turns.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is clinging to the intuitive belief that physical hardness causes waves to deflect, guessing that microwaves 'bounce off' the plate despite the tutor's previous analogy about light passing through a glass window. They need targeted guidance to explicitly map the transmission of light through glass to the transmission of microwaves through ceramic.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should directly challenge the 'bounce off' guess by asking the learner to recall or apply what light does when it hits a clear glass window, prompting them to conclude that microwaves pass through the plate.

rubric_items.title: Map Analogy to Ceramic Plate
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to deduce that microwaves pass through the ceramic plate by explicitly mapping it to the behavior of light with a glass window.

rubric_items.title: Challenge 'Bounce Off' Guess
rubric_items.description: Directly address the learner's 'bounce off' guess by contrasting it with the window analogy (e.g., asking if light bounces off a clear window).

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful: Giving Away Transmission
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that microwaves pass through the plate; they must make this connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful: Bare Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply say 'no' or ask the learner to guess again without using the window analogy or other scaffolding to guide their reasoning.

rubric_items.title: Premature Concept: Metal Reflection
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce the fact that microwaves bounce off metals, as this would inadvertently validate their incorrect reasoning about hardness and derail the current focus on transmission.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that $i^3$ simplifies to $-i$, but their phrasing indicates hesitation. They now need confirmation of their algebraic result and a prompt to connect this expression back to their original geometric goal of a 270-degree rotation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that $i^3 = -i$ and prompt the learner to explain or visualize how multiplying by $-i$ geometrically achieves the desired 270-degree rotation.

rubric_items.title: Affirmation of Correctness
rubric_items.description: Confirm that the learner's tentative answer of $-i$ is entirely correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Geometric Connection
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain, visualize, or deduce what multiplying a coordinate by $-i$ does to its position on the complex plane.

rubric_items.title: Reference to Original Goal
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tie the current algebraic step ($-i$) back to the learner's initial goal of achieving a 270-degree rotation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Geometric Meaning
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that multiplying by $-i$ points downwards or corresponds to a 270-degree counterclockwise (or 90-degree clockwise) rotation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-End Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely confirm the answer without asking a follow-up question that drives the learner to interpret the result geometrically.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that the interaction involves food from the hawk's perspective, but they are failing to realize that the chart categorizes the behaviors of the meerkats, not the predators. They are stuck in a loop because the tutor keeps explaining the column definitions rather than clarifying whose perspective the chart is about.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct observation about the hawk's motivation, and then ask a targeted question to shift their focus to whose behavior the chart is actually tracking (the meerkats).

rubric_items.title: Validate Hawk Perspective
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's correct observation that the hawk is indeed looking for food.

rubric_items.title: Target the Chart's Subject
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explicitly identify whose behavior or perspective the chart is tracking (the meerkats) to resolve the perspective confusion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating the Directive
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to put the behavior in the 'Staying Safe' column, which repeats a failed strategy and prevents the learner from resolving the misconception themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explicit Denial
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tell the learner they are wrong about the food aspect (e.g., 'No, it's not about food'), which dismisses their valid point about the hawk's motivation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Redirection
rubric_items.description: Ask a general question about the behavior or the columns (e.g., 'What do you think?') without specifically targeting the confusion between the hawk's and the meerkat's perspectives.

learning_objective: Whole Numbers, Place Value, and Fractions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confusing whole number place values with decimal place values, guessing 'tens' instead of 'hundredths' for the second decimal place. They need immediate scaffolding to distinguish between the naming conventions for whole numbers (left of the decimal) and fractions/decimals (right of the decimal, ending in '-ths').
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that 'tens' is a whole number place value and provide a pattern-based hint to help the learner deduce the correct decimal place value that follows 'tenths'.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Whole and Decimal Places
rubric_items.description: Explicitly address the learner's guess of 'tens' by distinguishing between whole number place values (left of the decimal) and decimal place values (right of the decimal, typically ending in '-ths').

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the 'Hundredths' Place
rubric_items.description: Provide a conceptual or pattern-based hint to help the learner deduce the 'hundredths' place (e.g., asking what fraction comes after 1/10, or relating the sequence of decimal places to the sequence of whole numbers).

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that 'tens' is a logical guess because of its phonetic similarity to 'tenths' or its role in the base-10 system.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Answer)
rubric_items.description: Directly state that the zero is in the 'hundredths' place without requiring the learner to do the cognitive work to find the name.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Non-Guidance (Vague Rejection)
rubric_items.description: Reject the learner's answer of 'tens' or ask them to guess again without explaining why 'tens' is incorrect or providing a concrete clue for the correct place value.

rubric_items.title: Premature Return to Comparison
rubric_items.description: Shift the conversation back to comparing the overall decimals (0.45 vs 0.50) or the compost mixtures before the learner has successfully identified the place value of the zero.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is persistently stuck on the intuition that doubling the diameter leads to a four-fold increase, likely conflating linear scaling of the circumference with area scaling. Because the tutor has repeatedly just stated the conclusion that 'it doubles' without unpacking why, the learner is pushing back and needs to prove the relationship to themselves.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should stop repeating the rule and instead prompt the learner to justify their 'four times' hypothesis, either by asking them to explain their reasoning or by having them calculate the circumference for two specific diameters to see the scaling for themselves.

rubric_items.title: Shift the Burden of Proof
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to justify their 'four times' hypothesis, either by asking them to explain their reasoning or by having them calculate the circumference for two specific diameters.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Area vs. Length
rubric_items.description: The tutor validates the learner's intuition by suggesting they might be thinking of the wheel's area (which does quadruple) before redirecting them to the 1D length of the rim.

rubric_items.title: Restating the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for simply repeating that the circumference or spacing only doubles, as merely stating this fact has already failed to convince the learner.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Calculation
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for performing a comparative calculation or explaining the mathematical proof themselves instead of leaving the cognitive work of proving the 2:1 ratio to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for simply rejecting the learner's guess (e.g., 'No, it is not four') without providing a concrete path forward, such as asking for their reasoning or directing them to the formula.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced the first half of the physical swap (attaching the red tip to the blue chromosome) but is seeking confirmation before acting. They need this validation along with a prompt to figure out the reciprocal action for the remaining blue tip to complete the crossing-over model.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm the learner's correct idea to put the red tip on the blue chromosome, and then prompt them to deduce where the detached blue tip should go.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Red-on-Blue
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly confirm or validate the learner's suggestion to attach the detached red tip to the blue chromosome.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Blue Tip
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to decide what to do with the remaining detached blue tip to complete the process.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Reciprocal Swap
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner to put the blue tip on the red chromosome, as this takes away the learner's opportunity to complete the logic of the swap.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Withholding Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The response should not answer the learner's direct, correct question with a vague 'What do you think?' or otherwise refuse to validate their correct physical step.

rubric_items.title: Connect to the 'Swap' Concept
rubric_items.description: The response may briefly reinforce the concept by using words like 'swap', 'trade', or 'exchange' to describe what is happening with the tips.

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly traces the energy but hits a cognitive roadblock because their macroscopic sensory experience (the room isn't noticeably warm) contradicts the principle of conservation. They need to reconcile this by understanding the concept of scale and dissipation—specifically, that a small amount of energy spread over a massive volume results in an undetectable temperature change.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's logical observation and prompt them to compare the relatively small amount of energy generated by a hand crank to the massive volume of the room it dispersed into.

rubric_items.title: Address Scale and Dissipation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider the ratio between the amount of energy produced (by a small hand crank) and the size of the space it spread into (a whole room).

rubric_items.title: Validate the Sensory Observation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly acknowledge that the learner's observation (the room not feeling warm) is a logical and scientifically sound point based on human senses.

rubric_items.title: Suggest a Dissipation Analogy
rubric_items.description: Introduce or ask the learner to imagine an analogy of a small amount of something spreading into a large volume (e.g., a drop of hot water in a swimming pool) to make the microscopic change concrete.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not directly state that the temperature increase is simply too small or microscopic for human skin to detect; the learner must be guided to deduce this.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Sensory Contradiction
rubric_items.description: Do not bypass the learner's specific point about the room not feeling warm by merely repeating the rule that 'energy is conserved' or asking a generic question about where it went.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the growth involves multiplying by 2, but they are superficially adjusting their previous quadratic guess by adding a coefficient of 2 ($y = 2x^2$). They still fail to recognize that for repeated multiplication, the independent variable must be in the exponent.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to test their new equation for a specific day where it fails (like day 2 or day 3) and compare the result to the target number of views, shifting the cognitive load of the calculation to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Test Against Target Views
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate their new equation ($y = 2x^2$) for a specific day where it fails (e.g., day 2 or day 3) and check if it produces the correct target number of views.

rubric_items.title: Shift Cognitive Load
rubric_items.description: Require the learner to perform the calculation for the test themselves, rather than the tutor doing the math for them as was done in the previous turn.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Coefficient Logic
rubric_items.description: Validate that the learner's attempt to include a 2 makes sense because they know the views are doubling, before moving to test it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the correct equation ($y = 2^x$) or explicitly tell the learner to move the $x$ into the exponent.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unsupported Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not reject the equation without providing a concrete step for the learner to evaluate it (e.g., penalize simply saying 'No, that's not it, try again').

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has hit a cognitive wall and is exhibiting resistance ('They just do') to abstract questions about why herons need frogs. They understand herons eat fish but cannot bridge the gap to realize a predator can survive by switching entirely to an alternative food source, requiring a shift in pedagogical tactics to bypass their frustration.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should pivot away from abstract 'why' questions and introduce a concrete, relatable scenario or analogy (such as a human's favorite food being unavailable while other food is present) to help the learner intuitively grasp the concept of food substitution.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Scenario Pivot
rubric_items.description: Shifts the dialogue from abstract reasoning to a concrete, relatable scenario or analogy about losing one food source but having another available (e.g., a human losing their favorite food, or a heron looking at a pond full of fish).

rubric_items.title: Preserves Learner Prediction
rubric_items.description: Requires the learner to predict the outcome or next action in the new scenario, rather than stating the conclusion for them.

rubric_items.title: De-escalates Resistance
rubric_items.description: Neutrally acknowledges the learner's 'They just do' response or normalizes the difficulty of the concept to reduce friction before introducing the new scenario.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repetitive Abstract Probing
rubric_items.description: Repeats an open-ended 'why' or 'how' question about the heron's specific need for frogs, which the learner has just rejected and will likely cause further shutdown.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner the biological answer (e.g., explicitly stating that herons will survive because they can just eat more fish instead of frogs).

learning_objective: LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in an unproductive guessing loop, having just guessed 'reptiles' despite the tutor's previous hint about 'warm-blooded' animals. They likely lack the specific biological vocabulary to retrieve 'mammals' and need direct intervention to break the cycle so they can return to the core concept of homologous structures.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly rule out reptiles by reminding the learner they are cold-blooded, and then either provide the term 'mammals' directly or give an unmistakable defining trait (e.g., 'they produce milk') to break the guessing loop.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Reptiles' Guess
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly address why 'reptiles' is incorrect, ideally by referencing the previous hint that the target group is warm-blooded.

rubric_items.title: Break the Guessing Loop (Target: Mammals)
rubric_items.description: The response must provide the term 'mammals' directly or give an unmistakable defining trait (e.g., 'they produce milk' or 'they have hair') to end the blind guessing.

rubric_items.title: Reconnect to the Shared Trait
rubric_items.description: The response should connect the concept of this shared mammalian group back to the original phenomenon being discussed (the five-finger bone structure).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prolonging the Guessing Game
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask the learner to guess yet another animal group without providing the answer or a definitive, unmistakable clue, as this leaves the learner stranded.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unprompted Lecture on Phylogeny
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that launch into a long, unprompted explanation of evolutionary trees or cladistics instead of simply establishing the mammalian connection and returning to the bone structure.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is relying on the visual appearance of the diagram ('drawn like that') rather than geometric properties, missing the fact that a sketch does not guarantee the physical rigidity or congruence of the triangles. They need to realize that without a specific mathematical constraint (like an angle), the shape could still physically change despite how it is currently drawn.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A cognitive-conflict prompt that challenges the assumption that a drawing guarantees physical measurements, ideally using the physical context of the chair or the 'swinging' analogy to help the learner realize a specific mathematical constraint is still needed.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Visual Reliance
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to question whether a sketch guarantees the actual physical measurements or rigidity of the chair brackets.

rubric_items.title: Re-anchor to the Dynamic Model
rubric_items.description: The tutor should use the physical context of building the chair or the previous 'swinging side' analogy to illustrate why relying on the static drawing is insufficient.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Visual Appearance
rubric_items.description: The tutor acknowledges that the drawing does indeed look fixed or symmetrical before challenging its reliability as a mathematical guarantee.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Rule-Dropping
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply states a geometric rule (e.g., 'we can't assume things from diagrams' or 'drawings aren't proofs') instead of guiding the learner to deduce why the drawing is insufficient.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Constraint
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly names the missing piece of information (such as the included angle or the third side) needed to lock the triangle's shape.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully constructed the left side of the circle's equation for a shifted center but forgot to square the radius value of 5 on the right side. They need a targeted prompt to reconcile their current right side (`= 5`) with the $r^2$ rule they correctly identified earlier in the dialogue.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct left side of the equation and prompt the learner to reconsider the right side by recalling that the radius must be squared.

rubric_items.title: Prompt to square the radius
rubric_items.description: The tutor must direct the learner's attention to the right side of the equation and prompt them to apply the $r^2$ rule to their chosen radius of 5.

rubric_items.title: Affirm the correct left side
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly validate that the learner successfully constructed the left side of the equation ($(x-3)^2 + (y+4)^2$).

rubric_items.title: Recall the learner's prior insight
rubric_items.description: The tutor reminds the learner of their own recent statement that the right side of the equation represents 'radius squared' or $r^2$.

rubric_items.title: Penalize giving away the answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not explicitly provide the corrected right side of the equation (e.g., by saying 'it should be 25' or 'write 5^2').

rubric_items.title: Penalize unguided rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not reject the learner's attempt vaguely (e.g., 'Almost!' or 'Try again') without specifically pointing to the radius term or the right side of the equation.

rubric_items.title: Penalize revisiting the center
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not ask further questions or provide instruction about the $x$ and $y$ terms or the center $(3, -4)$, as the learner has already demonstrated mastery of this part.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly deduced that the balanced equation means the laser hits the shield, but their phrasing ('It hits it?') shows slight hesitation. They need confirmation that the point lies exactly on the circle's boundary, followed by a prompt to extend this logic to points that might lie inside or outside the shield.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuition, clarify that the laser hits exactly on the boundary of the shield, and ask a targeted question about what a value less than or greater than 25 would represent geometrically.

rubric_items.title: Validate Intuition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative answer that the laser does indeed hit the shield.

rubric_items.title: Establish Boundary Concept
rubric_items.description: Establish (either by stating it or prompting the learner to specify) that the balanced equation means the laser hits exactly on the edge, boundary, or perimeter of the shield.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Inequality Reasoning
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to deduce the meaning of an unbalanced equation, either by asking generally what a result less than or greater than 25 would mean, or by proposing a new coordinate to test.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Rule
rubric_items.description: Directly state the geometric rules for inequalities (e.g., telling the learner that a result less than 25 means the point is inside the shield) instead of allowing them to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-End Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Confirm the learner's answer but fail to ask a follow-up question that extends their reasoning to points not on the boundary, leaving the conversation stalled.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has shifted from asking how the plant 'knows' to asking about the physical consequence of failure ('what if they get eaten?'), providing a perfect opening to discuss differential survival. They need to realize that getting eaten means the plant's 'recipe' dies with it and cannot be passed on to the next generation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce what happens to a plant's 'recipe' (and its ability to make baby cacti) if the plant gets eaten before it can reproduce.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Consequence of Being Eaten
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explain what happens to the plant's 'recipe' or its ability to make seeds if it gets eaten by an animal.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Survivors and Non-Survivors
rubric_items.description: Guide the learner to think about which recipes (spiky vs. non-spiky) will actually be left in the desert to grow the next generation of cacti.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Insight
rubric_items.description: Validate the learner's question (e.g., 'That is exactly the right question to ask!') to encourage their shift toward thinking about survival outcomes.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that eaten plants die and fail to pass on their recipes; the tutor must leave space for the learner to deduce this consequence.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Reverting to the 'No Brain' Explanation
rubric_items.description: Do not revert to explaining that plants lack brains, eyes, or feelings, as this ignores the learner's productive pivot toward the physical consequences of being eaten.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is hesitating to follow the tutor's instruction because the physical model they are using (likely clay) has the sister chromatids joined together, representing the centromere. They need explicit permission and mechanical guidance to break this physical attachment to accurately simulate the final division of meiosis.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A direct instruction that validates the learner's observation of the attachment but explicitly tells them to physically break or snap the chromatids apart at the center to model the final cell division.

rubric_items.title: Instruct Physical Separation
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly instruct the learner to physically break, snap, or pull apart the connection holding the sister chromatids together.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: The response should acknowledge that the learner is correct to notice they are attached, validating their attention to the physical model's current state.

rubric_items.title: Map to Biological Reality
rubric_items.description: The response should briefly connect this physical breaking action to the biological reality, such as mentioning that the attachment point (centromere) splits during this final division.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask vague questions (e.g., 'What do you think you should do?') instead of giving the learner the explicit permission they need to break the physical model.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overcomplicating the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that introduce unnecessary mechanical details about cell division (like spindle fibers, kinetochores, or Anaphase II phases) that distract from the immediate physical action required with the model.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner intuitively grasps that confounding means the causes are 'mixed up', but they hold a hidden belief that a formal justification requires numerical evidence of prior high performance rather than just pointing out the logical design flaw. They need to understand that the inability to separate the variables (due to self-selection) is itself the formal reason the causal claim is invalid.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that 'mixed up' means the effects of the app and motivation cannot be isolated, and prompt the learner to articulate why this logical design flaw is sufficient to invalidate the causal claim without needing numerical proof.

rubric_items.title: Clarify 'Mixed Up'
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's phrase 'mixed up' by confirming that it means it is impossible to isolate the effect of the app from the effect of the students' inherent motivation.

rubric_items.title: Target the Hidden Belief (Logical vs. Numerical Proof)
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider whether we need actual data (like past test scores) to prove the study is flawed, or if the logical presence of confounding (self-selection) is enough to invalidate the causal claim.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Formal Construction
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to try drafting a sentence that uses this inability to separate the variables as the formal reason we cannot claim the app caused the higher scores.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not write the formal justification or provide the final statistical conclusion for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely confirm that the variables are 'mixed up' without pushing the learner to connect this concept to the validity of the causal claim or the study's design.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the operation is meant to calculate the total cost, but they lack the conceptual link between multiplication and repeated addition in this context. They need concrete scaffolding to see exactly *how* multiplying the $2 price by the number of stickers is a shortcut for adding $2 for every sticker bought.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to calculate the total cost for a small, concrete number of stickers using addition, guiding them to discover for themselves that multiplication is just a shortcut for repeated addition.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Addition Prompt
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to express the total cost for a small, concrete number of stickers (e.g., 3 or 4) using addition instead of multiplication.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'How'
rubric_items.description: Frame the prompt as a direct way to explore or answer the learner's specific question of 'how' the operation gets the total.

rubric_items.title: Validate Partial Understanding
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's correct statement that the goal of the operation is 'to get the total'.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Link
rubric_items.description: Directly explain that multiplication is repeated addition, giving away the conceptual link instead of letting the learner construct it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Abstract Multiplication
rubric_items.description: Ask an abstract question about the definition of multiplication (e.g., 'What does multiplication mean?') without grounding it in the concrete $2 sticker scenario.

rubric_items.title: Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: Introduce new variables or move on to building the rest of the function before the learner has resolved how multiplication calculates the total.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is defending their incorrect algebraic coefficient (70x) by pointing out the correct arithmetic sum of the unit rate ($20) and the flat fee ($50). They are stuck on combining the visible numbers, failing to recognize that adding the flat fee before multiplying applies the setup fee to every single shirt.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's arithmetic but prompt them to contrast this sum with their own previous correct calculation for 5 shirts, helping them realize they did not add 20 and 50 together when doing the math step-by-step.

rubric_items.title: Address the Arithmetic Defense
rubric_items.description: Directly address the learner's defense ('20 plus 50 is 70') by prompting them to realize why adding the $20 shirt cost and the $50 setup fee together before multiplying is incorrect in this context.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Correct Calculation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly reference the learner's own correct arithmetic steps for 5 shirts ('5 times 20... plus 50') to demonstrate that they did not combine the 20 and 50 in their successful calculation.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Arithmetic
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's basic arithmetic (20 + 50 = 70) is mathematically correct in isolation before addressing why that sum doesn't apply to the formula.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Formula
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the correct algebraic formula (e.g., '20x + 50') or explicitly tell the learner to write the 20 and 50 as separate terms.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Do not leave the learner stranded by simply rejecting their answer, asking them to 'try again', or stating abstract rules ('unlike terms') without directing their attention to the real-world context or their prior calculation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner recognizes that division is required but is overwhelmed by simultaneously figuring out the algebraic rearrangement of the formula and the mechanics of dividing numbers in scientific notation. They need step-by-step scaffolding that separates setting up the equation from executing the arithmetic.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuition to divide, then prompt them to take the first step by either substituting the known values into the formula or isolating the wavelength variable, deferring the math rules for scientific notation until the setup is clear.

rubric_items.title: Elicit the Equation Setup
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks the learner to substitute the known values into $v = f \lambda$ or to algebraically isolate $\lambda$, ensuring the learner is the one who determines the setup.

rubric_items.title: Validate Division Intuition
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly acknowledges or confirms that the learner is correct to recognize that division will be required.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Algebraic Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner the rearranged formula ($\lambda = v/f$) or exactly what to divide (e.g., '$3 \times 10^8$ divided by $5 \times 10^9$'), bypassing the learner's opportunity to set it up themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Math Instruction
rubric_items.description: The tutor explains how to divide scientific notation (e.g., dividing coefficients and subtracting exponents) before the learner has successfully established what is being divided by what.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor gives a generic prompt (e.g., 'Use algebra' or 'What do you think?') that fails to direct the learner to focus specifically on the formula or the known values.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a repetitive loop, equating the physical disintegration of the solid iron nail with the complete destruction of its matter ('it's gone').
