rubric_items.description: Explicitly asks the learner to connect the physical support of the gas (or the analogy) back to the scale, encouraging them to deduce how the downward push eventually reaches the bottom of the bottle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unexplained Assertions
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that merely repeat that 'the scale measures everything inside' or 'gravity still pulls on it' without addressing the learner's specific mechanical confusion about how the scale feels a floating object.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Over-explaining the Physics
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that give away the answer by explicitly explaining the chain of force (e.g., 'the gas pushes on the air, which pushes on the bottle, which pushes on the scale') instead of letting the learner figure it out.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Question
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that wondering how a scale feels a floating object is an excellent, intuitive physics question, validating the learner's critical thinking.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has just experienced a paradigm shift, realizing that functions involve two simultaneously changing quantities rather than a single static 'answer' to solve for. They now need to understand the directional, cause-and-effect relationship between these two variables.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's realization that both quantities change, and then ask a targeted question prompting the learner to articulate which changing quantity determines the other.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Realization
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's insight that yes, both quantities are changing at the same time.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Causality
rubric_items.description: Ask a question that requires the learner to identify the cause-and-effect relationship between the two variables (e.g., asking which one affects or controls the other).

rubric_items.title: Maintain Concrete Context
rubric_items.description: Keep the prompt grounded in the specific analogy of gaming hours and battery life rather than immediately shifting back to abstract x and y.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explaining the Relationship
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner how the variables interact (e.g., 'Yes, the hours you play causes the battery to drop'); the learner must articulate this connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-end Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely say 'yes' or 'exactly' without providing a follow-up question that drives the learner to analyze how the two changing quantities relate.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Vocabulary
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce formal terminology like 'independent variable' or 'dependent variable' before the learner has conceptually described the relationship in their own words.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive overload because the tutor asked them to construct three decimal-based bins simultaneously before they had grasped how to represent a single continuous boundary. They understand the need to avoid double-counting but are blocked by the mechanics of decimal notation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should de-escalate the cognitive load by scaling the task back to defining just the first bin, using plain language (like 'up to but not including') or a familiar analogy (like money) to bypass the decimal confusion.

rubric_items.title: Reduce Task Complexity
rubric_items.description: The tutor scales back the previous request by asking the learner to focus on defining just the very first bin, rather than asking for multiple bins at once.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Continuous Boundaries
rubric_items.description: The tutor provides a simpler conceptual framing for the boundary (such as using the phrase 'everything from 7 up to right before 8' or a familiar analogy like dollars and cents) to bypass the confusion caused by decimal notation.

rubric_items.title: Validate Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly acknowledges the learner's correct prior understanding that an 8 mm beak cannot be counted twice, using it as an anchor for the next step.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Providing the Bins)
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly provides the correct non-overlapping intervals (e.g., 'Just write 7.0-7.9, 8.0-8.9...') instead of guiding the learner to construct the first one.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a broad question like 'What are you lost on?' or simply repeats the instruction to make bins without offering new scaffolding to address the decimal confusion.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The tutor introduces formal mathematical inequality notation (such as 7 ≤ x < 8) to solve the boundary issue, which risks further increasing the learner's cognitive overload.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner mistakenly believes that fertilizer in runoff will act as a poison and kill wetland plants. They need to connect their everyday knowledge of what fertilizer is used for (helping plants grow) to the wetland context to understand how plants process these nutrients.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to recall the primary purpose of fertilizer (e.g., why people put it on their lawns) to help them realize that it acts as food or nutrients for the plants rather than poison.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Fertilizer Purpose
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider the intended purpose of fertilizer or its typical effect on lawns.

rubric_items.title: Validate Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's intuition is reasonable for some types of toxic pollutants, before focusing specifically on the nature of fertilizer.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that fertilizer acts as plant food, provides nutrients, or causes plants to grow.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the learner's guess or ask a vague question (e.g., 'What else might happen?') without specifically directing them to think about what fertilizer is.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly believes that the insurance fee, like the cost of rain, must be multiplied by a fractional probability, guessing 70% (the probability of no rain). They need to realize that once the decision to buy insurance is made, paying the premium is a certainty regardless of the weather.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should ask a targeted question that challenges the learner to think about whether the insurance company only charges them in certain weather conditions.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Weather Dependency
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider whether paying the insurance fee depends on the weather outcomes (e.g., asking if they only pay when it's sunny, or if they pay regardless of rain).

rubric_items.title: Address the 70% Guess
rubric_items.description: Explicitly reference the learner's '70%' guess by asking what that number represents in the real world or testing if the fee only applies to that specific 70% outcome.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Focus on the Fee's Probability
rubric_items.description: Keep the immediate focus on establishing the probability of paying the insurance fee, without prematurely moving to comparing the $1,500 expected cost of rain to the insurance cost.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Conceptual Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that the fee is a 'fixed cost,' 'guaranteed,' 'certain,' or has a '100% probability.'

rubric_items.title: Avoid Procedural Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner the mathematical operation to perform (e.g., 'you don't need to multiply it,' 'just use the base fee,' or 'multiply it by 1').

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the sequential counting required for the y-axis but is confusing the spaces ('boxes') with the grid lines, a common formatting bottleneck in early data representation. They need immediate, concrete clarification on this spatial convention so they can successfully draw their scale.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly correct the 'box' misconception by directing the learner to write on the line itself, ideally using clear spatial language or referring back to the ruler analogy, without mapping out the rest of the numbers for them.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Box' Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly correct the learner's suggestion by clarifying that the number goes on the grid line itself, not inside the box or space.

rubric_items.title: Provide Concrete Spatial Grounding
rubric_items.description: The response should use clear descriptive language or an analogy (such as the previously mentioned ruler) to help the learner visualize exactly where the line is compared to the box.

rubric_items.title: Affirm the Correct Number
rubric_items.description: The response should briefly acknowledge that the learner correctly identified '2' as the next number in the sequence, separating their correct counting from their incorrect placement.

rubric_items.title: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that simply say 'no' or ask a generic question (e.g., 'Are you sure?', 'Where did we put the 1?') without explicitly clarifying the formatting convention.

rubric_items.title: Premature Completion
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that map out the rest of the axis for the learner (e.g., 'Put 2 on the next line, 3 on the next...') rather than just guiding this single placement and letting the learner continue.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is expressing valid physical skepticism, struggling to understand how a microscopic atomic shift (polarization) can generate enough macroscopic force to hold up a balloon. Their immediate need is a conceptual pivot that helps them bridge the gap between a tiny atomic movement and a noticeable macroscopic force.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that validates their skepticism and prompts them to consider either the massive quantity of atoms involved at the contact surface or the relative distance of the shifted charges.

rubric_items.title: Validate Skepticism
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validates the learner's intuition by acknowledging that a microscopic shift ('barely moving') does indeed seem intuitively too small to hold up a balloon.

rubric_items.title: Prompt on Scale or Relative Distance
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to consider either the massive number of atoms involved at the contact surface or the fact that the attracting charges are now strictly closer to the balloon than the repelling ones.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly explains that trillions of atoms add up to a large force or that the closer distance creates a stronger net attraction, giving away the physics concept rather than letting the learner deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Simply repeats the question about why a tiny lean causes attraction without offering a new conceptual pivot (like quantity of atoms or relative distance), leaving the learner stuck on their current bottleneck.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Conductor
rubric_items.description: Contrasts the tiny atomic shift in the wood with the free-flowing charges in the metal discussed earlier, contextualizing why the learner feels the movement is insufficient.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has formulated an accurate hypothesis that cacti open their pores at night to prevent water loss, but they have not yet realized that this creates a new timing conflict since making food requires sunlight, which is only available during the day.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's excellent hypothesis and then prompt them to identify the new problem this creates regarding the timing of sunlight and air collection.

rubric_items.title: Validate Nighttime Hypothesis
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm or praise the learner's hypothesis that the cactus opens its holes at night to save water.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Timing Conflict
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to consider the mismatch between when the plant collects air (night) and when it has access to sunlight (day).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Storage Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not reveal how the cactus solves this timing problem (e.g., by explaining that it stores the air or carbon dioxide chemically until daytime).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Continuations
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not simply ask a generic question like 'How does it make food then?' without specifically contrasting the nighttime air gathering with the daytime sunlight requirement.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully realized that the total capacity (64) must come first in the subtraction to avoid negative storage, overcoming their hidden belief that variables must always lead an equation. They now need to transition this concrete, conceptual understanding ('64 minus apps') into a formal algebraic expression using variables.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's logic about 64 being the maximum capacity, and then prompt them to represent 'the apps' with a mathematical variable to build the final expression.

rubric_items.title: Validate Size Constraint
rubric_items.description: Confirm the learner's realization that 64 is the maximum total capacity, which is why it must be the starting value we subtract from.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Variable Translation
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner how to represent the unknown size or number of 'the apps' using a mathematical variable.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Expression
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final algebraic expression or equation (e.g., '64 - x'); the learner must generate the variable term themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Formalization
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a generic question about writing the equation (e.g., 'So what is the equation?') without anchoring it to the '64 minus apps' structure they just built.

rubric_items.title: Highlight Variable Placement
rubric_items.description: Explicitly note that this real-world logic means the variable will come after the minus sign, directly addressing the common assumption that variables must always come first.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the formal mathematical terminology of 'input', which is preventing them from correctly ordering their coordinate pair. They already understand the concrete relationship between hours and battery percentage, so they need a conceptual bridge that connects the abstract term 'input' to the real-world concept of 'time' they already grasp.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a simple, non-technical definition of 'input', explicitly link it to the concrete concept of 'hours' in this scenario, and prompt the learner to try writing the coordinate pair again.

rubric_items.title: Plain Language Definition
rubric_items.description: Explains the term 'input' using simple, non-technical language (e.g., the starting information, what you put into a process, or the 'cause').

rubric_items.title: Contextual Grounding
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connects the concept of 'input' to the concrete scenario of the problem, specifically identifying 'time' or 'hours' as the input.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Output
rubric_items.description: Contrasts the 'input' with the 'output' or result (the battery percentage) to clarify the relationship between the two numbers.

rubric_items.title: Actionable Prompt
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to use this clarified meaning to attempt writing the (x, y) coordinate pair for B(12)=45 again.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Formal Jargon
rubric_items.description: Defines 'input' using additional formal mathematical jargon (such as 'domain' or 'independent variable') that does not resolve the learner's confusion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Coordinate
rubric_items.description: Directly provides the correct coordinate pair (12, 45) without requiring the learner to construct it themselves.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that solid wax is denser than liquid wax but trails off before connecting this relative density to the outcome of sinking and contrasting it with ice. They need a targeted nudge to finish their thought about wax and apply the inverse logic to the ice/water system.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to finish their sentence connecting the wax's higher density to sinking, and then direct them to contrast this with the density of ice relative to water.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Wax Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to complete their trailing thought by explicitly connecting the higher density of solid wax to the fact that it sinks.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Ice Contrast
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to complete the comparison by stating the density of ice relative to liquid water to explain why ice floats.

rubric_items.title: Validate Partial Answer
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or validates the learner's correct realization that the solid wax is denser before asking them to continue.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tells the learner that denser things sink and less dense things float, doing the comparative reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Continuations
rubric_items.description: Uses a generic prompt (e.g., 'So...', 'Keep going', 'What else?') that fails to focus the learner on connecting density to sinking and floating.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the starting and ending masses but is blindly guessing mathematical operations (first addition, now division) instead of reasoning about what 'lost mass' means. They need scaffolding to connect the concept of finding a lost amount to the operation of subtraction.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a simple, everyday analogy (like losing money or items) to help the learner intuitively recognize that finding a 'lost' amount requires subtraction.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Subtraction Concept
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to identify the correct mathematical operation by focusing on the meaning of 'lost' or 'difference' between the starting mass (5.030 u) and ending mass (5.012 u).

rubric_items.title: Use Everyday Analogy
rubric_items.description: Provide a simple, non-chemistry example involving whole numbers (e.g., starting with 5 items and ending with 3) to help the learner intuitively map the concept of loss to subtraction.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Operation or Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner to subtract, and do not provide the final calculated mass defect (0.018 u).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject division or repeat the previous question without providing new scaffolding, as the learner is currently stuck in a cycle of guessing operations.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that survivors pass down traits, but they are persistently conflating genetic resistance with 'built-up' (acquired) immunity. They need immediate help to realize that traits acquired or 'built' during a lifetime cannot be inherited by offspring.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a targeted probe or a relatable analogy (like building muscles or getting a scar) to create cognitive conflict, forcing the learner to distinguish between a trait an organism is born with and one it acquires during its lifetime.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Inheritance of Acquired Traits
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to evaluate whether a trait acquired or changed during an organism's lifetime can actually be passed down to its offspring.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Built-Up' Modifier
rubric_items.description: The tutor should specifically reference the learner's use of the word 'built-up' to ground the cognitive conflict in the learner's exact phrasing.

rubric_items.title: Use a Concrete Analogy
rubric_items.description: The tutor should introduce an everyday analogy (such as building muscles, dyeing hair, or getting a scar) to make the distinction between acquired and inherited traits intuitive.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not simply tell the learner that acquired traits cannot be inherited, nor directly replace 'built-up immunity' with 'genetic traits' without prompting the learner to realize the distinction themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Accepting the Misconception
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not accept 'built-up immunity' as correct or ignore the error to move forward with the broader natural selection model.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not merely ask 'Are you sure?' or 'Try again' without providing a specific conceptual probe about inheritance or the contradiction in the learner's words.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has accepted that radio waves are a form of light that can travel through space, but is now stuck on the mechanism of encoding: how a silent medium can carry audio information. They need a conceptual bridge to understand that information can be transmitted through patterns or changes in the light, rather than the light itself containing sound.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a relatable scenario involving visible light (like using a flashlight to send a message across a dark yard) and prompt the learner to deduce how they could use it to communicate, scaffolding the concept that information is carried through patterns or codes.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Light-Based Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response provides a concrete, relatable analogy or scenario involving visible light (such as a flashlight, signal fire, or Morse code) to serve as a conceptual bridge for how silent mediums can transmit messages.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner to Deduce Encoding
rubric_items.description: The response asks a question that requires the learner to figure out how to use the analogy to communicate (e.g., 'How could you use a flashlight to tell a friend a word?'), prompting them to generate the idea of using patterns or codes.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly validates the learner's question, acknowledging that it is a great point or that it is indeed counterintuitive for something silent like light to carry a voice.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Over-explaining the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The response prematurely gives away the concept by directly explaining that the light wave changes its pattern, shape, or flashes to match the voice, denying the learner the chance to deduce this mechanism themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Technical Jargon
rubric_items.description: The response introduces complex technical physics jargon (such as amplitude modulation, frequency modulation, or digital encoding) rather than sticking to the simple, grade-appropriate concept of patterns.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response asks the learner to explain how light carries voices without offering any analogy or scaffolding, leaving them stranded on a question they just admitted they don't understand.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused about how to find the vertical distance from the point (2,5) to the line y=-3, likely because they are conflating the x-coordinate (2) with the vertical distance, or struggling to calculate the gap between a positive and negative number. They need help isolating the y-coordinates and visualizing the vertical gap.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that '2' is the horizontal position, direct the learner's attention to the y-coordinate (5) and the line (y=-3), and scaffold the distance calculation by prompting them to visualize a vertical number line or break the distance into two parts (from 5 to 0, and from 0 to -3).

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Vertical Gap
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to visualize or calculate the distance specifically between y=5 and y=-3, such as by asking how far it is from 5 down to the x-axis (0), and then from 0 down to -3.

rubric_items.title: Address the X-Coordinate Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's guess of '2' by gently clarifying that 2 is the x-coordinate (horizontal position), which helps redirect their focus to the y-coordinates for vertical distance.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Overhelpful Arithmetic
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly state the distance is 8 or provide the explicit arithmetic setup (e.g., 'What is 5 minus negative 3?').

rubric_items.title: Penalize Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply reject the guess of '2' or ask 'How do you find distance?' without providing a concrete visualization or intermediate step for the y-coordinates.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Premature Return to Algebra
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that abandon the concrete point (2,5) to return to the algebraic expression 'y+3' or the distance formula before the numerical distance of 8 is successfully resolved.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is persistently falling back on macroscopic bulk properties (smoothness, gravity, and now density) to explain the water's behavior, struggling to apply the microscopic concepts of adhesion and cohesion. They need to realize that the water only interacts with the surface molecules, making bulk properties like density irrelevant to the strength of the intermolecular attraction.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that glass is indeed denser, but use a targeted probe or analogy to help the learner realize that water only interacts with the very top layer of molecules, making the bulk density underneath irrelevant to the adhesive force.

rubric_items.title: Address Density as a Bulk Property
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly address the learner's guess about density, guiding them to consider whether the density of the whole object affects the attraction at the very surface.

rubric_items.title: Refocus on Surface-Level Molecular Interaction
rubric_items.description: The response should redirect the learner's attention back to the microscopic scale, emphasizing that adhesion is about the specific attraction between the water molecules and the surface molecules they are directly touching.

rubric_items.title: Validate Factual Correctness
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that the learner is factually correct (glass is indeed denser than wax) before redirecting their reasoning.

rubric_items.title: Dismiss Without Explanation
rubric_items.description: The response simply tells the learner that density is wrong or irrelevant without helping them reason through why a bulk property doesn't apply to a surface interaction.

rubric_items.title: Premature Chemical Explanation
rubric_items.description: The response over-explains by introducing new, unprompted chemical concepts (like polarity, electronegativity, or specific intermolecular bonds) to explain the adhesion, doing the thinking for the learner.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identified the formula (speed / frequency) but is blocked by an arithmetic hesitation, doubting whether they can divide 340 by 1000 because the dividend is smaller than the divisor. They need reassurance that this division is mathematically valid and will simply result in a decimal or fractional wavelength.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's observation that 340 is smaller, confirm that it is perfectly fine to divide a smaller number by a larger one, and prompt them to execute the calculation (340 / 1000).

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Arithmetic Validity
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly confirm that it is mathematically acceptable to divide a smaller number (340) by a larger number (1000).

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Calculation
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to go ahead and execute the division (340 / 1000) despite their hesitation.

rubric_items.title: Contextualize the Decimal
rubric_items.description: The response reassures the learner by noting that dividing a smaller number by a larger one simply means the resulting wavelength will be a fraction or decimal (less than 1 meter).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Providing the Quotient
rubric_items.description: The response calculates the final answer (0.34) for the learner, bypassing their opportunity to perform the math.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Pivoting to Physics
rubric_items.description: The response ignores the learner's immediate arithmetic hesitation and instead re-explains wave physics concepts (like why speed is constant or the inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength).

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the delayed pain signal sent to the brain serves a long-term survival function: teaching the person to avoid the danger in the future. They need clear validation of this tentative hypothesis to solidify their understanding of why the brain still needs to receive the sensory information even after the spinal cord has handled the immediate reflex.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Validate the learner's correct insight and explicitly connect their idea of 'learning' to the brain's role in forming conscious memories to guide future behavior.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learning Hypothesis
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's hypothesis that the delayed pain signal is indeed meant to teach them not to touch the hot object again.

rubric_items.title: Connect Learning to Brain Function
rubric_items.description: Reinforce the concept by explicitly attributing this 'learning' to the brain, noting that the brain uses the signal to form a conscious memory for future protection.

rubric_items.title: Summarize the Dual Pathway
rubric_items.description: Briefly contrast the brain's role (long-term memory and learning) with the spinal cord's role (immediate reflex) to neatly wrap up the split-signal concept.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Merely saying 'yes' or 'correct' without echoing or expanding on the learner's specific idea of learning and future avoidance.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Introducing Unnecessary Anatomy
rubric_items.description: Overcomplicating the explanation by introducing specific brain regions (like the hippocampus or amygdala) rather than focusing on the functional concept of memory and learning.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited the core concept of inertia—that an object in motion stays in motion without needing a continuous forward force—but their phrasing ('Because... it's already moving?') shows hesitation. They need clear validation to solidify this conceptual shift and permanently discard their prior belief in a lingering 'forward force'.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should strongly affirm the learner's realization, explicitly confirm that being in motion is sufficient, and optionally introduce the formal term 'inertia' to cement the concept.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Breakthrough
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirm the learner's hesitant realization that the ball keeps moving simply because it is already in motion.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce the Absence of Forward Force
rubric_items.description: Connect the learner's insight back to the earlier established fact that the ball does not carry any lingering 'forward force' or 'push' from the throw.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Formal Terminology
rubric_items.description: Introduce the term 'inertia' or summarize Newton's First Law to give a formal name to the concept the learner has just successfully described.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Withholding Validation
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a vague probe (e.g., 'Why else?' or 'Can you elaborate?') or ask a new question without first clearly validating the learner's correct insight.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Topic Shift
rubric_items.description: Do not immediately introduce new forces (like gravity or normal force) or new complex scenarios before taking a turn to solidify this specific conceptual victory.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the genotype is identical everywhere and that temperature affects the trait, but they are struggling to conceptualize the absence of pigment (white fur) as an active part of the 'phenotype'. Additionally, there is an underlying misconception that temperature might be mutating the DNA rather than just affecting the enzyme's activity.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to explain the biological cause of the white fur using the previously discussed enzyme mechanism, guiding them to realize that the white fur is also an observable trait (phenotype) resulting from the same genotype.

rubric_items.title: Connect White Fur to Enzyme Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to explain how the white fur is produced (e.g., by asking what happens to the enzyme in the warm parts of the body), linking the trait back to the established mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Verify Genotype Consistency
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to reaffirm that the DNA sequence remains unchanged in the white areas, engaging the hidden belief that temperature mutates the DNA rather than just affecting the enzyme.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Inclusive Definition of Phenotype
rubric_items.description: The response should guide the learner to recognize that 'phenotype' encompasses all observable characteristics, including the absence of a feature like pigment.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply answer 'yes' and explain that white fur is a phenotype because it is an observable trait; it must require the learner to make the connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely ask 'What do you think?' or 'Is it?' without directing the learner's attention to the enzyme mechanism, the DNA, or the definition of phenotype.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully calculated the remaining fencing using concrete numbers (100 and 20) but still needs to articulate how this arithmetic maps to the algebraic expression '(budget/price) - 2x' they generated earlier. Their core bottleneck is translating the intuitive numerical operation into generalized algebraic logic.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct answer and prompt the learner to explicitly state the arithmetic operations they used to get 60, bridging those concrete steps back to the variables in their algebraic expression.

rubric_items.title: Elicit Concrete Arithmetic
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to articulate the specific mathematical operations they performed to calculate 60 (e.g., asking 'How did you get that number?' or 'What exactly did you subtract?').

rubric_items.title: Prompt Algebraic Mapping
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to connect their concrete calculation steps back to the variables ($x$) or the algebraic expression '(budget/price) - 2x'.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Explanation
rubric_items.description: Explains the arithmetic steps (e.g., 'You subtracted two 20s') or explicitly maps the concrete numbers to the variables for the learner, doing the cognitive work for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Asks a generic yes/no confirmation question (e.g., 'Do you see why we subtract 2x now?') or moves on to the next step without requiring the learner to actually articulate the connection.

rubric_items.title: Validate Concrete Answer
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirms that 60 is the correct answer to the hypothetical scenario before asking the follow-up question.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully conceptualized the magnetic field as an invisible, non-contact 'forcefield,' but they likely hold a hidden misconception that the North end of the compass is attracted to a magnetic 'North' pole. They need validation of their excellent analogy, followed by a targeted probe to surface their assumptions about how magnetic poles interact.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should enthusiastically validate the 'forcefield' analogy, then ask a guiding question about how the compass needle (a small magnet) interacts with this field to uncover the learner's belief about whether like or opposite poles attract.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Forcefield Analogy
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and affirm the learner's 'forcefield' analogy as an accurate and useful way to visualize an invisible magnetic field.

rubric_items.title: Probe Pole Interaction
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider how the compass needle (which is itself a magnet) behaves inside this forcefield, specifically to surface their underlying belief about how magnetic poles attract.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Scientific Terminology
rubric_items.description: Explicitly bridge the learner's intuitive 'forcefield' language to the scientific concept of a 'magnetic field'.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Explaining Magnetic South
rubric_items.description: Do not directly state that 'opposites attract' or reveal that Earth's geographic North is actually a magnetic South pole; leave this for the learner to deduce.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-end Validation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely say 'yes' to the forcefield analogy without asking a follow-up question that drives the physics reasoning forward.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited that the intersection represents 'both' categories, but they lack confidence and are highly fatigued. They need immediate validation of their correct insight and a very low-cognitive-load prompt to finalize the answer without further complex reasoning.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should enthusiastically validate the learner's 'both' insight, explicitly connect it to the 'Music' and 'less than 6 hours' labels, and ask a simple, highly scaffolded question to let the learner identify the final number.

rubric_items.title: Validate 'Both' Insight
rubric_items.description: Affirm the learner's correct intuition by explicitly confirming that the intersection indeed represents 'both' things.

rubric_items.title: Map to Specific Categories
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connect the concept of 'both' to the specific labels in the problem ('Music' and 'less than 6 hours').

rubric_items.title: Low-Cognitive-Load Prompt
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to find the final number using a highly scaffolded, direct question that requires minimal mental effort (e.g., 'What number is in that exact box?').

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: State the final intersecting number (32) for the learner, depriving them of the opportunity to complete the final step themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Provide a vague or unguided prompt (e.g., 'So what do we do next?') that leaves the exhausted learner stranded without clear direction.

rubric_items.title: High-Cognitive-Load Question
rubric_items.description: Ask an open-ended or complex reasoning question (e.g., 'Explain why...', 'How does that work?') that ignores the learner's explicit fatigue.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully identified the meaning of each individual component of the expression (the s-5 paying students, the $15 rate, and the $50 fixed fee). Their immediate need is to synthesize these isolated understandings to articulate what the entire expression calculates as a whole.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A synthesis prompt that asks the learner to combine their understanding of the individual parts to explain the overall meaning or purpose of the complete formula.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to explain what the entire expression or formula calculates when all the individual parts are put together.

rubric_items.title: Validate Constant Fee
rubric_items.description: Affirms the learner's correct conclusion that the $50 is a fixed cost that stays the same regardless of the student count.

rubric_items.title: Anchor to the Full Expression
rubric_items.description: Explicitly presents or refers back to the complete mathematical expression (e.g., 15(s-5) + 50) to visually ground the synthesis question.

rubric_items.title: Give Away the Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Tells the learner what the overall expression represents (e.g., 'So this formula gives us the total cost of the trip') instead of requiring them to deduce and state it.

rubric_items.title: Premature Calculation
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to plug in a specific number of students and solve, skipping the conceptual step of defining the whole expression's meaning.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating reflection ('bounce off') with absorption because they are struggling to visualize how a material can stop a high-energy wave without just deflecting it. They need to distinguish between light bouncing away and light energy being taken in by the material.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that bouncing off is one way light is blocked, but then prompt the learner to contrast 'bouncing off' with the specific word 'absorbed' using everyday knowledge.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Bouncing with Absorbing
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to explicitly distinguish their guess of 'bouncing off' from the concept of being 'absorbed'.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Definition of Absorption
rubric_items.description: The response should encourage the learner to think about what 'absorbing' means in a familiar, everyday context (e.g., a sponge absorbing water, or a dark shirt absorbing sunlight) to help them construct the definition.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Guess
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that 'bouncing off' (reflection) is indeed a logical way for light to be blocked from passing through.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Definition
rubric_items.description: The response should not directly tell the learner that absorption means the glass takes in the UV energy or converts it to heat.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Dismissive Rejection
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply say 'no' or 'incorrect' to the 'bounce off' guess without guiding the learner to analyze the word 'absorbed'.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly intuits that the coefficient 'a' represents the starting value, but they have not yet formalized the exact value of 'a' or constructed the full equation. Furthermore, they have not yet confronted the potential index mismatch: if 'Day 1' means x=1, then setting a=100 in y = a * 3^x would incorrectly yield 300 views on the first day.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuition that 'a' is the starting number, and then prompt them to either construct the full equation or test what happens if they use 100 for 'a' on Day 1.

rubric_items.title: Validate 'Starting Number' Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and validate the learner's correct intuition that the coefficient 'a' represents the initial or starting value of the function.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Equation Construction or 'a' Value
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to apply their idea by proposing a specific value for 'a' or by writing out the full equation using their base of 3.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Testing with Day 1 Data
rubric_items.description: Encourage the learner to test their proposed equation or 'a' value by plugging in x=1 (or asking what x represents on Day 1) to see if it actually outputs the required 100 views.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Equation
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly provide the final equation (e.g., y = 100 * 3^(x-1) or y = (100/3) * 3^x) or explicitly tell the learner the exact value of 'a' without making them do the work.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Index Shift Trap
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly validate y = 100 * 3^x as the correct final equation for this data, missing the mathematical error that plugging in x=1 for Day 1 would yield 300 instead of 100.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identified carbon dioxide as the gas released by decomposers, but they still need to connect this invisible gas emission to their original confusion about why the physical compost pile shrinks. The bottleneck is realizing that the physical mass of the food scraps is leaving the pile in the form of this gas.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the correct answer and prompt the learner to explain how the release of CO2 gas accounts for the disappearing physical matter or shrinking of the compost pile.

rubric_items.title: Affirmation of Carbon Dioxide
rubric_items.description: The response should confirm that carbon dioxide is the correct gas, providing necessary validation since the learner phrased their answer as a question.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Connection to Mass Loss
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to connect the release of this gas to the physical shrinking, weight loss, or disappearance of the solid compost pile.

rubric_items.title: Highlight Gas as Physical Matter
rubric_items.description: The response may briefly remind the learner that gases like CO2 are made of atoms and have physical mass, helping bridge the gap from solid food scraps to invisible gas.

rubric_items.title: Premature Explanation of Mass Transfer
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner that the carbon dioxide carries the mass/atoms away into the air, as the learner must make this connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Premature Topic Shift
rubric_items.description: The response should not pivot to discussing other ecosystem processes (like soil nutrients, plant growth, or the broader carbon cycle) before the learner resolves the immediate compost-shrinking phenomenon.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully deduced the core mechanism of recessive inheritance—that a 'weaker' trait requires the corresponding instruction from both parents to be visible—but their phrasing as a question indicates they are uncertain. They need immediate validation of this conceptual breakthrough before formalizing the vocabulary or generalizing the rule.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should enthusiastically validate the learner's correct deduction, and then either introduce formal vocabulary (dominant/recessive) mapped to their words or ask them to generalize this into a rule for all 'weaker' traits.

rubric_items.title: Explicit Validation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner's deduction is exactly right (e.g., 'Yes, exactly!' or 'You got it!'), addressing their uncertainty.

rubric_items.title: Generalize the Rule
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to generalize this specific discovery into a broader rule about what must happen for any 'weaker' trait to show up in an offspring.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Formal Vocabulary
rubric_items.description: Introduce formal scientific terms (like 'recessive', 'dominant', or 'genes/alleles') by explicitly mapping them onto the learner's grounded words ('weaker', 'stronger', 'instructions').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Redundant Questioning
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to explain why the orange kittens are orange or how they got their color, as this forces them to repeat the deduction they just successfully made.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Withholding Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a neutral probe (e.g., 'What do you think?') or move to a new topic without first clearly confirming that their answer about both parents giving orange instructions is correct.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the medium (air) determines wave speed, but remains stuck on the intuitive misconception that a higher frequency of local vibration must result in faster forward propagation. They need a new way to conceptually separate the speed of the back-and-forth particle motion from the forward speed of the wave itself, as the previous rope analogy did not resolve this confusion.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a new concrete analogy (such as placing boxes on a moving conveyor belt or mailing letters) that clearly separates the rate at which an action is repeated from the forward speed at which the result travels, prompting the learner to apply this distinction to the sound waves.

rubric_items.title: Target Local vs. Forward Motion
rubric_items.description: The response must focus the learner's attention on distinguishing between the speed of the local back-and-forth vibration (frequency) and the speed of the forward travel through the room (wave speed).

rubric_items.title: Provide a New Contrastive Scenario
rubric_items.description: The response should introduce a new concrete analogy or thought experiment that isolates 'how often' an action occurs from 'how fast' it moves forward.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response may acknowledge that the learner's intuition is very natural (e.g., validating that it makes intuitive sense to link 'faster vibration' with 'faster travel') before challenging it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply tell the learner that frequency does not affect wave speed or explain the difference outright, as the learner must reason through this distinction themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating the Rope Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely reiterate the previous rope analogy, since the learner has already indicated that it did not resolve their confusion.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response should not introduce the wave equation (v = f * λ) or the concept of wavelength to explain the constant speed, as this would bypass the current conceptual bottleneck.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that a steeper curve indicates faster speed, but they are still conflating the visual steepness of the graph with physical elevation ('uphill'). They need help untangling the concept of speed from the physical terrain.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct realization about speed, then ask a targeted question that prompts the learner to separate the concept of going faster from the physical act of going uphill.

rubric_items.title: Validate 'Faster'
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's correct insight that the steeper curve means they are going faster.

rubric_items.title: Prompt to Separate Speed from Incline
rubric_items.description: Ask a question or present a scenario that prompts the learner to realize they can go fast without going uphill (e.g., asking if it's possible to speed up on a flat road).

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Agreement
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of their own recent conclusion that the graph only tracks distance from home, not height.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not simply tell the learner that the graph doesn't mean uphill or that steepness only equals speed; leave the cognitive work of separating these concepts to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Misconception
rubric_items.description: Do not validate 'faster' and move on to a new topic without challenging the 'uphill' comment, as this would leave the core conflation intact.

learning_objective: LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identifies that biological instructions come from parents, but is experiencing cognitive dissonance because the parents are physically blind. They need to connect the parents' hidden genetic blueprint back to the sighted common ancestor discussed earlier.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct insight about parents, and then prompt them to trace where those blind parents originally inherited their instructions from.

rubric_items.title: Trace Instructions to Ancestor
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to think about where the blind parents got their instructions, guiding them to link the parents' blueprint back to the sighted common ancestor.

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirm the learner's hesitant but correct realization that the instructions do indeed come from the parents.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the parents still carry the DNA or leftover genes of the sighted ancestor; the response must leave the cognitive work of making that connection to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not use a generic probe (e.g., 'Why do you think that is?' or 'Keep thinking') that fails to focus the learner on the origin or nature of the parents' instructions.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Scientific Vocabulary
rubric_items.description: Introduce or prompt the learner to use the scientific term for these 'instructions' (e.g., DNA, genes, or genetics).

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that X-inactivation is inherited but assumes dividing cells move freely and mix together like a liquid. They need to realize that in solid tissues, dividing cells stay next to each other, forming localized clusters (clonal expansion) that appear as distinct color patches.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that prompts the learner to think about the physical location of daughter cells after division (e.g., whether they stay put or float away) to help them deduce why patches form instead of a blended color.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Spatial Constraint
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider the physical placement or movement of daughter cells immediately after they divide (e.g., asking if cells in skin/tissue stay together or float apart).

rubric_items.title: Connect to Visual Outcome
rubric_items.description: Guide the learner to connect the physical behavior of the dividing cells to the visible outcome of distinct color patches on the cat.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's intuition makes sense (e.g., validating that if cells were free to move around, the colors would indeed blend).

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Explaining Clonal Expansion
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that cells stay together in clusters or explicitly explain the concept of clonal expansion; leave the spatial deduction to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Unanchored Denial
rubric_items.description: Do not simply deny that the cells mix or ask a vague question (e.g., 'Why wouldn't they mix?') without providing a concrete physical or biological constraint for the learner to reason about.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner holds a common 'impetus' misconception, believing that the initial pushing force from the hand transfers to the car and continues acting on it even after release. They are expressing uncertainty ('I think so?'), indicating they need concrete scaffolding to realize that an applied force like a push requires ongoing physical contact.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should ask a targeted question about whether the hand is still touching the car, prompting the learner to deduce that a push cannot continue without physical contact.

rubric_items.title: Prompt on Physical Contact
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider whether the hand is still touching the car, or ask whether a push can happen without physical contact.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Uncertainty
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's hesitant tone ('I think so?') to normalize their guess before guiding them to the correct physical constraint.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that the force from the hand stops as soon as contact is broken.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Probing
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a generic 'Why do you think that?' or 'Are you sure?', which leaves the learner stranded with their misconception that force is stored in the object.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Concept Shift
rubric_items.description: Do not shift the topic to net force, inertia, or momentum before the learner resolves the specific question about the hand's applied force.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully calculated the digits 1 and 2 using long division but combined them into 1.2 instead of 12, likely because they are still anchored to the decimal in the original problem (4.5) or were confused by the tutor's phrasing to 'put the digits together'. They need to realize that 1.2 is mathematically unreasonable for the division they just performed.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to evaluate whether 1.2 makes sense as an answer, either by estimating the magnitude or by reviewing the place value of the digits they just calculated.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Mathematical Verification
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to resolve the 1.2 vs 12 confusion using a mathematical check, such as estimating the magnitude (e.g., 'Would 45 fit into 540 only 1.2 times?') or identifying the place value of the digits 1 and 2.

rubric_items.title: Anchor to the Division Problem
rubric_items.description: Explicitly reference either the scaled problem (540 ÷ 45) or the original problem (54 ÷ 4.5) to help ground the learner's reasoning about the expected size of the answer.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Source of Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that it is natural to expect a decimal in the answer since the original problem had one, validating their hesitation before guiding them to the correct whole number.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not directly give away the final answer of 12 or simply tell the learner to remove the decimal point.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not leave the learner stranded by merely repeating the vague instruction to 'put the digits together' without offering a mathematical scaffold to test if 1.2 is correct.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance because their mental model equates the direction of force with the direction of motion. They correctly observe the car is still moving forward, making it hard for them to accept that the frictional force is pushing backward.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt or concrete analogy that helps the learner separate motion from force by focusing on how a backward push affects the speed of a forward-moving object over time, rather than its immediate direction.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Speed vs. Direction
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to connect the backward force to the change in the car's forward speed (slowing down) rather than its current direction of travel.

rubric_items.title: Validate Forward Motion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's correct observation that the car is indeed still moving forward despite the backward force.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Explanation of Deceleration
rubric_items.description: Do not directly explain the physics principle that force direction does not dictate motion direction, or simply tell them that a backward force reduces forward speed.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Probing
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a generic question (e.g., 'Why not?' or 'What does it mean?') that leaves the learner stranded without a specific conceptual pivot (like speed, time, or an analogy) to resolve their dissonance.

rubric_items.title: Use a Relatable Analogy
rubric_items.description: Introduce or prompt for a relatable everyday analogy (e.g., walking into a strong wind, or someone pulling back on your shirt while you run forward) to ground the concept of a backward force acting on a forward-moving object.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is expressing surprise or confusion, likely doubting that the modeling software can automatically propagate indirect effects without a direct arrow drawn between the non-adjacent species. They need reassurance about the program's mechanics and guidance to trace how the software uses the intermediate link (the minnows) to calculate the effect on the herons.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that the program does not need a direct arrow and prompt the learner to trace the step-by-step logic of how a drop in the minnow population will affect the herons through the existing link.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Program Capability
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the program can calculate the connection automatically without needing a direct arrow drawn between the invasive fish and the heron.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Step-by-Step Tracing
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to trace the program's logic by asking how a change in the intermediate species (minnows) will affect the final species (herons) through the existing link.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner Surprise
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's surprise, recognizing that it can feel counterintuitive to rely on intermediate links rather than drawing a direct line.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner the final outcome (e.g., that the heron population will decrease); the learner must deduce this step themselves.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Dismissing the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Do not ignore the learner's 'Wait, it doesn't?' by simply repeating the previous question; the response must address their doubt about the program's mechanics.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that a small amount of water places the center of gravity near the bottom, but is confused why removing that last bit of water shifts the center of gravity back up to the middle. They need to realize that the center of gravity depends on what is actually providing the weight, and that emptying the can leaves only the evenly distributed metal.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to compare what material is providing the weight when there is a tiny splash of water versus when the can is completely empty.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Weight Contributors
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to identify or compare what is actually providing the weight in the 'tiny splash of water' scenario versus the 'completely empty' scenario.

rubric_items.title: Focus on the Metal Can's Distribution
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner's attention to the physical shape or weight distribution of the metal can itself now that the water is gone.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's surprise, acknowledging that it can seem counterintuitive for the center of gravity to move back up when the last bit of water is removed.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Explanation
rubric_items.description: Directly answers the learner's question by explaining that removing the water leaves only the evenly distributed metal can, doing the reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Asks a generic question (e.g., 'What changed?' or 'Think about the weight') without focusing the learner's attention specifically on the physical materials (water vs. metal).

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly calculated the total as six but is experiencing cognitive dissonance because the visual evidence (three literal faces) conflicts with the mathematical value (six votes). They need validation of their math and support in conceptualizing how a single physical symbol can represent multiple units.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's calculation of six, then provide a targeted prompt or analogy that helps the learner reconcile the physical object (one face) with its represented value (two votes or two people).

rubric_items.title: Validate Calculation
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly confirm that the learner's calculation of 'six' is correct before addressing their conceptual confusion.

rubric_items.title: Address Literal-to-Symbolic Mapping
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to connect the literal symbol ('faces') to the real-world entities they represent (e.g., asking who the faces represent, or what is 'inside' the face).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Over-Explanation
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for simply telling the learner the answer (e.g., 'It is 6 because each face is drawn to represent 2 people') rather than asking a question that requires the learner to make the connection.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Redirection
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for giving a generic instruction like 'Look at the key again' or 'Remember what we just said' without directly addressing the learner's specific fixation on the literal 'faces'.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Analogy
rubric_items.description: Rewards the tutor for introducing or referencing a concrete, familiar analogy where one physical item holds a higher value (e.g., a $2 bill, a single coin worth multiple cents, or a single ticket admitting two people) to bridge the conceptual gap.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the upward buoyancy force shifts to the tilted side, but is now asking a crucial clarifying question to anchor the opposing downward force of gravity. They need confirmation of gravity's location so they can mentally map the two forces and resolve their earlier confusion about whether the boat will capsize or right itself.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm (or guide the learner to confirm) that gravity still acts through the center of the boat, and then prompt the learner to visualize how the boat will rotate when gravity pulls down in the middle while buoyancy pushes up on the tilted side.

rubric_items.title: Establish Gravity's Location
rubric_items.description: Confirms, or prompts the learner to realize, that gravity continues to pull down from the center of the boat because the boat's mass distribution has not changed.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Two-Force Interaction
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to combine the two spatial anchors (gravity pulling down in the middle, buoyancy pushing up on the right) to deduce which way the boat will rotate.

rubric_items.title: Resolve Prior Conflict
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connects this two-force visualization back to the learner's earlier doubt ('wouldn't pushing up on that side just make it roll over more?') to help them resolve that specific mental block.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Rotation
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner the outcome of the force interaction (e.g., stating that it creates a restoring torque, flattens the boat, or pushes it upright) instead of letting the learner deduce the movement themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Stranding the Learner
rubric_items.description: Responds with a vague counter-question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that fails to validate or address the learner's direct question about gravity's location, leaving them without the spatial anchor they asked for.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is second-guessing their correct calculation ($90) because they are unsure whether the 10% depreciation applies to the original purchase price ($1000) or the current value of the phone ($900). They need to recognize that the phone's value has changed, so the percentage must be taken from its new, lower value.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to consider what the phone is actually worth at the beginning of the second year, guiding them to realize that taking 10% of $1000 would mean calculating the loss based on a value the phone no longer has.

rubric_items.title: Question the $1000 Premise
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate whether it makes sense to take 10% of $1000 by asking them to consider the phone's actual value at the start of the second year.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Depreciation Rule
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the percentage must be calculated on the new balance ($900) or directly answer their question by just saying 'no'.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not simply ask 'Are you sure?' or 'What do you think?' without specifically directing their attention to the phone's changing value.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Previous Insight
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that their earlier instinct to calculate 10% of $900 was actually on the right track before they second-guessed themselves.

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identifies the physical action (pushing) but lacks the conceptual framework to see this interaction as a transfer of an invisible quantity. They are stuck because a push feels like a mere event or physical contact rather than a substance-like transfer from the hand to the car.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's physical intuition and introduce a relatable scenario (like pushing something heavy and getting tired, or observing the car go from still to fast) that makes the 'invisible' cost or transfer of the push tangible.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Physical Intuition
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's perspective by acknowledging that a push feels like a simple action or contact rather than a physical object being handed over.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Tangible Evidence of Transfer
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to consider a concrete scenario where the 'cost' or result of pushing is obvious (e.g., getting tired from pushing a heavy box, or the car gaining speed) to help them deduce that something invisible is being used or given.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Prior 'Active' Concept
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connects the act of pushing back to the learner's own earlier definition of energy as being 'hyper' or 'active' to help them see that their own personal energy is being utilized.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that directly tell the learner that 'energy' is the thing passing from the hand to the car, bypassing the learner's opportunity to deduce the transfer themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Contradiction
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that simply contradict the learner or ask them to guess again (e.g., 'Are you sure nothing passes?' or 'Think harder about the push') without offering a new concrete scenario to help them rethink the interaction.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has just experienced cognitive conflict, realizing that their strategy of adding the visible numbers (8 + 5 = 13) results in 18 blocks on the right side, which breaks the scale's balance. They need the tutor to validate this realization and guide them to find the correct missing addend that will balance the 8 blocks on the left.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's realization that 18 blocks on the right side creates an imbalance, and prompt them to figure out what number of blocks actually needs to be combined with 5 to balance the 8 blocks on the left.

rubric_items.title: Validate the cognitive conflict
rubric_items.description: The tutor should validate the learner's realization by explicitly confirming that 18 blocks on the right side would be too many to balance the 8 blocks on the left side.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the balancing quantity
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to determine what number of blocks must be combined with the 5 blocks to perfectly match the 8 blocks on the left.

rubric_items.title: Maintain the scale analogy
rubric_items.description: The tutor should keep the explanation grounded in the physical scale analogy (e.g., using words like 'balance', 'sides', or 'heavy') rather than switching to abstract arithmetic rules.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge correct arithmetic
rubric_items.description: The tutor may briefly affirm that the learner correctly added 13 and 5 to get 18 before pointing out that this total breaks the balance.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving away the answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not tell the learner that the missing number is 3 or explicitly instruct them to calculate 8 minus 5.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague redirection
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not simply tell the learner they are wrong or ask them to try again without re-anchoring them to the goal of balancing the 8 blocks on the left.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited that multiplication is the right operation to find the number of feet in 12 miles, but phrased it as a question ('Times them?'), indicating a need for confirmation. They need validation of this choice and a prompt to execute the calculation before moving on to the more complex time conversion.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that multiplication is the correct operation and prompt the learner to set up or perform the calculation (12 * 5280).

rubric_items.title: Validate the Operation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's suggestion to multiply.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Calculation
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to identify which numbers to multiply or prompt them to perform the calculation of 12 times 5280.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Providing the Calculation Result
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that give the learner the answer to 12 * 5280 (63,360) instead of requiring them to calculate or set it up themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Jumping to Time Conversion
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that prematurely introduce the conversion of hours to seconds before the learner has finished calculating the distance conversion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely say 'yes' or confirm the operation without prompting the learner to take the next step of setting up or solving the math.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully constructed the left side of the circle's equation by squaring and adding the horizontal and vertical distances, but trails off, hesitating on how to complete it. Because they likely hold the hidden belief that the right side should just be the radius 'r' (the physical length of the hypotenuse), they need targeted guidance to apply the Pythagorean theorem's squaring rule to the right side of the equation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct left side of the equation and prompt the learner to complete it by specifically asking what happens to the hypotenuse (r) when plugged into the Pythagorean theorem.

rubric_items.title: Validate Partial Equation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner correctly squared and added the horizontal and vertical distances to form the left side of the equation.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Hypotenuse Completion
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to complete the equation by determining what happens to the hypotenuse (r) or the 'third part' when plugged into the formula.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Squaring Rule
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of the previously established rule that every side gets squared, or ask them to apply that specific rule to the hypotenuse, to preempt the misconception that the right side is just 'r'.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the equation equals r^2 or give away the final completed equation.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not use a generic prompt like 'keep going', 'what does it equal?', or 'finish it' that fails to direct the learner's focus to the hypotenuse or the squaring rule.

learning_objective: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is using the imprecise term 'disappear' to describe algebraic cancellation, bypassing the tutor's direct question about $5/5$. They need to explicitly recognize that dividing a number or variable by itself results in $1$, not $0$ or 'nothing', to understand why the $h$ terms cancel out without making the entire expression zero.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should redirect the learner to explicitly answer the $5/5$ question to establish that dividing a value by itself yields $1$, challenging the informal idea that the terms simply 'disappear'.

rubric_items.title: Re-prompt for the numerical division
