rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified that gravity points downward but is hesitating to state the direction of the magnetic force, leaving their sentence incomplete. They need a targeted nudge to finish their thought and explicitly recognize that the magnetic force must point upward to oppose gravity, a concept they briefly mentioned in their very first turn.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt or sentence-starter that encourages the learner to complete their thought and explicitly state that the magnetic force points upward to balance gravity.

rubric_items.title: Elicit Magnetic Force Direction
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to explicitly state the direction of the magnetic force acting on the hovering magnet.

rubric_items.title: Targeted Cueing
rubric_items.description: Provides a specific scaffold to help the learner answer, either by asking what direction is needed to balance the downward pull of gravity or by prompting them to complete their unfinished sentence ('but the other...').

rubric_items.title: Recall Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Reminds the learner that they already correctly stated earlier in the dialogue that the bottom magnet is 'pushing it up.'

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Answer)
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that the magnetic force points upward or instructs them to draw the arrow pointing up, bypassing their opportunity to articulate it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a generic question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that leaves the learner stranded without focusing their attention on the opposing magnetic force or their incomplete thought.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused by the conceptual leap of substituting a constant multiplier (B) with the variable x. They understand that B controls frequency and needs to grow, but they do not yet intuitively connect that because x represents time passing, using x as the multiplier causes the frequency to increase continuously as the sound plays.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to identify what x represents in the physical context of the game (time) and what happens to its value as the sound plays, guiding them to realize why x is a useful substitute for a growing multiplier.

rubric_items.title: Grounding 'x' as Time
rubric_items.description: The response must clarify, or prompt the learner to consider, what the variable x represents in the physical context of the sound wave or game (i.e., time passing).

rubric_items.title: Highlighting the Growth of 'x'
rubric_items.description: The response should guide the learner to connect the goal of an increasing multiplier to the behavior of x, specifically prompting them to realize that as time passes, the value of x continuously grows.

rubric_items.title: Validating the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that substituting a variable for a constant is a non-obvious or tricky conceptual leap, validating the learner's 'Wait, why...' question.

rubric_items.title: Avoiding Pure Algebraic Repetition
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely restate the previous turn's algebraic substitution (e.g., 'we replaced B with x because we wanted it to grow') without helping the learner understand why x specifically achieves that growth.

rubric_items.title: Avoiding Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly hand the learner the complete conceptual connection (e.g., 'x is time, and since time increases, x increases, which makes the frequency go up') without leaving at least one step for the learner to deduce.

rubric_items.title: Avoiding Formal Phase Calculus
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that attempt to justify the x^2 term by introducing the formal calculus relationship between instantaneous frequency and the derivative of phase, which would overwhelm the learner at this intuitive stage.

learning_objective: Whole Numbers, Place Value, and Fractions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the concrete analogy of sharing a pizza (more people means smaller slices), but is stuck on whole-number bias, conflating the denominator '4' with the overall value of the fraction. They need to explicitly map the '4' in '1/4' to the number of people sharing rather than the size of the slice.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the whole number 4 is indeed larger than 3, and then prompt the learner to identify what the '4' in the fraction '1/4' actually represents in their pizza analogy.

rubric_items.title: Validate Whole Number Fact
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's correct intuition that the whole number 4 is indeed bigger than 3 before redirecting their thinking.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Mapping of the Denominator
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to connect the '4' in the fraction '1/4' to the number of people sharing or the number of pieces cut in the analogy.

rubric_items.title: Distinguish Whole from Part
rubric_items.description: Explicitly contrast the whole number '4' with the fraction '1/4' (e.g., asking if 1/4 means 4 whole pizzas or something else) to help dismantle the whole-number bias.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Mapping
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the 4 in 1/4 represents the number of people or pieces; leave the cognitive work of making this connection to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Ignoring the Whole Number Bias
rubric_items.description: Do not ignore the learner's fixation on the number 4 by simply repeating the pizza analogy or asking which fraction is bigger without addressing what the 4 actually means.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing a geometric misconception, believing that the distance walked up and down the slanted sides of a hill (the fold) is equal to its straight vertical height. They need to recognize that the slanted path is longer before they can correctly determine how to measure the fold for the surface area calculation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted scaffolding question that introduces a concrete visualization (such as a ladder, an elevator, or a string) to help the learner intuitively grasp that a slanted path up and down a peak is longer than the straight vertical height.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Path Length Comparison
rubric_items.description: The response must direct the learner's attention specifically to comparing the length of the slanted path (up and down the sides) to the straight vertical height.

rubric_items.title: Provide Concrete Visualization
rubric_items.description: The response should introduce a relatable physical analogy or geometric visualization (like taking an elevator vs. walking a ramp, or comparing a straight string to a bent one) to make the length comparison intuitive.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: The response must not explicitly tell the learner that the slanted path is longer or simply state that their previous answer was wrong.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Prompting
rubric_items.description: The response must not merely ask 'Are you sure?' or 'Think about it again' without providing a new conceptual scaffold to help the learner re-evaluate the distances.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formula Focus
rubric_items.description: The response must not ask the learner how to calculate surface area or return to the length-times-width formula until this specific geometric misconception about the fold's dimensions is resolved.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the heavy bottom will pull the tilted bookshelf back down, overcoming the lighter top, but their phrasing ('?') shows they are still tentative. They need explicit validation of this specific mechanical insight before being asked to synthesize the final rule about book placement and stability.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's tentative conclusion about the heavy bottom overcoming the top, and then prompt them to state the final rule about where heavy items should be placed to maximize stability.

rubric_items.title: Validate Mechanical Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative conclusion that the heavy bottom's downward pull successfully overcomes the lighter top.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Final Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to apply their insight to state the final rule or answer the original question about where heavy books should be placed.

rubric_items.title: Formalize Concept
rubric_items.description: Reintroduce the terms 'stability' or 'center of mass' to connect the learner's grounded physical intuition back to the scientific vocabulary.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Stealing the Punchline
rubric_items.description: State the final conclusion about book placement for the learner instead of asking them to articulate it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Affirmation
rubric_items.description: Respond with only a generic 'yes' or 'correct' without explicitly confirming the mechanics of the heavy bottom overcoming the top, failing to fully anchor the learner's tentative understanding.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unnecessary Complexity
rubric_items.description: Introduce new physics concepts, such as torque or pivot points, that complicate the grounded intuition the learner has just successfully built.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner knows the components of an alpha particle (helium nucleus, mass 4, atomic number 2) but lacks knowledge of the arbitrary formatting convention for standard nuclear notation. They need direct instruction on where to place the numbers relative to the chemical symbol so they can assemble the final answer.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly state the rule for nuclear notation (mass number on top left, atomic number on bottom left) and then prompt the learner to apply this rule to assemble the alpha particle symbol.

rubric_items.title: Provide Notation Rule
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly state the standard nuclear notation convention, specifying that the mass number goes on the top left (superscript) and the atomic number goes on the bottom left (subscript) of the chemical symbol.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Application
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to apply the newly provided rule to assemble the specific symbol for the alpha particle using the numbers 4 and 2.

rubric_items.title: Remind of Chemical Symbol
rubric_items.description: The tutor may explicitly remind the learner to use 'He' as the central chemical symbol, since the learner has not yet typed it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not provide the final assembled symbol (e.g., ^4_2 He) for the learner, as the learner needs to practice constructing it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Guessing the Convention
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not ask the learner to guess or deduce where the numbers go (e.g., 'Where do you think the mass goes?'), because arbitrary formatting conventions cannot be deduced from first principles and withholding them causes unnecessary frustration.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confusing the independent variable (levels) with the dependent variable (XP), wondering if they should perform addition on the level numbers themselves. They need to understand that the 'constant amount added' applies to the XP values as they progress from one level to the next.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that the levels simply represent the sequential steps and redirect the learner to examine how the XP values change between those steps.

rubric_items.title: Redirect to Dependent Variable (XP)
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner's attention away from adding the level numbers and toward examining the XP values.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Role of Levels
rubric_items.description: Clarifies that the 'levels' represent the sequence or steps (e.g., moving from level 1 to level 2) rather than the quantities being added together.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Concrete Data
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to look at or share their actual XP numbers to ground the abstract idea of 'adding the same amount' in their specific game data.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Tells the learner exactly how to calculate the differences (e.g., 'subtract level 1 XP from level 2 XP') instead of letting them figure out how to apply their 'adding the same amount' rule to the XP.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a generic 'no' or vague question (e.g., 'What do you think?') without specifically addressing the learner's explicit confusion about adding the levels.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the conceptual and linguistic misconception that a 'dominant' allele inherently outcompetes others and increases in population frequency over time. Even though they previously accepted that the trait offers no survival advantage, they believe the genetic mechanics of dominance automatically force the trait to 'take over' the gene pool.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should present a concrete, simplified inheritance scenario (such as a single family where one parent has the dominant trait and the other has the recessive trait, having a set number of children) to help the learner mathematically or logically discover that dominant alleles do not replicate at a higher rate than recessive ones.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Inheritance Scenario
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to trace the actual inheritance of alleles in a specific, simplified scenario (e.g., a family or a small population) to test whether the dominant allele actually multiplies faster than the recessive one.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Equal Reproduction Constraint
rubric_items.description: Explicitly incorporates or reminds the learner of the previously established premise that individuals with and without the trait are having the exact same number of children.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful: Explaining the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for directly explaining that dominance only affects individual expression and does not change population frequency, which steals the cognitive work of dismantling the misconception.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful: Repeating the Definition
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for simply asking the learner to define 'dominant' again or repeating the definition, as the tutor already provided the definition in a previous turn and it failed to resolve the learner's bottleneck.

rubric_items.title: Validate Linguistic Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that the everyday use of the word 'dominant' makes it intuitively sound like the trait should overpower or take over the population.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully calculated the expected revenue for a single scenario and correctly hypothesized the next procedural step (repeating the calculation for all scenarios). They need confirmation of this step and a prompt to identify the final conceptual step: aggregating these values to find the total expected revenue.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Confirm the learner's intuition to repeat the calculation for each scenario, and prompt them to determine how to combine those individual results to find the overall expected revenue.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Repetition
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly validate the learner's hypothesis that the calculation (revenue × probability) needs to be repeated for each attendee scenario on the chart.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Aggregation Step
rubric_items.description: The tutor must ask the learner how they should combine those individual expected revenues once they are all calculated.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Operation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly tell the learner to 'add', 'sum', or 'total' the values, as the learner must identify the aggregation operation themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Dead End Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not merely confirm the learner's question (e.g., 'Yes, exactly') without asking a follow-up question that drives toward the final aggregation step.

rubric_items.title: Premature Arithmetic
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not ask the learner to immediately start calculating the remaining rows before the conceptual plan for combining them is established.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Goal
rubric_items.description: The tutor may explicitly mention that the ultimate goal of this process is to find the 'overall expected revenue' or 'expected value'.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner contrasts being 'just a liquid' with being made of particles, not realizing that liquids themselves are particulate. They need to transfer their newly established understanding of water (which they already agreed is made of moving molecules) to the food coloring.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to compare food coloring to water, prompting them to realize that since water is a liquid made of particles, food coloring must be too.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Water's State
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to recall or recognize that water is also a liquid, using this shared property to bridge the conceptual gap.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Particulate Deduction
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask a question that requires the learner to infer that if water is a liquid made of particles, the liquid food coloring must also be made of particles.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Macroscopic Appearance
rubric_items.description: The tutor validates the learner's observation by acknowledging that food coloring does indeed look like a continuous, normal liquid to the naked eye before prompting them to think about its microscopic structure.

rubric_items.title: Directly Stating the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner that liquids are made of particles or that food coloring is made of molecules, taking away the cognitive ownership of the deduction.

rubric_items.title: Vague Redirection
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks an overly broad question (e.g., 'What makes a liquid?' or 'Are you sure?') without scaffolding the connection back to the specific water molecules they just discussed.

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited that 'grams' indicates mass but lacks confidence and needs confirmation before proceeding. Their immediate bottleneck is verifying this unit so they can locate the correct number in their notes to use in the kinetic energy formula.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that grams measure mass and prompt the learner to state the specific number they have written down for it.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Grams as Mass
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's question by stating that grams are indeed a unit used to measure mass.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Mass Value
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to look at their notes and state the specific number associated with the grams.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or praise the learner for correctly identifying the unit of mass on their own.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the mass value for the learner or prematurely set up the kinetic energy calculation for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not stop at a simple confirmation (e.g., 'Yes'); the response must prompt the learner to take the next immediate step of finding the number.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly calculated that halving the speed results in one-fourth the kinetic energy, but their physical intuition is resisting the quadratic relationship for fractions ('seems too small'). They need validation of their math and a conceptual bridge to reconcile this dramatic decrease with their understanding.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the math is correct and prompt the learner to connect this fractional result back to the doubling scenario they already understand, helping them realize that if doubling speed quadruples energy, halving speed must quarter it.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Calculation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner's calculation of one-fourth is mathematically correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Conceptual Reconciliation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to reconcile their skepticism by connecting the halving scenario back to the doubling scenario they already mastered (e.g., asking what the reverse of 4x energy is).

rubric_items.title: Validate Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that it is normal or understandable to feel that one-fourth is surprisingly small, validating their physical intuition before challenging it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Over-explaining the Connection
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the logical or physical reason why one-fourth makes sense (e.g., explicitly stating 'Since 2x speed is 4x energy, half speed is 1/4 energy'); the learner must make this connection.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dismissing Skepticism
rubric_items.description: Do not ignore the learner's statement that 'it seems too small' by simply moving on to a new question or telling them to just trust the formula.

learning_objective: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused by the tutor's previous phrasing, which made it sound like 'the fraction' and 'the ratio' were two different things doing the same action. They are losing track of the mathematical referents and need a clear, concrete restatement that the fraction is the surface-area-to-volume ratio, and that this overall ratio is what shrinks as the cell grows.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly clarify that the fraction and the ratio are the exact same thing—the surface area divided by the volume—and confirm that this overall value is what shrinks as the cell gets larger.

rubric_items.title: Identify the Shrinking Quantity
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly state that the surface-area-to-volume ratio (or the overall value of the fraction) is the thing that shrinks.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Fraction-Ratio Equivalence
rubric_items.description: The response must clarify that the 'fraction' and the 'ratio' are the exact same thing, resolving the confusion caused by the tutor's previous turn.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Cell Growth
rubric_items.description: The response should contrast the shrinking ratio with the growing physical size of the cell (or its radius) to help the learner separate the two concepts.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Guessing Game
rubric_items.description: The response should not ask the learner to guess what shrinks (e.g., 'What do you think shrinks?'), as the learner is genuinely disoriented by the tutor's confusing previous wording.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Algebraic Correction
rubric_items.description: The response should not pivot to correcting the learner's underlying algebraic simplification of the cylinder formula, as the immediate need is to resolve the conceptual and terminological confusion.

learning_objective: LS1.B Growth and Development of Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner logically assumes the brain acts as the central control for gene expression, failing to realize that cell differentiation begins in early embryonic stages before a brain even exists. They need to shift their thinking from a macroscopic central nervous system to localized cellular mechanisms.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should create cognitive conflict by asking how cells know what to do early in development before the brain has formed, prompting the learner to consider alternative, localized sources of information.

rubric_items.title: Developmental Timeline Conflict
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider the timeline of development, specifically pointing out that an early embryo or a tiny cluster of cells does not yet have a brain.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Alternative Source
rubric_items.description: Ask a follow-up question that encourages the learner to hypothesize a different, more localized source of instructions once the brain is ruled out.

rubric_items.title: Validate Control Center Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the brain is a logical guess since it acts as the primary control center for the adult body.

rubric_items.title: Giveaway Chemical Signals
rubric_items.description: Directly state that cells use chemical signals, transcription factors, or neighboring cell interactions to regulate genes, bypassing the learner's opportunity to deduce a local mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Reject the 'brain' hypothesis without providing a specific biological constraint (like the lack of a brain in early embryos) to help the learner rethink.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly guessed that a dark moth would be easier to spot on a dark, soot-covered tree, indicating a temporary breakdown in basic visual logic regarding camouflage and background matching. They need scaffolding to visualize how contrasting colors stand out before they can connect this to predator survival rates.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a targeted probe or a simple everyday analogy about color contrast (e.g., drawing with white chalk versus black chalk on a blackboard) to help the learner self-correct their understanding of which moth stands out against the soot.

rubric_items.title: Prompting Contrast Logic
rubric_items.description: The response must guide the learner to consider how contrasting colors (a light object on a dark background) stand out visually, while matching colors (a dark object on a dark background) blend in.

rubric_items.title: Grounding in the Specific Scenario
rubric_items.description: The response should maintain the established context of the soot-covered tree trunk or the bird's perspective to help the learner apply the visual logic directly to the moths.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response must not explicitly tell the learner that the light moth is easier to see or state that the dark moth is camouflaged.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Empty Re-prompting
rubric_items.description: The response must not merely reject the learner's guess ('The dark one?') with generic phrases like 'Are you sure?' or 'Try again' without providing a cognitive stepping stone to help them visualize the color contrast.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has confused the 3D width of the ramp (which applies to the rectangular faces) with the 2D base of the side triangles. They need help distinguishing the overall side-to-side width of the ramp from the horizontal dimension of the side triangle itself.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the ramp's width is needed for the rectangular faces, but redirect the learner to visualize the side triangle specifically and prompt them to identify its horizontal edge along the ground.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Width' Suggestion
rubric_items.description: Address the learner's suggestion by either validating that the ramp's width is needed for the rectangular parts or prompting the learner to visualize where the width sits on the 3D ramp.

rubric_items.title: Direct Attention to the Triangle's Ground Edge
rubric_items.description: Guide the learner to focus specifically on the side triangle and prompt them to identify its horizontal dimension (e.g., the edge that sits on the ground).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Term
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the missing dimension for the triangle is the 'base,' 'length,' or 'depth.'

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject 'width' as incorrect without offering a geometric or spatial cue to help the learner re-evaluate.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully recognized that acquired traits (like disuse of eyes) do not change DNA and cannot be inherited, but they are experiencing cognitive dissonance because cavefish do, in fact, have smaller eyes. They need a bridge to understand that new traits arise from random genetic variations at birth rather than from a parent's lifetime experiences.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's confusion as the exact right puzzle to solve, and prompt them to hypothesize how a fish might end up with smaller eyes if the change didn't come from the parent's lifetime actions, guiding them toward the concept of random mutation or natural variation.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Dissonance
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and validate the learner's cognitive dissonance, affirming that their question ('But they still have smaller eyes?') is a great observation and exactly the right puzzle to solve next.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Source of Variation
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question that guides the learner to consider how a trait (like smaller eyes) could appear in offspring or how DNA might change if it wasn't caused by the parents' lifetime experiences (e.g., prompting for mutation, genetic variation, or being born different).

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Prior Realization
rubric_items.description: Explicitly reference or praise the learner's prior correct conclusion that DNA doesn't change from a parent's actions to anchor the new question.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that random mutations, genetic variation, or natural selection are the cause of the smaller eyes.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Jumping to Survival Advantage
rubric_items.description: Do not ask why smaller eyes would be beneficial or help the fish survive (selection) before the learner has established that the variation (being born with smaller eyes) exists in the population in the first place.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a completely open-ended question (e.g., 'So how do you think it happened?') that leaves the learner stranded without constraining their thinking to genetics, birth, or differences within a population.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is clinging to their initial belief that more water equals a higher pitch, leading them to incorrectly guess that slow vibrations produce high sounds. They need an intuitive bridge to correctly associate slow vibrations with low pitch and fast vibrations with high pitch before applying this rule back to the water glasses.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a familiar, everyday example of slow versus fast vibrations or movements (e.g., a slow, heavy bass drum vs. a fast, tiny whistle) to help the learner intuitively grasp that slow vibrations produce low sounds.

rubric_items.title: Target the Slow-High Misconception
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to re-evaluate their guess that slow vibrations produce high sounds, keeping the pedagogical focus entirely on the relationship between vibration speed and pitch.

rubric_items.title: Use an Intuitive Analogy
rubric_items.description: Provide a concrete, everyday example contrasting slow and fast movements or vibrations (such as a slow, heavy drum versus a fast, buzzing mosquito) to help the learner intuitively grasp the correct relationship.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Rule
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner the correct answer (e.g., do not state that slow vibrations make a low sound or fast vibrations make a high sound).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the learner's guess (e.g., 'Not quite') or ask 'Are you sure?' without offering a concrete example or scaffold to help them rethink it.

rubric_items.title: Defer the Water Glass Context
rubric_items.description: Do not apply the concept back to the water glasses or the volume of water until the general rule connecting vibration speed to pitch is firmly established.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited that 'local environments' refers to distinct geographic areas, but needs to consolidate how the permanent genetic trade-off (slowness for resistance) drives divergent adaptation across these areas over generations, overcoming any lingering belief that the traits are merely temporary reactions.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the learner's spatial intuition ('different areas') and prompt them to predict how the permanent nature of the genetic trade-off causes the snake populations in these distinct areas to diverge from each other over multiple generations.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Spatial Intuition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's realization that 'local environments' translates to distinct geographic areas.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Divergent Prediction
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain or predict how the permanent genetic trade-off (speed vs. resistance) will cause the snake populations in these different areas to look different from each other over multiple generations.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Permanent Trade-off
rubric_items.description: Frame the prompt in a way that requires the learner to treat the slowness as a permanent genetic trait tied to the population, implicitly challenging any residual belief that snakes only slow down when actively digesting a newt.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Explanation
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly explain the outcome of divergent adaptation (e.g., telling the learner that one area will become entirely slow snakes and another entirely fast snakes) instead of making the learner predict it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Agreement
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply say 'yes' or 'exactly' without prompting the learner to apply this spatial concept to the snakes' traits.

learning_objective: PS3.D Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identifies 'heat' as the answer but expresses surprise ('Wait...'), indicating cognitive dissonance as they realize that cellular chemical reactions—not their initial idea of stomach friction—are the true source of body heat. They need to explicitly articulate and resolve this contradiction to consolidate their new understanding.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that the reaction releases heat and prompt the learner to explicitly contrast this cellular process with their original idea about stomach grinding.

rubric_items.title: Affirmation of Heat Release
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm that the cellular chemical reaction does indeed release heat.

rubric_items.title: Prompting Conceptual Contrast
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to compare this cellular source of heat to their initial idea about stomach muscles grinding.

rubric_items.title: Energy Conversion Link
rubric_items.description: The tutor should encourage the learner to connect the release of heat to the transformation of the 'chemical energy' they identified in previous turns.

rubric_items.title: Explaining the Contrast (Takeover)
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for explicitly stating that cellular reactions replace stomach grinding as the source of heat, rather than giving the learner the space to articulate this realization themselves.

rubric_items.title: Ignoring the Dissonance
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for simply accepting the answer 'heat' and moving on to a new topic without addressing the learner's expressed surprise or their earlier misconception.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a loop, stubbornly clinging to the heuristic that 'loud equals scary' and ignoring the tutor's repeated factual corrections about the predator-prey dynamic. Because direct contradiction has failed, the learner needs a new conceptual frame to realize why a large, hungry predator would not be deterred by a small prey's alarm call.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should pivot from direct contradiction to targeted inquiry, using a perspective-taking prompt or analogy that forces the learner to deduce why a loud noise wouldn't frighten a hungry predator in this specific context.

rubric_items.title: Shift to Targeted Inquiry
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a specific question that prompts the learner to actively reason about the coyote's reaction, breaking the unproductive cycle of direct contradiction.

rubric_items.title: Perspective-Taking or Analogy
rubric_items.description: The tutor introduces a new conceptual frame—such as asking the learner to imagine being a hungry predator, or comparing the situation to a human facing a tiny but loud object—to challenge the 'loud equals scary' rule.

rubric_items.title: Validate Intuition
rubric_items.description: The tutor acknowledges that the learner's logic is generally sound by validating that loud noises are indeed startling in many everyday situations.

rubric_items.title: Unproductive Contradiction
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply repeats the factual assertion that the coyote is not scared or is too big to care, continuing a cycle of contradiction that has already proven ineffective.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor introduces a new analogy or perspective but immediately explains the conclusion for the learner (e.g., 'Just like you wouldn't be scared of a loud bug, the coyote isn't scared'), depriving them of the 'aha' moment.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a generic pushback question (e.g., 'Are you sure?' or 'Why would he be scared?') that is likely to just elicit the same 'because it's loud' response, rather than offering new framing to break the loop.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identified that there are 3 items left over (5 total - 2 winning), but mistakenly attached a percentage sign to this raw count instead of calculating the complement percentage. They are confusing the raw number of items with the percentage representation of the whole.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that 3 is the correct number of remaining items, then prompt the learner to either convert 3/5 into a percentage or subtract the 40% winning chance from the 100% total.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Raw Count
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's '3' correctly represents the raw number of losing items left in the box.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Percentage Calculation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to calculate the percentage by either subtracting the 40% winning chance from 100%, or by converting the fraction 3/5 into a percentage.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Items vs. Percentages
rubric_items.description: Explicitly clarify the difference between the raw count of items (3) and the percentage out of 100.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the final answer of 60%.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the answer or repeat that the whole is 100% without providing a concrete mathematical step (like 100 - 40 or 3/5) to help them move forward.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is taking the concept of digital encoding too literally, struggling to bridge the gap between a physical phenomenon (light) and abstract data (numbers). They need to understand that the physical state of the light (on or off) is simply a signal that we assign the meaning of '1' or '0' to, rather than the light physically containing literal digits.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use or prompt for a simple, everyday analogy (like using a flashlight or a light switch to send a message) to help the learner realize how physical states can represent abstract information.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Pattern vs. Literal Digits
rubric_items.description: The response must clarify that the light itself does not contain literal numbers, but rather the physical states of the light (being turned on or off) are used to represent the numbers 1 and 0.

rubric_items.title: Ground in Everyday Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response should introduce or ask the learner to imagine a familiar, non-digital analogy where a physical action sends a message (e.g., a flashlight, a light switch, or Morse code).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner Application
rubric_items.description: The response should ask a targeted question that requires the learner to apply the concept of encoding, such as asking how they would use a light switch to communicate two different options.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overcomplicating with Binary Math
rubric_items.description: The response should not introduce complex binary math, bytes, or base-2 calculations (e.g., explaining how 8 bits make 255), as this bypasses the foundational conceptual gap of how a physical signal becomes a number in the first place.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Tautological Explanation
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply repeat that 'the pulses are binary code' or 'the computer reads it as numbers' without explaining the physical-to-abstract mapping.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully accepted that gravity acts through the vacuum of space without needing air, but they are now facing a cognitive conflict: if Earth's gravity is pulling on the astronauts, why do they appear to float instead of falling to the floor? They need scaffolding to understand that 'floating' in orbit is actually the experience of continuous free fall where both the astronaut and the ship are falling at the same rate.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a relatable thought experiment (like a falling elevator or a dropping amusement park ride) to help the learner deduce what happens when a person and their container are pulled downward by gravity at the exact same time.

rubric_items.title: Targeted Scaffold: Simultaneous Falling
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to consider what happens to a person's movement relative to their container if both the person and the container (the spaceship) are being pulled by gravity at the exact same rate.

rubric_items.title: Use of Earth-Bound Analogy
rubric_items.description: Introduces a concrete, familiar thought experiment (such as a falling elevator, a dropping amusement park ride, or jumping off a diving board holding a ball) to ground the concept of weightlessness before applying it to orbit.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Contradiction
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's question by explicitly acknowledging that 'floating' seems to contradict the newly established fact that gravity is pulling on them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Explaining Orbital Mechanics
rubric_items.description: Directly gives away the answer by telling the learner that the astronauts are in 'free fall' or explaining that they are 'moving sideways so fast they miss the Earth' without letting the learner deduce the falling concept first.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unguided Rebound
rubric_items.description: Responds with a vague, unguided question (e.g., 'Why do you think they float?' or 'What else could cause floating?') that leaves the learner stranded without any new conceptual tools to resolve their confusion.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has just experienced an 'aha' moment, realizing that the 'mixing paint' analogy fails because genes do not blend. They are asking a direct question to confirm this realization of discrete (particulate) inheritance and need validation to fully resolve their initial misconception.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's realization that genes do not mix, reinforcing the concept that genes remain separate, intact units from generation to generation.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Non-Mixing
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirms the learner's deduction that genes do not blend or mix together.

rubric_items.title: Emphasize Intact Units
rubric_items.description: Reinforces the concept of discrete inheritance by explaining that genes remain separate, intact units even when they are hidden by a dominant gene.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for New Analogy
rubric_items.description: Encourages the learner to think of, or provides, a new analogy (such as shuffling cards or mixing marbles) to replace the discarded 'mixing paint' model.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Withholding Validation
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for responding with a vague probe or counter-question that fails to clearly say 'yes' to the learner's correct conceptual deduction.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Introducing Exceptions
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for prematurely introducing concepts like incomplete dominance or codominance, which actually do resemble mixing and would severely confuse the learner's newly formed understanding of discrete Mendelian inheritance.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that a changing rate eliminates a linear model, but lacks the specific mathematical procedure to test for a quadratic model. They need to be introduced to the concept of 'second differences' using the first differences (2 cm and 1.7 cm) they have already identified.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explain that quadratic models have a constant change in their differences (second differences) and prompt the learner to calculate the difference between the two drops they just found.

rubric_items.title: Grounded Calculation Prompt
rubric_items.description: The response must direct the learner to look at or calculate the difference between the two specific drop sizes they already found (2 cm and 1.7 cm).

rubric_items.title: Quadratic Rule Explanation
rubric_items.description: The response should explain the rule being tested: that for a quadratic model, the change between the steps (the 'second difference') must be constant.

rubric_items.title: Foreshadowing the Next Data Point
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges or hints that because they currently only have one 'second difference', they will eventually need a fourth data point (at 3 seconds) to verify if the pattern is truly constant.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Math Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response calculates the second difference for the learner (e.g., explicitly stating 'the difference between 2 and 1.7 is 0.3') rather than leaving that calculation to them.

rubric_items.title: Ungrounded Jargon
rubric_items.description: The response tells the learner to 'find the second differences' or 'use the formula' without explicitly connecting this concept back to the 2 cm and 1.7 cm drops, leaving the learner stranded.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly used the horizontal alignment strategy to identify that the child's second band matches the mom's, but their phrasing ('Um, the mom?') indicates lingering hesitation. They now need confirmation of their success and a prompt to synthesize their two findings (one band from dad, one from mom) into a conclusion about inheritance.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the learner's correct alignment to build confidence, then prompt them to synthesize what these two band matches mean for the child's overall inheritance.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Alignment
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's correct identification that the second band aligns with the mom.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Ask a question that requires the learner to combine their two observations (one band matching dad, one matching mom) into a conclusion about where the child gets their traits.

rubric_items.title: Reconnect to Biology
rubric_items.description: Use terms like 'DNA', 'fragments', or 'inheritance' to transition the conversation from the visual 'ruler trick' back to the biological concept.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Overcoming the Bottleneck
rubric_items.description: Praise the learner for successfully using the horizontal alignment strategy across columns to figure out the matches.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the child gets one band or DNA fragment from each parent; the learner must articulate this synthesis themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-End Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely say 'Yes' or 'Correct' without providing a follow-up question that drives the biological synthesis.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce a new gel, a new child, or a new concept before the learner has articulated the synthesis for this current child's bands.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully set up the Punnett square for an Ai x Bi cross and correctly deduced the genotype for the first box (AB), though they are slightly tentative. They now need to complete the remaining boxes to resolve their original question of how these parents can produce a type O (ii) child.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct 'AB' answer and prompt the learner to fill in the remaining three boxes of the Punnett square to locate the 'ii' genotype.

rubric_items.title: Validate First Cross
rubric_items.description: Affirms the learner's correct deduction that crossing 'A' and 'B' in the first box results in the 'AB' genotype.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Remaining Boxes
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to continue crossing the alleles to fill in the remaining three boxes of the Punnett square.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Original Goal
rubric_items.description: Frames the completion of the Punnett square around the original goal of finding the type O child (the 'ii' genotype).

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Square
rubric_items.description: Provides the genotypes for any of the remaining boxes (Ai, Bi, or ii) or tells the learner exactly which box will contain the 'ii' genotype before they work it out.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Unstructured Prompt
rubric_items.description: Asks a vague question like 'What's next?' or 'Keep going' without explicitly anchoring the next step to the remaining boxes of the Punnett square.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating partitioning lines with measurement lines; because the altitude line visually splits the middle triangle into two smaller right triangles, they are now counting 4 total triangles instead of the original 3. They need to reconcile their accurate visual observation with the conceptual goal of measuring the original shapes.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's visual observation that the line creates two smaller triangles, but prompt the learner to recognize that these two smaller pieces still combine to form the single original middle triangle.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Visual Reality
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's observation that drawing the height line does indeed visually create two smaller triangles inside the middle one.

rubric_items.title: Re-establish the Original Shape
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to articulate the relationship between the new smaller triangles and the original middle triangle (e.g., asking what shape is formed when those two new pieces are combined).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Flat Denial
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply correct the learner by stating 'No, it's still three' or instruct them to just 'ignore' the new triangles, which leaves the learner's visual conflict unresolved.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that introduce area formulas (like 1/2 * base * height) or calculations before the learner has resolved the spatial composition of the shapes.

rubric_items.title: Positive Framing of Observation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly praise the learner for noticing the new shapes, framing their count of 'four' as a good geometric observation rather than just a mistake.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that placing a telescope on a mountain would help bypass the lower-altitude water vapor that blocks infrared light. They now need to evaluate the limits of this strategy to understand why space telescopes are still ultimately necessary for complete infrared observation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's excellent deduction about mountain observatories and prompt them to consider whether a mountain is high enough to escape all atmospheric water vapor.

rubric_items.title: Validate Mountain Deduction
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's deduction is correct and that building telescopes on mountains does indeed help get above the dense, lower-altitude water vapor.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Limitations
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question that prompts the learner to consider whether a mountain is high enough to escape all the water vapor or if there is still some atmospheric interference above it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that mountains still have some atmosphere or water vapor above them, or that space is still required for perfect infrared observation; leave this for the learner to deduce.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dismissing the Idea
rubric_items.description: Do not dismiss the learner's mountain idea as incorrect, as high-altitude observatories are a real, effective, and widely used strategy for infrared astronomy.

rubric_items.title: Ground with Real-World Example
rubric_items.description: Briefly mention that astronomers actually do build telescopes on high mountains for exactly this reason before asking the follow-up question.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner recognizes the physical tension ('tightness') in the static rubber band but is blocked by the misconception that energy requires active motion. They need to connect this physical readiness or tension to the concept of stored energy.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce that the 'tightness' represents a readiness or capacity to cause motion, thereby justifying why it counts as energy.

rubric_items.title: Connect Tension to Capacity for Motion
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to explain what the 'tightness' has the ability to do (e.g., snap back, cause motion) to help them conclude on their own that it is energy.

rubric_items.title: Incorporate Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly validate or use the learner's word 'tight' or the concept of physical tension in the prompt.

rubric_items.title: Recall Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: The response connects the current 'tightness' back to the learner's earlier insight that energy was 'just waiting there' in the squeezed spring.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply answer 'Yes' to the learner's question or directly define 'potential energy' for them, which would bypass their cognitive work.

rubric_items.title: Ungrounded Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response should not reply with a generic 'What do you think?' or ask for a definition of energy that abandons the concrete rubber band example.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner calculated the simple average of 15 and 30 to get 22.5, failing to account for the 80/20 probability distribution. They need to realize that because the 15-minute trip happens much more frequently, the long-term average is weighted heavily toward 15 rather than sitting exactly in the middle.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that acknowledges 22.5 as the simple average, but asks the learner to calculate how many days out of a concrete timeframe (like 10 or 100 days) would actually take 15 minutes versus 30 minutes.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Simple Average
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly recognize that the learner's guess of 22.5 makes sense as the exact middle or simple average of 15 and 30.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Concrete Frequencies
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to apply the 80% and 20% probabilities to a hypothetical number of days (e.g., 'Out of 10 days, how many would take 15 minutes?') to reveal why the outcomes aren't weighted equally.

rubric_items.title: Highlight the Conceptual Pull
rubric_items.description: The response prompts the learner to intuitively consider which travel time the final average should be closer to, based on which outcome happens more often.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Frequencies
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly tell the learner how many days each outcome occurs (e.g., 'Since it's 80%, 8 out of 10 days will be 15 minutes') instead of asking the learner to figure it out.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Abstract Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely reject 22.5 or vaguely remind the learner to 'use the percentages' without providing a concrete scenario (like a 10-day timeframe) to ground their reasoning.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck because they do not know the definition of the vocabulary word 'quantitative', which is preventing them from distinguishing between numerical measurements and categorical groups. They need a direct, simple definition of the term to resolve this vocabulary bottleneck before they can apply it to their original question about 'hours'.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a clear, simple definition of 'quantitative' (such as relating it to 'quantity' or 'amount') and briefly connect it back to the 'hours' example, rather than asking the learner to guess the definition.

rubric_items.title: Provide Clear Definition
rubric_items.description: The response must directly define 'quantitative' in simple, grade-appropriate terms, such as explaining that it means measuring an 'amount' or 'how much' of something.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Root Word
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly points out that 'quantitative' comes from the word 'quantity' to give the learner a helpful mnemonic.

rubric_items.title: Apply to Current Context
rubric_items.description: The response connects the definition back to the learner's original variable by explaining how 'hours' represents an amount or quantity.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Guessing Games
rubric_items.description: The response should not respond to 'What is quantitative?' by asking the learner to guess what it means, as this leaves the learner stranded when they have explicitly signaled a vocabulary gap.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overcomplicating
rubric_items.description: The response should not introduce new statistical concepts (like continuous vs. discrete data or histograms) or re-explain the concept of mathematical averages before the basic definition of 'quantitative' is established.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identified the 2D shape of the cereal box top (a square/rectangle) but is highly hesitant, phrasing their answer as a question. They need immediate validation to build confidence, followed by a scaffolded prompt to compare the physical attributes of the square and the circle.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's correct observation to boost their confidence, then ask a targeted question about a specific feature of the square (like its corners or straight sides) to contrast it with the circle.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly affirm the learner's hesitant answer (e.g., 'Yes, exactly!' or 'You got it!') to build their confidence.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for 2D Attributes
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to identify a specific physical feature of the square/rectangle (such as corners, points, or straight sides) that makes it different from the circle.

rubric_items.title: Shape Refinement
rubric_items.description: The response gently accepts 'square' while naturally introducing or acknowledging 'rectangle' as an accurate description of the cereal box top, without making the learner feel they were wrong.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Attributes
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner the difference between the shapes (e.g., 'A square has four corners and a circle has none') instead of prompting the learner to describe the difference.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Unanchored Comparison
rubric_items.description: The response asks a generic follow-up like 'Why?' or 'How are they different?' without anchoring the question to the physical features of the square and circle they just named.

rubric_items.title: Premature 3D Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response introduces formal 3D geometric terms (like 'cylinder', 'rectangular prism', 'faces', or 'vertices') before the learner has successfully articulated the simpler 2D differences.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has made an accurate and insightful connection: learning a trick physically changes the brain. Their bottleneck is understanding why this specific physical change (in the brain) does not alter the 'instructions' that are passed down to the puppies.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's insight that the brain does change, and then ask a targeted question prompting the learner to consider whether changes in the brain can rewrite the instructions passed to the puppies.

rubric_items.title: Validate Brain Insight
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or validates the learner's accurate insight that learning a trick does physically change the dog's brain.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Brain-to-Instruction Connection
rubric_items.description: Asks a targeted question that prompts the learner to consider whether a physical change in the brain can reach or rewrite the 'instructions' that are passed down to the puppies.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Metaphor
rubric_items.description: Uses the established 'instructions' metaphor to help the learner reason through the problem, rather than abruptly shifting to formal genetic terminology (like DNA or germ cells).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that brain changes do not affect the inherited instructions, stealing the opportunity for the learner to deduce this boundary themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Dismissal
rubric_items.description: Ignores the learner's point about the brain changing, or simply repeats the rule that 'instructions don't change' without addressing the learner's specific cognitive conflict.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the variable $h$ (the input of 5 total hours) with the evaluated result of the expression $(h-2)$ (the output of 3 growth hours), despite the tutor's previous clarification. They are struggling to hold the two distinct values in their working memory and map them to the correct mathematical symbols.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that corrects the value of $h$ to 5 and asks the learner to substitute that 5 into the expression $(h-2)$ to see how it produces the 3.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Value of h
rubric_items.description: Explicitly clarify, or guide the learner to recognize, that $h$ is 5, not 3.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Substitution
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to substitute 5 for $h$ in the expression $(h - 2)$ to see how the math produces the 3.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Contextual Meaning
rubric_items.description: Reinforce the physical meaning of the numbers by linking $h=5$ back to the total time and 3 back to the growth time.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Doing the Math
rubric_items.description: Do not do the math for the learner by explicitly stating the full equation '5 - 2 = 3' or 'since h is 5, 5 minus 2 is 3'.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply say 'No' or vaguely tell the learner to re-read the previous message without actively guiding them to map the numbers 5 and 3 to their respective parts of the expression.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the newly calculated increase (11) needs to be added to a previous value, but they are incorrectly attempting to add it back to the original base (100) instead of the current accumulated value (110). They need scaffolding to recognize that each level builds on the immediately preceding level's total.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's instinct to add the 11, but prompt them to identify what the character's value actually was right before reaching level 2.

rubric_items.title: Redirect to Current Level Value
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to consider the character's value at level 1 (110) as the correct starting point for the level 2 addition.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Addition Operation
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that the learner's instinct to add the 11 is correct, separating the correct operation from the incorrect target number.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner to add 11 to 110 or provides the final answer of 121, taking away the cognitive work of identifying the correct base.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: The response simply rejects the learner's guess (e.g., 'Not quite' or 'Try again') without directing their attention to the level 1 total.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response attempts to introduce multipliers (like 1.1) or algebraic functions before the learner has successfully resolved this concrete step-by-step calculation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly understands the pattern for creating intervals of size 5 and realizes their current list stops at 24, which falls short of their maximum value of 29. They are now perfectly positioned to apply the pattern to generate the final interval(s).
rubric.ideal_next_move: Prompt the learner to generate the next interval(s) following the established pattern until the maximum value of 29 is included.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Next Intervals
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to determine the next interval or intervals in the sequence.

rubric_items.title: Reference the Target Value
rubric_items.description: The tutor should connect the prompt to the goal of reaching or covering the highest value of 29.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not provide the final interval (e.g., '25 to 29') for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Next Steps
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not ask a vague question (e.g., 'What should we do next?') that fails to focus the learner specifically on extending the current interval pattern.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly deduced that if gravity stopped pulling at the peak, the ball would 'just float there.' They now need to contrast this hypothetical scenario with the ball's actual behavior to realize that gravity must still be acting at the peak to prevent it from floating.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's hypothetical deduction and prompt them to state what the ball actually does in reality instead of floating.

rubric_items.title: Elicit Real-World Behavior
rubric_items.description: The tutor prompts the learner to state what the ball actually does in reality to contrast with their 'float there' hypothesis (e.g., 'But does it actually float?' or 'What happens instead?').

rubric_items.title: Validate the Hypothetical
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly affirms the learner's logical deduction that the ball would indeed float if gravity were turned off.

rubric_items.title: Premature Conclusion (Takeover)
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner that gravity is still pulling at the peak, bypassing the learner's opportunity to make that connection themselves based on the ball's behavior.

rubric_items.title: Stating the Obvious (Takeover)
rubric_items.description: The tutor tells the learner that the ball falls back down or doesn't float, depriving the learner of the chance to state this obvious real-world fact themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor responds with a generic prompt (e.g., 'Are you sure?' or 'Think about it again') that fails to anchor the learner on comparing their 'floating' hypothesis to the ball's actual behavior.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance because the tutor stated that steepness depends on ratios, but the learner is fixated on the fact that both ramps have a height-to-base difference of 2 (5-3=2 and 8-6=2). They are pushing back and are not ready to simplify the fraction 6/8 until they understand why their additive rule is incorrect.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should temporarily drop the fraction simplification and introduce an extreme counterexample (like a ramp with height 100 and base 102, or height 1 and base 3) to help the learner intuitively realize that a constant difference of 2 does not result in the same steepness.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Observation
rubric_items.description: The response should briefly validate that the learner is mathematically correct about the difference being 2 before challenging its relevance to the concept of steepness.

rubric_items.title: Create Cognitive Conflict via Counterexample
rubric_items.description: The response should present an extreme case of a ramp where the base and height have a difference of 2 (e.g., height 100 and base 102, or height 1 and base 3) to test the learner's additive rule.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Focus on Steepness
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly ask the learner to consider the physical steepness of the new counterexample ramp, prompting them to realize that a constant difference does not mean constant steepness.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explaining the Flaw Directly
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly explain why subtraction doesn't work for steepness (e.g., 'Steepness is about multiplication, not addition') instead of allowing the learner to discover this through the counterexample.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Insisting on Fraction Simplification
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that dismiss the learner's question and repeat the prompt to simplify the fraction 6/8, which would leave the additive misconception unaddressed.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is deeply entrenched in the misconception that plants recycle heat for photosynthesis, leading them to incorrectly guess that chlorophyll absorbs heat. They need a targeted hint that breaks this fixation by connecting chlorophyll's function directly to light rather than warmth.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a concrete clue about chlorophyll (such as its nature as a green pigment or its reliance on the sun) and prompt the learner to deduce that it absorbs light, not heat.

rubric_items.title: Address the Heat Guess
rubric_items.description: The response must clearly indicate that heat is not the specific type of energy chlorophyll is shaped to absorb.

rubric_items.title: Provide a Light-Oriented Clue
rubric_items.description: The response must offer a specific conceptual bridge—such as mentioning that chlorophyll is a green pigment, or reminding the learner of the sun—that helps the learner deduce the correct energy type.

rubric_items.title: Require Learner Articulation
rubric_items.description: The response must ask a question or leave a blank that requires the learner to actively generate the word 'light' or 'sunlight' themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that tell the learner they are wrong but merely ask them to guess again without providing a new conceptual clue, leaving them stranded.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly tell the learner that chlorophyll absorbs light, bypassing their opportunity to connect the clue to the answer.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that move on to the next step of the energy cycle (e.g., what happens after photosynthesis) before resolving the immediate bottleneck about what energy chlorophyll absorbs.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a semantic loop, correctly observing that $x^2$ contains an exponent but incorrectly assuming this makes it an 'exponential' function. They are growing frustrated by the tutor's repeated abstract definitions and need to break away from terminology to see the mathematical difference through concrete calculation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's correct literal observation that 2 is an exponent, acknowledge the confusing terminology, and then prompt the learner to plug concrete numbers into $x^2$ and $2^x$ to discover the difference in behavior for themselves.

rubric_items.title: Validate Literal Observation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner is correct in stating that the number 2 in $x^2$ is indeed an exponent.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Concrete Comparison
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to plug specific numbers (e.g., 3 or 4) into both $x^2$ and $2^x$ to discover how the position of the variable changes the output.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Confusing Terminology
rubric_items.description: Validate the learner's frustration by acknowledging that the mathematical naming convention is counterintuitive since both quadratic and exponential expressions contain exponents.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating Abstract Definitions
rubric_items.description: Do not merely restate the abstract rule about where the variable is located, as this semantic explanation has already failed multiple times.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Calculation
rubric_items.description: Do not calculate the outputs of the concrete examples for the learner; leave the actual evaluation of $x^2$ and $2^x$ to them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not simply agree that 2 is an exponent without providing a concrete mathematical task (like evaluating expressions) to help the learner break out of the semantic loop.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has lost track of the sequential flow of the calculations and forgotten that they themselves just derived the 800-calorie value for the ladybugs from the aphids' energy two turns ago. They need to be re-grounded in their own prior work and the biological context before they can confidently proceed to calculate the energy for the next trophic level.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should pause the forward progression of the math and prompt the learner to look back at their own previous calculation to re-establish the link between the aphids' 8,000 calories and the ladybugs' 800 calories.

rubric_items.title: Trace Back to Previous Trophic Level
rubric_items.description: Address the learner's confusion by connecting the 800 calories back to the previous step in the food chain (the aphids' 8,000 calories).

rubric_items.title: Reference Learner's Prior Work
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner that they themselves just calculated this 800-calorie value two turns ago.

rubric_items.title: Normalize the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that it is easy to lose track of what the numbers mean in a multi-step problem.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Question
rubric_items.description: Ignoring the learner's question about where the 800 came from and insisting they answer the pending math problem for the bird (800 / 10).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Math Without Biology
rubric_items.description: Explaining the mathematical origin of the 800 (e.g., '8000 divided by 10') without mentioning the organisms (aphids or ladybugs) those numbers represent.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has explicitly voiced the core misconception that air is 'nothing' because it is invisible, preventing them from understanding how it could physically block water. They need a concrete anchor to realize that air is a physical substance that interacts with the world, even if it cannot be seen.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to think of a familiar, everyday physical experience where they can feel or observe air acting as a physical substance (such as wind, blowing up a balloon, or feeling their breath).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Concrete Evidence of Air
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to identify or reflect on a specific physical experience where air can be felt or observed acting as a physical substance (e.g., wind, blowing up a balloon, or feeling breath on a hand).

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's perspective that air seems like 'nothing' because it is invisible or cannot be easily seen.
