rubric_items.title: Focus on the Combined Effect
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner's attention to the 'winning' force or the combined result of the two unequal forces, rather than letting them focus solely on the existence of the opposing force.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that it is natural to think an opposing force causes slowing down (since in everyday life, friction often acts alone to slow things down), validating their thought process before challenging it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating the Abstract Rule
rubric_items.description: Do not simply restate that 'because gravity is stronger, the net force is downward so you speed up', as the tutor already stated this rule two turns ago and the learner's intuition rejected it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Abstract Physics Jargon
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to define 'net force', 'acceleration', or 'vectors' abstractly without grounding it in a physical scenario, as their block is intuitive, not definitional.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is mid-thought, trying to process the tutor's direct instruction on algebraic notation (writing '2d') and apply it to their specific problem. They understand the concept of multiplication but need a moment to map the rule to the actual shampoo cost.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A gentle, brief prompt that encourages the learner to finish their thought and apply the 'number next to variable' rule to the actual shampoo cost from their problem.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Application of Notation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to apply the newly explained rule (writing the number and variable next to each other) to the actual cost of the shampoo in their specific problem.

rubric_items.title: Provide Space to Finish
rubric_items.description: Keep the response brief and open-ended enough to allow the learner to complete the thought they started with 'Wait, so...'.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Final Term
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state the final algebraic term for the actual shampoo cost (e.g., do not say 'So if the shampoo is $5, you write 5d').

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce the next part of the equation (such as the flat-rate rental fee) before the learner has successfully written the shampoo term.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the paint moves from the sprayer to the target, but they are struggling to map this physical action onto a spatial coordinate system (X and Y). They need concrete scaffolding to describe the physical orientation of the setup in everyday spatial terms before they can connect it back to the math.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's basic intuition and prompt them to describe the physical direction of the target relative to the sprayer using concrete spatial terms (e.g., up/down, left/right, horizontal/vertical).

rubric_items.title: Establish Spatial Orientation
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to specify the physical direction of the target relative to the sprayer using concrete spatial concepts (e.g., horizontal/vertical, up/down, left/right).

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Logic
rubric_items.description: The response should briefly affirm the learner's correct, albeit basic, statement that the paint moves towards the target to build confidence.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Math
rubric_items.description: The response must not reintroduce mathematical terms like X, Y, vectors, or triangles until the physical space is clearly defined.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Layout
rubric_items.description: The response must not state the physical orientation of the sprayer and target for the learner (e.g., 'Since the target is in front of you...').

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Probes
rubric_items.description: The response must not ask an open-ended question (e.g., 'Can you be more specific?') that fails to guide the learner toward thinking in terms of physical dimensions.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the misconception that 'f' is an independent algebraic variable that needs a numerical value, rather than understanding it as the name of the function. They need to realize that 'f' is not calculated, but rather the output is calculated by applying the '5x' rule to a specific input.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly clarify that 'f' is just a name or label, and then prompt the learner to calculate the distance for a specific number of turns to demonstrate that the actual math happens on the '5x' side of the equation.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Nature of 'f'
rubric_items.description: Explicitly address the learner's question by stating that 'f' is just a name or label for the rule/machine, not a number or variable to be calculated or solved for.

rubric_items.title: Direct Focus to the Rule
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to engage with the '5x' side of the equation (e.g., by asking them to calculate the distance for a specific number of turns) to help them discover where the actual math happens.

rubric_items.title: Maintain the Story Context
rubric_items.description: Refer back to the 'toy car' or 'distance' context to keep the abstract notation grounded in the physical scenario the learner already understands.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Process
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly tell the learner the steps to evaluate the function (e.g., 'You calculate it by replacing x with a number and multiplying by 5') instead of prompting them to perform a concrete calculation themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Reassurance
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply tell the learner 'You don't calculate f' without providing a concrete next step (like a specific input value or a question about the 5x rule) to help them see how the equation actually works.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has overlooked the text labels in the t-table header and only noticed the decimal values. They need to be guided to find the specific words (like 'one-tail' and 'two-tail') that categorize those decimals so they can apply their earlier reasoning.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to look more closely at the text or words immediately above or next to the decimals, specifically hinting that they should look for terms related to their previous discussion about 'tails'.

rubric_items.title: Direct Attention to Text Labels
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to look for words, text, or specific labels (rather than just numbers) in the table's header area.

rubric_items.title: Connect to the 'Tail' Concept
rubric_items.description: The response should remind the learner that they are specifically looking for headings related to the 'one-tail' or 'two-tail' concepts discussed moments ago.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Decimals
rubric_items.description: The response may briefly validate that the decimals are indeed there before redirecting the learner to look for the text above them.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Column
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply tell the learner which specific column to use (e.g., 'Look at the 0.05 under two-tails') or bypass the table-reading step entirely.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: 'Look Again'
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely tell the learner to 'look closer' or 'try again' without specifying that they should be looking for words or text.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified that the hawk risks getting hurt by the mobbing birds. They now need to connect this risk of injury to the hawk's decision to retreat, which ultimately explains how the small birds' group behavior successfully deters a larger predator.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's realization about the risk of injury and prompt them to predict what the hawk will decide to do as a result.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Risk of Injury
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly acknowledge or validate the learner's correct realization that the hawk risks getting hurt.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Hawk's Decision
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to deduce what the hawk will choose to do when faced with this risk of injury (e.g., asking what the hawk will decide to do next).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Outcome
rubric_items.description: The response must not explicitly tell the learner that the hawk will fly away, give up, or leave the flock alone.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Continuation
rubric_items.description: The response must not ask a generic question (like "What happens next?" or "Why does that matter?") that fails to focus the learner on the hawk's specific behavioral response to the risk.

rubric_items.title: Optional: Connect to Group Safety
rubric_items.description: The response may prompt the learner to connect the hawk's likely decision to the ultimate benefit for the group of small birds.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully calculated the probabilities of avoiding the traps (1/2 and 1/3) but is confusing the probability of the hazard with the probability of safety, leading to the mistaken belief that a smaller percentage is safer. They need help distinguishing between the chance of hitting a trap and the chance of avoiding it before they can correctly evaluate which path is better.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuition that we want the chance of danger to be small, explicitly contrast this with the fact that these percentages represent the chance of safety, and prompt the learner to conclude whether the chance of safety should be high or low.

rubric_items.title: Distinguishing Safety from Hazard
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly draw a contrast between the chance of hitting the trap (the hazard) and the chance of avoiding the trap (safety) to address the learner's specific confusion.

rubric_items.title: Preserving Learner Conclusion
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask a question that requires the learner to deduce that a larger percentage is desirable when measuring safety, rather than stating this conclusion for them.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly tells the learner that a larger percentage means it is safer or explicitly tells them to pick the 50% path, doing the reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply repeats their previous question (e.g., 'Do you want it to be high or low?') or offers a generic 'Are you sure?' without providing new scaffolding to help the learner distinguish hazard from safety.

rubric_items.title: Prematurely Addressing Compound Probability
rubric_items.description: The tutor attempts to address the learner's broader hidden belief by discussing consecutive traps or multiplying probabilities, which is premature and distracts from resolving the immediate confusion about what the current percentages represent.

rubric_items.title: Validating the Intuition
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly acknowledges the logic behind the learner's confusion, validating that it makes sense to want a small number when thinking about encountering traps.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance because the tutor's biological rule (pots don't pass traits) conflicts with their visual observation (short plants are consistently in red pots). They need help distinguishing between a correlation (where the plants were placed) and causation (what made them short).
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted hypothetical question that forces the learner to separate the seed's inherited instructions from its physical container, such as asking what would happen if a 'tall' seed were planted in the red pot.

rubric_items.title: Hypothetical Separation Prompt
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner with a hypothetical scenario that separates the seed's instructions from the pot, such as asking what would happen if a 'tall' seed were planted in the red pot.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner correctly noticed a pattern (the short plants actually are in the red pots) to validate their observation before challenging their conclusion.

rubric_items.title: Dismissive Repetition
rubric_items.description: Merely repeat that pots aren't alive or cannot pass traits, which ignores the learner's valid visual evidence and fails to resolve their cognitive dissonance.

rubric_items.title: Giving Away the Explanation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tell the learner why the correlation exists (e.g., 'The gardener just put the short seeds in the red pot') instead of guiding them to realize the pot is just a location.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully grasps the concept of accumulation (gallons in a bucket) but is tripped up by everyday language, incorrectly assuming the unit is a rate ('Watts per hour') rather than a product. They need to connect the mathematical operation they already performed (multiplication) to the name of the unit.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's grasp of accumulation ('Gallons') and then prompt them to reflect on their earlier math (300 * 5) to realize that 'per' implies division, whereas they actually multiplied Watts by hours.

rubric_items.title: Contrast 'Per' with Multiplication
rubric_items.description: The response must address the word 'per' by guiding the learner to recognize that 'per' implies division, whereas accumulating energy requires multiplication.

rubric_items.title: Re-anchor to the Initial Calculation
rubric_items.description: The response should reference the learner's own earlier math (multiplying 300 by 5) to help them see why the resulting unit is a product (Watt-hours) rather than a rate.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Accumulation Insight
rubric_items.description: The response should briefly affirm the learner's correct answer ('Gallons') to reinforce their conceptual understanding of accumulation before correcting the terminology.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Unit Correction
rubric_items.description: The response simply tells the learner that the unit is 'Watts times hours' or that 'per' means division, without prompting them to deduce this from their own math.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response asks a generic question about units or math (e.g., 'What does the math tell you?') without specifically targeting the 'per' misconception.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response introduces new physics units like Joules to explain Watt-hours, which abandons the current intuitive grounding and overcomplicates the immediate terminology fix.

learning_objective: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully identified the correct numerator and restricted denominator from the data table but lacks an intuitive understanding of why the 'given' condition shrinks the sample space. They are struggling to conceptually justify why the rest of the school population must be excluded from the denominator.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a concrete thought experiment or targeted question (such as asking if it is possible to pick a freshman if we already know the student is a sophomore) to help the learner intuitively realize why non-sophomores have a zero percent chance of being selected and must be excluded.

rubric_items.title: Provide an Intuitive Anchor
rubric_items.description: Provide a concrete scenario or intuitive question that makes the restriction of the sample space obvious, such as imagining physically separating the sophomores or asking if a non-sophomore could possibly be chosen.

rubric_items.title: Redefine 'Everyone'
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connect the intuitive explanation back to the learner's exact words ('everyone'), helping them see that the 45 sophomores have effectively become the new 'everyone' for this specific scenario.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Conceptual Hurdle
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that asking 'why not everyone?' is a great question, validating that this restriction is the trickiest conceptual shift in conditional probability.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating Previous Logic
rubric_items.description: Do not merely repeat the logic from the previous turn ('we only look at sophomores because we are told they are a sophomore') without offering a new conceptual anchor or thought experiment.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Do not attempt to answer the 'why' by introducing formal conditional probability formulas or notation (like P(A|B)), which would bypass the intuitive bottleneck the learner is currently facing.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly deduced that the dominant 'freckles' trait will be expressed, but is now confusing physical expression (phenotype) with genetic presence (genotype), wondering if the unexpressed allele physically vanishes.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the learner's correct answer about freckles, then prompt them to recall where the alleles are physically located (on the chromosomes) to help them deduce that the 'no freckles' allele remains safely in the cell.

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Deduction
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative answer ('Freckles?') so they know their reasoning about dominance was correct.

rubric_items.title: Ground in Physical Location
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to use their recent knowledge about chromosomes or cells to reason out whether the 'no freckles' allele physically disappears.

rubric_items.title: Praise the Insight
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that asking about the fate of the hidden allele is an excellent, deep biological question.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Answer)
rubric_items.description: Directly tell the learner that the allele does not disappear, stays in the DNA, or is simply 'hidden', thereby doing the reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Respond with a completely unguided question like 'What do you think?' without directing the learner's attention back to the physical reality of the chromosomes discussed in the previous turn.

learning_objective: LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has expressed persistent skepticism that whales are more closely related to hippos than sharks, but has finally agreed to look at the genetic evidence. They now need concrete, step-by-step guidance to begin comparing the amino acid sequences without being overwhelmed by the full dataset.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should direct the learner to compare a specific, small section of the sequence (e.g., the first five letters) for just one pair of animals, prompting the learner to do the actual counting themselves.

rubric_items.title: Isolate a Pair
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to begin by comparing the whale to just one of the other animals (either the hippo or the shark) rather than trying to look at all three at once.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Small-Scale Counting
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to look at a specific, manageable chunk of the sequence (e.g., the first 5 letters) and count the matches themselves.

rubric_items.title: Frame as a Test
rubric_items.description: Connect this mechanical counting step back to the learner's skepticism by framing it as a test to see if the DNA matches the whale's appearance or its ancestry.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor counts the matches or explicitly lists the matching letters for the learner, depriving them of the chance to examine the data themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply tells the learner to 'compare the sequences' or 'start counting' without specifying a pair of animals or a starting section to focus on.

learning_objective: LS2.C Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly assumes that insect-eating animals can simply switch their diet to grass to survive the loss of their primary food source. They need to recognize the biological constraints of food webs—specifically that insectivores cannot digest or survive on grass—in order to understand how the pesticide disruption cascades to other species.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to consider whether an animal adapted to eat insects is physically capable of eating and surviving on grass.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Dietary Flexibility
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to evaluate whether insect-eating animals are biologically capable of eating or surviving on grass.

rubric_items.title: Use Concrete Animal Examples
rubric_items.description: Grounds the question in a specific, familiar example of an insect-eating animal (e.g., a bird, frog, or spider) to make the dietary constraint more intuitive.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Abundance Logic
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's underlying logic that grass is the most abundant food source left in the park, before challenging whether the animals can actually use it.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Consequence
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that the animals will starve, die, or have to leave the park, rather than letting the learner deduce this consequence from their dietary constraints.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Generic Rejection
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's guess with a generic 'No' or 'Are you sure?' without specifically directing their attention to the animals' dietary needs or physical adaptations.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully deduced that the 'bb' genotype corresponds to the brown fur phenotype but is hesitant and seeking validation. They now need to combine this phenotype with their earlier 25% calculation to state the final probability of the offspring having brown fur.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that 'bb' means brown fur and prompt the learner to combine this with their previous 25% calculation to state the final probability of a brown offspring.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Phenotype
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly confirm that the learner is correct about the 'bb' genotype resulting in brown fur.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Final Synthesis
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask a question that requires the learner to state the final conclusion regarding the probability of the offspring having brown fur.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Calculation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly remind or point the learner back to the 25% figure they calculated earlier to scaffold the final synthesis.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Progress
rubric_items.description: The tutor may briefly praise the learner for successfully connecting the genotype to the phenotype.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving the Final Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not state the final combined conclusion (e.g., 'Yes, so there is a 25% chance of brown fur') for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-end Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not merely say 'Yes' or 'Correct' without prompting the learner to take the final step of stating the overall probability.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that the maternal grandma passed down the swirled fur, but questions why they need to check the maternal grandpa. This hesitation stems from a hidden belief that traits must be a blend from both parents, making the learner confused about how the grandpa fits in if the grandma already has the complete trait.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's observation about the grandma, then frame checking the grandpa's fur pattern as a way to test whether the mom inherited the trait from just one parent or a blend of both.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Logic
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's correct realization that the swirled fur trait has already been successfully traced to the grandma.

rubric_items.title: Frame the Purpose of Checking Grandpa
rubric_items.description: Explain that checking the grandpa helps us discover whether the mom got the trait from only one parent or if both parents had to contribute to it.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Observation of Grandpa
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to look at the maternal grandpa's picture and identify his specific fur pattern.

rubric_items.title: Surface the Blending Misconception
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner for their hypothesis on whether the grandpa needs to have the trait too, directly engaging their hidden belief about blended inheritance before they check the picture.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the grandpa lacks the trait or state that traits can come from just one parent before the learner observes the picture themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unjustified Command
rubric_items.description: Do not simply repeat the instruction to look at the grandpa without addressing the learner's underlying 'why' question.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive overload from the complex algebra and is confused by the tutor's mention of a 'middle term,' as they hold the misconception that squaring a sum simply squares each individual term. They need scaffolding to understand why squaring the equation as-is fails before they can meaningfully engage with the strategy of rearranging it.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should step back and use a simpler abstraction (like substituting A and B for the radicals) or a basic example (like expanding (A+B)^2) to help the learner realize why squaring the sum creates a middle term.

rubric_items.title: Target the Squaring Misconception
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate a simpler example of squaring a sum (such as expanding (A+B)^2 or a numerical example) to help them realize that squaring does not simply eliminate the individual square roots.

rubric_items.title: Simplify the Visual Representation
rubric_items.description: Suggest replacing the complex radical expressions with simple variables (like A and B) to help the learner focus on the algebraic structure without being overwhelmed by the coordinates.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the algebra for this specific derivation is notoriously messy or that feeling lost at this transition is completely normal.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Expansion)
rubric_items.description: Directly tell the learner the correct binomial expansion (e.g., 'Remember that (A+B)^2 is A^2 + 2AB + B^2') instead of prompting them to expand it or realize it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Unscaffolded Push for Rearrangement
rubric_items.description: Repeat the request to rearrange the equation without offering a simpler abstraction (like A + B = 2a) or clarifying the squaring misconception.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Respond with a generic question like 'What part are you lost on?' or 'Let's take it step by step' without providing a concrete mathematical scaffold to anchor their thinking.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the physical event of getting bitten with the medical consequence of getting Lyme disease. They need to realize that while biodiversity doesn't stop ticks from biting humans, it changes the outcome of those bites from disease transmission to a mere nuisance.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that validates the learner's observation that bites still happen, but asks them to deduce or contrast the actual health outcome of being bitten by an uninfected tick versus an infected one.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Bite Outcome
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to articulate the difference in the medical outcome or danger between being bitten by an infected tick versus an uninfected tick.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Bite Event
rubric_items.description: Explicitly acknowledges or validates the learner's correct observation that humans will indeed still get bitten by ticks.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Concrete Example
rubric_items.description: References the earlier example of the tick that fed on the opossum to ground the concept of an 'uninfected bite' in the dialogue's established context.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Answer)
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that an uninfected bite is just a normal bug bite (or harmless) rather than asking them to conclude what happens.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Repetition (Sticking to Math)
rubric_items.description: Repeats the explanation about percentages, probabilities, or 'chances dropping' without addressing the learner's specific fixation on the physical bite itself.

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that mass, temperature change, and specific heat must be multiplied to find the total thermal energy, but they are seeking confirmation before formalizing the math. They need validation of this specific operation and a prompt to construct the actual equation, ideally building on their earlier realization that the heat of the washer and the water should be set equal.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm that multiplying the three variables is correct and prompt the learner to write out the resulting mathematical expression or equation.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Multiplication
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's correct deduction that multiplying mass, temperature change, and specific heat is the right mathematical operation.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Mathematical Formulation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to write out the mathematical expression or equation using these three variables.

rubric_items.title: Recall Equality Insight
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of their earlier idea to set the washer and water equal to each other, encouraging them to apply the multiplication to both sides.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Equation
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final mathematical formula (e.g., q = mcΔT) or set up the equality for them before they have a chance to construct it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a non-committal question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that withholds the confirmation the learner explicitly asked for and needs in order to proceed.

learning_objective: LS1.B Growth and Development of Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully located and listed the raw data for their plant group and now needs to calculate the average to make sense of the varied heights. Their immediate bottleneck is procedural, requiring guidance on the first mechanical step of calculating an average: summing the values.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to add the five numbers together as the first step toward finding the average, without doing the math for them or giving away the full multi-step formula all at once.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Addition
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to add or find the total sum of the five numbers they just provided.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Average
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connects this mathematical step to the broader goal of finding the 'average' or 'typical' height for this group of plants.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Data Retrieval
rubric_items.description: Briefly affirms that the learner successfully found the correct data points before moving to the math step.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful: Doing the Math
rubric_items.description: Calculates the sum (30) or the final average (6) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful: Full Formula Dump
rubric_items.description: Provides the complete multi-step formula for an average (e.g., 'add them up and then divide by 5') rather than focusing only on the immediate next step of adding.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful: Vague Next Step
rubric_items.description: Asks a completely open-ended procedural question (e.g., 'What do we do next with these numbers?') without providing enough scaffolding to point the learner toward addition.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the concept of a 'field' with a physical 'pull' (force), leading to the logical contradiction of a pull existing with nothing to pull on. They need to separate the potential for a force (the field) from the actual force itself (the pull).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's logic by confirming there is indeed no 'pull' in empty space, and then prompt the learner to conceptualize the field as a 'potential' or 'readiness' to pull rather than an active force.

rubric_items.title: Validate the 'No Pull' Intuition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's correct intuition that there is absolutely no 'pull' (force) happening if there is no second object present.

rubric_items.title: Shift from Action to Potential
rubric_items.description: Guide the learner to reframe the field as a 'potential', 'readiness', or 'zone of influence' waiting for an object, rather than an active physical action.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Reconceptualization
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question that requires the learner to articulate what is actually present in the empty space if it isn't a 'pull' (e.g., 'If it's not a pull yet, what is it waiting to do?').

rubric_items.title: Over-explaining Potential
rubric_items.description: Giving away the complete explanation of how a field represents a potential force without leaving a conceptual gap for the learner to resolve.

rubric_items.title: Ignoring the 'Pull' Conflation
rubric_items.description: Responding with generic statements about fields (e.g., repeating 'fields are properties of space') without directly addressing and dismantling the learner's specific use of the word 'pull'.

learning_objective: LS2.C Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands how to calculate the retention percentage based on their success with the low-density plot, but they have lost their train of thought while trying to locate the corresponding data for the high-density plot, likely exacerbated by their recurring distraction about the beach. They need immediate, targeted guidance to extract the correct 'before' and 'after' values from their dataset to set up the next calculation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should direct the learner to look specifically at their dataset to find the 'before' and 'after' soil mass values for the high-density cordgrass, using their previous successful setup as a model.

rubric_items.title: Direct to High-Density Data
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly directs the learner to locate the 'before' and 'after' soil mass values for the high-density cordgrass in their dataset.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Success
rubric_items.description: The tutor connects the current task to the learner's previous successful step by suggesting they use the same fraction setup they just used for the low-density plot.

rubric_items.title: Manage Beach Distraction
rubric_items.description: The tutor gently acknowledges, tables, or redirects the learner's recurring 'beach' thought to help them focus on the immediate data extraction task.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Data Provision
rubric_items.description: The tutor provides the specific data values, the fraction setup, or the final retention percentage for the high-density plot, bypassing the learner's need to extract the information themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor gives a generic prompt (e.g., 'What's next?' or 'Keep going') that fails to specify looking for the high-density data, leaving the distracted learner stranded.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the binary arithmetic logic that any sample mean below the claimed population mean (9 < 10) automatically disproves the claim, resisting the tutor's previous mention of a calculation. They need the tutor to validate their literal observation while concretely framing the upcoming calculation as a way to test if a specific difference of 1 chip is statistically significant.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's observation that 9 is less than 10, then shift the focus to the magnitude of the difference (1 chip) and prompt the learner to identify what information is needed to calculate if a 1-chip difference is unusual.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Inequality
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's literal observation that 9 is indeed less than 10 before adding statistical context.

rubric_items.title: Focus on the Magnitude of Difference
rubric_items.description: The tutor should shift the learner's focus from the absolute value (9) to the magnitude of the difference (1 chip), explaining or prompting the learner to recognize that the calculation tests whether being exactly 1 chip off is due to random chance.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Calculation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to identify what specific information (e.g., the typical spread, standard deviation, or variance) is needed to perform this calculation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Formula Dump
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for simply handing the learner the formula for standard error or z-score without first establishing what the calculation is trying to solve conceptually.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Generic Repetition
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for merely repeating that 'samples vary' or 'we need a calculation' without grounding the response in the specific 1-chip difference or moving the calculation forward.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly calculated that 4.3 squared is 18.49 and realized it is too large, meaning the exact side length must fall strictly between 4.2 and 4.3. They are at the threshold of discovering that no simple terminating decimal in tenths will work, setting the stage for the concept of irrational numbers.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that 18.49 is too big, establish that the exact value must lie between 4.2 and 4.3, and prompt the learner to consider how they could find a more precise number in that range.

rubric_items.title: Synthesize the Current Bounds
rubric_items.description: Confirm that 18.49 is too big and explicitly state (or prompt the learner to state) that the exact side length must therefore be between 4.2 and 4.3.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Increased Precision
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner how they might find a number between 4.2 and 4.3, encouraging them to consider adding another decimal place (such as hundredths).

rubric_items.title: Praise the Systematic Approach
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's logical progression in narrowing down the possibilities from the initial 4 and 4.5 to the much tighter 4.2 and 4.3 range.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the decimal will go on forever, introduce the term 'irrational', or give away the square root of 18; allow the learner to first experience the need for infinite precision.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not simply ask 'What's next?' or 'Try again' without anchoring the next step in the newly established 4.2 to 4.3 interval.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that a gamete receives only one allele per gene, but their tentative phrasing ('Just one?') indicates they need validation before they can confidently use the four gamete combinations they derived to set up the Punnett square.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct deduction and prompt them to apply the four gamete combinations (VS, Vs, vS, vs) to the axes of the Punnett square, returning to their original question of 'What goes where?'.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative answer that exactly one copy of the gene ends up in a single gamete.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Punnett Square Setup
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to take the next step by asking how or where the four gamete combinations they derived earlier should be placed on the Punnett square.

rubric_items.title: Reference Original Question
rubric_items.description: Connect this biological realization back to the learner's initial question of 'What goes where?'.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Doing the Setup
rubric_items.description: Do not tell the learner exactly where to write the gametes (e.g., 'Put those four combinations along the top and side of the square'), which would give away the step they are now ready to take.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Lingering on Meiosis
rubric_items.description: Do not ask further conceptual questions about meiosis or chromosome separation, as the learner has grasped the necessary concept to move forward.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the semantic meaning of the category label ('large' shoes) with the quantitative meaning of the bar's height (frequency). They are stuck on the intuitive idea that the 'large' category must have the biggest bar because the shoes themselves are the biggest, struggling to decouple the size of the object from the count of the students.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that 'large' indeed means the biggest shoes, but prompt the learner to explicitly state what the height of the bar is measuring (the number of kids) to help them decouple the two concepts.

rubric_items.title: Target the Semantic Conflation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explicitly contrast what 'large' describes (the shoes) with what 'biggest' or 'tallest' describes on the graph (the number of kids).

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Intuition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's statement by confirming that 'large' does indeed refer to the biggest shoes.

rubric_items.title: Reference the Previous Hypothetical
rubric_items.description: Refer back to the tutor's previous hypothetical about 'only one person' wearing large shoes to help ground the distinction between shoe size and student count.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Resolution
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state the resolution for the learner (e.g., 'The bar is tall because of the number of kids, not the shoe size'); leave the cognitive work of separating the two concepts to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not ignore the learner's specific reference to 'large' or 'biggest' by asking a generic question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that fails to address the immediate semantic clash.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that fiber optic cables transmit binary numbers and that the screen has its own colored pixels, but they are stuck on the abstract mapping of how a number (like zero) can represent a qualitative property (like the color blue). They need a conceptual bridge explaining how arbitrary codes or on/off signals can be assigned to specific colors.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Provide a simple, concrete example or analogy showing how combinations of numbers can act as a lookup table, or how 1s and 0s act as on/off switches for the screen's specific colored lights, avoiding real-world technical complexity.

rubric_items.title: Binary-to-Color Mapping
rubric_items.description: The response must explain or prompt the learner to consider how binary values map to colors (e.g., by explaining that combinations of 1s and 0s form unique codes, or that 1s and 0s act as simple on/off switches for the different colored lights).

rubric_items.title: Concrete Example or Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response uses a simple, hypothetical example (e.g., 'maybe 001 means blue') or a relatable analogy (like ordering from a numbered restaurant menu or a paint-by-numbers canvas) to illustrate how numbers can represent something that isn't a number.

rubric_items.title: Grounding in Pixel Instructions
rubric_items.description: The response connects the mapping back to the previously established idea that these numbers are instructions telling the screen's existing red, green, and blue pixels what to do.

rubric_items.title: Overcomplication Pitfall
rubric_items.description: The response introduces real-world technical color depth concepts (like 24-bit RGB, hexadecimal codes, or 0-255 values) that overcomplicate the basic conceptual mapping the learner needs right now.

rubric_items.title: Vagueness Pitfall
rubric_items.description: The response merely repeats that 'it is a code' or 'the computer decodes it' without providing any conceptual mechanism for how numbers can actually represent colors.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly predicts that the iron filings will stick to the magnet, but this treats the interaction as a simple contact event rather than revealing the spatial structure of the field. They need to realize that the filings form a specific pattern in the space around the magnet, which visualizes the 'invisible push' they were previously confused by.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the filings stick, describe the unique pattern they form in the space around the magnet (e.g., lines or arcs), and prompt the learner to infer what that pattern tells us about the invisible space.

rubric_items.title: Validate Sticking
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's intuition is correct and that the iron filings will indeed be attracted to or stick to the magnet.

rubric_items.title: Describe Filing Pattern
rubric_items.description: Describe or introduce the specific visual pattern the filings form before or as they stick (e.g., lining up, forming arcs, or spreading out into the space around the magnet).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Inference About the Field
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner what the pattern of the filings suggests about the 'invisible' space or the 'nothing' around the magnet that they asked about earlier.

rubric_items.title: Give Away the Inference
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly state that the filings map out the magnetic field lines or prove the field has a shape, doing the conceptual connection-making for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Vague Prompting
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask the learner to guess the specific pattern the filings make without providing any descriptive or visual scaffolding, as the learner has never seen this phenomenon.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating 'inside the frog' with 'inside the cells', leading to the paradox that a frozen frog must have frozen cells. They need help distinguishing between the macroscopic freezing of the frog's body (extracellular spaces) and the microscopic liquid state inside the protected cells.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe or visualization that helps the learner distinguish between 'inside the frog' and 'inside the cell', prompting them to deduce exactly where the natural antifreeze must be concentrated to keep the cells safe while the rest of the body freezes.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Ambiguity of 'Inside'
rubric_items.description: The response must help the learner distinguish between the general space 'inside the frog' (which does freeze) and the specific space 'inside the cells' (which does not).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Localization of Antifreeze
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to use their prior insight about antifreeze to deduce where it must be located to allow the body to freeze while the cells remain safe.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner that the antifreeze is concentrated inside the cells or that ice only forms in the spaces between them.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Pivot to Evolution
rubric_items.description: The response should not introduce or attempt to correct the learner's hidden belief about how the frog acquired this trait (e.g., DNA changes from winter temperatures) before resolving the immediate physiological paradox.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely repeat the previous question about 'inside vs. outside the cells' without offering new scaffolding, analogies, or clarification to address the learner's block.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the abstract algebraic structure of $5(x+2)$ and denies that the $2$ gets multiplied, clinging to the idea that it is a flat fee added at the end. They need to evaluate the expression with a concrete number to experience how the parentheses force the addition to happen before the multiplication.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to substitute a small, concrete number for $x$ (e.g., 1 or 2 friends) and ask them to perform the first step of the calculation.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Numerical Test
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to substitute a specific, small number for $x$ (e.g., 1 or 2 friends) to test how the expression $5(x+2)$ actually behaves.

rubric_items.title: Step-by-step Evaluation
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to perform the calculation one step at a time, specifically asking what must be calculated first according to the parentheses.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Abstract Distribution
rubric_items.description: Explains the distributive property abstractly (e.g., 'The 5 distributes to both the x and the 2') instead of letting the learner discover the effect through numerical calculation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that the 2 gets multiplied by 5 to become 10, doing the math for them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: Simply contradicts the learner (e.g., 'Yes it does get multiplied') or asks them to look at the parentheses again without providing a concrete numerical path to test their claim.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the everyday meaning of 'burned up' (destruction), equating the ash-like appearance of the product with the loss of the original iron. They need to realize that the iron atoms are not destroyed but are still present as part of the new iron oxide compound.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that redirects the learner to the name or composition of 'iron oxide' to help them deduce for themselves that the iron is still physically present.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Iron Oxide Composition
rubric_items.description: The response should direct the learner's attention to the name or composition of 'iron oxide' to help them deduce that the iron is still present in the new compound.

rubric_items.title: Challenge 'Burned Up'
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to reconsider their definition of 'burned up' in this context, shifting their focus from 'destroyed' to 'chemically combined.'

rubric_items.title: Validate Visual Change
rubric_items.description: The response should acknowledge that the substance looks different or resembles ash, validating the learner's visual intuition before challenging their conclusion about the iron.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving Away Conservation)
rubric_items.description: The response should not directly tell the learner that the iron is still there, that atoms cannot be destroyed, or that burning is just a chemical reaction.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response should not ask a broad, unguided question (e.g., 'What do you think happens when things burn?') that fails to anchor the learner to the specific elements in the iron oxide.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner tentatively recognizes that multiplying the frame weight by the number of batteries leads to an absurd physical result (multiple frames), but they remain insecure about whether an equation can have a number without a variable. They need confirmation that their equation T = 300 + 50x is correct and a clear link between the single physical frame and the constant term.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's realization, explicitly confirm that T = 300 + 50x is correct, and solidify the connection that unchanging physical quantities are represented by constant terms without variables.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Equation Correctness
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly confirm that the learner's previously proposed equation (T = 300 + 50x) is absolutely correct.

rubric_items.title: Connect Physical Reality to Constant Term
rubric_items.description: The response must explain, or prompt the learner to articulate, that because the single frame does not change when batteries are added, the 300 stands alone without an 'x'.

rubric_items.title: Normalize Constants
rubric_items.description: The response reassures the learner that it is normal and mathematically expected to have a 'lonely' number (a constant) in an equation when representing a fixed quantity.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unelaborated Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The response simply says 'Correct' or 'Right' without grounding the confirmation in why the 300 lacks an 'x', leaving the learner's underlying conceptual insecurity unaddressed.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: The response moves on to a new topic, asks the learner to graph the equation, or asks them to solve for a specific total weight before solidifying their confidence in the equation's structure.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that a mutation caused blindness but does not grasp the biological cost of eyes, specifically how 'saving energy' works and why it matters. They need a concrete explanation of biological energy (food/calories used for tissue growth and maintenance) and a prompt to connect this saved energy to survival in a food-scarce cave.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should concretely explain that building and maintaining eyes requires food-energy, establish that food is scarce in a cave, and prompt the learner to deduce how having extra energy helps the blind fish survive or reproduce.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Explanation of Biological Energy
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explain that biological 'energy' comes from food, and that growing, repairing, and using complex organs like eyes consumes a significant amount of this food-energy.

rubric_items.title: Establish Cave Resource Scarcity
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly mention or prompt the learner to consider that food is very scarce in a dark cave environment, which makes energy conservation critical.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Survival Advantage
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to deduce what a blind fish can do with the food-energy it saves by not growing eyes, prompting them to connect the saved energy to survival or reproduction.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Evolutionary Advantage
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly tell the learner the final answer (e.g., 'they use the saved energy to live longer and have more babies'), leaving this connection for the learner to make.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Reverting to Mutation Mechanics
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not return to explaining how random mutations happen or Lamarckian inheritance, as the learner's current bottleneck is strictly about the mechanics of energy and survival.

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified the number 12 from their diagram, which corresponds to the leftover hydrogen atoms, but they have not specified which element this count refers to or accounted for the oxygen atoms. They need validation of their count and a prompt to explicitly link this number to hydrogen, as well as to find the corresponding count for oxygen.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the count of 12 and prompt the learner to specify whether it refers to the leftover hydrogen or oxygen atoms.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Count
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's number '12' is a correct count for one of the leftover elements on their sheet.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Element
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to look at their diagram and specify whether the '12' refers to the leftover hydrogen atoms or the leftover oxygen atoms.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Second Element
rubric_items.description: Encourage the learner to also find the count for the other element they need to make water (e.g., 'And how many of the other?').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Element or Math
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the 12 refers to hydrogen, state the number of leftover oxygens, or give away the final number of water molecules that will be formed.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Validation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply accept the answer 'twelve' or say 'yes' without requiring the learner to attach that number to a specific element.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is applying a linear subtraction model to half-life, assuming the original amount is divided into two 50% chunks that decay sequentially. This likely stems from their hidden belief that atoms have a deterministic 'timer' that starts when the organism dies, rather than understanding that decay is a constant, probabilistic process for each individual atom.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a concrete analogy (like flipping coins or repeatedly halving a physical object) or a targeted prompt to help the learner realize that the remaining atoms behave exactly like a new starting batch, each with a 50% chance of decaying.

rubric_items.title: Shift to the Remaining Pool
rubric_items.description: The response must guide the learner to treat the remaining 50% of atoms as a new starting pool for the next half-life, rather than a leftover chunk that is 'due' to decay.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Analogy or Visualization
rubric_items.description: The response should introduce a concrete analogy (such as flipping a set of coins, or repeatedly cutting a physical object in half) to ground the abstract math of repeated halving.

rubric_items.title: Address Biological Stabilization Belief
rubric_items.description: The response should engage the learner's hidden belief by clarifying that individual carbon-14 atoms don't have a 'decay timer' that starts at death; they decay randomly all the time, even when the organism is alive.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Linear Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's linear intuition (that the second half should decay next) is a very common and logical way to think about everyday processes before introducing the exponential concept.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Restating the Math Rule
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely repeat the mathematical rule (e.g., 'you always divide the current amount by two') without providing a conceptual or analogical reason why, as the learner has already shown this abstract explanation is not clicking.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply tell the learner the outcome (e.g., 'No, only half of the remaining half decays, leaving 25%') without requiring them to think through the mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that just ask 'What do you think?' or 'Why might that be wrong?' without providing any new conceptual scaffolding or analogy to help the learner break out of their linear mindset.

learning_objective: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has incorrectly guessed that 30 (the total number of skipped songs) represents the total number of indie songs, confusing the outcome with the given condition. They need to explicitly distinguish what the numbers 30 and 40 represent in their dataset to select the correct denominator.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to check the label or meaning of the number 30 in their data to help them realize it represents total skipped songs, not total indie songs.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Meaning of '30'
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to identify what the number 30 actually represents or counts in their playlist data.

rubric_items.title: Re-anchor to the Condition
rubric_items.description: The tutor should remind the learner that the goal for the denominator is to find the total number of *indie* songs.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly tell the learner that the correct number is 40, nor should they directly state that 30 is the 'total skipped' songs.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not simply say 'No' or 'Try again' without directing the learner's attention to the specific meanings of the numbers in the data.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Mix-up
rubric_items.description: The tutor may briefly validate that it is easy to mix up these numbers, since both relate to the categories being discussed.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a guessing cycle, fixated on the environmental mechanism of 'sleeping' and failing to integrate the tutor's previous hint that traits are present at birth. They need scaffolding that explicitly connects the timeline of birth back to their own earlier observation that the puppies' traits match the parents.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly contrast the 'sleeping' guess with the fact that puppies are born with their ear shapes, and then scaffold the answer by reminding the learner of their earlier observation that the puppies' ears match the mom and dad dogs.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Prior Matching
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner's attention back to the mom and dad dogs, prompting them to use their earlier successful matching to explain where the traits come from.

rubric_items.title: Confront the Sleeping Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Explicitly addresses the learner's 'sleeping' guess by highlighting the logical impossibility of acquiring a trait from sleeping if the puppy is already born with it.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Gives away the answer by explicitly stating that the puppies get their traits from their parents, genes, or DNA, rather than prompting the learner to make the connection.

rubric_items.title: Open-Ended Guessing Loop
rubric_items.description: Merely rejects 'sleeping' or repeats the previous open-ended question ('Where do they come from?') without introducing the parents as a scaffold, leaving the learner to guess blindly.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identified '10' as a factor but incorrectly split the grouped quantity '(m-3)', guessing only 'm' as the second factor. They need to be reminded that parentheses bind the expression into a single factor.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate '10' as correct, remind the learner how parentheses group terms into a single quantity, and prompt them to identify the entire grouped expression as the second factor.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Correct Factor
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate that the learner correctly identified '10' as one of the factors.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Grouped Factor
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner's attention to the parentheses or the concept of grouping to help them realize that the 10 is multiplied by the entire expression, not just 'm'.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Second Factor
rubric_items.description: Ask a question that requires the learner to articulate the full second factor themselves.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly remind the learner of their own earlier realization that the parentheses keep the expression together.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the answer by stating that the second factor is '(m-3)'.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not reject 'm' without providing specific scaffolding about the grouping or parentheses.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the algebraic mechanics of exponent decomposition and does not know how to apply exponent rules to break $i^5$ into known components like $i^2$. They need a concrete stepping stone to translate the tutor's previous hint into an actionable algebraic step before they can test their hypothesis about odd powers.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a scaffold for exponent decomposition, either by asking how to split the exponent 5 into smaller parts or by offering a parallel example with a standard variable (like $x^5$), while leaving the actual calculation of $i^5$ to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Exponent Decomposition
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to break down the exponent 5 into smaller parts (e.g., asking what adds up to 5) or ask them to apply the product rule of exponents to split $i^5$.

rubric_items.title: Activate Prior Knowledge of Exponents
rubric_items.description: The response should use a familiar algebraic analogy (such as asking how to break down $x^5$) or explicitly remind the learner of the general exponent rule (like $x^a \cdot x^b = x^{a+b}$) to bridge the gap.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Expansion or Answer
rubric_items.description: The response must not explicitly provide the fully decomposed form of $i^5$ (e.g., $i^2 \cdot i^2 \cdot i$ or $i^4 \cdot i$) or reveal its final simplified value ($i$).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response must not merely repeat the instruction to 'use $i^2$' or 'break it down' without offering a new, concrete hint about how exponents combine.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the conceptual setup for the Simpson's index but is currently stuck on the mathematical mechanics of multiplying fractions (squaring 12/16). They need targeted scaffolding on how to execute this specific arithmetic step.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a concrete strategy for squaring the fraction—such as multiplying the numerators and denominators separately, simplifying the fraction first, or converting to a decimal—and then prompt the learner to attempt the calculation.

rubric_items.title: Provide a Calculation Strategy
rubric_items.description: The response must offer a specific method for squaring the fraction, such as multiplying the numerators together and the denominators together, or converting the fraction to a decimal first.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Result
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to perform the calculation using the suggested strategy, keeping the cognitive work on the learner.

rubric_items.title: Suggest Simplifying First
rubric_items.description: The response suggests simplifying the fraction 12/16 (e.g., to 3/4) before squaring to make the arithmetic easier.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Doing the Math
rubric_items.description: The response calculates the final squared value (e.g., 144/256, 9/16, or 0.5625) for the learner, removing their opportunity to practice the math.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Math Guidance
rubric_items.description: The response tells the learner to 'just multiply them' or 'use fraction rules' without explaining the actual mechanics of how to multiply fractions.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has made a basic multiplication fact error, guessing that 8 times 6 is 54. Since they previously correctly calculated that 8 times 5 is 40, their immediate need is a strategy to bridge from that known anchor fact to the correct product.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to find the answer for 8 times 6 by adding one more group of 8 to their previous correct calculation of 40.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Incremental Addition Strategy
rubric_items.description: The response must guide the learner to figure out 8 times 6 by adding one more group of 8 to 40.

rubric_items.title: Anchor on the 5-Game Total
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly remind the learner of their own previous calculation that 5 games equal 40 gigabytes to contextualize the addition step.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response must not simply provide the correct answer (48) or perform the addition (40 + 8) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: The response must not simply reject the guess of 54 and ask the learner to try again without offering a mathematical strategy to find the correct answer.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Zoom-Out
rubric_items.description: The response must not shift focus back to the overall tablet storage or the photo library subtraction until this specific multiplication error is resolved.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the speed of oscillation ('vibrating faster') with the speed of forward propagation ('going faster'). Because this intuitive block is preventing them from absorbing the tutor's previous explanation about wavelength, they need a conceptual bridge to decouple these two distinct types of motion.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a relatable analogy (like taking quick, short steps versus slow, long strides) or a physical visualization to help the learner separate the rate of a repeating action from overall forward speed, and prompt the learner to resolve how the two balance out.

rubric_items.title: Validate Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's intuition makes logical sense on the surface (e.g., validating that it is natural to assume faster vibration equals faster forward travel).

rubric_items.title: Decouple Oscillation from Propagation
rubric_items.description: Provide a conceptual bridge (such as an analogy like walking steps, or a physical visualization) that explicitly distinguishes the up-and-down/back-and-forth rate of vibration from the forward travel speed.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Compensating Variable
rubric_items.description: Ask a question that requires the learner to deduce how the wave can vibrate faster without traveling forward faster, guiding them to connect this to the shrinking wavelength.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Resolution
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner the resolution to the paradox (e.g., do not state 'because the wavelength gets shorter, the speed stays the same' or give away the punchline of an analogy).

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Repeating the Rule
rubric_items.description: Do not merely repeat that all EM waves travel at the speed of light or that frequency doesn't affect speed without providing a conceptual way for the learner to understand why.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner logically hypothesizes that mucus might act as an internal shield against alpha particles, similar to dead skin. They need to be guided to realize that the lungs' primary function (gas exchange) requires the internal lining to be extremely thin and vulnerable, preventing the existence of a thick, dead protective barrier.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's logical guess about mucus, then prompt them to consider the biological function of the lungs (like absorbing oxygen) to deduce why the internal lining must remain thin and vulnerable.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Mucus Hypothesis
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that mucus is a logical guess or confirm that it does exist in the respiratory tract.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Functional or Structural Reasoning
rubric_items.description: Ask a guiding question about the lungs' primary function (e.g., absorbing oxygen, gas exchange) to help the learner deduce why a thick protective barrier cannot exist deep inside the lungs.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Direct Explanation (Overhelpful)
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that the lung lining is too thin, that mucus isn't thick enough, or that alveoli lack protection; the learner must deduce this.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Flat Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not flatly reject the 'mucus' idea (e.g., 'No, that is wrong') without validating the underlying logic of looking for an internal barrier.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Vague Rejection (Underhelpful)
rubric_items.description: Do not merely ask the learner to guess again (e.g., 'Not quite, what else?') without providing a biological or structural constraint to guide their thinking.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a pattern of blind guessing, agreeing that room temperature determines human hair color rather than applying common sense. They need to be grounded in a relatable, everyday reality to break this misconception before they can understand genetic variation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should present a simple, undeniable everyday scenario about human hair color (e.g., asking if hair changes color when going out in the cold, or if siblings sharing a room have identical hair) to trigger the learner's common sense and create cognitive conflict with their temperature guess.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the Temperature Guess
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to critically evaluate their affirmative guess that room temperature determines human hair color.

rubric_items.title: Use Everyday Concrete Scenario
rubric_items.description: Ground the question in a highly familiar, undeniable everyday scenario (e.g., asking if hair changes color in the winter, or if siblings in the same house have identical hair) to trigger the learner's common sense.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that their guess is wrong or provide the correct scientific explanation (e.g., mentioning DNA or genes).

rubric_items.title: Stay on the Human Analogy
rubric_items.description: Do not return to the snake example or the incubator until the learner has successfully resolved the human hair color analogy.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Do not simply ask 'Are you sure?' or 'Why do you think that?'; the learner is guessing and needs a specific scenario to help them reason.

learning_objective: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the scenario and previously identified 'taking the class' ($C$) as the condition, but they are now confusing the notation order, guessing that $C$ goes first despite the tutor's rule. They need help mapping the specific variables ($P$ and $C$) to the roles of 'target event' and 'condition' to self-correct their notation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that reminds the learner of their own prior realization that $C$ is the condition, and asks them to apply the tutor's previously stated rule to determine where the condition belongs.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Variable Mapping
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explicitly map the variables ($P$ and $C$) to their roles (target event vs. condition) to help them deduce the correct order.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of their own correct realization from two turns ago that $C$ (taking the class) is the condition.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly tell the learner that $P$ goes first or provide the final correct notation $P(P|C)$.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely say 'no' or 'read the rule again' without scaffolding the connection between the specific variables and the notation rule.

rubric_items.title: Normalize Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the order in conditional probability notation can be counterintuitive or confusing at first.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that individual sand grains do not change shape, but they are stuck on the macroscopic observation that a collective pile of sand mimics the flowing behavior of water. They need help distinguishing between a continuous liquid flowing and a collection of tiny, discrete solids tumbling over one another.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that extends the previously established marble analogy to a large-scale pouring motion, prompting the learner to realize that 'flowing' sand is actually just many individual solids tumbling past each other.

rubric_items.title: Probe the 'Flowing' Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to analyze the 'flowing' motion by comparing water's continuous flow to the movement of discrete objects (e.g., by asking what happens if you pour a massive bucket of marbles).

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Insight
