rubric_items.title: Provide Problem Context
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to the original word problem or provides the specific text from the problem that defines what 0.40 and 0.25 represent.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Focus on the Conditioning Event
rubric_items.description: Reiterates that the immediate goal is to find the probability of 'high humidity' on its own to use as the denominator.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Answer
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that 0.40 is the probability of high humidity or that 0.40 belongs in the denominator.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to keep looking at their unlabeled notes or to guess between the numbers without providing the missing problem context.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Roadblock
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or normalizes the learner's realization that unlabeled numbers make it impossible to proceed.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the distinction between matter and physical energy, unable to see how physical chemicals can act as a power source in the way that light does. They need a conceptual bridge to understand that energy can be stored within physical structures (chemical bonds) as potential energy and released when those structures change.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a concrete analogy for stored potential energy (like a compressed spring, a stretched rubber band, or a battery) and prompt the learner to connect this analogy back to the concept of chemical bonds.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Analogy for Stored Energy
rubric_items.description: Introduces a familiar physical analogy or example (such as a compressed spring, a battery, or a stretched rubber band) to help the learner visualize how physical matter or structures can store potential energy.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Mapping
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to apply the provided analogy back to the chemical bonds, prompting them to explain how the chemicals might act like the physical example.

rubric_items.title: Validates the Matter vs. Energy Distinction
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges the learner's valid intuition that chemicals (matter) seem fundamentally different from light (pure energy) before explaining how they connect.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Circular Restatement
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that merely repeat that breaking chemical bonds releases energy without offering a new conceptual tool or analogy to explain *how* matter can hold energy.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Jargon
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that introduce advanced biochemical mechanisms (like ATP, electron transport chains, or enthalpy) instead of focusing on the basic concept of stored potential energy.

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance because they intuitively view gases as weightless or insubstantial, making it hard to conceptualize how an invisible gas can serve as the physical building block for a solid leaf.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's surprise and prompt them to consider the particulate nature of matter, guiding them to realize that gases are made of physical atoms that can be rearranged and connected to build solid structures.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Counterintuitive Concept
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that it is naturally surprising or unintuitive that an invisible gas can turn into a solid physical structure like a leaf.

rubric_items.title: Ground in Particulate Matter
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner's attention to the fact that carbon dioxide gas is made of physical building blocks (atoms or molecules) that have actual substance and mass.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Chemical Rearrangement
rubric_items.description: Ask a guiding question or use a structural analogy (like Lego bricks) to help the learner think about how individual atoms from the gas can be connected together to build larger, solid molecules.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Explanation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply explain the chemical process of photosynthesis or glucose formation outright; leave the cognitive work of connecting atoms to solid structures to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Inaccurate Phase Change Analogy
rubric_items.description: Do not use analogies involving freezing or condensation (e.g., water vapor turning to ice), as this conflates a physical phase change with the chemical rearrangement occurring in plants.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely confirm that gas turns into leaves (e.g., 'Yes, it does!') without providing a conceptual stepping stone to help the learner understand how this is physically possible.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the function's limiting value (terminal velocity) with its initial value, asking if the speed starts at 120. They need to evaluate the beginning of the jump to distinguish the starting speed from the eventual flattened-out speed.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to test their hypothesis by determining the value of time (t) at the very start of the jump and plugging it into the equation.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Initial Time Evaluation
rubric_items.description: The response must direct the learner to consider what happens at the start of the jump by asking them to evaluate the equation at t = 0.

rubric_items.title: Ground in Physical Reality
rubric_items.description: The response should connect the mathematical evaluation to the physical scenario by asking what the skydiver's actual speed is the exact moment they step out of the plane.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Source of Confusion
rubric_items.description: The response may briefly validate why the learner guessed 120 (e.g., acknowledging that it is the prominent number at the front of the equation) before redirecting them to test it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Initial Value
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner that the starting speed is 0, nor should it do the math for them by stating that e^0 = 1.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Redirection
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely tell the learner to 'look at the equation again' or 'check the math' without specifically focusing their attention on the time variable (t) at the start.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the eyes and tongue perform different functions but is stuck on why they cannot simply be wired directly together for maximum speed. They need to realize that without a central processor to interpret the visual input, the frog would not be able to distinguish between appropriate targets (bugs) and inappropriate ones (rocks, predators).
rubric.ideal_next_move: Ask the learner to predict what would happen if the eyes and tongue were directly connected, specifically prompting them to consider how the frog would react to seeing things other than food.

rubric_items.title: Test the Direct Connection Hypothesis
rubric_items.description: Asks a question that requires the learner to evaluate the logical consequence of the eyes and tongue being directly connected.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Non-Target Stimuli
rubric_items.description: Incorporates the idea of the frog seeing non-food items (e.g., a rock, a leaf, or a predator) to challenge the direct-connection model.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly explains the consequence of a direct connection (e.g., 'The frog would shoot its tongue at everything it sees') instead of letting the learner deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Biological Dead-Ends
rubric_items.description: Explains why the eyes and tongue cannot connect using complex anatomical facts (e.g., nerve types or tissue differences) rather than focusing on the logical need for information processing.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating Previous Analogies
rubric_items.description: Merely repeats that the brain is a 'middleman' or 'translator' without providing a new scenario to help the learner understand why that role is functionally necessary.

learning_objective: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that the adjusted numerators should be added together, but is seeking validation before committing to the final expression. They need confirmation of their intuition and a direct prompt to actually construct the combined numerator.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuition to add the parts together and prompt them to write out the resulting combined numerator or the full rational expression.

rubric_items.title: Validate Addition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner is correct in their intuition to add the two scaled numerators together.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Construction
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to write out the actual expression for the new combined numerator (or the full fraction).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Providing the Expression
rubric_items.description: Do not write out the combined numerator or the final fraction for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Do not leave the learner stranded by merely saying 'Yes' or answering their question with another question (e.g., 'What do you think?') without prompting them to actually write the expression.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Expansion
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to expand or simplify the numerator before they have successfully written down the unsimplified combined expression.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the first part of the projection formula yields a scalar, but is using imprecise language ('multiply by the boat') for the final step. They need to connect their conceptual understanding to the formal mathematical operation of multiplying the scalar by the boat's path vector.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the learner's intuition while refining their terminology to 'the boat's path vector', and prompt the learner to construct the final mathematical expression.

rubric_items.title: Refine Terminology
rubric_items.description: The tutor must clarify or guide the learner to specify that we are multiplying by the boat's path vector ($\vec{v}$), rather than the physical boat.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Formula Assembly
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to put the pieces together and state or write out the complete vector projection formula.

rubric_items.title: Connect to the Shadow Concept
rubric_items.description: The tutor should reinforce that multiplying the scalar by $\vec{v}$ scales the path vector so its length perfectly matches the wind's 'shadow' while keeping its direction.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Final Formula
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not write out the complete final formula (e.g., $\frac{\vec{w} \cdot \vec{v}}{\|\vec{v}\|^2} \vec{v}$) themselves, as the learner is capable of assembling it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Magnitude Calculations
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not pivot to discussing how to calculate the magnitude of the wind's parallel or perpendicular components (such as subtracting one from the total wind speed) before the vector projection formula is fully constructed.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is overwhelmed by trying to hold overlapping imaginary triangles in their head and has resorted to superficial guessing, offering a line segment ('puppet to the wall') when asked for a starting point. They need to step back from verbal descriptions and use a visual representation to anchor the shared vertex at the flashlight.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should break the learner's cycle of verbal guessing by prompting them to draw or visually trace the scenario, starting with the single shared point of the flashlight.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Single Starting Point
rubric_items.description: The tutor must address the learner's 'puppet to the wall' guess by clarifying that a starting point is a single location (a vertex), or by guiding them to identify the flashlight as that single shared point.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Visual Representation
rubric_items.description: The tutor prompts the learner to draw the scenario, sketch the triangles, or physically trace the light's path, providing a concrete visual anchor to help them see the nested shapes.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Visualization Difficulty
rubric_items.description: The tutor normalizes the learner's confusion by acknowledging that it is difficult to keep track of overlapping imaginary triangles in one's head.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply rejects the guess and repeats the question about where the triangles start, leaving the guessing learner stranded without new scaffolding.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Verbal Explanation
rubric_items.description: The tutor attempts to resolve the confusion by verbally explaining the full layout of the bases and vertices again, which has already proven ineffective and removes the learner's cognitive ownership.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused by the introduction of the 'normal force' and cannot proceed with the friction formula until this concept is clarified. They need to temporarily shift their focus from the horizontal motion to the vertical forces acting on the stone in order to conceptualize and calculate the normal force.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should pause the algebraic substitution and prompt the learner to identify the vertical forces acting on the stone (gravity and the ice pushing up) to build a grounded understanding of the normal force.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Vertical Forces
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to identify the vertical forces acting on the curling stone (e.g., gravity, weight, or the ice pushing up).

rubric_items.title: Contextualize Normal Force
rubric_items.description: Frame the normal force conceptually as the upward support force from the surface (the ice) acting on the stone.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Vertical Balance
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the normal force equals mass times gravity ($mg$) or the stone's weight; leave this for the learner to deduce from the vertical forces.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Return to Horizontal Forces
rubric_items.description: Do not push the learner to complete the friction formula ($f_k = \mu_k F_N$) or return to the $ma$ equation before their confusion about the normal force is addressed.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified the 4 corner tiles but is still answering tentatively. They need to combine the 8 side tiles and 4 corner tiles to find the total for the 2x2 garden, which will provide the concrete value (12) needed to disprove their earlier assumption that the total would be 16 (8n).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the 4 corners and prompt the learner to calculate the total number of border tiles for the 2x2 garden, ideally reminding them of the physical components (sides plus corners) to prepare for the connection to the algebraic structure.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Corner Count
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner's tentative guess of 4 corner tiles is correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Concrete Total
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to calculate the total number of border tiles for the 2x2 garden.

rubric_items.title: Highlight the Physical Structure
rubric_items.description: Frame the prompt for the total in a way that explicitly mentions the physical components being combined (e.g., the 8 side tiles and the 4 corners) to reinforce the structure of the upcoming expression.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Comparison
rubric_items.description: Invite the learner to consider how this actual total compares to their earlier prediction of 16.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Doing the Math
rubric_items.description: Do not calculate the final total number of border tiles (12) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Algebra
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to evaluate or construct algebraic expressions involving 'n' (like 4n+4 or 8n) before they have established the concrete numerical total for the 2x2 garden.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly believes that interior angles scale proportionally with side lengths, guessing that halving the sides halves the 90-degree angle to 45 degrees. They need to realize that changing the angle would alter the fundamental shape, which contradicts the definition of similarity they just discussed.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should create cognitive conflict by asking the learner to visualize what happens to the shape if the corner becomes 45 degrees, or by prompting them to apply their earlier realization about the square's corners to this triangle.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the 45-Degree Guess
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate their 45-degree guess by asking how changing a 90-degree corner to a 45-degree corner would affect the overall shape of the bracket.

rubric_items.title: Recall the Square Analogy
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connect the current triangle scenario back to the learner's earlier realization that a square's corners remain square when shrunk.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Proportionality Logic
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the intuitive logic behind the learner's guess by noting that it makes sense they halved the angle because the sides were halved.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not directly state that the angle remains 90 degrees or that angles do not scale with side lengths.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the learner's guess (e.g., 'Not quite') without providing a concrete geometric visualization or analogy to help them self-correct.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has accepted that an object in a frictionless environment will move indefinitely, but they are trying to reconcile this with their misconception that motion requires force by concluding the force must be permanently stored 'inside' the object. They need to shift from viewing force as a consumable internal property to understanding it as an external interaction that changes motion.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that challenges the idea of force as a storable substance, either by asking the learner to apply the 'force changes motion' rule to an object whose motion isn't changing, or by asking them to define what a force actually is (a push or pull) to see if it can exist 'inside' an object.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Force Inside' Hypothesis
rubric_items.description: The response must directly engage with the learner's specific claim that force 'stays inside,' prompting them to evaluate whether force is a substance or property that can be contained within an object.

rubric_items.title: Re-anchor to the 'Change' Principle
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to apply the rule introduced in the previous turn—that force is only needed to change motion—to their current scenario where the probe's motion is constant.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Logic
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's deduction makes logical sense based on their current assumption (i.e., validating that if motion required force, an object moving forever would indeed need force forever).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that outright tell the learner that force is not stored inside objects or that objects don't need internal force to keep moving, doing the cognitive work for them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply ask 'Why do you think that?' or 'Does it?' without providing a physical concept (like the definition of a push/pull or the rule about changing motion) for the learner to reason with.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is anchored to the concept of area conservation ('it's still the same space'), failing to recognize that the rigid dimensions of the rectangular space constrain the placement of the circular sprinklers. They need a concrete, extreme counter-example that breaks the 'area is area' assumption by showing a situation where the area is the same but the shape mismatch drastically changes the required number of sprinklers.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should present an extreme geometric counter-example (such as a very long, narrow lawn with the same total area) and ask the learner if the same number of sprinklers would still work.

rubric_items.title: Extreme Counter-Example
rubric_items.description: Propose a concrete, extreme scenario where the total area of the lawn remains the same but its dimensions are drastically altered (e.g., a very long, narrow strip).

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Evaluation
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to visualize or deduce whether the original number of sprinklers would successfully cover this new extreme shape.

rubric_items.title: Validate Area Equivalence
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's correct intuition that the total square footage of the space remains exactly the same.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Abstract Repetition
rubric_items.description: Do not merely repeat the abstract concepts from the previous turn (e.g., 'circles are rigid' or 'geometry matters') without introducing a new concrete scenario to visualize.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the actual method for calculating the layout (e.g., dividing the lawn's length and width by the sprinkler's diameter) before the learner recognizes why dimensions matter.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has shifted their gaze to the horizontal x-axis (the bottom of the graph, likely seeing 12 months) instead of looking at the top of the vertical y-axis. They need help distinguishing the bottom horizontal line from the top of the vertical side line.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted redirect that clarifies the '12' is on the bottom horizontal line and prompts the learner to shift their gaze to the very top of the vertical side line.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Vertical Top
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner's attention specifically to the top of the vertical (up-and-down) line on the left side.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Bottom
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges the learner's observation by clarifying that the 'bottom' where they see the 12 is the horizontal line (or the x-axis).

rubric_items.title: Contextualize the Error
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connects the '12 at the bottom' to the lizard's age in months, reinforcing the meaning of the horizontal axis discussed earlier.

rubric_items.title: Giveaway Pitfall
rubric_items.description: Directly states the highest number on the vertical y-axis instead of letting the learner locate and read it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Vagueness Pitfall
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's answer (e.g., 'No, look again') without providing specific visual cues to re-orient them to the correct physical location on the graph.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is disconnected from the physical meaning of the 'steps' and is guessing rather than observing the pattern. They need to ground the abstract labels back into the concrete objects they have already built.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to count the blocks in the first few towers they have already built to establish a concrete, visual connection between the tower and its block count.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Concrete Counting
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to physically or visually count the blocks in the towers they have already built.

rubric_items.title: Anchor to Initial Steps
rubric_items.description: Focuses the counting task specifically on the first and second towers to rebuild the pattern from its simplest foundation.

rubric_items.title: Normalize Guessing
rubric_items.description: Validates or normalizes the learner's admission of guessing before redirecting them to a concrete strategy.

rubric_items.title: Give Away the Rule
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tells the learner the rule connecting the step number to the number of blocks.

rubric_items.title: Premature Prediction
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to predict the number of blocks for a future step (like Step 3 or 4) before they have grounded the pattern in the existing towers.

rubric_items.title: Vague Directive
rubric_items.description: Responds with a vague directive (e.g., 'Look closer at the blocks' or 'Try to find a pattern') without giving the learner a specific, concrete action to perform.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully overcome their prior misconception and synthesized the nuclear change (an added proton) with the atomic state (only one orbital electron remaining) to correctly deduce that the immediate product is a positively charged Helium ion. They are now tentatively seeking validation for this accurate, albeit counter-intuitive, conclusion.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly and enthusiastically validate the learner's correct deduction that the immediate result is a positive Helium ion (He⁺), confirming their breakthrough before moving on.

rubric_items.title: Explicit Validation
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm that the learner's conclusion is correct and that the immediate product is indeed a positively charged Helium ion.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Reasoning
rubric_items.description: The tutor should briefly praise or reflect back the specific logic the learner used (comparing the two protons in the nucleus to the single remaining electron in the cloud) to reinforce how they arrived at the right answer.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Vocabulary
rubric_items.description: The tutor may explicitly affirm the learner's correct use of the term 'ion' to describe the charged atom.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Contradicting with Long-Term Neutrality
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not contradict the learner by stating the atom is neutral, which would confuse the immediate product of the decay (an ion) with its eventual stable state (after it captures an electron from the environment).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Question to Formalize
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not ignore the learner's tentative question by immediately jumping into writing the formal nuclear equation or moving to a new topic without first providing clear confirmation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that genetic variation provides defenses, but their question 'Do they just adapt to it?' reveals a Lamarckian misconception that individual organisms actively change their DNA on demand in response to a threat. Additionally, their hidden belief suggests they conflate individual physical responses to the environment (like growing taller) with population-level genetic variation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a targeted probe or cognitive conflict question to make the learner consider the timeline of these defenses—specifically, whether a plant can change its DNA after the fungus attacks, or if the genetic differences must exist beforehand.

rubric_items.title: Probe the Timeline of Defense
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to consider the timeline of the genetic defense, specifically asking whether the plant changes its DNA after the fungus attacks or if the genetic differences must exist beforehand.

rubric_items.title: Engage the Physical vs. Genetic Distinction
rubric_items.description: The tutor should guide the learner to differentiate between an individual plant physically reacting to its environment (such as growing taller or greener) and possessing actual pre-existing genetic differences, directly challenging the learner's hidden belief.

rubric_items.title: Leverage the Learner's Analogy
rubric_items.description: The tutor incorporates the learner's own 'cold' analogy (e.g., asking if people change their DNA when they catch a cold, or if they were born with that resistance) to help them reason about whether defenses are acquired on demand.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Validating Active Adaptation
rubric_items.description: The response agrees with or validates the phrase 'adapt to it' without clarifying that individuals cannot intentionally change their DNA in response to an immediate threat.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Explaining Mutation
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner that genetic variation comes from 'random mutations' or 'sexual reproduction', giving away the mechanism before the learner realizes that defenses must be pre-existing.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response asks a generic clarification question like 'What do you mean by adapt?' without offering a conceptual pivot (like the timeline of the attack or the cold analogy) to help the learner evaluate their misconception.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the idea of blending inheritance, struggling to understand how a dominant allele completely masks a recessive one without the traits mixing together physically. They need a clear contrast between blending and Mendelian dominance to realize that the dominant trait determines the single physical outcome.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly clarify that the dominant trait completely hides the recessive one rather than blending with it, and then prompt the learner to deduce the physical appearance of the Ee rabbit.

rubric_items.title: Address the Mixing Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly address the learner's question about 'mixing' by explaining that the dominant allele completely masks or overrides the recessive one, rather than blending with it.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Phenotype Deduction
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to apply the rule of dominance to determine what the Ee rabbit's ears will actually look like.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly state the final physical appearance (e.g., 'The rabbit will have straight ears') before the learner has a chance to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Ignoring the Question
rubric_items.description: The response should not ignore the learner's specific question about 'mixing' by merely repeating the previous prompt or offering a generic definition of dominance without contrasting it with blending.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response validates the learner's intuition by acknowledging that mixing is a logical guess or happens in other situations (like mixing paint), before clarifying how dominance works here.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is attempting to stack a triangular prism by balancing its vertex ('pointy side') on the cylinder, failing to recognize that stable stacking requires aligning two flat surfaces. They need to realize that a point cannot stably rest on a flat surface, regardless of the cylinder's overall roundness.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to predict or physically test what happens when they try to balance the pointy side of an object on a flat surface.

rubric_items.title: Target Pointy Side Instability
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to consider the physical stability of resting the 'pointy side' (vertex) of the triangle block on a surface.

rubric_items.title: Elicit Prediction or Test
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to visualize, predict, or physically test what happens when a point rests on a flat surface (e.g., trying to stand a pencil on its tip), preserving their cognitive ownership of the outcome.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the next step by explicitly telling the learner to turn the triangle block over or to use one of its flat faces.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the learner's choice or ask a generic 'Will that work?' without grounding the question in the physical mechanics of the pointy side.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Prior Flatness Insight
rubric_items.description: Briefly reinforce that the cylinder's top is flat (as established in previous turns) to help the learner isolate the triangle's pointy side as the true source of the stacking problem.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the procedure of division and has reverted to subtraction (12 - 3 = 9) despite the tutor's previous correction. They understand the goal is to share the cars but lack a concrete, actionable strategy to execute the 'sharing equally' concept.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a concrete method for the learner to figure out 12 divided by 3, such as dealing items out one by one, drawing a picture, skip counting, or using a related multiplication fact.

rubric_items.title: Provide Concrete Division Strategy
rubric_items.description: The response must offer a specific, actionable strategy for dividing 12 by 3, such as dealing items out one by one, skip counting by 3s, or asking what number times 3 equals 12.

rubric_items.title: Address the Subtraction Error
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly note that 9 is the result of subtracting 3, helping the learner recognize they repeated the subtraction error.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response must not give away the final answer (4 cars per box).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Abstract Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response must not merely repeat the instruction to 'divide' or 'share equally' without offering a concrete way to execute that operation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified the two terms needed for the expression ($S$ and $0.2S$) but has arranged them in the wrong order, subtracting the original amount from the decrease. They need to realize that to represent a decrease, they must start with the original amount and subtract the removed amount.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the learner has the correct components while prompting them to reconsider the order of subtraction by asking which term represents the starting amount and which represents what is being taken away.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Correct Components
rubric_items.description: Validate that the learner has correctly identified the two terms needed for the expression ($S$ and $0.2S$).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Subtraction Order
rubric_items.description: Guide the learner to correct the order of subtraction by prompting them to identify which term represents the starting amount and which represents the amount being removed.

rubric_items.title: Optional: Concrete Analogy
rubric_items.description: Reward referencing the previous concrete example (e.g., starting with 100 and taking away 20) to help the learner map the logical order of subtraction to the variables.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Expression
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly provide the correct expression ($S - 0.2S$) instead of requiring the learner to construct it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply tell the learner the order is wrong or tell them to 'flip it' without grounding the correction in the conceptual meaning of the terms.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Simplification
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that jump to discussing the simplified form ($0.8S$) before the learner has successfully formulated the unsimplified subtraction.

learning_objective: LS2.C Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing a semantic conflict between their everyday definition of 'stable' (perfectly unchanging) and the ecological reality of 'wobbling' populations just described by the tutor. They need to bridge this gap by understanding that stability in a system means staying within safe boundaries (dynamic equilibrium) rather than remaining frozen.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a conceptual bridge—such as a familiar analogy involving active balance (like riding a bike or a thermostat) or a concrete boundary scenario—and ask a guiding question that prompts the learner to explain how continuous small adjustments prevent the system from collapsing.

rubric_items.title: Reframe Stability
rubric_items.description: The response must directly address the learner's semantic confusion by contrasting the idea of being 'frozen/unchanging' with the idea of 'staying within safe boundaries' or 'avoiding collapse'.

rubric_items.title: Provide a Conceptual Bridge
rubric_items.description: The response must offer a scaffold to help the learner rethink stability, such as a familiar analogy (e.g., balancing on one foot, steering a bike, a thermostat) or a concrete scenario about what happens if the 'wobble' gets too big.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner Articulation
rubric_items.description: The response must end with a targeted question that requires the learner to explain *how* or *why* small changes actually maintain balance, preserving their cognitive ownership of the insight.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Lecturing the Answer
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that over-explain the resolution by simply telling the learner that fluctuations act as a balancing mechanism (or lecturing on 'dynamic equilibrium') without leaving them the work of making that connection.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unscaffolded Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely reflect the question back (e.g., 'Well, what do you think stable means in a forest?') without providing an analogy or boundary concept to help the learner resolve their current semantic block.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is falling back on a macroscopic, mechanical analogy ('a wall') because they cannot yet connect their earlier microscopic insight (charges moving due to electric forces) to the macroscopic outcome (the signal being blocked). They need scaffolding to realize that the movement of these charges actively opposes or cancels the incoming electromagnetic signal.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should gently challenge the mechanical 'wall' analogy by redirecting the learner back to their own prior insight about moving charges, prompting them to consider what those moving charges might do to the incoming signal.

rubric_items.title: Redirect from Mechanical to Electrical
rubric_items.description: Contrasts the mechanical 'wall' analogy with the electrical mechanism by explicitly reminding the learner of their own prior statement about moving charges or electric forces.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Consequence of Movement
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to hypothesize what effect those moving charges have on the incoming signal or what they might generate to cause the 'blocking' effect.

rubric_items.title: Validate Macroscopic Outcome
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that the foil does act like a wall in terms of the final result (stopping the signal) before pivoting to the underlying mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Explaining Cancellation
rubric_items.description: Directly explains the physics mechanism (e.g., stating that moving charges create an opposing electric field or wave that cancels the signal) instead of prompting the learner to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Unconstrained Rejection
rubric_items.description: Merely rejects the 'wall' analogy or asks a generic question like 'how else might it work?' without explicitly anchoring the learner back to the moving charges or electric forces.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that saving family helps pass on genes, but is currently stuck on a paradox: if siblings are different individuals, how can they possess the exact same 'warning' gene? They need to reconcile overall genetic variation among siblings with the inheritance of specific shared genes from common parents in order to fully grasp kin selection.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct intuition that siblings are not identical, but use a targeted probe or analogy to help them realize that siblings still draw from the exact same pool of parent genes, meaning they share many specific individual traits.

rubric_items.title: Reconcile Variation with Shared Source
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to consider how siblings drawing from the exact same parents can share specific individual genes (like the warning gene) even if their overall genetic combination is different.

rubric_items.title: Validate Sibling Variation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly acknowledges or validates the learner's correct observation that siblings are indeed different individuals and not identical clones.

rubric_items.title: Over-explaining Inheritance
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner the answer by explaining that parents pass down identical copies of genes or by stating the exact percentages of shared DNA, rather than prompting the learner to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Merely repeats the previous question about 'where they got their genes' without providing new scaffolding to help the learner resolve the specific 'but they're different' paradox.

rubric_items.title: Broadening to Species Level
rubric_items.description: Shifts the focus away from immediate family genetics to the survival of the whole meerkat group or species, which would inadvertently reinforce the learner's hidden belief about species-level altruism.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Trait Analogy
rubric_items.description: Uses a relatable everyday example (e.g., human siblings having different hair color but inheriting the exact same nose shape from a parent) to ground the concept of sharing specific genes despite overall differences.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly understood that baking soda is not a reactant, but this elimination has left them momentarily disoriented about what is actually reacting, despite the tutor having just described the interaction between aluminum and tarnish. They need a targeted prompt to synthesize the previous clues and explicitly name the two reacting substances.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's clarifying question and prompt them to deduce the two reactants based on the previously stated fact that aluminum pulls sulfur from the tarnish.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Reactants
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to explicitly state which two substances are undergoing the chemical change.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Prior Clues
rubric_items.description: The response should guide the learner by referring back to the specific interaction just described, where aluminum pulls sulfur out of the tarnish.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Question
rubric_items.description: The response should briefly validate the learner's question, acknowledging that it is the logical next step to figure out the actual reactants after ruling out baking soda.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Answer
rubric_items.description: The response must not explicitly give away the answer by stating that aluminum and silver sulfide (or tarnish) are the reactants.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Deflection
rubric_items.description: The response must not ask a generic question (e.g., "What do you think?") that fails to point the learner toward the clues already provided in the dialogue.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is fixated on the idea that having flat feet is sufficient for balance, ignoring the tutor's previous hint about where their weight is concentrated. They need to realize that if their center of mass (belly button) moves horizontally beyond their base of support (toes), the flat feet can no longer hold that weight up.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A concrete thought experiment or physical analogy that forces the learner to visualize what happens when heavy weight extends past a base of support, challenging their assumption that flat feet alone guarantee balance.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Unsupported Weight
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider what is physically underneath their shifted weight (belly button) once it moves past their toes.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the 'Flat Feet' Sufficiency
rubric_items.description: Ask a question that leads the learner to realize that flat feet cannot prevent a fall if the body's weight is no longer positioned over them.

rubric_items.title: Introduce a Concrete Analogy
rubric_items.description: Provide a tangible physical scenario (e.g., holding a heavy box out in front of you, or pushing a book off the edge of a table) to help the learner visualize weight shifting beyond a base.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is correct that their feet are still flat on the floor before introducing the complication of the shifted weight.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tell the learner the physics rule (e.g., 'your center of gravity moved outside your base of support') or directly state that unsupported weight causes tipping.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Merely repeat the previous question about weight concentration without offering a new angle, analogy, or visualization to help the learner break out of their 'flat feet' loop.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a binary assumption where organisms must either have identical traits (be the exact same fruit) or be completely different fruits, lacking the concept of variation within a species. They need to reconcile how two things can be the same 'kind' of fruit but possess different genetic instructions for color.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's logical deduction and prompt them to think of a familiar example of variation within a single kind of living thing (such as humans with different eye colors or dogs of different breeds) to bridge this conceptual gap.

rubric_items.title: Targets Variation Within a Kind
rubric_items.description: Guides the learner to realize that being the 'same kind' of organism does not mean having identical genetic traits.

rubric_items.title: Prompts Familiar Analogy
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to think of a familiar example of variation within a single species (such as humans with different hair colors or dogs of different breeds) to ground the concept.

rubric_items.title: Validates Logical Deduction
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validates the learner's question, recognizing that wondering if they are different fruits is a logical deduction from just learning they have different genetic instructions.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner the answer by simply defining 'varieties' or stating 'they are the same fruit, just different types' without prompting the learner to construct the understanding themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Leaves the learner stranded by asking a vague question (e.g., 'What do you think?') or simply saying 'No' without providing scaffolding or an analogy to resolve their confusion about fruit classification.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully grasped the human family analogy, recognizing that offspring inherit only 'some things' rather than being identical copies. The immediate bottleneck is mapping this analogical insight back to the target domain: the variation observed between the parent oak tree and the sapling.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's insight about human families and prompt them to apply that exact same logic back to the oak tree and its sapling.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Analogical Mapping
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask a question that prompts the learner to apply their realization about human families back to the oak tree and its sapling.

rubric_items.title: Validate Partial Insight
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly affirm the learner's conclusion that offspring only share 'some things' or features with their parents.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Making the Connection
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly states the connection for the learner (e.g., 'Exactly, and trees are the same way, they only share some features') instead of requiring the learner to articulate the mapping.

rubric_items.title: Premature Advancement: Introducing Mechanisms
rubric_items.description: The tutor introduces underlying biological mechanisms (like DNA, genes, or two parents) before the learner has fully established the observable phenomenon of variation in the trees.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor gives a brief affirmation (e.g., 'Right!') without providing a clear prompt or question to direct the learner's focus back to the plants.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that males inherit a Y chromosome from their father, but has overgeneralized this to mistakenly believe that males only possess Y chromosomes (rather than being XY). They need to recognize that the father, like the son they just discussed, has both an X and a Y chromosome.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce the father's full sex chromosome genotype (XY) by asking them to recall the genotype of the male son they just discussed.

rubric_items.title: Address Father's Genotype
rubric_items.description: The tutor's response must focus on establishing that the father (or any male) has both an X and a Y chromosome, directly addressing the learner's 'only Y' misconception.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold via the Son's Genotype
rubric_items.description: The tutor should scaffold the realization by prompting the learner to recall the son's genotype (XY), which they just discussed, and applying that logic to the father.

rubric_items.title: Validate Prior Reasoning
rubric_items.description: The tutor briefly validates why the learner might have thought this (e.g., by acknowledging that the father is indeed the source of the Y chromosome for sons).

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner that males are XY or that the father has an X chromosome, rather than prompting the learner to deduce it from prior knowledge.

rubric_items.title: Ignoring the Misconception
rubric_items.description: The tutor ignores the learner's question about the father's chromosomes and simply repeats the prompt about where the daughter gets her second X chromosome.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has realized that checking an infinite decimal for repeating blocks is practically impossible, prompting them to ask how we can ever be certain a number is irrational. They need to transition from relying on decimal calculation (which they suspect might eventually reveal a pattern) to using the fractional definition of rational numbers as a basis for logical proof.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's insight that we cannot simply calculate decimals forever, and prompt them to recall the alternative definition of a rational number (being writable as a fraction) as the key to proving irrationality.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Limitation of Decimals
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's insight by confirming that we cannot know a number is irrational simply by calculating its decimal expansion, since we cannot calculate infinitely.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Fraction Definition
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to recall the other main characteristic of rational numbers (being writable as a fraction of integers) as the alternative method we must use to test a number.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Artificial Pattern
rubric_items.description: Do not get bogged down in explaining why the specific constructed example '0.101001...' never repeats, as this distracts from the broader question of how we prove naturally occurring numbers like roots are irrational.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Proof Delivery
rubric_items.description: Do not outline the logical steps of a proof by contradiction (e.g., assuming the root is a fraction and showing that fails) before the learner has established that fractions are the necessary starting point.

rubric_items.title: Connect Back to the Root
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tie the conversation back to the twelfth root of two, shifting the focus away from the constructed decimal example.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner now successfully visualizes that shifting the wave by half a wavelength aligns the first wave's peak with the second wave's valley, but they do not yet know the physical consequence of this alignment. Their immediate bottleneck is deducing how these opposing wave parts combine (destructive interference) to affect the light signal.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce the net result of combining an upward displacement (peak) and a downward displacement (valley) of equal size, without giving away the concept of cancellation.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Wave Combination
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to deduce what happens when a peak and a valley are added together at the exact same spot.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Opposites
rubric_items.description: Provides a conceptual scaffold for combining the waves, such as asking what happens when you add equal positive and negative numbers, or when two equal but opposite forces pull on an object.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away Cancellation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tells the learner that the waves cancel out, destroy each other, result in zero amplitude, or create 'destructive interference'.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Interference Prompts
rubric_items.description: Asks a generic question about 'wave behavior' or 'interference' without anchoring it to the specific peak-meets-valley alignment established in the previous turn.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Technology Context
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's question by framing this specific wave combination as the exact mechanism the CD/DVD sensor uses to read data.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the foil's purpose is to redirect more light toward the pot, but may still harbor a hidden belief that the foil is transferring heat rather than light. They now need validation of their insight and a prompt to synthesize how this additional light increases the total heat absorbed by the pot.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's idea about bouncing, clarify that it is light being bounced, and prompt the learner to conclude how this extra light affects the pot's overall temperature or heat generation.

rubric_items.title: Validate Insight
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and validate the learner's correct deduction that the foil's purpose is to 'bounce' more.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Light vs. Heat
rubric_items.description: Explicitly specify that it is light (rather than heat) that the foil is bouncing, which helps counter the hidden belief that the foil itself gets hot and transfers heat.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to synthesize how this additional bounced light affects the total amount of heat generated by the black pot.

rubric_items.title: Formalize Terminology
rubric_items.description: Introduce or reinforce the formal term 'reflect' alongside the learner's word 'bounce'.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state the final conclusion (e.g., 'so it gets even hotter' or 'which creates more heat'); the learner must be the one to state that more light means more heat.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not merely praise the learner or ask a generic 'And then what?'; the prompt must specifically direct the learner to consider the effect of the extra light on the pot's heat or temperature.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that surface glare is polarized and underwater light is not, but they lack a physical model for why this difference exists. They need to recognize that uniform polarization in this context requires reflection off a uniform flat surface, whereas light from underwater bounces off varied, uneven objects.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to contrast the flat, horizontal surface of the lake with the varied shapes of the objects the light is bouncing off of underwater, prompting them to deduce how those shapes affect the light waves.

rubric_items.title: Contrast the Reflecting Surfaces
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to compare the flat, uniform surface of the lake with the varied objects (like fish, rocks, or particles) that light bounces off of underwater.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Effect on Light Waves
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to predict how bouncing off uneven or varied underwater objects would affect the direction or orientation of the light waves compared to bouncing off a flat surface.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away Scattering
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for directly explaining that underwater objects scatter light in random directions or randomize the polarization, rather than letting the learner deduce it from the geometry of the surfaces.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Missing the Physical Grounding
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for asking a generic question (e.g., 'Why do you think it is different?') without directing the learner's attention to the physical surfaces or the nature of the bounce.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Logic
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that the learner's question is an excellent, logical extension of the previous step, reinforcing their cognitive ownership.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is still trying to map a static physical state ('light') directly to a binary value ('zero'), missing the tutor's previous point that the *constancy* of the state is what represents zero. They need to shift their mental model from 'state = value' to 'steady = 0 / change = 1'.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that corrects the premise by emphasizing 'steady light' equals zero, and then asks the learner to identify what would represent a '1' to reinforce the contrast.

rubric_items.title: Emphasize "Steady" over "Light"
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly clarify that *steady* or *constant* light represents a zero, correcting the learner's implication that the mere presence of light equals zero.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the "1" Condition
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to explain what would represent a '1' (e.g., a change or an edge), requiring them to actively contrast the steady state with a transition.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unqualified Agreement
rubric_items.description: The response must not simply say 'yes' or 'correct' to the question 'light is zero?', as this would validate the learner's flawed state-to-value mapping.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating the Full Rule
rubric_items.description: The response must not give away the answer by restating the entire rule (e.g., 'steady is 0 and change is 1'); it must leave the cognitive work of defining the '1' to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Shift
rubric_items.description: The response may validate that the learner is on the right track by letting go of their initial assumption that light must equal '1'.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating individual physical growth with inherited genetic potential, believing that without fishing pressure, fish will simply grow large regardless of their DNA. They have missed the implication of the tutor's previous question and need to realize that an organism cannot grow beyond the limits set by its inherited genes.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted cognitive-conflict probe that asks the learner whether a fish can physically grow to a large size if it only inherited genes for maturing at a small size.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the 'Just Grow' Assumption
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to evaluate whether an organism can physically grow to a large size if its DNA only contains instructions for maturing at a small size.

rubric_items.title: Revisit the 'Hungry Fish' Contrast
rubric_items.description: The tutor references the learner's earlier insight (that a hungry fish still has 'big' genes) to help them see that the current fish have the opposite problem: they have a safe environment to grow, but lack the 'big' genes.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Explaining the Constraint
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly tells the learner that fish cannot grow beyond their genetic limits, giving away the answer instead of prompting the learner to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor rejects the learner's answer (e.g., 'Not quite') or asks them to 'think again' without providing a specific conceptual probe about the relationship between genes and growth.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Premature Recovery Mechanisms
rubric_items.description: The tutor introduces new evolutionary concepts (like mutation or migration) to explain how the population might eventually get 'big' genes back, rather than addressing the immediate misconception about individual growth.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly intuits that the fast neutron's extra kinetic energy is highly disruptive, but they misapply a classical mechanical model by assuming this energy 'shatters' the nucleus like glass. They need to realize that this excess internal energy instead overpowers the nuclear 'glue,' causing the neutron to break free or be ejected before the nucleus has time to undergo the slow deformation required for fission.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that validates the learner's intuition about the energy being disruptive, but redirects them to apply that disruption specifically to the newly formed 'glue,' prompting them to deduce that the bond breaks and the neutron escapes.

rubric_items.title: Target the 'Glue' Breaking
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to deduce how the massive extra energy affects the newly formed 'glue' or bond, guiding them toward the realization that the energy breaks the bond itself.

rubric_items.title: Dismantle the 'Shatter' Misconception
rubric_items.description: Address the mechanical 'shatter' concept by contrasting a rigid impact (like breaking glass) with internal excitation or instability.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Energy Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is correct to think the extra kinetic energy has a highly disruptive or violent effect on the system.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving Away the Escape)
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that the neutron escapes, bounces off, or is spat back out; the response must leave room for the learner to deduce the outcome of the broken glue.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness (Naked Rejection)
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the word 'shatter' without providing a conceptual bridge (like focusing on the glue or internal energy) to help the learner rethink the energy's effect.

rubric_items.title: Re-invoke the Water Droplet Analogy
rubric_items.description: Reference the previously established 'water droplet' analogy to help the learner visualize internal excitation (e.g., boiling or splashing) rather than a solid object shattering.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly calculated the combined width of 6 inches but is struggling to visualize the full 2D net of the mylar sheet, specifically how this new combined width pairs with the existing length of the panels.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the 6-inch width and prompt the learner to identify the length of the combined sheet so they can complete their mental model of the final rectangle.

rubric_items.title: Validate Combined Width
rubric_items.description: The response must confirm that 6 inches is the correct total width for the three panels laid side-by-side.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Length Dimension
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to determine or recall the length of this combined sheet.

rubric_items.title: Ground in Physical Object
rubric_items.description: The response helps the learner visualize the net by referring back to the physical tube, such as asking if the 8-inch length of the tube changes when the panels are laid flat.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Dimension Reveal
rubric_items.description: The response gives away the final dimensions of the sheet (e.g., 'So it will be 6 by 8') instead of requiring the learner to supply the length.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response asks a generic question like 'What do you think comes next?' without specifically directing the learner's attention to the missing length dimension.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that more carbon leaves the mouse through breathing than through solid waste, but their phrasing indicates hesitation. They need validation to build confidence and a prompt to articulate the underlying reasoning to solidify this conceptual shift.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct answer to resolve their hesitation, and then prompt them to explain why this is the case based on the prior discussion of energy use and digestion.

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Deduction
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm that the learner is correct that more carbon leaves through breath.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Reasoning
rubric_items.description: The tutor must ask the learner to explain why breath accounts for more carbon loss than poop.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Prior Concepts
rubric_items.description: The tutor should encourage the learner to use the previously discussed concepts (cellular respiration, energy use, or digestion) to build their explanation.

rubric_items.title: Address Hesitation
rubric_items.description: The tutor may explicitly reassure the learner or acknowledge their tentative tone to build confidence.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the 'Why'
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not explain the reasoning for the learner (e.g., by stating that most food is absorbed and used for energy while only a small fraction is undigested waste).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Moving On Prematurely
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not move on to the next topic (such as the next trophic level or the broader carbon cycle) before the learner has articulated the reasoning behind their answer.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly added the coefficient (3) and the subscript (2) to get 5, struggling to translate the concept of 'three separate CO2 molecules' into the correct mathematical operation (multiplication or repeated addition).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should scaffold the counting process by having the learner add the oxygens across three distinct molecules (e.g., 2 + 2 + 2) to help them realize why multiplication is the correct operation.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Repeated Addition
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to calculate the total by considering the oxygens in each of the three separate molecules (e.g., asking 'If one has 2, how many do three have?' or 'What is 2 + 2 + 2?').

rubric_items.title: Address the Addition Error
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or points out that the learner got 5 by adding the coefficient and the subscript, clarifying that this is not the right operation.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Rule or Answer)
rubric_items.description: Directly gives the answer (6) or simply states the rule ('you need to multiply them') without having the learner derive the total from the concept of separate molecules.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Tells the learner they are wrong or asks them to guess again without providing a concrete visualization or counting strategy for the three molecules.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that surviving birds pass on short wings, but holds a hidden Lamarckian belief that the birds acquired these short wings through the physical effort of dodging cars during their lifetime. Before consolidating how the population shifts over time, the learner must first recognize that the variation in wing length existed before the cars exerted selective pressure.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that short wings are passed on, and then ask a targeted question that contrasts whether the birds were born with short wings or acquired them by dodging cars.

rubric_items.title: Validate Inheritance Insight
rubric_items.description: The response should confirm the learner's partial thought by explicitly agreeing that the surviving birds pass on the trait for shorter wings.

rubric_items.title: Probe Trait Origin (Target Hidden Belief)
rubric_items.description: The response should ask a targeted question that prompts the learner to consider whether the surviving birds were already born with shorter wings or if their wings shrank during their lifetime from the effort of dodging cars.

rubric_items.title: Complete the Learner's Thought
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly supplies the word 'wings' or 'traits' to complete the learner's trailing sentence ('So they only pass on short...?').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away Natural Variation
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly tell the learner that the birds were born with short wings or explicitly explain 'natural variation' rather than prompting the learner to realize the distinction.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Advancing to Population Shift
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that immediately ask how the overall population changes over many generations without first dismantling the misconception that individual birds acquired shorter wings during their lifetime.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask a generic follow-up (e.g., 'What does that mean for the species?') that fails to specifically target the origin of the short wings.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is struggling to visualize the physical scenario of the sun directly overhead (0 degrees from the vertical), incorrectly guessing it would produce an infinite shadow like the 90-degree sunset scenario. They need concrete scaffolding to mentally simulate a light shining straight down on an object to realize the shadow length would be zero.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Provide a concrete, everyday analogy or visualization prompt (like standing directly under a streetlamp) to help the learner deduce the shadow's length when the light is directly overhead.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Shadow Length at 0 Degrees
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to deduce the length or location of the shadow for the specific scenario where the sun is directly above the flagpole.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Visualization
rubric_items.description: Provide new scaffolding to help the learner visualize the 'straight down' scenario, such as introducing a relatable analogy (e.g., standing under a streetlamp at noon, holding a flashlight over a pencil) or asking them to trace the light ray.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with 90-Degree Scenario
rubric_items.description: Contrast the current 0-degree scenario with the previously discussed 90-degree scenario (where rays were parallel to the ground) to help the learner see why the shadow cannot be infinite here.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tell the learner that the shadow length is zero, that there is no shadow, or that the tangent of zero is zero.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Leave the learner stranded by merely rejecting their guess of 'infinite' or repeating the previous question without offering any new conceptual support.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified that the short, wide cylinder holds more volume, overcoming their initial misconception. They now need to consolidate this understanding by articulating how the physical dimensions of the wide cylinder result in a larger radius, which is squared in the volume formula.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the correct answer and prompt the learner to explain their reasoning by connecting the physical shape of the wide cylinder to the outsized impact of the radius in the volume formula.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Correct Choice
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner correctly chose the wide cylinder.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Justification
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain why the wide cylinder holds more, specifically prompting them to connect its physical shape (or how the paper is rolled) to the mathematical rule they just discovered about the radius.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Connection
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly explain how the paper's orientation creates a larger circumference and therefore a larger radius, as this steals the learner's opportunity to articulate the final connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Closure
rubric_items.description: Do not end the problem or transition to a new topic without requiring the learner to articulate the final 'why' behind their correct choice.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance because they firmly believe offspring must physically match their parents, leading them to insist that genuine physical changes to a parent's body (unlike 'fake' hair dye) must rewrite DNA. They need a conceptual bridge to realize that while offspring inherit baseline genetic traits, they do not inherit environmentally acquired physical changes to body cells.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should present a scenario involving a genuine, undeniable physical change to a parent's body cells (such as building muscle from exercise or getting a scar) and ask the learner to predict if the offspring is born with that same physical change.

rubric_items.title: Introduce a Genuine Cellular Change Scenario
rubric_items.description: The response must introduce an analogy or scenario involving a real, environmentally caused physical change to a parent's body cells (e.g., building muscle, getting a scar, or losing a limb) to directly address the learner's distinction between 'fake' changes and 'real' cellular changes.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Inheritance Prediction
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to predict whether the offspring in the new scenario will be born with that acquired physical trait.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: The response should acknowledge or validate the learner's correct observation that eating extra food genuinely changes the parent's body cells, before challenging the assumption that this changes the DNA.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly state the outcome of the new scenario (e.g., telling the learner that a baby isn't born with a scar or big muscles), but must leave that deduction to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating the Stalled Rule
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply repeat the rule that 'DNA doesn't change' or refer back to the 'instruction manual' analogy, as this approach has already failed to resolve the learner's dissonance.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response should not offer a vague, open-ended prompt like 'Why do they have to?' without introducing a new conceptual anchor, which would leave the learner stranded in their current logical loop.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully constructed and evaluated the equation, demonstrating procedural competence and resolving their initial confusion about variable placement. They now need to connect the numbers in their calculation back to the physical quantities in the word problem to consolidate their conceptual understanding of linear equations.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct calculation and prompt the learner to explain the physical meaning of the numbers 2 and 3 in the context of the backpack problem, without giving the explanation away.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Correct Calculation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's step-by-step calculation ('2 times 5 plus 3') is completely correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Contextual Meaning
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain what the numbers 2 and 3 represent in the real-world context of the backpack, textbooks, and binder.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Meaning
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the 2 represents the textbook weight and the 3 represents the binder weight; the learner must articulate this connection themselves.
