rubric_items.title: Avoid Unfocused Continuation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply praise the learner and end the problem or move to a new topic without requiring them to reflect on why the equation's components make sense.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Redundant Calculation
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to evaluate the equation for yet another value of x (e.g., 10 textbooks), as they have already demonstrated procedural mastery.

rubric_items.title: Highlight Conceptual Shift
rubric_items.description: Contrast their final correct logic with their initial guess (3x+2) to highlight what they have learned about variable placement.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the yellow parents carry hidden 'B' alleles and correctly deduces that these 'B' alleles are passed to the puppies, but they are confused about why this doesn't result in black puppies. They need to connect the inheritance of the 'B' alleles with the simultaneous inheritance of the 'ee' alleles, realizing that the blocking mechanism still applies to the offspring.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that the puppies do indeed inherit the 'B' alleles, but prompt the learner to recall what happens to those 'B' alleles when the puppy also inherits 'ee' from its parents.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge 'B' Inheritance
rubric_items.description: Confirm that the learner is correct to ask about the 'B's, affirming that the puppies do indeed inherit these pigment genes from their parents.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Epistatic Interaction
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explain what happens to those inherited 'B' alleles given that the puppy also inherits the 'ee' genotype from its parents.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Interaction
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the 'ee' genotype blocks the inherited 'B' alleles; the tutor must leave the application of this blocking rule to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Dismissing the 'B's
rubric_items.description: Do not dismiss the 'B' alleles as irrelevant or ignore the learner's question to simply repeat the previous statement that the puppies are 'ee'.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Insight
rubric_items.description: Praise the learner for remembering that the hidden pigment genes are still being passed down to the next generation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive overload from trying to visualize an abstract 2D grid based purely on the tutor's verbal description. They need to transition from abstract layout concepts to concrete data entry by focusing on constructing just one piece of the matrix.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should scaffold the visualization by asking the learner to identify or write out the specific numbers from their data that belong in the first row for Courier A.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Concrete Numbers
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to state the actual numerical values from their data for Courier A's price and delivery time to ground the abstract row concept.

rubric_items.title: Isolate a Single Row
rubric_items.description: Restrict the immediate task to constructing or visualizing only the first row (Courier A) rather than asking about the entire matrix or the other couriers.

rubric_items.title: Normalize the Difficulty
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that visualizing a grid mentally from a text description is tricky, validating their confusion before prompting the next step.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Re-explaining Abstractly
rubric_items.description: Do not attempt to re-explain the concepts of rows, columns, or matrix dimensions using abstract descriptions, as this just repeats the move that caused the current confusion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Providing the Row Data
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state the numbers that go into the row (e.g., 'So if Courier A costs $5 and takes 2 days...') instead of making the learner retrieve and place them.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified that they need to ask 'random people' to avoid bias, but likely conflates the everyday meaning of 'random' (haphazardly picking anyone they bump into) with systematic statistical random sampling. They need to bridge this gap by operationalizing how to actually execute a random selection from the whole grade.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the learner's insight to use 'random' people, then prompt them to invent a concrete method for how they would actually select random eighth graders without accidentally just picking their friends again.

rubric_items.title: Affirm 'Random' Insight
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's suggestion of asking 'random people' as the correct conceptual step toward an unbiased sample.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Operationalization
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to propose a specific, concrete method for how they would actually choose these 'random' students.

rubric_items.title: Ground in the Target Population
rubric_items.description: Ensures the prompt specifically targets how to select from the whole eighth grade, keeping the focus on the population they are trying to represent.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Previous Bias
rubric_items.description: Reminds the learner of the risk of accidentally picking friends again to emphasize why a strict random system is needed.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Method
rubric_items.description: Provides a specific example of random sampling (e.g., drawing names from a hat, using a student roster, or a random number generator) instead of letting the learner invent one.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Abstract Definitions
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner for a dictionary definition of 'random' rather than asking them how to execute a random selection in this specific scenario.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully calculated the individual component products (8 and 15) but lacks a conceptual understanding of why a dot product yields a single scalar value (a sum) rather than a new vector (a coordinate pair). Their question 'Wait, why add?' indicates a need to bridge the procedural steps with the physical or contextual meaning of the operation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a conceptual explanation or analogy—ideally grounded in the 'guard and player' context of the problem—that illustrates why the two separate products represent parts of a single accumulated total rather than independent directional coordinates.

rubric_items.title: Conceptual Justification for Addition
rubric_items.description: The response must provide, or prompt the learner to discover, a conceptual reason why the two products (8 and 15) are combined into a single accumulated total rather than kept separate.

rubric_items.title: Grounding in Problem Context
rubric_items.description: The response references the specific context of the problem (the 'guard and player') to illustrate what the numbers 8 and 15 practically represent, making the act of summing them intuitive.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Scalar vs. Vector Meaning
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly contrasts the meaning of a scalar (a single total amount or magnitude) with a vector (independent coordinates or directions) to resolve the learner's lingering confusion about the (8, 15) format.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response validates the learner's question by acknowledging that it is a common and logical intuition to want to keep x and y separate as coordinates.

rubric_items.title: Procedural Dismissal
rubric_items.description: The response dismisses the learner's 'why' question by simply restating the mathematical rule or formula (e.g., 'that is just how dot products are calculated' or 'because the formula says to add') without offering conceptual grounding.

rubric_items.title: Premature Geometric Shift
rubric_items.description: The response attempts to explain the addition by introducing the geometric definition of the dot product (magnitudes and cosine theta), which overcomplicates the immediate algebraic question and abandons the current component-based reasoning.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is caught in a cycle of asking for definitions because the tutor keeps introducing new, abstract terminology ('genes', 'chromosomes', 'chemical code') without grounding them. The learner is currently stuck on the word 'code' and needs a concrete, everyday analogy to understand how abstract instructions translate into physical traits.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a simple, everyday analogy for 'code' (like a recipe or a building manual), explicitly connect it back to the duck's physical traits, and avoid introducing any new biological jargon.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Everyday Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response must explain the word 'code' using a familiar, non-biological concept of instructions, such as a recipe, a blueprint, or a Lego building manual.

rubric_items.title: Connection to Physical Traits
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly link the explanation of 'code' back to the duck's physical characteristics (like feather color or size) to show what the code actually produces.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Application
rubric_items.description: The response should end with a question that asks the learner to apply the analogy or share their own understanding of how instructions work in everyday life.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Introducing New Biological Jargon
rubric_items.description: The response introduces new, complex biological terminology (such as proteins, nucleotides, base pairs, or RNA) instead of simplifying the current concept.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Abstract or Circular Definition
rubric_items.description: The response defines 'code' using dictionary definitions, computer science jargon, or abstract synonyms (e.g., 'a system of symbols', 'data') that fail to provide a visualizable, concrete anchor for the learner.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has overgeneralized the 'multiply by 2' shortcut, failing to realize that while 50 times 2 equals the required percentage base of 100, 60 times 2 equals 120. They need to recognize this denominator mismatch before learning a more general conversion method.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that asks the learner to calculate what 60 times 2 actually is, so they can see for themselves that the resulting denominator is 120 rather than the required 100.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Denominator Evaluation
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to identify the actual denominator they get when multiplying 60 by 2 and compare it to the target denominator for percentages (100).

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Previous Success
rubric_items.description: Contrasts the current situation with the previous one by reminding the learner why multiplying by 2 worked for 50 (because 50 x 2 = 100).

rubric_items.title: Premature Method Introduction
rubric_items.description: Provides the correct percentage (40%) or immediately introduces a new method (like division or cross-multiplication) before the learner understands why their current 'times 2' method failed.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Dismissal
rubric_items.description: Simply states that 120 is not 100 or says 'no' without prompting the learner to reflect on the math (60 x 2) that led to the incorrect denominator.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly understands the physical mechanism of a barrier (equating it to the game Red Rover), but remains stuck in the hidden belief that group animal behavior is for play rather than survival. They need to bridge their accurate mechanical analogy to the actual biological purpose: coordinating to get food.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the physical accuracy of the 'Red Rover' analogy (forming a line to block), but prompt the learner to identify the life-or-death consequence of 'winning' this block for the pelicans.

rubric_items.title: Validate Physical Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that 'Red Rover' is an accurate comparison for the physical action of forming a line to block an escape.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Survival Purpose
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question that prompts the learner to state what the pelicans actually get out of 'winning' this block, shifting the focus from play to food or survival.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Outright Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply reject the game analogy again (e.g., 'No, it's not a game'), as this ignores the mechanical accuracy of the learner's insight and repeats a previously failed tutor strategy.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Consequence
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly tell the learner the difference in purpose (e.g., 'In Red Rover you play for fun, but pelicans do it to eat') rather than making the learner articulate the pelicans' reward.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly combined both the dominant 'A' and recessive 'a' alleles into a single gamete ('AaBC'), violating the law of segregation. They need to understand that each gamete receives only one allele from the 'Aa' pair, and then apply this rule to generate the remaining combinations starting with 'a'.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted correction or probe that reminds the learner that 'A' and 'a' separate into different gametes, followed by a prompt to generate a 3-letter combination starting with 'a'.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Aa' Co-occurrence
rubric_items.description: The tutor must address the learner's error of grouping 'A' and 'a' together by reminding them (or asking them to recall) that each combination can only receive one allele from the first gene pair.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for an 'a'-Starting Combination
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to construct a new combination that includes the 'a' allele but not the 'A' allele.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Successful Combinations
rubric_items.description: The tutor suggests using the four combinations the learner already successfully built (ABC, AbC, ABc, Abc) as a pattern for generating the new ones.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor provides the actual correct combinations starting with 'a' (e.g., 'aBC') instead of leaving the work of generating them to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Surface Rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor rejects 'AaBC' based purely on surface features (e.g., 'That has four letters' or 'Too many letters') without referencing the biological rule of segregation or the principle that each gene contributes exactly one allele.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that without kelp to anchor them, holding paws does not physically attach the otters to the environment, leading to the realization that they might still drift. The tutor needs to validate this deduction and probe the learner's underlying assumption about what the group does when they drift, specifically to surface the hidden belief that the otters might actively paddle together.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A validating probe that confirms the otters do indeed drift, followed by a targeted question asking the learner to theorize what the connected group does next or how holding hands helps them survive the drift.

rubric_items.title: Validate Drift Deduction
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly confirm the learner's realization that without kelp, the group of otters does indeed drift.

rubric_items.title: Probe Group Dynamics During Drift
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to theorize what the connected group does while drifting or how holding hands helps them survive the drift, creating space for the learner to reveal their assumption about paddling.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Benefit of Rafting
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly state the biological benefits of holding paws (e.g., preventing separation, looking larger to predators) before the learner attempts an explanation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Preempting the Passive Floating Concept
rubric_items.description: The response should not prematurely state that otters float passively or explicitly tell the learner they do not paddle together, which would rob the learner of the chance to voice their hidden belief.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely confirm that the otters float away without asking a targeted follow-up question to guide the learner's next reasoning step.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is clinging to an assumption that the fret spacing decreases by a constant 5 mm, rather than consulting their actual data. Before addressing deeper misconceptions about quadratic versus exponential models, the learner must first calculate the actual differences between consecutive frets to discover that the decrease is not constant.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt directing the learner to calculate the actual difference between at least two pairs of consecutive frets to empirically test their 'always minus 5' hypothesis.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Data Verification
rubric_items.description: The response must direct the learner to look at their actual measurements and calculate the differences between consecutive frets to test their 'minus 5' assumption.

rubric_items.title: Specify Multiple Intervals
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to compare at least two specific intervals (e.g., the gap between frets 1 and 2 versus the gap between frets 2 and 3) to establish whether the change is constant.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Linear Test
rubric_items.description: The response may acknowledge that checking for a constant subtraction of 5 is exactly the right mathematical way to test if the model is linear.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Math
rubric_items.description: The response should not tell the learner that the differences are not constant, nor should it provide the calculated differences for them.

rubric_items.title: Premature Model Discussion
rubric_items.description: The response should not jump into explaining why non-constant differences mean the model is exponential rather than quadratic before the learner has actually done the math to see that the differences are non-constant.

learning_objective: PS3.D Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that more energy is released during bond formation than is absorbed during bond breaking, overcoming their initial misconception. Because their answer is tentative ('More is released?'), they need explicit validation followed by a prompt to consolidate this realization into a complete explanation of why the engine releases energy.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's correct deduction and prompt them to synthesize how this difference in energy explains where the car engine's heat and motion actually come from.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Deduction
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative conclusion that more energy is released (when forming exhaust bonds) than is absorbed (when breaking gasoline bonds).

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Phenomenon Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to connect this net difference in energy back to the observable phenomenon, asking them to articulate in their own words where the engine's heat and motion actually come from.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Conceptual Shift
rubric_items.description: Explicitly contrast this new conclusion with the learner's initial idea, highlighting that the energy comes from forming new bonds rather than just breaking the old ones.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Tutor Summarizes
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for taking over the cognitive work by stating the final conclusion themselves (e.g., 'Yes, that extra energy is what powers the car') rather than asking the learner to articulate it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Topic Shift
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for validating the answer and immediately moving on to a new topic (like the chemical formula for combustion or a new reaction) before the learner has explicitly summarized the energy transfer in this engine.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance, wondering how two substances made of the exact same element (carbon) can have entirely different physical properties. They need to connect their prior realization about the different bonding structures (three vs. four bonds) to the core chemical principle that the physical arrangement of atoms, not just their identity, determines a substance's properties.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Validate the learner's excellent question, then prompt them to use the structural differences they just discussed (the number of bonds and electron mobility) to explain how the same building blocks can create different properties.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Dissonance
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's observation that it is counterintuitive or surprising for two materials made of the exact same element (carbon) to behave so differently.

rubric_items.title: Anchor to Prior Structural Discoveries
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner's attention back to the specific differences in bonding (three vs. four bonds) or electron mobility they just uncovered as the key to resolving their confusion.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Punchline
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner the core takeaway that 'structure determines properties' or introduce the term 'allotrope' before they have articulated the connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Questions
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a vague, open-ended question (e.g., 'Why do you think they are different?') that fails to point the learner back to the structural differences established in the previous turns.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has accepted that air consists of invisible particles but is now struggling to map a macroscopic physical property (weight) onto something microscopic. They need to bridge the gap between a single, seemingly weightless particle and the cumulative mass of trillions of them.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that acknowledges a single particle is extremely light, but asks the learner to predict what happens to the total weight when trillions of them are combined.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Individual Lightness
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or establishes that a single air particle is incredibly light, addressing the intuition that microscopic things don't feel 'heavy' on their own.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Accumulation
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to reason about what happens to the weight when a massive number (e.g., 'trillions') of these tiny particles are added together.

rubric_items.title: Validate Scientific Intuition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly praises the learner's question, validating that wondering about the physical properties of invisible things is a strong scientific insight.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that air has weight or that the particles add up to make things heavy, bypassing the learner's opportunity to deduce the concept of accumulation themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a vague counter-question (e.g., 'What do you think?' or 'Are they?') without providing a conceptual scaffold like scale, accumulation, or a concrete analogy to help them answer.

learning_objective: PS3.C Relationship Between Energy and Forces

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the satellite's gravitational potential energy decreases as it gets closer to Earth, overcoming their earlier misconception, but their question mark indicates lingering hesitation. They need confirmation of their reasoning and a final prompt to confidently connect this decreasing trend back to their original answer about where the potential energy is at its minimum.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly affirm the learner's correct deduction to build confidence, and then prompt them to state where in the orbit the potential energy must therefore be at its lowest.

rubric_items.title: Affirmation of Correct Deduction
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm that the learner's answer ('it decreases') is correct in order to resolve their hesitation.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Final Consolidation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to apply their realization to conclude exactly where in the satellite's orbit the gravitational potential energy is at its minimum.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not do the cognitive work of stating that the potential energy is lowest at the closest point; the response must leave this final articulation to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Topic Shift
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not shift the focus to new orbital mechanics concepts (like the satellite's kinetic energy or speed) before the learner has firmly stated the conclusion about minimum potential energy.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Overcoming the Misconception
rubric_items.description: The tutor may explicitly contrast this correct conclusion with the learner's earlier reasoning by noting that potential energy decreases even though the gravitational pull is getting stronger.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating 'half of the original amount' with 'half of the current amount,' insisting that losing half always means losing a fixed 50 mg regardless of the starting value. They are stuck on the absolute loss and need to explicitly confront what 'half' means when the starting quantity is only 50.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should induce cognitive conflict by pointing out that losing 50 from 50 means losing *all* of it, or directly prompt the learner to calculate what half of 50 actually is.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Calculation of Half of 50
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to explicitly determine what 'half' of 50 is, either directly (e.g., 'What is half of 50?') or through a concrete analogy.

rubric_items.title: Highlight the 'Losing All' Contradiction
rubric_items.description: The response should highlight the logical consequence of the learner's claim by pointing out that losing 50 mg when only 50 mg is left means losing 100% (or 'all') of it, which contradicts the rule that only 'half' is lost.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not do the math for the learner by stating that half of 50 is 25 or that they will lose 25 mg.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a vague prompt (e.g., 'Think about it again' or 'Are you sure?') that fails to direct the learner to the specific calculation of half of the remaining 50 mg.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Refocusing on Time
rubric_items.description: Do not shift the focus back to the 5-hour time interval; the response must keep the learner focused on the amounts (the milligrams).

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly, though tentatively, deduced that stored energy reaches zero at the bottom of the ramp. They now need validation of this insight and a prompt to connect the disappearance of stored energy to the maximization of motion energy, completing the concept of continuous energy transformation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Validate the learner's conclusion that stored energy runs out, and prompt them to deduce what this means for the amount of motion energy at the bottom of the ramp.

rubric_items.title: Validate Tentative Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and validate the learner's tentative conclusion that the stored energy 'runs out' or reaches zero at the bottom of the ramp.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Motion Energy
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to deduce what happens to the amount of motion energy (or speed) at the exact point when the stored energy runs out.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Transformation Context
rubric_items.description: Frame the follow-up question by reminding the learner of the continuous transformation discussed in the previous turn (e.g., 'Since that stored energy was turning into motion energy...').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Climax
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the motion energy is at its maximum or highest at the bottom; the learner must deduce this.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-End Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply say 'Yes' or 'Exactly' without asking a follow-up question that drives the learner to consider the other half of the energy transfer.

rubric_items.title: Optional: Connect to Zero Height
rubric_items.description: Explicitly connect the stored energy 'running out' to the physical reality of the skateboarder reaching the ground and having no more height to lose.

learning_objective: LS2.C Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the misconception that a lake functions like a simple pipe where stopping the input allows the water flow to easily 'wash away' all remaining contaminants. They are failing to account for the physical reality of heavy sediment at the bottom of the lake and how bound nutrients resist being swept away by water currents.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that creates cognitive conflict by asking the learner to consider the physical mechanics of water flowing through a lake versus the heavy, bound sediment sitting at the bottom.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the Mechanics of 'Washing Away'
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to reason about the physical interaction between the water flowing through the lake and the heavy mud at the bottom (e.g., asking if the water current is strong enough at the bottom to sweep away thick mud).

rubric_items.title: Leverage the 'Binding' Concept
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to incorporate the previously established fact that the nutrients are 'bound' to the sediment, making them fundamentally different from freely floating particles that easily wash away.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Partial Correctness
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's intuition by acknowledging that the water itself, or freely dissolved nutrients, do indeed wash away, before pivoting to why the sediment behaves differently.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Directly explains that water flows over the top of the mud without moving it, or explicitly states that sediment is too heavy to wash away, rather than prompting the learner to deduce this physical constraint.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's answer (e.g., 'Not quite') or asks a generic question (e.g., 'Are you sure it washes away?') without introducing a specific physical constraint (like weight, water flow, or binding) for them to reason about.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully deduced that the upward drag force increases as the skydiver speeds up. Their immediate need is to connect this velocity-dependent upward force to the constant downward force of gravity to understand how the net force and acceleration change over time.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's deduction and prompt them to compare this growing upward drag force against the constant downward force of gravity to determine what happens to the skydiver's net force.

rubric_items.title: Validate Drag Increase
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or confirm the learner's correct deduction that the upward drag force gets bigger as speed increases.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Gravity Comparison
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider the downward force of gravity (or weight) in relation to the increasing upward drag force.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Net Force or Acceleration
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to deduce how the combination of the constant downward force and the increasing upward force affects the skydiver's overall net force or acceleration.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away Terminal Velocity
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the forces will eventually balance, that the net force becomes zero, or that the skydiver stops accelerating.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Lingering on Particle Collisions
rubric_items.description: Do not ask further questions about the air particles or the mechanics of the collisions, as the learner has already successfully grasped why drag increases with speed.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a generic question (e.g., "What does that mean for the skydiver?" or "What happens next?") that fails to explicitly direct the learner to consider gravity, net force, or acceleration.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that a complex number can be represented by its components 'a' and 'b', but is erroneously trying to force this representation (which belongs on the complex plane) onto the real Cartesian plane of their physics problem. They are resisting the conceptual boundary that a mathematical result of complex roots physically means 'no intersection' on a real graph.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct intuition that (a,b) is used to graph complex numbers, but then use a targeted prompt to make the learner realize why plotting that specific real coordinate pair on their current graph would not represent an actual intersection of the line and parabola.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Evaluation of the Proposed Point
rubric_items.description: Evaluates whether the tutor asks the learner to consider the physical or mathematical consequences of plotting the real point (a,b) on their current graph (e.g., asking if the point (a,b) would actually sit on both the line and the parabola).

rubric_items.title: Validate Complex Plane Intuition
rubric_items.description: Evaluates whether the tutor affirms the learner's correct mathematical intuition by acknowledging that (a,b) is indeed exactly how we graph complex numbers on a complex plane.

rubric_items.title: Connect Back to Intersection Goal
rubric_items.description: Rewards the tutor for explicitly reminding the learner that the original purpose of the graph is to find the specific location where the two shapes (the line and the parabola) touch.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover of Plane Rules
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for simply stating the rule that (a,b) belongs to the complex plane and cannot be put on a real plane, thereby doing the reasoning for the learner instead of letting them discover the incompatibility.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for ignoring the learner's specific (a,b) proposal and merely repeating prior statements that the shapes don't intersect or that the roots are imaginary.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the physical size of a shape (side lengths) with its angular measure (the spread between the sides), assuming that scaling up a triangle scales all its properties proportionally. They need a conceptual bridge to realize that extending the length of two intersecting lines does not change the angle between them.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should offer a concrete thought experiment or visualization—such as extending the sides of a single corner, zooming in on a picture, or imagining a larger square—that prompts the learner to separate the concept of side length from the 'pointiness' or spread of an angle.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Visualization of Angle vs. Length
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to visualize or reason about whether making the sides of a corner longer actually changes the spread or 'pointiness' of that corner.

rubric_items.title: Contextualize with the Sail or Familiar Shape
rubric_items.description: The response should ground the visualization in the learner's sail project (e.g., looking at one specific corner of the sail) or a familiar everyday object (like the 90-degree corner of a piece of paper or a room).

rubric_items.title: Validate the Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that the learner's assumption is a natural intuitive leap (e.g., 'It makes total sense to think the angles would double too since the sides are doubling').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Direct Explanation of Angle Measure
rubric_items.description: The response directly explains that angles measure rotation or spread rather than length, giving away the conceptual insight instead of letting the learner deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague or Repetitive Questioning
rubric_items.description: The response leaves the learner stranded by merely repeating that triangles must be 180 degrees or asking how it's possible to be bigger but stay at 180, without offering a new way to visualize the problem.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully answered a series of scaffolded questions tracing the mechanism of natural selection in elephants and has just correctly identified poachers as the selective pressure, albeit with slight hesitation. Their immediate need is to consolidate these isolated, guided steps into a cohesive, independent explanation of the evolutionary process.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the learner's correct answer and prompt them to synthesize the entire step-by-step process of natural selection in the elephants in their own words.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Selective Pressure
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner is correct about poachers being the selective pressure, resolving the uncertainty indicated by their question mark.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to synthesize the previously discussed steps (hunting, survival, inheritance, population shift) into a single cohesive explanation of how the elephant population changed.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Formal Concept
rubric_items.description: Frame the requested synthesis around the formal term 'natural selection' to help the learner map their concrete understanding of the elephants to the scientific vocabulary.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Tutor Takeover of Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Do not summarize the full mechanism of the elephants' evolution for the learner, as this robs them of the opportunity to consolidate the steps themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: Do not move on to a new topic, a new example, or close the lesson simply because the learner correctly identified the final piece of the puzzle.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the hydrophobic tails hide from water, but is unsure about the chemical properties of the phospholipid head. They are perfectly positioned to deduce that if the tails point inward to hide, the heads must face outward toward the water, meaning they must have the opposite property (water-loving/hydrophilic).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce the head's relationship with water by asking them to consider where the heads must be positioned if the tails are hiding on the inside of the double layer.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Deduction via Spatial Reasoning
rubric_items.description: The response must guide the learner to figure out the head's relationship with water by asking where the heads end up if the tails are pointing inward.

rubric_items.title: Recall Environmental Context
rubric_items.description: The response should remind the learner (or prompt them to recall) the previously established fact that there is water on both the outside and inside of the cell.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Opposite Term
rubric_items.description: The response may introduce or hint at the etymology for 'water-loving' (hydrophilic) to parallel the earlier breakdown of the word 'hydrophobic'.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly tell the learner that the head likes water, is hydrophilic, or faces outward, bypassing the learner's opportunity to deduce this themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Unanchored Question
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply ask 'What do you think?' or 'Does it?' without anchoring the question to the physical structure of the bilayer or the location of the water.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly guessed that the dot represents multiplication ('Times?') but expresses hesitation ('But how...') about executing the final step. They need confirmation that their guess is correct and a direct prompt to multiply the initial value (15) by the evaluated exponent (8).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's identification of multiplication and prompt them to calculate 15 times 8.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Multiplication
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's realization that the dot means 'times' or multiplication.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Final Calculation
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to multiply 15 by the 8 they calculated in the previous step.

rubric_items.title: Optional: Calculation Scaffolding
rubric_items.description: Offer a brief mental math strategy for calculating 15 times 8 (e.g., breaking it into 10 times 8 and 5 times 8) to address the learner's 'But how...'.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Doing the Math
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final answer (120) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Stranding the Learner
rubric_items.description: Do not merely say 'Yes' to 'Times?' without explicitly guiding them to multiply 15 and 8.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Regressing to Previous Steps
rubric_items.description: Do not re-explain the order of operations or the $2^3$ step, as the learner has already moved past this and just needs to finish the multiplication.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is struggling to visualize how an object can fall continuously without hitting the ground, as the abstract explanation of 'the ground curving away' is not intuitive. They need a concrete, step-by-step analogy to bridge the gap between everyday projectile motion and orbital mechanics.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a relatable thought experiment (like throwing a ball or shooting a cannon horizontally) and ask the learner to predict what happens to the landing spot as the sideways speed increases.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Grounding Analogy
rubric_items.description: Introduces a concrete, everyday thought experiment or analogy involving an object moving sideways and falling (such as throwing a ball or shooting a cannon off a high peak).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner Prediction
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to predict the trajectory or outcome of the object in the analogy (e.g., asking what happens to the landing spot if the object is thrown faster).

rubric_items.title: Normalize Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that continuous falling without crashing is a highly counterintuitive concept, validating the learner's 'Wait, what?' reaction.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Punchline
rubric_items.description: Explicitly states the conclusion of the analogy (that if the object moves fast enough it will orbit or never hit the ground), bypassing the learner's opportunity to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating Abstract Concepts
rubric_items.description: Merely repeats or rephrases the abstract explanation of the Earth's curvature and falling, without introducing a simpler grounding scenario.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a generic clarification request (e.g., 'What part is confusing?') without providing any new conceptual scaffold to help the learner visualize the physics.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the complex number's position ($7i$) with its geometric distance along the imaginary axis, struggling to see how $i$ functions purely as a directional marker in this context. They need to realize that while the point is located at $7i$, the physical distance used in the coordinate formula is just the real number 7.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that $7i$ is the correct location, then prompt the learner to determine the physical distance (number of units) from the origin to that location on the imaginary axis.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Geometric Distance
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to determine the physical distance or number of units from the origin to the point $7i$ on the imaginary axis.

rubric_items.title: Validate Location vs. Distance
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that $7i$ is indeed the correct location or name of the point on the axis, validating their statement before shifting focus to the distance.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Coordinate
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that the distance is 7 or instruct them to simply drop the $i$ from their formula.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Algebraic Detour
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce algebraic manipulation of $i$ (such as explaining that $i^2 = -1$) to resolve the formula, as this abandons the geometric coordinate approach the tutor is building.

rubric_items.title: Directional Analogy
rubric_items.description: Offer a concrete analogy involving physical direction (e.g., walking '7 steps North') to help the learner separate the magnitude from the directional label.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly predicts that more urchins lead to less kelp, but is experiencing cognitive dissonance because the energy arrow points from the kelp to the urchin, which feels contradictory to the kelp population decreasing. They need to connect the abstract concept of 'giving energy' to the physical reality of 'being eaten' to resolve this visual-conceptual mismatch.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that asks the learner to articulate the physical mechanism of how the urchin gets its energy from the kelp (eating/consuming), bridging the gap between the abstract arrow and the population decrease.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Physical Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to explain what physically happens to the kelp when its energy is transferred to the urchin (e.g., asking what the urchin has to do to get that energy).

rubric_items.title: Reference the Visual Dissonance
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly link the learner's confusion about the arrow to the population decrease, framing the question around reconciling these two ideas.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that it is normal or understandable to be confused by an arrow pointing toward a growing population while the source population shrinks.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Answer)
rubric_items.description: The response directly explains the connection for the learner (e.g., 'The arrow means the urchin is eating the kelp, so the kelp dies and its population goes down').

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response asks a generic question (e.g., 'What does the arrow mean again?' or 'Think about it') without directing the learner's attention to the physical act of consumption or the fate of the individual kelp.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner hypothesizes that the brain's response command travels backward along the same sensory nerve they just drew. They need to realize that because the sensory nerve connects to the skin (to feel touch), sending a signal back along it wouldn't reach the muscles needed for movement, necessitating a separate pathway.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to trace their drawn 'touch nerve' backward to see where it leads (the skin/tentacle tip) and ask if that is where the 'move' command needs to go (the muscles).

rubric_items.title: Test Hypothesis via Endpoints
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate their 'same string' idea by considering where that specific string leads (the tentacle tip/skin) versus where the movement command needs to go (the muscles).

rubric_items.title: Ground in the Diagram
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to look at the specific line they just drew on their diagram to make the abstract pathway concrete.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that sending the signal back along the same path is a logical initial guess.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Revealing the Separate Pathway
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the signal uses a different string, a separate pathway, or a 'motor nerve'; the learner must deduce this.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unscaffolded Reversal
rubric_items.description: Do not simply bounce the question back (e.g., 'What do you think?') without guiding them to consider the physical endpoints of the nerves.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner distinguishes between active human effort ('I'm pushing') and passive resting, failing to see that gravity pulling the book down also causes the book to exert a downward force on the desk. They need to connect their earlier realization about gravity's downward pull to the concept of the book pressing against the desk.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to consider whether gravity pulling the book down causes the book to press or push against the desk, bridging the gap between active human pushing and the book's weight.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Book's Downward Press
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to consider whether the book is also pressing, pushing, or exerting a downward force on the desk.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Gravity Insight
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly reference the learner's earlier statement about gravity pulling the book down to help them realize why the book would be pressing on the desk.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Active Push Observation
rubric_items.description: The response may acknowledge or validate the learner's correct observation that their hand is actively pushing, before pivoting to the book.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Force
rubric_items.description: The response should not directly state that the book pushes on the desk or that the desk pushes back on the book, as the learner must make this connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Ignoring the Agency Bottleneck
rubric_items.description: The response should not ask a generic question (e.g., 'Are you sure?' or 'What is a force?') that fails to address the learner's specific bottleneck regarding active human pushing versus passive resting.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a conceptual loop, unable to separate the surface interaction (friction/grip) from the mechanics of balance and tipping. Even when presented with a scenario where grip is infinite, they default to 'not enough grip' because they lack a mental model for how weight distribution causes rotational falling (tipping) independently of sliding.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a highly relatable, everyday physical analogy—such as leaning one's own body forward while wearing perfectly grippy shoes—to definitively isolate the concept of weight distribution from surface friction.

rubric_items.title: Isolate Tipping via Relatable Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response must use a relatable physical analogy or thought experiment (e.g., leaning over in grippy shoes, or a tall object bolted to a hinge) that definitively proves perfect grip cannot prevent tipping.

rubric_items.title: Shift Focus to Weight Distribution
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to consider the physical location of the object's weight, its shape, or how much of it is hanging over empty space.

rubric_items.title: Validate Friction's Role
rubric_items.description: Reward responses that briefly validate the learner's intuition by confirming that grip is indeed the perfect answer for sliding, before pivoting to why tipping is a different mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly introduce formal terms like 'center of mass', 'center of gravity', or 'base of support' before the learner has articulated the physical concept in their own words.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely reject the 'grip' hypothesis and ask another open-ended question (e.g., 'No, remember they are glued. What else could it be?'), which will leave the learner stranded in their current loop.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the constant vertical value (temperature) of the flat line with the horizontal value (time), leading them to incorrectly conclude that moving left-to-right means the time numbers don't change. They need immediate scaffolding to explicitly read the increasing numbers on the x-axis to break this conflation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to explicitly read or compare the specific numbers on the horizontal axis at different points along the flat line.

rubric_items.title: Prompting X-Axis Reading
rubric_items.description: The tutor prompts the learner to explicitly read, trace, or identify the numbers on the bottom (time) axis as they move from left to right.

rubric_items.title: Distinguishing Variables
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly contrasts the height of the line (temperature, which is constant) with the horizontal position (time) to help the learner separate the two variables.

rubric_items.title: Point Comparison Strategy
rubric_items.description: The tutor suggests picking two specific points on the flat part of the line (e.g., the beginning and the end of the flat section) to compare their time values.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly tells the learner that the time numbers are increasing, getting bigger, or that time continues to pass, rather than making the learner read the graph to discover this.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply rejects the learner's answer (e.g., 'No, they do change') or asks a generic 'Are you sure?' without providing a concrete strategy for reading the axis.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the enzyme's shape change prevents target molecules from fitting, but they still harbor the hidden belief that the cytoplasm is a highly basic environment that actively destroys escaped enzymes. They need confirmation of their insight followed by a targeted probe to distinguish between temporary inactivation and permanent destruction in a neutral environment.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's insight that the molecules won't fit, and then use a targeted probe to help the learner realize that the neutral cytoplasm merely renders the enzyme inactive rather than actively destroying it.

rubric_items.title: Validate "Won't Fit" Insight
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm the learner's correct deduction that the shape change prevents the target molecules from fitting into the enzyme.

rubric_items.title: Probe Inactivation vs. Destruction
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to consider whether the enzyme is permanently destroyed by the cytoplasm or simply rendered inactive because the molecules no longer fit.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Neutrality of Cytoplasm
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly state or prompt the learner to recognize that a pH of 7 means the cytoplasm is neutral, countering the misconception that it is a highly basic environment.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Inactivation)
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not directly state that the enzyme is merely inactive or that the shape change is reversible; they must leave room for the learner to reason about the enzyme's fate.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not simply say 'Yes' or ask a generic 'What happens next?' without specifically guiding the learner to consider the enzyme's state (destroyed vs. inactive) in the cytoplasm.

rubric_items.title: Premature Conclusion
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not immediately conclude the lesson by stating how this keeps the cell safe without first addressing the learner's misconception that the enzyme is actively destroyed.

rubric_items.title: Introduce "Active Site" Terminology
rubric_items.description: The tutor can optionally introduce the formal term 'active site' to label the 'specific spot' the learner just correctly reasoned about.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully connected a higher RPM to a shorter period and correctly visualized this as the peaks of the wave being closer together on a graph. They now need validation of this correct intuition and a scaffolded transition to representing this horizontal compression mathematically within a trigonometric equation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the learner's graphical intuition and prompt them to consider how to modify the input of a basic sine or cosine function to make the wave repeat more quickly.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Graphical Intuition
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly validates the learner's tentative conclusion that the peaks and valleys of the wave will be closer together.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Mathematical Representation
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks the learner how to alter a basic trigonometric function (like sine or cosine) to reflect this compressed wave or shorter period.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Parameter
rubric_items.description: The tutor does not explicitly provide the period formula (e.g., T = 2π/B) or directly state that a coefficient must be multiplied by the input variable.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Equation Prompts
rubric_items.description: The tutor does not ask the learner to generate the full equation all at once without focusing their attention specifically on the part of the function that controls the period.

rubric_items.title: Reference the Input Variable
rubric_items.description: The tutor specifically directs the learner's attention to the input variable (e.g., time or t) inside the trigonometric function as the target for modification.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is strongly anchored to the geometric definition of 'center' and 'middle', causing their intuition to fail on the tutor's ruler-and-coin thought experiment. They need to mentally simulate the physical forces in this specific scenario to realize that supporting the geometric middle will no longer balance the uneven weight.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A cognitive-conflict prompt that asks the learner to mentally test their prediction by imagining what would physically happen to the heavy side of the ruler if they tried to balance it exactly in the geometric middle.

rubric_items.title: Test the Middle Prediction
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to mentally simulate what would happen if they actually placed their finger in the geometric middle of the ruler with the heavy coin on one end.

rubric_items.title: Highlight the Weight Discrepancy
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly draw the learner's attention to the difference in weight between the two sides of the ruler (the side with the coin vs. the side without).

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Geometric Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that the learner's answer would be perfectly correct for a normal, unweighted ruler before challenging it for the weighted one.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly tell the learner where the ruler would balance (e.g., 'It would balance closer to the coin') or explicitly state that the center of mass moves toward the heavier side.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Analogy Hopping
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that abandon the ruler-and-coin scenario to introduce a completely new analogy or revert to abstract definitions before resolving the current thought experiment.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a loop of superficial guessing because they lack a solid conceptual grasp of the physical difference between a radius and a diameter, causing them to conflate the total height of the wheel with its amplitude. The immediate need is to pause the trigonometric mapping and have the learner articulate the basic geometry of a circle.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that temporarily drops the trigonometric terminology and asks the learner to define or visualize the difference between a 'radius' and a 'diameter' in their own words.

rubric_items.title: Eliciting Geometric Definitions
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to define or describe the physical difference between a 'radius' and a 'diameter' on a basic circle or wheel in their own words.

rubric_items.title: Suspending the Mapping Task
rubric_items.description: The tutor's response should temporarily drop the terms 'amplitude' and 'vertical shift' to focus exclusively on the physical geometry of the wheel.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Providing the Geometric Definition
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not define 'radius' or 'diameter' for the learner, nor state the mathematical relationship between them (e.g., telling them that the radius is half the diameter).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating the Failed Explanation
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not repeat the assertion that amplitude is the radius or that amplitude only measures from the middle to the top, as this didactic approach has already failed multiple times.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is misinterpreting the tutor's analogy, incorrectly mapping the 'grass' as the mechanism that holds the rug to the floor, rather than realizing the grass and topsoil are the rug itself. They still do not grasp that securing the top layer is insufficient if that entire layer can slide over the deeper soil.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify the analogy mapping (grass = the rug) and prompt the learner to identify what is actually needed to secure a loose rug to a slippery floor.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Analogy Mapping
rubric_items.description: Clarify that the grass (and the topsoil it holds together) represents the rug itself, rather than the mechanism that secures the rug to the floor.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Anchor
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to identify what additional mechanism is needed to keep a rug from sliding on a slippery floor (e.g., nailing it down, a heavy weight, or a non-slip pad).

rubric_items.title: Validate Topsoil Cohesion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is correct that the grass holds the top layer of dirt together, reinforcing that this is exactly like the tightly woven rug.

rubric_items.title: Prematurely Explaining the Solution
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that deep roots (or bushes/trees) act as the anchors connecting the topsoil to the deep soil; leave the mapping of the anchor back to the plants for the learner to deduce.

rubric_items.title: Abandoning the Analogy
rubric_items.description: Do not drop the rug-on-floor analogy to explain the soil mechanics directly; the response must resolve the learner's confusion within the context of the analogy.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is comparing the raw numbers (1,500 and 8) while ignoring the units, leading to confusion about how 1,500 megabytes can represent a smaller capacity than 8 gigabytes. They need to realize that comparing the size of two quantities requires evaluating them in the same unit.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's numerical observation and then prompt them to resolve the paradox by recalling the common-unit conversion they established earlier in the dialogue (that 8 GB is 8,000 MB).

rubric_items.title: Validate Numerical Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is mathematically correct that the raw number 1,500 is larger than the number 8.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Common Unit Comparison
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to compare the two amounts using the same unit, ideally by prompting them to recall their earlier realization that the 8-gigabyte drive holds 8,000 megabytes.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Resolution
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly spell out the conclusion (e.g., 'Since 8 GB is 8,000 MB, 1,500 is actually smaller'); leave the cognitive work of making that connection to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Unit Hints
rubric_items.description: Do not give a generic, unanchored hint like 'check your units' without specifically contrasting the 1,500 megabytes with the 8 gigabytes or referencing their prior conversion.

rubric_items.title: Everyday Analogy
rubric_items.description: Offer a familiar everyday analogy (such as pennies vs. dollars or inches vs. feet) to illustrate how a larger number can represent a smaller total amount if the unit is smaller.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that 18 falls between the 15 and 20 markers but incorrectly assumes it lies exactly in the middle. They need to evaluate the relative distances from 18 to the boundary markers to determine its proportional placement.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to mathematically verify their guess by comparing the distance from 18 to 15 versus 18 to 20, or by counting out the integers between the markers.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Mathematical Verification
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to check their 'middle' guess by either counting the integers between 15 and 20 or calculating the distance from 18 to each endpoint.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Correct Range
rubric_items.description: Validate that the learner correctly identified that 18 belongs between 15 and 20 before addressing its exact position.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that 18 is closer to 20 or calculate the exact distances for them.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unstructured Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the 'middle' guess (e.g., 'Not quite') without offering a specific mathematical strategy to re-evaluate it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Accepting Incorrect Placement
rubric_items.description: Do not accept 'in the middle' as correct or move on to the next step of plotting without addressing the proportional placement.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused about which specific pair of tripod feet to use for their measurement, missing the implication of the tutor's previous instruction to use 'any' two feet. They do not yet realize that because the tripod base is symmetrical, the distance to the tipping edge is identical for all three pairs.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to observe the shape of the base or compare the different pairs of feet to deduce for themselves why any pair will work.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Symmetry Deduction
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to consider the shape of the base or compare the different pairs of feet to deduce that the choice of which two feet to use does not matter.

rubric_items.title: Suggest Physical Verification
rubric_items.description: The response should encourage the learner to physically look at or measure multiple edges of their tripod model to prove to themselves that the distances from the center are identical.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Answer
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner that 'all sides are equal,' 'it is an equilateral triangle,' or 'it doesn't matter.'

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply repeat the phrase 'any two feet' or tell them to 'just pick one' without providing a conceptual or observational prompt to help the learner understand why.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive conflict and guessing ('Yellow? No, wait... black?') because they lack a formal understanding of genetic dominance. They are beginning to realize that their previous assumption—that a single yellow gene is enough to make a dog yellow—might be flawed, but they need conceptual scaffolding to understand why one gene masks another.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a conceptual anchor (such as introducing the concept of dominance or referencing the black parents' phenotypes) and prompt the learner to use it to definitively deduce the color of the heterozygous dog.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Dominance Concept
rubric_items.description: The tutor provides scaffolding to help the learner determine which gene 'wins', either by introducing the concept of dominant/recessive traits or by prompting the learner to consider the parents' actual physical color as evidence of which gene is stronger.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Heterozygous Outcome
rubric_items.description: The tutor directs the learner to apply the scaffolding to explicitly conclude the physical color of the dog with the mixed gene combination (one black, one yellow).

rubric_items.title: Validate Cognitive Conflict
rubric_items.description: The tutor acknowledges or validates the learner's hesitation and self-correction (e.g., 'You're right to second-guess that!').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly confirms that the dog will be black, or directly states that black is dominant, thereby giving away the answer before the learner has articulated the reasoning.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unscaffolded Prompting
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply asks the learner to justify their guess (e.g., 'Why black?' or 'Are you sure?') without offering any conceptual support, leaving the learner stranded in their confusion.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that claws provide a strong grip but is stuck on why this grip alone cannot stabilize the bird during the backward push of pecking. They need to visualize the difference between holding on at a single point (which creates a pivot) and bracing (which prevents swinging backward) to see why the tail is necessary.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt, ideally using a relatable physical analogy, that asks the learner to predict what happens to a body when it is pushed backward at the top while only gripping at the bottom.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Consequence of Push
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to predict what physical motion would happen to the bird's body if it only held on with its claws while its upper body is pushed backward by the tree.

rubric_items.title: Relatable Physical Analogy
rubric_items.description: Introduces a concrete, relatable scenario (such as holding onto a pole or rope while being pushed back at the shoulders) to help the learner visualize the mechanics of gripping versus bracing.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Grip
rubric_items.description: Explicitly acknowledges that the claws are indeed holding on tightly, validating the learner's intuition before challenging its sufficiency.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Mechanics
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner the answer (e.g., explaining that the bird would swing backward, pivot, or hinge around its feet) instead of asking them to deduce the motion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dismissing the Claws
rubric_items.description: Ignores the learner's specific question about the claws, or simply repeats that the tail is needed without addressing why a strong grip is insufficient to stop the backward motion.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has just experienced a conceptual breakthrough, realizing that the highly coordinated penguin huddle operates without central leadership or conscious planning, which directly challenges their hidden belief about animals making conscious agreements. They now need to solidify this understanding of decentralized behavior by articulating what actually drives the system in the absence of a leader.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm the learner's insight that no one is in charge, and then prompt the learner to summarize what actually drives the group's rotation (the individual physical response to cold) to replace their old 'conscious agreement' model.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Decentralization
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly validate the learner's realization that there is no leader, boss, or central control directing the penguin huddle.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Alternative Driver
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to articulate what actually causes the organized rotation if there is no leader, prompting them to connect the lack of a leader back to the individual penguins pushing inward to get warm.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Conceptual Shift
rubric_items.description: The tutor praises the learner for grasping a counterintuitive biological concept (that complex, seemingly planned group behavior can happen without anyone actually being in charge).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explaining Emergence Directly
rubric_items.description: The tutor over-explains how self-organizing or emergent systems work, giving away the answer rather than asking the learner to explain how individual actions replace the need for a leader.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-End Confirmation
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply agrees that nobody is in charge but fails to ask a follow-up question, leaving the learner stranded without prompting them to consolidate their new understanding of the mechanism.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced the concept of dominance at the individual kernel level (purple + yellow = purple). They now need to connect this micro-level genetic rule back to the macro-level observation of the whole cob to fully dismantle their prior belief that the cob is a single offspring with uniform traits.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct deduction and then prompt them to apply this rule to explain how a yellow kernel could possibly appear on the cob, given that purple 'wins'.

rubric_items.title: Validate Deduction
rubric_items.description: Confirm that the learner is absolutely right: a kernel with both instructions will indeed be purple.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Macro-Application
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to use this 'winning' rule to explain the variation on the cob, such as asking what instructions a kernel must inherit to actually end up yellow.

rubric_items.title: Integrate Multiple Pollen Sources
rubric_items.description: Link the question about color variation back to the earlier established fact that pollen comes from 'different dads' (e.g., 'Given all those different dads...').

rubric_items.title: Optional: Formalize Terminology
rubric_items.description: Introduce the formal term 'dominant' for the winning instruction and/or 'recessive' for the hidden one, now that the learner has fully grounded the concept.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Recessive Condition
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that a yellow kernel requires two yellow instructions; this is the exact deduction the learner should make next.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unmoored Praise
rubric_items.description: Do not simply praise the learner and ask a vague question (e.g., 'Great job! Does that make sense?'); the response must anchor the next step in the cob's color variation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing a procedural bottleneck with the slope formula, specifically hesitating over how to assign the points (4, 2) and (2, 4) to the variables x1, y1, x2, and y2. They likely believe there is a strict mathematical rule dictating which point must be designated as 'point 1'.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that either point can be designated as the first point and prompt the learner to make a choice and assign the coordinates themselves.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Arbitrary Assignment
rubric_items.description: Explain or guide the learner to realize that it does not matter which of the two points, (4, 2) or (2, 4), is chosen as 'point 1' as long as they are consistent.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner Choice
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to pick one of the points to be (x1, y1) and explicitly state what x1 and y1 would be.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Question
rubric_items.description: Validate the learner's hesitation, as asking which point is first is a common and good clarifying question when setting up the slope formula.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Doing the Assignment
rubric_items.description: Do not assign the coordinates for the learner (e.g., 'Let x1 be 4 and y1 be 2').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Calculating the Slope Prematurely
