rubric_items.description: The response asks a generic question (like 'What do you think?' or 'Are you sure?') without directing the learner's attention to the physical constraints of feeding or warming 100 chicks.

rubric_items.title: Premature Shift to Frogs
rubric_items.description: The response shifts the focus back to the frogs' survival rates or compares the two animals again before the learner has resolved why the robin's high-care strategy fails with 100 eggs.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the sensor's number is irrational, but is experiencing cognitive dissonance because they still equate 'predictable' with 'rational.' They need to separate the everyday concept of a predictable pattern from the strict mathematical definition of a repeating fixed block.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the number is irrational, validate that it is indeed predictable, and prompt the learner to realize that a number can have a predictable pattern without having a repeating fixed block.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Irrationality
rubric_items.description: Confirm the learner's correct conclusion that the sensor's number is irrational.

rubric_items.title: Validate Predictability
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and validate the learner's observation that the number's pattern (adding a zero each time) is indeed predictable.

rubric_items.title: Reconcile Predictable vs. Repeating
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to articulate or recognize that a pattern can be predictable without being a repeating fixed block.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dismissing Predictability
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that claim the number is not predictable, which is factually incorrect and undermines the learner's valid observation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Dissonance
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that confirm the number is irrational but fail to address the learner's explicit confusion about how an irrational number can be predictable.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Introducing New Examples
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that introduce other irrational numbers (like pi or square roots) to explain irrationality, which distracts from resolving the confusion about this specific predictable decimal.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating shape or density with weight, mistakenly believing that crumpling a piece of paper makes it heavier. Before they can isolate the effect of surface area on air resistance, they must first recognize the principle of mass conservation—that changing the paper's shape does not change its weight.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to consider whether any material was added or removed when the flat sheet was crumpled into a ball, guiding them to realize the weight remains identical.

rubric_items.title: Target Material Conservation
rubric_items.description: The response must direct the learner to consider what happens to the actual amount of paper during the crumpling process (e.g., asking if any paper was added or taken away).

rubric_items.title: Preserve Cognitive Ownership
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to deduce for themselves whether the weight changes, rather than simply stating that the two pieces of paper weigh the same.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges why the learner might intuitively think the ball is heavier (e.g., noting that it feels more solid, looks denser, or falls faster).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner that the flat paper and the crumpled ball weigh exactly the same.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Discussing Falling Speed
rubric_items.description: The response attempts to discuss which object falls faster or brings air resistance back into the conversation before the learner has explicitly resolved the weight misconception.

learning_objective: LS1.B Growth and Development of Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly but tentatively deduced that the tire swing does not move upward, overcoming their initial belief that the trunk stretches. However, they still need to consolidate this deduction with the mechanism of apical growth to fully resolve their earlier confusion about how the tree gets taller.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct conclusion about the swing and prompt them to explain in their own words why it stays in place despite the tree growing taller.

rubric_items.title: Validate Deduction
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirm the learner's tentative conclusion that the tire swing stays at the exact same height.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain in their own words why the swing stays at the same height while the tree gets taller, connecting the swing's position to the concept of top-only growth.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final summary of why the swing stays in place for the learner; leave the cognitive work of connecting the growth mechanism to the swing's position to them.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: Do not move on to a new topic or scenario without first having the learner articulate the complete explanation for the swing's position.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Prior Misconception
rubric_items.description: Explicitly contrast this correct conclusion with the learner's earlier idea that the trunk stretches like playdough, highlighting how their understanding has changed.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly concluded that there is no outward force, relying on their understanding of inertia, but their language ('I guess not') shows they are still tentative. They need validation of this counterintuitive conclusion to solidify their new understanding and resolve any lingering cognitive dissonance.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's conclusion and synthesize the concept, contrasting the feeling of an outward push with the physical reality of inertia.

rubric_items.title: Validate Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's conclusion that there is no physical outward force pulling them.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Feeling vs. Reality
rubric_items.description: Address the learner's tentativeness by acknowledging that while it strongly feels like an outward push, it is actually just the body's inertia.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Bare Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not provide a simple 'Correct' or 'Yes' without reinforcing the conceptual takeaway, as the learner's 'I guess not' indicates they still need conceptual support.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Jargon
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce new terminology (such as 'centrifugal' or 'centripetal' force) that could overcomplicate the learner's newly grounded conceptual understanding.

rubric_items.title: Check for Confidence
rubric_items.description: Ask a brief, low-stakes question to gauge whether the learner feels more confident about this explanation now.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive conflict, correctly recognizing that lighter objects generally require less force, but struggling to reconcile this with the idea that a light, crumpled piece of paper would get stuck. They are fixated on the variable of weight and need help isolating how the object's uneven shape interacts with the bumpy surface.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct intuition about weight, then prompt them to consider how the paper's uneven shape physically interacts with the bumps (e.g., by catching or failing to roll) despite its light weight.

rubric_items.title: Validate Weight Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges the learner's valid point that a lighter object generally requires less force to move.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Physical Interaction
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to explain how the uneven or wrinkly edges of the paper physically interact with the bumps on the bubble wrap.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tells the learner that the paper gets stuck because it cannot roll or because its edges catch on the bumps.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Ignoring the Learner's Point
rubric_items.description: Dismisses or ignores the learner's statement about weight by simply repeating the previous question about shape without bridging the two concepts.

rubric_items.title: Isolate Variables Prompt
rubric_items.description: Suggests a contrastive thought experiment that holds weight constant but changes shape (e.g., comparing the crumpled paper to a perfectly round, equally light hollow bead).

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a loop, insisting that light energy directly powers cellular functions during the day because they cannot distinguish between capturing energy (photosynthesis) and utilizing it (cellular respiration). They need a conceptual bridge to realize why light, despite being available, cannot be the direct fuel for immediate cellular work.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a cognitive conflict—such as asking how underground roots survive without light, or why the plant bothers making sugar if light works directly—to help the learner deduce that energy must be converted into a chemical form to be usable.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Cognitive Conflict
rubric_items.description: The response introduces a logical contradiction or concrete scenario (e.g., asking about plant parts in the dark like roots, or asking why the plant makes sugar at all) to challenge the belief that light directly powers cell functions.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Agreement
rubric_items.description: The response prompts the learner to reconcile their 'just light' answer with the fact established earlier in the dialogue that the plant stores energy in glucose.

rubric_items.title: Validate Ultimate Source
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that the learner's intuition has merit because light is indeed the original, ultimate source of the plant's energy.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner that cells run on chemical energy, ATP, or glucose, doing the reasoning for them instead of letting them deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response merely rejects the learner's answer ('No, not light') or repeats the previous question ('What form of energy do cells run on?') without providing a new conceptual scaffold.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully deduced the components of the expression for the total weight (15x + 75). The immediate next step is to transition from building this expression to setting up an inequality by incorporating the 200-gram maximum weight limit.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the learner's correct addition of 75, synthesize the full expression (15x + 75), and prompt the learner to relate this total weight to the 200-gram limit without giving away the inequality symbol.

rubric_items.title: Affirm and Synthesize Expression
rubric_items.description: The tutor should confirm that adding 75 is correct and establish the complete expression (15x + 75) for the total weight.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Constraint
rubric_items.description: The tutor should introduce or remind the learner of the 200-gram weight limit and ask them how to represent that the total weight cannot exceed this amount.

rubric_items.title: Contextualize the Limit
rubric_items.description: The tutor frames the 200-gram limit using the physical context of the problem (e.g., 'maximum capacity' or 'can only carry up to') rather than just presenting it as a naked number.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Inequality
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not provide the mathematical symbol (e.g., <=, <) or write out the full inequality (15x + 75 <= 200) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Solving
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not ask the learner to start calculating or solving for 'x' before the inequality itself has been explicitly formulated.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the mechanics of mutation and inheritance but still attributes the evolutionary shift to an internal, purposeful drive ('survival instinct') rather than an external environmental pressure. They need help shifting the locus of control from the butterfly's internal desires to the predator's external actions.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that redirects the learner's focus from the butterfly's internal feelings to the external environmental factor (the predators) that actually determined which butterflies lived and died.

rubric_items.title: Shift Focus to External Pressure
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to identify the external factor or agent (e.g., asking 'who or what was eating them?') that actually determined survival, shifting focus away from the butterfly's internal drive.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Intentionality
rubric_items.description: Explicitly addresses or questions the concept of 'survival instinct' to help the learner separate conscious behavioral drives from passive physical traits like wing color.

rubric_items.title: Anchor in Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Reminds the learner of their own previous correct statement that the orange butterflies 'wouldn't get eaten' to help them deduce the external driver.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Naming the Driver)
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for directly telling the learner that predators, birds, or the environment drove the change, rather than making the learner identify it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness (Simple Rejection)
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for simply saying 'no' or 'not quite' to 'survival instinct' without providing a concrete prompt that guides the learner toward the environmental cause.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly multiplied the planet's distance (10 AU) by the scale factor (2.5) instead of dividing, resulting in an answer of 25 inches. They need to recognize that this answer is physically impossible because it exceeds the total 12-inch length of their paper model.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should draw the learner's attention to the physical constraint of their 12-inch paper to create cognitive conflict with their 25-inch answer, prompting the learner to realize their mathematical operation was incorrect.

rubric_items.title: Induce Cognitive Conflict via Paper Length
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to compare their calculated distance (25 inches) to the total physical length of their paper model (12 inches).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that they should have divided instead of multiplied, and do not provide the correct answer of 4 inches.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not reject the learner's answer with a generic 'try again' or 'check your math' without grounding the feedback in the physical impossibility of fitting 25 inches on the paper.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Correct Components
rubric_items.description: Validate that the learner correctly identified the two numbers needed for the calculation (10 AU and 2.5 AU/inch) before addressing the error in how they were combined.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confusing the starting height (2) with the elapsed time (3 hours) when trying to translate 'adding 0.5 three times' into a multiplication expression. They need to recognize that the multiplication should involve the growth rate and the number of hours, not the starting height.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should gently address the learner's misuse of '2' by reminding them of its role as the starting height, and prompt them to focus specifically on what numbers to multiply to represent 'adding 0.5 three times'.

rubric_items.title: Address the Misused Value
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly address the learner's use of '2', either by reminding them that 2 is the starting height or by asking them what the 2 represents in this context.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Correct Multiplication
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to determine the correct numbers to multiply to represent the 3 hours of growth (or 'adding 0.5 three times').

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Correct Factor
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that the learner correctly identified 0.5 as one of the numbers to multiply.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Expression
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly give the learner the correct multiplication expression (e.g., 'It should be 0.5 times 3').

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Equation Building
rubric_items.description: The response should not jump ahead to combining the starting height and the multiplication into a full expression (e.g., '2 + 0.5 * 3') before the learner has successfully formulated the multiplication part.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply reject the learner's attempt (e.g., 'No, try again') without referencing the specific numbers (0.5, 2, or 3) involved in the confusion.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully calculated the score for a single target (150 + 25) but is hesitating because they realize the number of targets could vary ('if there's more?'). They are at the crucial pivot point between concrete arithmetic and algebraic generalization, needing to establish a pattern before formalizing it with a variable.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's foresight and prompt them to calculate the score for a specific, small number of multiple targets (e.g., 2 or 3) to establish the pattern of repeated addition or multiplication.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Pattern Building
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to consider a specific, concrete number of targets greater than one (e.g., 'What if you hit 2 targets?' or 'Let's say there are 3 targets.').

rubric_items.title: Focus on the Operation
rubric_items.description: The response should ask the learner to explain the math or steps they would use for that new number of targets, maintaining focus on the operation rather than just the final score.

rubric_items.title: Validating Learner Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges or praises the learner's foresight in asking 'what if there's more?' as a strong mathematical instinct.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response introduces a variable (e.g., 'x', 't', 'n') or provides the general algebraic expression (150 + 25x) before the learner has explored the concrete pattern.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response asks a completely open-ended question (e.g., 'What do you think happens?' or 'How would you write that?') without anchoring the learner to a specific, concrete number of targets first.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly guessed that the 'angle at the tip' is the one to measure, but they may not fully realize that this angle is required specifically because it is the 'included angle' between the two known sides. They now need to connect this physical setup (two known sides and the angle between them) to the formal Side-Angle-Side (SAS) congruence theorem.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's choice of the tip angle, explicitly highlight that it is located between the two known sides, and prompt the learner to name the corresponding geometry theorem.

rubric_items.title: Validate Tip Angle
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner correctly identified the 'angle at the tip' as the right angle to measure.

rubric_items.title: Highlight the Included Angle
rubric_items.description: Establish (either by stating it or prompting the learner to notice) that the tip angle is the one located exactly between the two outer sides whose lengths are already known.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Congruence Theorem
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to identify the specific geometry rule or theorem that proves congruence using two sides and the angle between them.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Base Angles
rubric_items.description: Reward responses that briefly ask or explain why the tip angle works but a base angle would not, addressing the necessity of the included angle.

rubric_items.title: Prematurely Naming SAS
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that give away the name of the theorem ('Side-Angle-Side' or 'SAS') instead of asking the learner to provide it.

rubric_items.title: Missing the Formal Connection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that confirm the angle is correct but fail to prompt the learner to connect this setup to a formal congruence theorem.

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that mold gets energy by breaking down sugar from the strawberry, but they lack a mental model for the molecular mechanism, assuming the energy release 'just happens.' They have hit a conceptual wall and need concrete scaffolding to visualize how the connections (bonds) within the sugar molecules store energy that is released during chemical rearrangement.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a targeted scaffold or a concrete analogy (such as a compressed spring, a stretched rubber band, or snapping a glow stick) to help the learner visualize energy stored in the connections between atoms, bridging the gap between 'breaking apart' and 'energy release'.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Molecular Connections
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner's attention to what holds the pieces of the sugar molecule together (the chemical bonds) as the source or location of the stored energy.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Visualization
rubric_items.description: Introduces a relatable analogy or visual scaffold (e.g., a compressed spring, a stretched rubber band, or snapping apart linked blocks) to make the abstract concept of releasing stored energy concrete.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Breaking Step
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or validates the learner's previous correct insight that breaking the sugars down is indeed the necessary trigger, normalizing their current confusion about the invisible mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Mechanism)
rubric_items.description: Directly explains the scientific mechanism (e.g., 'energy is stored in chemical bonds and released when they are broken and rearranged') instead of guiding the learner to conceptualize it themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness (Stranding the Learner)
rubric_items.description: Asks another broad, open-ended question about 'how' or 'why' energy is released without providing any new conceptual scaffolding, ignoring that the learner has already hit a wall with 'It just happens?'.

learning_objective: LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is expressing a classic 'use and disuse' misconception, believing that unused structures naturally shrink over generations even if they aren't harmful. They need to realize that for a trait to shrink across generations, the change must be tied to inheritance and survival, not just an individual's lack of use.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe or analogy that asks the learner to explain the mechanism of inheritance, specifically how an unused trait in a parent would cause their offspring to be born with a smaller version of that trait.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the Mechanism of Inheritance
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explain how an unused eye socket would shrink across generations, focusing their attention on the mechanism of passing traits from parent to offspring.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Intuition of Atrophy
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that it makes intuitive sense for unused things to shrink or weaken during an individual's lifetime (like an unused muscle), before questioning how that affects the next generation.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Lamarckian Fallacy Directly
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that traits acquired or lost during a lifetime aren't passed on to offspring; leave the cognitive work of realizing this to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Ignoring the 'Shrinking' Misconception
rubric_items.description: Do not simply repeat the previous question ('But why would it disappear?') or ignore the learner's specific idea that unused traits naturally shrink.

rubric_items.title: Use a Somatic Analogy
rubric_items.description: Introduce a brief, relatable analogy about an acquired physical change (like lifting weights or losing a finger) to help the learner distinguish between individual lifetime changes and inherited traits.

learning_objective: LS1.B Growth and Development of Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a loop, repeatedly suggesting that the shell itself grows despite the tutor's previous explanations that it is a dead snail shell. They need a direct intervention that breaks this pattern by explicitly contrasting 'dead' with 'growing' and guiding them back to their earlier correct insight about finding an already-bigger shell.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted correction that explicitly states dead shells cannot grow, followed by a prompt for the learner to recall their earlier idea of finding a shell that is already bigger.

rubric_items.title: Confront 'Growing Shell' Misconception
rubric_items.description: Explicitly addresses the learner's 'growing shell' utterance by stating or guiding the learner to conclude that dead objects cannot grow.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Static Size Search
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to deduce what kind of shell the crab must look for on the beach, given that the shells' sizes are permanently fixed.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Correct Insight
rubric_items.description: Reminds the learner of their own earlier correct statement ('Go find a bigger shell') to help them break out of their current loop.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vague Repetition
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that simply repeat a variation of 'what does it search for?' without first directly shutting down the 'growing shell' misconception, as this questioning loop has already failed.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that give away the final answer by explicitly telling the learner 'it finds a shell that is already bigger' rather than prompting them to deduce it from the fact that shells don't grow.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating their physical appearance (phenotype) with their genetic makeup (genotype), assuming that because the 'no-dimple' allele is hidden in them, it cannot be passed on. They need to realize that reproduction passes on the DNA stored in their cells, not their physical traits.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should guide the learner to distinguish between their physical appearance and their DNA, prompting them to consider what exactly gets passed down to children.

rubric_items.title: Distinguish Trait from DNA
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to distinguish between having the physical trait (dimples) and carrying the genetic instruction (the hidden allele) when thinking about what gets passed to children.

rubric_items.title: Re-anchor to Hidden Allele
rubric_items.description: Reminds the learner, or asks them to recall, the fact established in the previous turn: that the 'no-dimple' allele is still physically present in their cells.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Intuitive Logic
rubric_items.description: Validates why the learner's assumption makes intuitive sense (e.g., acknowledging that it is logical to assume you only pass on the traits you actually show).

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that they can pass on the hidden allele, failing to let them deduce it from the presence of the allele in their cells.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Introduces probabilities, Punnett squares, or the mechanics of meiosis (e.g., 'there is a 50% chance') before the learner grasps the qualitative possibility of passing on a hidden allele.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully adopted the 'tug-of-war' analogy and is asking the logical next question about which force dominates. They need to connect this conceptual tug-of-war to the observable reality that atomic nuclei actually exist and stay together, which will allow them to deduce the winner themselves.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to deduce the winner of the tug-of-war by considering the fact that protons actually do manage to stay together inside the nucleus.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Deduction from Reality
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce the winner of the tug-of-war by pointing out the observable outcome (e.g., asking them to consider the fact that the nucleus stays together or that atoms exist).

rubric_items.title: Reinforce the Distance Constraint
rubric_items.description: The response should maintain the crucial context that this outcome (who wins) is strictly dependent on the incredibly tiny distances inside the nucleus.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Logic
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly validate that 'who wins?' is exactly the right logical question to ask based on the tug-of-war analogy.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly tell the learner that the strong nuclear force wins; the learner must be allowed to deduce this.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Deflection
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not respond with an unguided question like 'What do you think?' or 'Who do you think wins?' without anchoring it to the physical clue that the nucleus stays together.

learning_objective: PS3.D Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is likely looking at a data table with multiple mass values (e.g., water mass, initial candle mass, final candle mass) and is confused because the tutor's phrase 'change in the candle's mass' does not match a single raw measurement they can just read off the page. They need help bridging the tutor's abstract instruction to the concrete 'before' and 'after' data points they actually collected.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to locate the candle's specific starting and ending mass values from their data so they can calculate the difference themselves.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Initial and Final Values
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to look at their data and identify the candle's specific mass before it burned and after it burned.

rubric_items.title: Clarify it is a Calculated Value
rubric_items.description: Explicitly clarifies that the number they need is not a single raw measurement on their data sheet, but a difference they must calculate from two separate readings.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Multiple Masses
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's confusion by acknowledging that having multiple mass readings in the experiment (water, candle before, candle after) makes this step tricky.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating Abstract Terms
rubric_items.description: Repeats phrases like 'change in mass,' 'mass lost,' or 'the candle's mass' without breaking them down into the concrete starting and ending measurements.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving the Numbers
rubric_items.description: Provides the exact numerical values for the candle's mass or performs the subtraction for the learner.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands how to find the hypotenuse but is now asking for the 'adjacent' side without realizing that 'adjacent' (unlike the hypotenuse) is relative to a specific reference angle. They need to understand that they must choose one of the acute angles in the projector setup before they can identify the adjacent side.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explain that 'adjacent' depends on which angle we are looking from, and prompt the learner to identify or choose a specific reference angle in their projector setup.

rubric_items.title: Establish Reference Angle Dependency
rubric_items.description: The tutor explains or guides the learner to realize that the 'adjacent' side changes depending on which acute angle is being used as the starting point.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Specific Angle
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks the learner to choose or identify a specific angle in the projector setup (e.g., the angle at the projector lens or the angle at the wall) to focus on.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Hypotenuse Identification
rubric_items.description: The tutor clarifies that the adjacent side will be the side next to their chosen angle that is *not* the hypotenuse (the beam) they just identified.

rubric_items.title: Premature Identification
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly names a side as the adjacent side, or tells the learner which side it is, without first establishing which reference angle is being used.

rubric_items.title: Unstructured Guessing
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply asks 'Which one do you think it is?' or 'What does adjacent mean?' without introducing the necessary prerequisite of picking a reference angle, leaving the learner to guess blindly.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly intuits that a single high-amplitude wave carries more energy than a single low-amplitude ripple, but they are conflating the energy of an individual wave with the total energy transferred over time by a continuous stream. Furthermore, their hidden belief suggests they assume that because wave speed is constant, the overall energy transfer must also remain constant regardless of frequency.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that a single big wave carries more energy than a single tiny ripple, but then prompt the learner to visualize how the energy arrives at the edge of the pan over time (e.g., one large impact versus a continuous series of smaller impacts).

rubric_items.title: Validate Single-Wave Comparison
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's intuition is correct if they are comparing the energy of one giant wave to just one tiny ripple.

rubric_items.title: Shift Focus to Cumulative Delivery
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate the total energy delivered by the continuous stream over time, shifting their focus from individual wave amplitude to the rate of energy transfer.

rubric_items.title: Incorporate Wave Speed and Arrival Rate
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to consider how the constant travel speed of the waves affects how many tiny ripples will arrive at the edge of the pan compared to the single big wave, directly challenging their hidden belief.

rubric_items.title: Recall Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of their own recent conclusion ('more ripples means more energy') to help them resolve their current confusion about the fast stream.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explicitly Stating the Difference
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for doing the cognitive work of explaining how the energy delivery differs (e.g., telling the learner 'The big wave is one big burst, while the ripples are a steady stream').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for rejecting the learner's guess ('Not quite') or asking them to try again without introducing a specific physical parameter (like time, speed, or the edge of the pan) to help them re-evaluate.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner recognizes that the pole's weight is key to stability but is guessing at the mechanism ('pulls them back up') without a clear physical model. They need scaffolding to visualize how the distribution of that heavy weight interacts with the walker's tipping motion.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a concrete thought experiment—such as asking what happens to the opposite end of the pole when the walker tilts to one side—to help the learner reason through the mechanics of the balancing act.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Tilting Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to analyze the physical behavior of the pole during a tilt, such as asking what happens to the ends of the pole or how the weight shifts when the walker leans to one side.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Counteracting Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response should acknowledge that the learner's instinct is on the right track—that the pole does indeed help counteract the tilt or bring them back to center.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly explain the underlying physics concepts (like center of gravity, torque, or rotational inertia) before the learner has reasoned through the physical behavior themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ungrounded 'How' Question
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply ask the learner to explain their guess (e.g., 'How does a downward pull pull them up?') without providing a concrete scenario or visualization to help them figure it out.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is fixated on the arithmetic operation of subtraction as strictly 'taking away' or reducing a total, which conflicts with their recent realization that the bill increases. They need to reconceptualize subtraction in this specific context as finding a difference or measuring an excess over a limit.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's observation and prompt them to reflect on what the subtraction actually accomplished when they calculated the extra minutes earlier, helping them see it as finding a difference rather than taking away.

rubric_items.title: Validate Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is absolutely correct to notice the subtraction sign and that it usually means 'taking away'.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Reconceptualization of Subtraction
rubric_items.description: Ask a question that guides the learner to consider an alternative meaning for subtraction in this context, such as finding a difference, distance, or the amount over a limit.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Concrete Example
rubric_items.description: Explicitly refer back to the specific calculation the learner already performed (e.g., 210 - 200 = 10) to ground the conceptual question in their own prior work.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Give Away the Concept
rubric_items.description: Directly tell the learner that subtraction can mean finding a difference or excess, doing the conceptual reconciliation for them instead of prompting them to realize it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Change the Subject
rubric_items.description: Ignore the learner's specific fixation on the subtraction operation and attempt to move on to the multiplication or addition parts of the formula.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly assumes that a sudden shift in predator behavior (hawks switching to eating rabbits) will leave the new prey population unaffected. They need to recognize that a sudden increase in predation pressure directly reduces the prey population size.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a targeted probe to help the learner visualize the physical consequence of all the hungry hawks suddenly hunting rabbits, guiding them to deduce that the rabbit population will decrease.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the 'Fine' Assumption via Predation Pressure
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to evaluate how a sudden influx of hawks actively hunting rabbits would affect the number of surviving rabbits.

rubric_items.title: Reference the Hawks' Hunger
rubric_items.description: Explicitly mentions that the hawks are hungry or eating a lot of rabbits to replace their lost food source, emphasizing the intensity of the new predation.

rubric_items.title: Draw Parallel to Previous Logic
rubric_items.description: Encourages the learner to apply the same cause-and-effect reasoning they just used for the acorn/mouse relationship to the new hawk/rabbit dynamic.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for directly stating that the rabbit population will decrease, shrink, or not be fine, which would bypass the learner's own reasoning.

rubric_items.title: Penalize Generic Pushback
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that merely question the learner's guess (e.g., "Are you sure?") without directing their attention to the specific mechanism of hawks eating the rabbits.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the intimidating 10-foot figure and needs clarification that the required foam thickness is only a fraction of that total wavelength. They lack the specific domain knowledge (the quarter-wavelength rule) to determine what that fraction is.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly state that the wave's energy peaks at one-quarter of its wavelength, reassure the learner that this is much less than 10 feet, and prompt them to calculate what one-quarter of 10 feet would be.

rubric_items.title: Direct Reassurance
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly answer the learner's 'Still ten feet?' question by confirming that the required thickness is significantly less than 10 feet.

rubric_items.title: Introduce the Quarter-Wavelength Rule
rubric_items.description: The tutor must provide the specific domain knowledge that the wave's air movement peaks at one-quarter (1/4) of its wavelength.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Application to the 10-Foot Wave
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to apply the newly provided fraction to the 10-foot example to determine the practical panel thickness.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Doing the Math
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not calculate the final thickness (e.g., 2.5 feet) for the learner, leaving the arithmetic step for the learner to complete.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Guess-the-Fraction
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not ask the learner to guess the fraction (e.g., 'What fraction do you think it is?'), as the learner has no physics background to derive the quarter-wavelength rule.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing a semantic confusion, taking the scientific term 'field' literally and mapping it to a familiar physical space (a soccer field). They need a direct, grade-appropriate clarification that distinguishes the everyday use of the word from the scientific concept of an invisible area of influence.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should gently validate the linguistic connection, explicitly clarify that a magnetic field is an invisible space rather than a physical place, and describe it simply as the area around the magnet where its pull can be felt.

rubric_items.title: Disambiguate 'Field'
rubric_items.description: Explicitly distinguishes the scientific meaning of 'field' from a physical sports field, clarifying that a magnetic field is an invisible space or area.

rubric_items.title: Define Magnetic Field Simply
rubric_items.description: Defines the magnetic field in simple, concrete terms as the specific area around the magnet where its pulling power works.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Misinterpretation
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's literal interpretation of the word 'field' (e.g., acknowledging it's the same word or that both are types of spaces) to maintain engagement and prevent them from feeling foolish.

rubric_items.title: Ground in Sensory Experience
rubric_items.description: Suggests a concrete sensory example, such as feeling two magnets pull or push before they actually touch, to help the learner visualize the invisible field.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Technical Overcomplication
rubric_items.description: Introduces overly technical physics jargon (e.g., vector fields, electrons, field lines) that exceeds the learner's current conceptual level and distracts from the basic definition.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a vague question (e.g., 'What else could a field mean?' or 'Think about science instead') that leaves the learner stranded without the necessary vocabulary correction.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly evaluated their expression to find that their 40-minute guess results in a 95% charge, which is just short of the 100% goal. They now need to transition from evaluating a specific guess to formally setting up an equation to find the exact time required for a full charge.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the 95% calculation, point out that it is close to but not quite a full charge, and prompt the learner to set their expression equal to 100 to create the final equation.

rubric_items.title: Validate Calculation
rubric_items.description: Confirms that 95% is the correct battery percentage after 40 minutes.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Equation Creation
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to state what their expression (15 + 2m) should be set equal to in order to find the exact time for a fully charged battery (100%).

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Estimate Quality
rubric_items.description: Notes that the learner's initial guess of 40 minutes was a very close estimate.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Equation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly provides the final equation (e.g., '15 + 2m = 100') instead of requiring the learner to construct it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Bypassing Equation Creation
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to calculate the final time directly (e.g., 'How many more minutes to reach 100%?') without first having them state the formal equation, which undermines the 'Creating Equations' objective.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly moved past the idea of lifetime DNA changes and understands that survival drives the population shift, but they are now oversimplifying natural selection as an all-or-nothing event ('Only they survived?'). They need guidance to transition from binary survival to the concept of differential reproductive success—that the trait provided a relative advantage over time.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's focus on survival but ask a targeted question that challenges the absolute word 'Only', prompting the learner to consider if those without the trait could still survive but perhaps have a harder time or fewer children.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Absolute Survival
rubric_items.description: The tutor must specifically question the all-or-nothing assumption in the learner's utterance (e.g., by focusing on the word 'Only' or asking if every single person without the trait died).

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Relative Advantage
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask a guiding question that directs the learner to consider differential success, such as asking who might be healthier, live longer, or have more children, rather than just who lives or dies.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Survival Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The tutor should validate that the learner is correctly looking at survival and reproduction as the core driver of the population change.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explaining Differential Reproduction
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not explicitly tell the learner that natural selection is a gradual process of relative reproductive advantage; they must leave the cognitive work of realizing this to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unstructured Rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not simply reject the learner's guess (e.g., 'No, not only them') without providing a concrete follow-up prompt about the rest of the population's ability to survive and reproduce.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited that an attractive force ('pulling') must counteract the protons' repulsion, successfully moving past their previous mechanical 'blocking' misconception. They now need to consolidate this insight by comparing the relative strength of this attractive pull to the electromagnetic push in order to explain nuclear stability.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's 'pulling' intuition and prompt them to deduce how strong this pulling force must be compared to the protons' repulsive force to keep the nucleus from flying apart.

rubric_items.title: Affirm the 'Pull' Intuition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's insight that there is an attractive force or 'pull' keeping the particles together.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Relative Strength
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to compare the strength of this new 'pulling' force to the repulsive 'pushing' force of the protons (e.g., asking which one must be stronger for the nucleus to stay intact).

rubric_items.title: Introduce Formal Vocabulary
rubric_items.description: Provide the formal name for this pulling force (the 'Strong Nuclear Force') to give the learner the correct scientific terminology for their correct intuition.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Force Balance
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that the pulling force is stronger than the pushing force, as this steals their opportunity to deduce the mechanics of nuclear stability themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Continuations
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a generic confirmation followed by an unanchored question (e.g., 'Yes! What else?') that fails to contrast the new 'pull' with the previously discussed 'push'.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that memory is required to evaluate the shadow but incorrectly guesses that these memories are stored in the sensory organ (the eyes) rather than the processing organ (the brain). They need help distinguishing the act of gathering immediate visual information from the act of storing and retrieving past information.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should ask a guiding question that prompts the learner to define the actual job of the eyes (seeing/sensing) to help them realize that a different organ must be responsible for storing memories.

rubric_items.title: Probe Eye Function
rubric_items.description: Rewards prompting the learner to articulate what the eyes actually do (e.g., seeing, taking in light) to spark the realization that they do not store memories.

rubric_items.title: Reconnect to Prior Brain Insight
rubric_items.description: Rewards referencing the learner's earlier realization that 'the brain has to decide' to help them deduce where the memories needed for that decision must live.

rubric_items.title: Validate Sensory Input
rubric_items.description: Rewards acknowledging that the eyes are indeed the necessary first step in the process (because they see the shadow) before redirecting to where the memory is stored.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Penalizes explicitly telling the learner that memories are stored in the brain or directly stating that the eyes are only for seeing.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalizes simply saying 'No', 'Not quite', or 'Try again' without offering a conceptual probe about the function of the eyes or the brain.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that an equation needs a dependent variable and an equals sign ('y ='), but is hesitant to assemble the full expression. They need validation for this step and a final nudge to combine it with the components they already identified.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Confirm that starting with 'y =' is correct, and prompt the learner to complete the equation by appending the expression they built earlier.

rubric_items.title: Validate Equation Start
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that starting the equation with 'y =' is correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Completion
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to finish the equation by combining 'y =' with the mathematical pieces they already identified.

rubric_items.title: Recall Prior Pieces
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of the specific components they already found (100, 0.75, and x) to help them assemble the final answer.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Equation
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the complete final equation (e.g., 'y = 100 * 0.75^x') for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a generic prompt (e.g., 'What do you think?') that leaves the learner unsure if their proposal of 'y =' was correct.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on their familiar schema of X-rays showing bones, failing to apply the immediately preceding fact that terahertz waves stop at the skin. They need a prompt that directly contrasts their guess ('bones') with the physical reality of where bones are located relative to the skin.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should gently challenge the learner's guess by asking them to consider whether waves that stop at the skin can actually reach the bones.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the 'Bones' Guess
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate their guess by reminding them that bones are located beneath the skin, or asking if waves that stop at the skin can reach the bones.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Reflecting Surface
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to identify what the waves actually bounce off of or what the scanner will show, guiding them to state the correct surface.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the waves bounce off the skin or that the scanner shows the skin surface.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the answer ('no') or repeat the previous question without specifically addressing the physical impossibility of the 'bones' guess.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge X-ray Confusion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly note or validate that the learner is likely thinking of how X-rays work, which do show bones.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a loop, repeatedly defaulting to environmental explanations (soil, vitamins) for disease resistance because they lack a mental model for internal, inherited traits. The tutor's previous abstract corrections ('instructions, not vitamins') failed to dismantle the learner's core belief that plant health is entirely dictated by the dirt it grows in.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a concrete analogy or contrasting question (e.g., comparing inherited traits like eye color to environmental factors like food) to help the learner distinguish between what a living thing gets from its environment versus what it is born with.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Plant vs. Environment
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly clarify that the inherited instructions change the internal makeup of the plant itself, not the soil or the environment it grows in.

rubric_items.title: Provide a Conceptual Bridge
rubric_items.description: The response must use a familiar analogy, example, or contrast (such as comparing inherited physical traits to food/environment) to help the learner conceptualize the difference between genetics and soil.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Soil's General Role
rubric_items.description: The response briefly validates the learner's intuition by acknowledging that while good soil is important for general health, it is a separate mechanism from inherited disease resistance.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repetitive Denial
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely repeat the abstract assertion that 'it is not the soil, it is the instructions' without offering a new conceptual bridge, as this approach has already failed.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Lecturing Genetics
rubric_items.description: The response should not launch into a complex, unprompted explanation of DNA, genes, or evolutionary mechanisms, which would overwhelm the learner and bypass their immediate need to separate internal traits from external environment.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that the stems will span from 4 to 12, but expresses this tentatively and has not yet explicitly listed the individual numbers. They need validation of their range and a prompt to generate the full, consecutive list of stems before moving on to the leaves.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the learner's correct range and prompt them to explicitly list out all the consecutive integers from 4 to 12.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Range
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's tentative answer that the stems will indeed go from 4 to 12.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Explicit Listing
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explicitly state or write out all the individual numbers that make up the stems between 4 and 12.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Providing the List
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that list out the intermediate numbers (e.g., 4, 5, 6, 7...) for the learner instead of requiring the learner to generate the sequence.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Prematurely Moving to Leaves
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask the learner to start finding or plotting the leaves (the ones digits) before the full list of stems has been explicitly established.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Consecutive Rule
rubric_items.description: Briefly note or hint that stems in a stem-and-leaf plot must include every consecutive number in the range, without skipping any.

learning_objective: Whole Numbers, Place Value, and Fractions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly multiplied the numerators (4 * 8 = 32) but incorrectly multiplied the denominator by 4 as well (getting 12 instead of 3), showing they are still applying their earlier flawed logic of multiplying both parts of the fraction by the whole number. They need to realize that the denominators to be multiplied are 1 and 3.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct numerator (32) and prompt the learner to specifically multiply the denominators (1 and 3) to fix the bottom of the fraction.

rubric_items.title: Isolate the Denominator Error
rubric_items.description: The response must direct the learner to re-evaluate the denominator, either by asking how they got 12 or by prompting them to multiply the bottom numbers (1 and 3).

rubric_items.title: Validate the Numerator
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly confirm that the top part of the fraction (32) is correct, ensuring the learner does not discard their successful step.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Prior Question
rubric_items.description: The response may explicitly point out that the learner multiplied the bottom by 4 instead of 1, directly addressing the exact confusion they voiced in their previous turn ('do I do 4 times 8 and 4 times 3?').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Providing the Correct Answer
rubric_items.description: The response must not give away the correct denominator (3) or the final fraction (32/3), leaving the calculation to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: The response must not reject the learner's attempt vaguely (e.g., 'Not quite' or 'Check your math') without specifically focusing their attention on the denominators.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully computed the partial products (160 and 32) but lacks a conceptual understanding of the distributive property, leading them to guess multiplication for recombining the parts. They need to understand that 160 and 32 represent the ounces in 10 pounds and 2 pounds respectively, which must be added to find the total for 12 pounds.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should ground the partial products in the problem's context (e.g., the ounces in 10 pounds and 2 pounds) to help the learner conceptually deduce that addition is required to find the total.

rubric_items.title: Contextualize the Partial Products
rubric_items.description: Explains or prompts the learner to consider what the numbers 160 and 32 actually represent in the real-world context (e.g., 160 is the ounces in 10 pounds, and 32 is the ounces in 2 pounds).

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Operation
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to determine how to combine the two amounts to find the total for 12 pounds, rather than just asking them to guess the math operation again.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Operation
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner to add the numbers or provides the final answer of 192.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Ungrounded Rejection
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's guess (e.g., 'No, we don't multiply') or asks them to guess again without providing any conceptual grounding to help them understand why.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully skip-counted by twos up to the fifth group (ten) and correctly remembers their ultimate goal is seven groups, but feels overwhelmed by the remaining gap. They need scaffolding to take just the next incremental step rather than jumping to the end.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's progress and prompt them to find the value for just the sixth finger, breaking the remaining distance into manageable single steps.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Sixth Finger
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to take exactly one step forward by asking what number corresponds to the sixth finger, or what they get when they add two to ten.

rubric_items.title: Validate Current Progress or Goal
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly confirm that 'ten' is correct for five fingers and/or validate that seven fingers is indeed the correct final goal.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not provide the number for the sixth finger (12) or the seventh finger (14).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Requesting a Double-Step Leap
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not ask the learner to figure out the seventh finger directly from the fifth finger without guiding them through the sixth finger first.

learning_objective: LS2.C Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that biodiversity creates ecological resilience ('harder to destroy'), but they hold a hidden assumption that if moderate fire increases biodiversity, increasing fire frequency or intensity will continuously improve it. They need validation for their correct insight before being prompted to consider the limits of the fire disturbance.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuitive definition of resilience, optionally introduce the formal term, and then ask a hypothetical question about what happens if fires become too frequent or intense in order to surface the hidden belief.

rubric_items.title: Validate Resilience Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirm the learner's conclusion that having many species makes the ecosystem 'harder to destroy'.

rubric_items.title: Probe Fire Frequency or Intensity
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question about what would happen if fires occurred much more frequently or intensely to test the limits of the fire-biodiversity relationship.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Formal Terminology
rubric_items.description: Connect the learner's intuitive phrase 'harder to destroy' to the formal ecological terms 'resilience' or 'stability'.

rubric_items.title: Give Away the Limit
rubric_items.description: Directly state that too much fire will harm the ecosystem or reduce biodiversity, rather than prompting the learner to predict the outcome of increased fire.

rubric_items.title: Vague Continuation
rubric_items.description: Ask a generic follow-up question (e.g., 'What else happens?' or 'Why is that?') that fails to specifically introduce the variables of fire frequency or intensity.

learning_objective: LS2.C Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the cause-and-effect relationship (mussels eat plankton, leaving less for fish) but is confusing the agent causing the shortage (the mussels) with the ecological term for the resource that is running out (the limiting factor). They need a clear distinction between the competitor and the resource before they can apply this vocabulary to broader ecosystem stability.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should provide a clear, simple contrast between the consumer causing the problem (mussels) and the resource that is actually running out (plankton)—perhaps using an everyday analogy—and ask a targeted question to check the learner's understanding of this distinction.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Consumer and Resource
rubric_items.description: The response must clearly contrast the mussels' role as the competitor or cause of the shortage with the plankton's role as the actual resource that is limited.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner Application
rubric_items.description: The response should ask a question that requires the learner to articulate or apply the distinction between the mussels and the plankton, rather than just lecturing them on the difference.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Advancing to Stability
rubric_items.description: The response must not ask the learner to analyze the stability of the broader food web, as the foundational vocabulary confusion regarding the limiting factor must be resolved first.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating the Abstract Definition
rubric_items.description: The response should avoid merely restating the formal definition of a limiting factor, as the tutor's previous attempt to define it did not resolve the learner's confusion.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Focus on Mussels
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that it is understandable for the learner to focus on the mussels, since they are the invasive species actively causing the problem.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly realized that the horizontal tension components do not interact with the vertical weight force. They now need to return to the task of writing an equation that shows the two horizontal forces canceling each other out, free from their previous confusion about weight.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that horizontal and vertical forces are independent, and prompt the learner to write an equation using only the two horizontal forces to show they are equal or cancel out.

rubric_items.title: Validate Independence
rubric_items.description: Confirm the learner's realization that the horizontal forces do not relate to or equal the downward weight.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Horizontal Equation
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to write the mathematical equation showing that the two horizontal forces cancel each other out or are equal.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Horizontal Components
rubric_items.description: Refer back to the specific horizontal forces the learner already identified (T1 cos(30) and T2 cos(45)) to help ground the equation.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Equation
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final equation (e.g., T1 cos(30) = T2 cos(45) or T1 cos(30) - T2 cos(45) = 0).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Vertical Shift
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to write the equation for the vertical forces (involving the weight) until the horizontal equation is fully resolved.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not merely confirm the learner is correct without providing a clear prompt to construct the horizontal equation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner recognizes that both sides are actively exerting force, but they are stuck on the additive misconception, unable to understand why two opposing 100 N forces result in 100 N of tension rather than 200 N. They need to reconcile their correct intuition that 'both pull' with the concept that tension is a single transmitted internal force rather than the sum of external forces.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A cognitive-conflict prompt that asks the learner to apply their 'both pull' addition logic to the wall scenario (where the wall and the team both pull 100 N, yet the learner already agreed the tension is 100 N) to help them dismantle the addition misconception themselves.

rubric_items.title: Leverage the Wall Analogy for Cognitive Conflict
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to compare their 'both pull' logic to the wall scenario by asking why they didn't add the wall's 100 N pull to the person's 100 N pull.

rubric_items.title: Validate the 'Both Pull' Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is absolutely correct that both sides are pulling, validating their physical intuition before addressing why those pulls don't add up to 200 N.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Mechanism Directly
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner the rule for tension (e.g., 'you don't add opposing forces' or 'tension is just the force of one side') without requiring them to reason through the contradiction.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not give a generic response (e.g., 'Think about Newton's laws' or 'What is the definition of tension?') that fails to specifically target the learner's confusion about why the two 100 N forces aren't added together.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Internal Measurement
rubric_items.description: Suggest visualizing a spring scale in the middle of the rope or looking at a single point inside the rope to help the learner conceptualize tension as an internal transmitted force rather than a sum of the ends.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is fixated on 'weight' as the missing variable and is failing to connect the tutor's geometric prompt to the concept of 'radius'. They likely cannot retrieve the word 'radius' from the current prompt and need clarification that weight is not a distance, followed by stronger scaffolding to complete the formula.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should briefly clarify that weight is a force rather than a distance, provide a stronger hint or explicitly supply the term 'radius', and then prompt the learner to assemble the final formula.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Weight and Distance
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly address the learner's guess by pointing out that 'weight' is a force or property of the car, whereas the missing component is a measurement of distance or length.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold or Supply 'Radius'
rubric_items.description: The tutor must help the learner arrive at the term 'radius', either by providing a stronger hint (such as the starting letter) or by directly supplying the word.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Formula Assembly
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to combine their previously recalled piece (mv squared) with the new concept (radius) to state the complete formula.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating the Same Question
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely repeat the definition of a circle's distance without offering additional scaffolding, as the learner has already shown they cannot retrieve the word 'radius' from that prompt alone.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Tangent on Weight Physics
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that launch into a detailed explanation of how weight relates to normal force or friction, which distracts from the immediate goal of identifying the geometric divisor.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Formula
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly state the final assembled formula (e.g., 'So the formula is mv^2/r'), depriving the learner of the chance to construct it themselves.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is seeking final confirmation that without a functional enzyme, and with heat unable to break the stable sugar molecule, the lactose simply remains intact and unreacted. They use the phrase 'just sits there,' which correctly captures the lack of chemical reaction but slightly misrepresents the physical reality of heated molecules bouncing around.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the sugar remains chemically unbroken, gently clarify that it is still physically bouncing around rather than sitting still, and ideally prompt the learner to consider the macroscopic consequence of this unbroken sugar.

rubric_items.title: Validate Chemical Intactness
rubric_items.description: Affirms the learner's intended meaning that the lactose remains chemically intact and the breakdown reaction does not happen.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Molecular Motion
rubric_items.description: Gently corrects the phrase 'just sits there' by reminding the learner that the sugar molecules are still physically moving or bouncing around due to the heat, even though they aren't reacting.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Macroscopic Consequence
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to consider the broader consequence of the lactose remaining unbroken (e.g., what this means for the organism's digestion or the overall system).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Endorse Molecular Stillness
rubric_items.description: Uncritically confirms the phrase 'just sits there' without clarifying that the molecules are in motion, endorsing a physically inaccurate picture of heated molecules.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overcomplicate with Thermodynamics
rubric_items.description: Introduces unnecessary advanced biochemical terminology (like activation energy or bond energy) to explain why the sugar doesn't break, rather than relying on the established concepts of enzyme shape and molecular stability.

learning_objective: LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully deduced that python ancestors had legs, but their phrasing as a question indicates slight uncertainty. They now need to consolidate this insight by reasoning about why these now-useless bones remain, which bridges to the concept of vestigial structures as evidence of evolution.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct deduction and prompt them to explain why the modern python still retains these pelvic bones if it no longer uses them for legs.

rubric_items.title: Affirmation of Inference
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner's deduction about python ancestors having legs is correct, addressing the uncertainty in their question.

rubric_items.title: Prompting the 'Leftover' Concept
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question that prompts the learner to consider why the modern python still retains a pelvis and pelvic spurs if it no longer has legs.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for directly providing the term 'vestigial structure' or explaining the evolutionary mechanism before the learner has attempted to explain the presence of the leftover bones.

rubric_items.title: Vague Continuation
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for merely confirming the answer and asking a generic follow-up (e.g., 'What does that mean for evolution?') without focusing the learner on the specific anomaly of the unused bones.

rubric_items.title: Tying Back to Physical Evidence
rubric_items.description: Reinforce that the pelvic spur they just examined is the physical evidence for this conclusion, connecting their abstract realization back to the skeleton.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the SSS shortcut relies on side measurements, but they do not yet realize that sides are defined by their endpoints (corners), causing confusion about how to write a vertex-based congruence statement. They need help bridging the conceptual gap between the sides they measured and the corners they are being asked to match.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to consider what geometric features (corners) make up the ends of the specific sides they just measured.

rubric_items.title: Target the Side-Endpoint Relationship
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to think about what geometric features (corners or vertices) form the ends of the sides they just measured.

rubric_items.title: Use a Concrete Tent Feature
rubric_items.description: Reference one of the specific sides of the tent flap previously discussed (e.g., the vertical middle, the bottom, or the slanted side) to ground the question.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly acknowledge that the learner is correct in pointing out that they have only focused on measuring sides up to this point.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Connection
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that sides connect corners or that matching sides automatically means matching their endpoints.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Non-Guidance: Repeating the Prompt
rubric_items.description: Do not simply repeat the instruction to match the corners or write the congruence statement without addressing the learner's confusion about how sides relate to corners.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has lost track of the premise that the playground's actual wind speed is 10, mistakenly concluding that the calculated average (6) is the playground's speed. They need to confront the contradiction between the individual data point and the average to realize that the average represents the whole group, not a single location.
