rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe asking the learner to visualize a straight vertical line drawn from the center to the bottom flat side, and to compare the length of that straight line to the slanted side of the internal equilateral triangle.

rubric_items.title: Trace the Vertical Height
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to visualize or trace a vertical line passing from the center of the hexagon straight down to the bottom flat side (or all the way from bottom to top) through the internal triangles.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Altitude with Side Length
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to explicitly compare the straight vertical path through an internal triangle with the triangle's slanted outer side to see if they are the same length.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Corner vs. Flat Side Distinction
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's prior correct reasoning by reminding them that the side length is the distance from the center to the corners, setting up a contrast with the distance to the flat sides.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Geometric Answer
rubric_items.description: Penalizes telling the learner that the height is made of two triangle altitudes, or directly providing the formula for the height of the hexagon.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Pushback
rubric_items.description: Penalizes simply telling the learner 'no' or asking a vague question like 'Are you sure?' without directing their attention to the internal geometry of the triangles.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Shift to Area or Packing
rubric_items.description: Penalizes shifting the conversation to the area of the hexagon or how the logs fit inside it (the packing problem) before the learner has correctly resolved their misconception about the geometric height.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner equates biological death with system failure, ignoring that mechanical filters break down and require replacement, whereas a living oyster reef reproduces and self-heals. They need to contrast the inevitable decay of machines in saltwater with the self-sustaining nature of a biological population.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted question that prompts the learner to consider what happens to machines submerged in harsh saltwater over time, or how a living reef compensates for the death of individual oysters.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Mechanical Permanence
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to evaluate what happens to mechanical parts submerged in a saltwater environment over time (e.g., wear and tear, rust, or breaking down).

rubric_items.title: Highlight Biological Resilience
rubric_items.description: Guides the learner to consider how a living oyster reef sustains itself as a system despite the death of individual oysters (e.g., through reproduction or new oysters growing on old shells).

rubric_items.title: Validate Literal Truth
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that the learner is factually correct that individual oysters do indeed die.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tells the learner that machines rust and break down or that oysters reproduce to replace themselves, rather than prompting the learner to deduce these realities.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Disagreement
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's statement with a generic prompt (e.g., 'Are you sure?' or 'Think about the whole ecosystem') without directing their attention specifically to lifespan, maintenance, or reproduction.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully calculated the 80% probability but is disconnected from its real-world meaning, failing to see how the abstract percentage translates to the physical outcome of seeds growing. They need to bridge the gap between the mathematical value and the concrete scenario to understand why a higher percentage is preferable.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to recall their earlier definition of a percent ('out of 100') and apply it to the seeds to explain what an 80% chance physically means.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Concrete Meaning
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks the learner to explain what an 80% chance means in terms of the actual number of seeds that would be expected to grow.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Prior Definition
rubric_items.description: The tutor directs the learner back to their earlier discussion that a percent is a fraction out of 100 to help them deduce the answer.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explaining the Meaning Directly
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner that 80% means 80 out of 100 seeds will grow, doing the translation work for them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Purely Mathematical Justification
rubric_items.description: The tutor justifies the choice merely by stating that 80 is a bigger number than 70, failing to address the physical meaning of the probability.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly affirms that asking 'why' the number matters in real life is a good or important question.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly believes that an infinite, non-repeating decimal can be written as a simple fraction, and their focus is currently split between the math and their drawing. They need a concrete, step-by-step prompt to realize why constructing a fraction for a never-ending, non-patterned decimal is mathematically impossible.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that asks the learner to consider the mechanics of turning a decimal into a fraction (such as determining the denominator) to help them realize why an endless, non-repeating decimal cannot be written this way.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Decimal-to-Fraction Mechanics
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider the mechanics of converting a decimal to a fraction (such as asking what the denominator would be, or comparing it to a terminating decimal like 0.5) to help them discover why an endless, non-repeating decimal breaks this process.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Distraction
rubric_items.description: Briefly acknowledge the learner's drawing or their 'blue marker' comment to maintain rapport before redirecting their focus back to the math.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Impossibility
rubric_items.description: Directly state that it is impossible to write an endless, non-repeating decimal as a fraction, doing the reasoning for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unscaffolded Pushback
rubric_items.description: Ask a generic 'Are you sure?' or 'Why do you think so?' without providing any concrete mathematical scaffolding to help the learner evaluate their incorrect assumption.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Prematurely introduce the formal term 'irrational' or state the final rule before the learner has actually recognized the impossibility of the fractional representation.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has tentatively but correctly deduced that particle collisions cause a 'push' on the walls. They now need to consolidate this microscopic mechanism by comparing the collisions of the slower inside particles to the faster outside particles to fully explain why the bottle collapses.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct understanding of how particles push, and then prompt them to compare the particle collisions on the outside of the bottle to those on the inside.

rubric_items.title: Affirm the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative answer that the crashing particles are what push on the walls.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Microscopic Comparison
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to compare the particle collisions on the outside of the bottle to the collisions on the inside.

rubric_items.title: Reference Particle Speed
rubric_items.description: Incorporate the previously established fact that the inside particles are moving slower (or are colder) to scaffold the comparison.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Comparison
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the outside particles hit harder, faster, or more frequently than the inside particles.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Prompt
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a broad question (e.g., 'So why does it squish?') that fails to specifically direct the learner to compare the particles on the inside versus the outside.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Reintroducing Distractions
rubric_items.description: Do not bring up the learner's previous off-task topics (iPad, dog, being cold) since the learner's latest turn was finally entirely on-task.

learning_objective: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing a disconnect between their intuitive count-based calculation (which correctly yielded 1/4) and the formal probability formula. They do not understand the pedagogical purpose of calculating the formal probabilities when they already have the correct answer, leading to valid confusion and resistance.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that 1/4 is indeed the correct answer, explain that the current goal is to prove that the formal formula mathematically simplifies to that exact same result, and then prompt the learner again for the grand total of flies.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Answer
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner's previous answer of 1/4 is correct and does not need to be changed.

rubric_items.title: Establish the Purpose of the Formal Formula
rubric_items.description: Explain that the current exercise is to show how the formal formula produces the exact same result as their intuitive count-based method.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Grand Total
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner back to the immediate next step of finding the grand total of flies in the study so they can calculate P(B).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Invalidating the Count Method
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that imply the learner's count-based method (6/24) was incorrect, incomplete, or inferior to using the formal formula.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Denominator Cancellation
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly explain how the grand total denominators will cancel out to leave 6/24, giving away the mathematical punchline before the learner calculates the parts.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unresponsive Task Persistence
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply repeat the prompt to find the total number of flies without acknowledging or addressing the learner's valid question ('But we already got 1/4?').

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the changing raw values of diameter and intensity with the ratio between them, failing to recognize that a constant ratio is the defining feature of a proportional (and in this case, quadratic) relationship. They need to connect their calculated constant ratio back to what it means for the relationship between the variables.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce what a constant ratio implies about the relationship between intensity and squared diameter, guiding them to realize this confirms their model.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Implication of Constant Ratio
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explain what getting the same ratio (0.5) implies about the relationship between the intensity and the squared diameter.

rubric_items.title: Distinguish Raw Values from Ratio
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's observation by explicitly contrasting the raw measurements (which do change) with the ratio (which stays the same).

rubric_items.title: Reference Original Goal
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of their original hypothesis or the reason they decided to square the diameter in the first place.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Punchline
rubric_items.description: Directly state that a constant ratio means the relationship is proportional or quadratic, doing the conceptual work for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Non-guidance: Just Saying 'No'
rubric_items.description: Simply state that the ratio is not supposed to change or that the learner's math is correct, without prompting them to reason about why the constant ratio matters.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is applying a sequential physical collision model ('bounce') to the tutor's prompt about opposing forces, failing to realize that simultaneous equal and opposite pushes result in cancellation. They need a conceptual scaffold to recognize that when an electron is pushed equally in opposite directions at the exact same time, it does not move.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a relatable analogy or targeted question about simultaneous opposing forces (such as two people pushing a door from opposite sides with equal strength) to help the learner deduce that the electron stays still.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Simultaneous Opposing Forces
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to deduce the outcome of two equal forces pushing in opposite directions at the exact same time.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Bounce' Guess
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly address the learner's 'bounce' guess by emphasizing the simultaneous nature of the forces, contrasting it with the sequential nature of a bounce.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response should not directly tell the learner that the electron stays still, does not move, or that the forces cancel out.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely reject the 'bounce' guess (e.g., 'Not quite, try again') without providing a concrete analogy or scaffold about simultaneous forces.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Terminology
rubric_items.description: The response should not introduce formal terms like 'destructive interference' or 'net zero force' before the learner has articulated the physical concept of the electron not moving.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the inputs (carbon dioxide gas and sunlight) but lacks the conceptual model for how an invisible gas can be transformed into solid plant matter. They are genuinely stuck on the mechanism of chemical synthesis and need the process broken down into a relatable, visible concept rather than just being told to think harder.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Provide a simple, concrete analogy or guided question (such as comparing molecules to building blocks) to scaffold how plants use the energy from sunlight to assemble the carbon from the gas into solid food.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Gas-to-Solid Transformation
rubric_items.description: Addresses the learner's specific confusion by scaffolding the idea that plants use energy to connect or rearrange the invisible gas molecules into solid structures (like sugar/food).

rubric_items.title: Use a Concrete Analogy
rubric_items.description: Introduces a concrete, everyday analogy (e.g., building blocks, Legos, or a factory) to help the learner visualize how sunlight provides the energy/power to assemble the carbon dioxide.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Confusion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly normalizes or validates the learner's question (e.g., 'It is pretty amazing to think about a gas becoming a solid!' or 'That's a great question.'), acknowledging that this is a counter-intuitive concept.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Jargon Drop
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for simply giving away the scientific terms 'photosynthesis' or 'glucose' as the answer without first breaking down the 'how' of the mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for leaving the learner stranded by merely repeating the previous prompt (e.g., 'Just think about what sunlight does to the gas') when the learner has explicitly stated they cannot picture the mechanism.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is applying their everyday experience with friction to a frictionless scenario, revealing the core Aristotelian misconception that force is required to sustain motion rather than change it. They need to realize that without an opposing force like friction to slow the ball down, no continuous forward push is needed to keep it moving.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should create cognitive conflict by asking the learner to identify what is physically pushing the ball after it leaves their hand, or what specific force would cause it to stop if there is truly zero friction.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the Continuous Push
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to critically examine their claim by asking what is physically pushing the ball after it leaves their hand, or what force would cause it to stop if there is no friction.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Frictionless Context
rubric_items.description: Keep the reasoning grounded in a frictionless environment (like the smooth ice or deep space) to isolate the concept of inertia from the learner's everyday experience with friction.

rubric_items.title: Validate Everyday Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that in everyday life (where friction is always present), objects do seem to need a continuous push to keep moving.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Rule
rubric_items.description: Do not directly state Newton's First Law or simply tell the learner that the ball will keep moving forever without a push.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply tell the learner they are wrong or ask a generic 'Are you sure?' without introducing a specific physical question to guide their reasoning.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has grasped the geometric concept of the base of support (the rectangle) and the line of gravity (the dropped marble) but does not yet understand how their spatial relationship determines stability. They need to connect the location of the downward force (inside vs. outside the base) to the physical consequence (balancing vs. tipping).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to predict the physical behavior of the cat tree if the downward push (the marble) lands outside the rectangle, rather than telling them it will tip.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Prediction for Outside Force
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to predict the physical consequence for the cat tree if the downward push (the marble) lands outside the boundary of the rectangle.

rubric_items.title: Contrast Inside vs. Outside
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to compare or contrast the outcome of the force landing outside the rectangle with the outcome of it landing inside.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the cat tree will tip, fall, or become unstable if the force lands outside the rectangle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a generic question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that fails to direct the learner's attention to the specific physical relationship between the marble/push and the rectangle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce formal physics terms like 'center of gravity,' 'center of mass,' or 'torque' to explain why it matters before the learner has articulated the physical intuition.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully deduced that the pendulum's period remains constant because increased distance is offset by increased speed, but their phrasing ('It doesn't change?') indicates lingering hesitation. They now need validation of this physical insight and a prompt to explicitly connect it back to the mathematical model of the sine function to fully resolve their initial misconception.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confidently validate the learner's physical conclusion and prompt them to state how this confirms their earlier thoughts about the period or frequency of the sine graph.

rubric_items.title: Validate Physical Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Confidently confirm the learner's conclusion that the time for a swing does not change, addressing the hesitation implied by their question mark.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Mathematical Consolidation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to connect this constant physical time back to the mathematical model, such as asking what this means for the period or frequency of their sine function.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Reasoning Process
rubric_items.description: Praise or explicitly mention the learner's successful reasoning about the increased distance and speed canceling out.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not do the final cognitive work for the learner by explicitly stating that the period or frequency of the sine graph remains constant.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Validation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely say 'Yes' or 'Correct' without asking a follow-up question that requires the learner to apply this physical insight back to the sine function.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has tentatively realized that food, rather than oxygen, is the actual fuel for the fish, but their question mark indicates uncertainty. They now need to consolidate this insight and figure out how oxygen interacts with that food to release energy, completing the conceptual shift away from their initial misconception.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's realization that food is the fuel and prompt them to use the campfire analogy to explain what the oxygen's role is now that the fuel has been identified.

rubric_items.title: Validate Tentative Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative answer that food is the fuel, building their confidence in this new idea.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Oxygen's Role
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain what the oxygen does to the food now that they have identified food as the body's fuel.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Campfire Analogy
rubric_items.description: Refer back to the campfire analogy to help the learner map the relationship between wood/oxygen and food/oxygen.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Interaction
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that oxygen 'burns', 'breaks down', or 'reacts with' the food to release energy; leave this connection for the learner to articulate.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Moving On Prematurely
rubric_items.description: Do not simply affirm 'yes' and move on to a new topic (like the food web or what the fish eats) without resolving how oxygen and food work together to provide energy.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Jargon
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce terms like 'cellular respiration', 'mitochondria', or 'ATP' before the learner has articulated the conceptual relationship between food and oxygen in their own words.

learning_objective: LS1.B Growth and Development of Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has temporarily lost track of the specific substance being transported by the pumps, despite having correctly identified it as 'hydrogen' in their very first turn. They need a targeted cue to recall their own prior insight rather than being re-taught the fact.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to recall their own earlier statement, optionally using the concept of acidity as a hint, so the learner remembers that hydrogen ions (protons) are the substance being pumped.

rubric_items.title: Prompting Recall of Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: The tutor directs the learner's attention back to their own earlier statement in the conversation to help them recall the substance they already identified.

rubric_items.title: Using Acidity as a Cue
rubric_items.description: The tutor provides a targeted hint by referencing the 'acid' in the acid growth hypothesis or asking what makes the wall acidic, to trigger the connection to hydrogen.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Answer)
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly names 'hydrogen' or 'protons' as the substance being pumped, doing the recall work for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness or Topic Jumping
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a completely unguided question (e.g., 'What do you think?') or ignores the learner's immediate question to push forward into the broader chemical steps.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is taking the tutor's 'button' analogy too literally and is stuck trying to visualize a mechanical button on a butterfly's foot. They need the tutor to clarify that this was just a figure of speech and provide a simpler, more intuitive explanation of how chemical contact triggers an electrical response.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly clarify that there is no literal button, provide a simpler explanation or a more relatable analogy (like a doorbell) for how contact triggers a signal, and prompt the learner to apply this concept.

rubric_items.title: De-literalize the Analogy
rubric_items.description: Explicitly clarify that the 'button' was just a figure of speech and that the butterfly does not have a literal mechanical button on its foot.

rubric_items.title: Explain the Trigger Concept
rubric_items.description: Provide a simpler, direct explanation or a highly relatable alternative analogy (e.g., a doorbell) to illustrate that the chemical's physical touch on the outside simply triggers the nerve to fire an electrical signal.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Learner Application
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question that requires the learner to actively apply the trigger concept, such as asking what the nerve does immediately after being touched or why the chemical doesn't enter the leg.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the 'button' analogy was confusing or validate the learner for questioning it (e.g., 'Good catch, I didn't mean a real button!').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overcomplicating the Explanation
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce advanced biological jargon (e.g., 'action potentials' or 'neurotransmitters') or explain the entire pathway to the brain; keep the focus strictly on how the signal is triggered at the foot.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not leave the learner stranded by asking them to guess how the mechanism works or by asking them to analyze the 'button' analogy without first clarifying that it is not a literal button.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is clinging to a Lamarckian misconception, insisting that bedbugs actively 'built' their tolerance even when explicitly prompted to consider traits existing before exposure. They are currently unable to conceptualize that a defense could exist as a natural, pre-existing variation prior to an environmental threat.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should create cognitive conflict by asking the learner to explain the logical impossibility of an organism actively building a defense against a chemical it has never encountered.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Pre-Exposure 'Building'
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to explain the chronological contradiction of how a bedbug could actively 'build' a defense against a spray it has not yet experienced.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Natural Variation
rubric_items.description: The response should use a familiar analogy (e.g., natural differences in human height or animal fur) or a targeted question to help the learner recognize that individuals in any population are born with natural differences.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Explanation of Mutation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly tell the learner that traits arise from random genetic mutations; the learner must be allowed to realize that variation can be innate on their own.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Advancement to Selection
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not shift the discussion to which bedbugs survive, die, or reproduce; the focus must remain strictly on the origin of the trait itself.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not merely ask 'Are you sure?' or 'Why do you think that?' without specifically targeting the logical flaw in building a defense prior to exposure.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully realized that continuous numerical data connects at boundary values (like 5), explaining why histogram bars touch. They now need validation of this insight and an opportunity to synthesize the final rule distinguishing histograms from bar graphs.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly affirm the learner's correct insight about the connecting value and prompt them to summarize the overall rule for when to use a bar graph versus a histogram.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Connection Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirm the learner's correct realization that the boundary value (5) connects the two weight categories.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to summarize the overall rule or difference between when to use a bar graph (gaps) and a histogram (touching bars) based on the type of data.

rubric_items.title: Formalize Terminology
rubric_items.description: Introduce or reinforce the term 'continuous' to formalize the learner's insight about the numerical data flowing together.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Rule)
rubric_items.description: State the final conclusion or rule distinguishing the two graphs for the learner instead of requiring them to articulate it.

rubric_items.title: Abrupt Transition
rubric_items.description: Move on to a new topic or problem without solidifying the conceptual takeaway regarding graph types.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that the overall reaction happens 'faster' at higher temperatures, but they are conflating this increased reaction rate with a lowered activation energy barrier. They need to reconcile how a reaction can be faster overall (more molecules reacting per second) while the minimum energy required for a single collision to react remains unchanged.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the overall reaction is indeed faster, and then prompt the learner to use the established hurdle analogy to explain why the 'race' finishes faster even if the hurdle's height hasn't changed.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Rate Increase
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's correct intuition that the overall process (the reaction or the race) is indeed faster.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Reconciliation of Rate vs. Barrier
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain how the overall process can be faster if the barrier or hurdle height remains exactly the same.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Established Analogy
rubric_items.description: Utilize the established 'runners and hurdles' analogy to help the learner visualize the difference between the speed of the race and the height of the obstacle.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not directly explain that the reaction is faster because more molecules are clearing the same barrier; leave this causal connection for the learner to articulate.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Invalidating the Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: Do not tell the learner they are wrong about it being 'faster', as this would incorrectly imply that the macroscopic reaction rate does not increase with temperature.

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identified ATP as the essential product of glycolysis, successfully completing the conceptual chain for why fermentation is necessary. However, based on their earlier phrasing ('dumps it') and the hidden belief, they likely still hold the misconception that NADH releases electrons freely into the cytoplasm rather than transferring them to a specific acceptor molecule.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct answer (ATP) to consolidate the purpose of fermentation, and then use a targeted probe to ask *what* exactly catches the electrons when NADH 'dumps' them, exposing and correcting the hidden belief.

rubric_items.title: Validate ATP as the Goal
rubric_items.description: Confirm that ATP is the correct answer, validating the learner's successful deduction about why yeast needs glycolysis to continue.

rubric_items.title: Probe the 'Dumping' Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner what specifically catches or accepts the electrons when NADH 'dumps' them, directly challenging the hidden belief that electrons are released freely into the cytoplasm.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Prior Byproducts
rubric_items.description: Reference the 'pyruvate byproduct' or 'alcohol' discussed earlier in the dialogue as a hint to help the learner deduce what accepts the electrons.

rubric_items.title: Prematurely Naming the Acceptor
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the electrons go to the pyruvate byproduct or acetaldehyde, as this robs them of the chance to recall the earlier explanation.

rubric_items.title: Moving On Without Clarifying the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Do not simply accept 'ATP' and conclude the topic or move to a new lesson phase without addressing the incomplete 'dumps it' model of electron transfer.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly realized that motion (spinning) is necessary for the process, but they mistakenly believe the spinning creates the energy rather than transferring it. They need to trace the energy back to its source (their own physical effort) to distinguish between energy transfer and energy creation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should challenge the word 'makes' and prompt the learner to identify where the energy is actually coming from, ideally scaffolding the question by referencing the biological energy discussed earlier.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Energy Source
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to identify the original source of the energy being transferred to the radio.

rubric_items.title: Challenge 'Makes'
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly address the learner's use of the word 'makes' by questioning or challenging the idea that the spinning creates the energy.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Prior Context
rubric_items.description: The response should remind the learner of their own physical effort or the 'biological energy' discussed in previous turns to help them connect their pushing to the energy transfer.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response directly tells the learner that the energy comes from the person or explicitly states that energy cannot be created, doing the reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Validation
rubric_items.description: The response simply agrees with the learner or validates the role of spinning without addressing the misconception that energy is being 'made'.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is focusing solely on the slower speed of the waves, logically concluding that slower waves take longer to arrive and thus the time gap between them must increase. They have temporarily lost sight of their own earlier observation that the waves also compress ('squished closer together'), which is the necessary compensating factor.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's logic regarding the slower speed, then prompt them to recall that the waves are 'squished closer together' and ask how that shorter distance affects the arrival time.

rubric_items.title: Reintroduce Wavelength Compression
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner's attention back to their earlier observation that the waves get 'squished closer together' (or ask them what happens to the physical distance between the wave crests).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Integration of Speed and Distance
rubric_items.description: Ask a guiding question about how having less distance to travel between crests affects the time gap, prompting the learner to weigh this against the slower speed.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Speed Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's logic is correct if speed were the only factor changing (e.g., 'If they were the same distance apart, yes, it would take longer.').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Cancellation
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the shorter distance perfectly cancels out the slower speed to keep the time gap constant; leave this realization for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unscaffolded Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the learner's guess ('No, the gap doesn't get bigger') or ask them to 'think again' without pointing them to the compensating factor of the waves being closer together.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has lost track of the specific time interval they were originally discussing and is now confused about which numbers to use. They need to be re-grounded in the problem statement to identify the specific hours before they can find the corresponding elevations.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should direct the learner to look back at the original problem text to find the specific time interval or hours mentioned.

rubric_items.title: Direct to Problem Text
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to re-read or look back at the original problem statement to find the specific hours mentioned.

rubric_items.title: Do Not Give Away the Hours
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly tell the learner which hours to use, doing the work of reading the problem for them.

rubric_items.title: Do Not Ask for Elevations Yet
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask the learner to find or subtract the elevations before they have successfully re-identified the hours.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Recall
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask the learner to rely solely on their memory of the conversation (e.g., 'What did you say earlier?') rather than pointing them to the concrete problem text.

rubric_items.title: Normalize the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Briefly validate or normalize that it is easy to lose track of the specific numbers after spending time discussing the underlying concepts.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is using the big player's lack of movement to incorrectly conclude he experienced less force, temporarily losing sight of their own earlier realization that heavy objects barely move even when subjected to the same force.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to apply their earlier insight about the parked car to the big player, asking if his lack of movement could simply be due to his weight rather than a smaller force.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Conclusion Using Weight
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider whether the big player's lack of movement is due to his heavier weight rather than experiencing a smaller force.

rubric_items.title: Re-invoke Parked Car Analogy
rubric_items.description: Explicitly reference the learner's own earlier insight about the parked car to help them bridge the gap between that analogy and the soccer players.

rubric_items.title: Validate Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's physical observation ('He barely moved') is completely correct before challenging the inference they drew from it.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Answer)
rubric_items.description: Directly tell the learner that the forces are equal, doing the reasoning for them instead of letting them connect the dots.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Ask a generic question (e.g., 'Are you sure?' or 'Think about it again') that fails to direct the learner's attention to the relationship between the player's weight and his movement.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Introduce formal physics terms like 'acceleration', 'mass', or 'Newton's Third Law' before the conceptual understanding of the interaction is fully grounded in the learner's intuitive language.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly guessed that rotating (1,1) by 90 degrees counterclockwise results in (0,1), likely confusing it with the rotation of their previous point (1,0). They need geometric scaffolding to correctly visualize where a point off the axes lands before they can derive the algebraic formula.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Prompt the learner to visualize or sketch the rotation of (1,1), perhaps by asking which quadrant it moves to or how its horizontal and vertical components shift, so they can discover the correct coordinates (-1, 1) themselves.

rubric_items.title: Address the Incorrect Coordinate Guess
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to re-evaluate their guess of (0,1) by considering the geometric properties of the rotation or the distance from the origin.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Visual or Geometric Reasoning
rubric_items.description: Provide a specific geometric scaffold to help the learner find the new point, such as asking them to sketch it, asking which quadrant a 90-degree counterclockwise rotation moves it to, or breaking the movement into horizontal and vertical steps.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Previous Correct Insight
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that (0,1) is the correct landing spot for their previous point (1,0), but prompt them to consider how starting at (1,1) changes the outcome.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Coordinates
rubric_items.description: Provide the correct rotated coordinates (-1, 1) or prematurely introduce the algebraic rotation matrix formula before the learner has visually grounded the transformation.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Bare Rejection
rubric_items.description: Reject the learner's guess (e.g., 'Not quite' or 'Try again') without offering a specific visual, spatial, or geometric strategy to help them find the correct point.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully overcome their misconception and correctly simplified the square root of -16 to 4i. They now need confirmation of their tentative answer and guidance to apply this result back to the original equation they were solving.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm that 4i is correct and prompt the learner to substitute this value back into the quadratic formula or original equation.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Simplification
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner's answer of 4i is correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Substitution
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to substitute 4i back into the original equation or quadratic formula they were working on.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Doing the Substitution
rubric_items.description: Do not perform the substitution of 4i or state the resulting updated equation for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Next Steps
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a generic 'What do we do next?' without referencing the original equation or the quadratic formula.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Process
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or praise the learner for successfully applying the square root to both the 16 and the negative sign.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has lost the connection between their concrete calculation and the algebraic expression, guessing that the variable 'x' represents the starter loop rather than the number of extension pieces. They need to remap the variable to the specific quantity it replaced in their earlier example.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that directs the learner to recall exactly what the number 3 represented in their previous '5 times 3' calculation, so they can map that meaning onto the variable x.

rubric_items.title: Reference Concrete Example
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to recall what the number 3 represented in their previous '5 times 3' calculation in order to map it to the variable x.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Loop' Guess
rubric_items.description: Addresses the learner's incorrect guess by reminding them that the starter loop is a different part of the track than the extension pieces being multiplied.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Variable Definition
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that x represents the number of extension pieces, doing the mapping work for them.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Simply tells the learner they are wrong or asks them to 'guess again' without pointing them back to the concrete example.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Equation Building
rubric_items.description: Attempts to move forward with writing the full equation (e.g., asking for the loop's length again) before the learner has correctly defined what x means.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the two 100-meter edge zones add up to 200 meters, but they are stuck on how to translate this into a total corridor width. They need immediate, step-by-step scaffolding to connect this 200-meter edge penalty to the minimum total width required to retain any interior habitat.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the '200' calculation and then prompt the learner to figure out the total width by asking what happens if they want a specific amount of interior space left over.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Edge Calculation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and validate the learner's realization that 200 meters is the total width taken up by the two edge zones.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Total Width Relationship
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to determine how the 200-meter edge requirement dictates the total width of the corridor if they want to have any protected interior space.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with a Concrete Interior Target
rubric_items.description: Provide a simple hypothetical interior width (e.g., 'If we want 50 meters of safe interior space...') to help the learner construct the addition step themselves.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Formula
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly state the formula (e.g., 'Total Width = 200 + Interior') or calculate a final total width for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Premature Advancement: Jumping to Area or Ratios
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask the learner to calculate the total area or the edge-to-interior ratio before the learner has successfully articulated how to find the 1D total width.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply say 'Yes, what's next?' or leave the learner stranded without anchoring the next step to their '200' calculation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has observed the duck moving forward, likely because they accidentally created a water current when making the ripple, which reinforces their misconception that waves carry objects forward. The immediate need is to validate their honest observation while guiding them to refine their experiment to isolate pure wave motion from bulk water movement.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should accept the learner's observation and prompt them to create a ripple in a controlled way (such as tapping straight down or dropping a small object) to eliminate accidental water currents.

rubric_items.title: Validate Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or accepts the learner's reported observation that the duck moved, treating their empirical report as valid rather than a mistake.

rubric_items.title: Isolate Wave Generation
rubric_items.description: Directs attention to how the ripple was created to help the learner avoid accidentally pushing the water (e.g., asking 'How did you make the ripple?' or suggesting a controlled method like tapping straight down).

rubric_items.title: Prompt New Controlled Test
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to perform a new observation using the controlled wave-generation method to see if the duck still drifts away from their finger.

rubric_items.title: Normalize Accidental Currents
rubric_items.description: Mentions that it is very easy or common to accidentally push water and create a current when trying to make a wave.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Deny Observation
rubric_items.description: Contradicts the learner's observation or insists the duck didn't actually move, which undermines the learner's trust in their own senses.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Explain the Current Prematurely
rubric_items.description: Gives away the answer by explaining that the learner must have created a water current, or states the scientific conclusion (that waves only transfer energy) instead of letting the learner discover it through a better test.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the correct mathematical operation (20 divided by 1.50) but is stuck on the procedural execution because of the decimal in the divisor. They need targeted scaffolding to figure out how to transform the problem into one with whole numbers.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the decimal is the tricky part and offer a conceptual hint—such as converting the dollar amounts to cents or multiplying by a power of 10—to help the learner transform the expression into whole numbers.

rubric_items.title: Target the Decimal Bottleneck
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to find a way to eliminate or bypass the decimal in the divisor (1.50) to make the division easier.

rubric_items.title: Provide a Conceptual Stepping Stone
rubric_items.description: The tutor should offer a specific conceptual hint to help the learner perform the transformation, such as suggesting they think about the amounts in cents instead of dollars, or asking what factor they could multiply by to remove the decimal.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Identification
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's intuition by agreeing that the decimal is indeed the challenging part of the calculation.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Procedural Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not explicitly state the procedural rule (e.g., 'move the decimal point two places to the right') or give away the transformed expression (e.g., 'divide 2000 by 150').

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Prompts
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not leave the learner stranded by simply asking 'What do you do with the decimal?' or 'How do you divide decimals?' without offering a conceptual or strategic hint.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is seeking confirmation that the number 2 is rational before they feel confident applying the multiplication rule to the term 2π. They have all the necessary pieces but need validation of this single premise to overcome their hesitation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Directly confirm that 2 is rational, then prompt the learner to apply the established rule to the product of the rational 2 and the irrational π.

rubric_items.title: Confirm the Premise
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's statement that 2 is indeed a rational number.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to apply the established 'rational times irrational' rule to determine the nature of the product 2π.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Careful Thinking
rubric_items.description: Validate the learner for checking their premises or correctly identifying the components of the expression before jumping to a conclusion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the product 2π is irrational, as the learner must make this final connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not answer the learner's direct question with a generic deflection (e.g., 'What do you think?'), which leaves them stranded and unsure of their premise.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the genetic dominance of an allele (its ability to mask a recessive allele in an individual) with a physical or reproductive 'strength' that would allow it to outcompete other alleles in a population. They need to realize that a gene's dominance does not alter the basic mechanism of inheritance: it cannot spread to new families unless the people who carry it actually reproduce.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that validates the learner's intuition about dominance being 'stronger' in an individual, but challenges them to explain how that internal strength would actually cause the gene to spread to new families or change how many children a person has.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the Mechanism of 'Strength'
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to explain how a gene being 'stronger' (dominant) would actually change the physical process of passing genes down, such as whether it causes people to have more children.

rubric_items.title: Re-invoke the Learner's Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to reconcile their idea of 'strength' with their own earlier realization that a trait cannot spread if very few parents have it to begin with.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Individual-Level Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that a dominant gene is indeed 'stronger' in the sense that it masks the recessive gene inside a single individual, validating their intuition before pivoting to population spread.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Correction
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner that dominance does not mean a gene will take over the population or does not provide a reproductive advantage, bypassing the learner's opportunity to reason this out.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a generic question (e.g., 'What do you mean by stronger?') without scaffolding the learner to think about the mechanism of reproduction or population spread.

learning_objective: PS3.C Relationship Between Energy and Forces

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that the restoring force is strongest at the top of the swing, but experiences cognitive dissonance because the pendulum's speed is zero at that point. They are struggling to decouple the concept of force (the pull) from the concept of speed (how fast it is currently moving), which stems from their underlying belief that maximum force requires maximum speed.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the pendulum is indeed stopped at the top, acknowledge why that feels counterintuitive, and prompt the learner to consider what that strong pull is about to do to the stopped pendulum.

rubric_items.title: Validate Correct Observations
rubric_items.description: Confirm that the learner is correct on both counts: the pull is strongest high up, and the pendulum is momentarily stopped there.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Effect of the Pull
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner what the strong pull is about to do to the stopped pendulum, guiding them to realize that the force is what causes the object to start moving again.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Paradox
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's intuition that it feels counterintuitive or surprising for the strongest force to occur when the object has zero speed.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Resolution
rubric_items.description: Do not directly explain the physics principle that force causes a change in speed (acceleration) rather than requiring speed; leave the realization of what the pull does to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely confirm the pendulum is stopped without providing a prompt that helps the learner resolve how a strong pull can act on a stationary object.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has lost track of the different mass variables in this multi-step problem, specifically confusing the mass of the carbon (8,500 kg) with the total biomass of the tree. They need to re-establish the biological distinction between the whole tree and the carbon contained within it before finishing the math.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe or reminder that helps the learner distinguish between the whole tree and its carbon content, either by asking what else makes up a tree's mass or by prompting them to recall how they originally calculated the 8,500 kg figure.

rubric_items.title: Address Biological Mass Distinction
rubric_items.description: The response must address the conceptual difference between the total tree mass and the carbon mass, helping the learner recognize that the tree consists of more than just carbon.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner Recall
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to think about the tree's composition (e.g., water, other elements) or recall their previous calculation steps to deduce what the 8,500 kg represents, rather than just giving them the answer.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Variable Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate that it is easy to lose track of the different mass values (total tree, dry mass, carbon, CO2) during a long, multi-step conversion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely repeat 'No, 8,500 is the carbon' without explaining or prompting the learner to consider the biological difference between the whole tree and its carbon content.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Advancement to Conversion
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ignore or brush past the learner's confusion about the tree mass to push them into finishing the division by 1,000 for the metric ton conversion.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is unsure how adding mass to the top of the system affects stability, tentatively guessing that adding weight might help. They need to connect the addition of top-weight to an upward shift in the center of gravity, which they previously established decreases stability.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe asking the learner to predict how adding a heavy coin to the top of the phone will change the location of the center of gravity.

rubric_items.title: Focus on Center of Gravity Shift
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to determine how adding weight to the very top of the phone changes the vertical position of the center of gravity.

rubric_items.title: Recall Height-Stability Relationship
rubric_items.description: Encourages the learner to apply their earlier realization that a lower center of gravity increases stability to evaluate this new scenario.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Intuition
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's instinct that adding weight can sometimes increase stability (e.g., if added to the base) before redirecting them to consider the specific placement at the top.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that the center of gravity will move up or that the phone will become less stable.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's guess (e.g., 'No, it wouldn't') without directing their attention to the center of gravity or mass distribution.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly intuits that the wind 'pushes' the boat, but their phrasing indicates hesitation and they have not yet connected this macroscopic push to the transfer of kinetic energy. They need validation of their idea and guidance to articulate how the microscopic particle collisions actually transfer energy to the boat.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Validate the learner's intuition that the wind 'pushes' the boat, connect this push to the microscopic collisions discussed previously, and prompt the learner to explain what happens to the boat's energy as a result of these collisions.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and validate the learner's correct suggestion that the wind 'pushes' the boat.

rubric_items.title: Connect 'Push' to Microscopic Collisions
rubric_items.description: Explicitly link the macroscopic concept of 'pushing' back to the microscopic particle collisions (e.g., the 'bouncy balls' smashing into the sail) established in the previous turn.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Energy Transfer Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Ask a targeted question that requires the learner to explain what happens to the kinetic energy during this push (e.g., asking how the boat gains energy from the collisions).

rubric_items.title: Address Learner Hesitation
rubric_items.description: Provide explicit encouragement or praise to build the learner's confidence, addressing the hesitation implied by their question mark.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Transfer Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that the particles transfer their kinetic energy to the boat; the response must leave room for the learner to articulate this connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness or Moving On
rubric_items.description: Do not simply accept 'pushes' as a complete answer and move on to a new topic without requiring the learner to unpack how the energy actually transfers.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is persistently stuck on the misconception that the concave shape of the bowl amplifies gravity, which is preventing them from engaging with the tutor's questions about the normal force. Because direct factual correction has failed multiple times, the learner needs an opportunity to unpack or test their belief about how the bowl affects gravity before moving on.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should pause the discussion of normal force and vector addition, and instead directly investigate the learner's belief that the bowl's shape amplifies gravity by asking them to explain their reasoning or proposing a thought experiment.

rubric_items.title: Pivot to the Gravity Misconception
rubric_items.description: The tutor must pause the progression toward vector addition and explicitly focus the turn on the learner's persistent belief that the bowl's shape changes the strength of gravity.

rubric_items.title: Elicit the Learner's Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The response should ask the learner to explain *why* or *how* they think the inside of the bowl makes gravity pull harder.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Pushing Normal Force
rubric_items.description: Penalize the response if it ignores the learner's bottleneck and insists they answer the previous prompt about adding forces or identifying the support force.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating the Factual Correction
rubric_items.description: Penalize the response if it simply tells the learner again that gravity is the same or depends only on mass, as this direct telling has already proven ineffective.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: Penalize the response if it merely asks a generic question like 'Are you sure?' or 'Why do you say that?' without anchoring the inquiry in the specific physical setup of the bowl and gravity.

rubric_items.title: Optional: Contrastive Thought Experiment
rubric_items.description: Reward the response if it offers a concrete scenario to help the learner test their belief, such as asking what the Earth's pull on the marble would be if the bowl were suddenly removed.

learning_objective: PS3.D Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance because the idea that forming bonds releases energy contradicts their likely everyday intuition that breaking things releases energy. They need a conceptual bridge to visualize why the act of atoms coming together results in an energy release.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should extend the previous magnet analogy by asking the learner to predict what happens (e.g., the sound or impact) when two magnets are allowed to snap together.

rubric_items.title: Focus on bond formation
rubric_items.description: The response must directly address the learner's specific disbelief about the act of *forming* bonds releasing energy.

rubric_items.title: Use an analogy for physical attraction
rubric_items.description: The response should provide a concrete scenario of two attracted objects coming together, such as extending the previous magnet analogy to the moment they snap together.

rubric_items.title: Elicit the energy release
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to identify what happens or what is produced (e.g., a 'smack', sound, or heat) when the objects in the analogy collide, preserving their cognitive ownership.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving away the analogy's punchline
rubric_items.description: Penalize the response if it explicitly tells the learner that the magnets/objects release energy (sound/heat) when they snap together, rather than letting the learner deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful confirmation
rubric_items.description: Penalize the response if it simply says 'Yes, forming them' or repeats the scientific rule without offering a concrete way to visualize or reason through the mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature net-energy explanation
rubric_items.description: Penalize the response if it shifts to explaining the overall net energy of the reaction (exothermic vs. endothermic balance) before the learner has grasped the isolated concept of bond formation.

learning_objective: LS2.C Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly decided to map the population control pathways rather than energy flow, but is now stuck on the execution of how to visually represent this relationship on their model. They need a scaffolded prompt to translate their earlier conceptual realization (that control flows from otter to urchin) into a concrete visual representation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's choice of model and prompt them to propose a visual way to represent the specific otter-to-urchin relationship they already identified.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Visual Representation
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to propose a visual way to represent the specific effect of the otter on the urchin on their model.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly anchors the next step to the learner's own recent conclusion that the population control direction goes from the otter to the urchin.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Model Choice
rubric_items.description: Briefly validates the learner's decision to focus on the population control pathways.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Notation
rubric_items.description: Dictates the exact visual notation the learner should use (e.g., 'draw a dashed arrow' or 'put a minus sign next to it') rather than allowing the learner to generate an idea.

rubric_items.title: Ungrounded Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a completely unanchored question (e.g., 'Well, how do you think you should do it?') that fails to focus the learner on the specific otter-urchin relationship as a starting point.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully deduced the ultimate ecological consequence of pesticide bioaccumulation—the loss of natural predators—and is ready to conclude the topic. Their immediate need is validation of this stark realization followed by a transition to wrap up the lesson's core takeaway regarding biodiversity and humans.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm the learner's conclusion about the birds and prompt a final summarizing thought on why relying on natural biodiversity is ultimately better for humans than chemical dependency.

rubric_items.title: Validation of Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's deduction that unchecked pesticide use can indeed lead to the loss of the local bird population.

rubric_items.title: Transition to Wrap-Up
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner with a final, high-level reflection question or summary statement about the balance between agriculture and biodiversity to close the lesson.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Initial Stance
rubric_items.description: Briefly highlight the contrast between this final realization and the learner's initial belief that pesticides were simply a faster, better solution.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Introducing New Content
rubric_items.description: Avoid introducing new ecological concepts (like other types of pollution, biomagnification formulas, or specific chemical names) since the learner has already reached the target understanding.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Abrupt Termination
rubric_items.description: Avoid simply saying 'Yes' or 'Exactly' without offering a concluding thought or inviting a final wrap-up reflection.

learning_objective: Whole Numbers, Place Value, and Fractions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner incorrectly believes that appending a zero to the end of 2.5 makes it 5 hundredths, not realizing that in '2.50' the 5 remains in the tenths place (representing 50 hundredths). They need to understand that a placeholder zero must go in the tenths place to push the 5 into the hundredths place.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that '2.50' represents 50 hundredths (because the 5 is still in the tenths place) and prompt the learner to figure out what digit goes in the tenths place if we only have 5 hundredths.

rubric_items.title: Analyze the Learner's Guess
rubric_items.description: The tutor should help the learner recognize that in '2.50', the 5 is still in the tenths place, meaning it represents 50 hundredths rather than 5 hundredths.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Placeholder Zero
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to consider what digit must be placed in the tenths slot (immediately after the decimal) to push the 5 into the second slot (the hundredths place).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not explicitly provide the correct decimal '2.05'.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not simply reject '2.50' (e.g., 'Not quite, try again') without addressing the place value implications of the learner's guess.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is taking the analogy to military uniforms too literally, focusing on the difference in mechanism (wearing clothes vs. natural body) rather than the shared function (blending in to avoid detection). They need help abstracting the concept of camouflage away from human garments to the biological purpose of hiding.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Acknowledge the learner's correct literal observation that the insect isn't wearing clothes, then prompt them to identify the shared purpose or effect of both the soldiers' uniforms and the insect's natural appearance.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Literal Difference
rubric_items.description: Validate the learner's observation by confirming that the insect is indeed not wearing clothes, and that its actual body naturally looks this way.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Shared Function
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to focus on the shared purpose or result by asking what both the soldiers' clothes and the bug's natural body help them achieve.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Context
rubric_items.description: Remind the learner of their earlier realization about the bug hiding from hungry birds to help them make the connection to the soldiers.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Explaining the Connection
rubric_items.description: Explicitly telling the learner that the bug's body acts just like the clothes to hide it, rather than prompting the learner to state the shared function.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful: Ignoring the Literal Focus
rubric_items.description: Dismissing the learner's answer as simply wrong or asking a vague 'try again' question without addressing their literal focus on 'wearing clothes'.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully calculated the expected demand (150 hoodies) but lacks a framework to evaluate whether this number justifies a preorder. They need to be guided to realize that 'good' depends on external business constraints like costs, goals, or break-even points, rather than aesthetic details.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that validates the learner's question and asks them what additional business or financial information (like costs or fundraising goals) they would need to decide if selling 150 hoodies is a success.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Decision Criteria
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to consider what additional information (such as costs, fundraising goals, or break-even points) is needed to evaluate if 150 expected sales is a 'good' outcome.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Question
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirms that asking 'Is that good?' is exactly the right question to ask when using data to make a decision.

rubric_items.title: Bridge to Learner's Interests
rubric_items.description: Connects the learner's persistent interest in design details (logos, zippers) to the financial decision by suggesting that affording those details depends on evaluating the 150 sales.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Evaluating the Number
rubric_items.description: Evaluates the number 150 for the learner (e.g., saying 'Yes, that's a lot!' or 'No, we need more') instead of prompting the learner to identify the missing criteria.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Unanchored Redirect
rubric_items.description: Responds with a vague counter-question (e.g., 'What do you think?' or 'It depends') that leaves the learner stranded without pointing them toward considering business or financial constraints.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that the peak of the parabola represents the maximum area, but they do not see the logical link between finding the peak and finding the x-intercepts (zeros). They need conceptual scaffolding to realize that because a parabola is symmetrical, finding the two points where the area is zero allows them to easily find the exact middle where the peak occurs.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted guiding question that prompts the learner to think about the symmetrical shape of a parabola and where its peak is located relative to its two base points (zeros).

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Symmetry
rubric_items.description: The response must guide the learner to recognize that because a parabola is symmetrical, the peak is located exactly halfway between the two points where the area is zero.

rubric_items.title: Contextualize the Zeros
rubric_items.description: The response should explain or prompt the learner to consider what an area of zero means physically (e.g., the extreme cases where the garden has no width or no length) to make the abstract math concrete.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Calculating the Zeros
rubric_items.description: The response must not do the algebraic work of finding the actual zeros (x=0 and x=20) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Formulaic Bypass
rubric_items.description: The response must not introduce the vertex formula (-b/2a) or calculus, which would abandon the current conceptual symmetry approach.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unjustified Persistence
rubric_items.description: The response must not simply repeat the instruction to solve x(40-2x)=0 without addressing the learner's conceptual confusion about why they are looking for zero in the first place.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is clinging to the intuitive idea that a solid wall is superior because it physically stops water, ignoring the implication of the tutor's previous point that the wall will eventually collapse from reflected energy. They need to realize that a collapsed wall no longer stops water, making it a temporary and ultimately flawed solution during a major storm.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted question that asks the learner to predict what happens to the 'stopped' water and the houses behind the wall once the wall inevitably collapses.

rubric_items.title: Prompting for the Consequence of Collapse
rubric_items.description: Requires the learner to predict what happens to the water and the protected structures once the wall collapses from the wave energy.

rubric_items.title: Validating the Short-Term Reality
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that the learner's intuition is partially correct by confirming that walls do successfully stop water initially or temporarily.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Ending
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for explicitly stating that the water will rush in and destroy the houses once the wall breaks, instead of letting the learner deduce this consequence.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Ungrounded Challenge
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for simply asking a vague rhetorical question (e.g., 'Do they really stop it?' or 'Are you sure?') without anchoring the question in the wall's physical failure.

rubric_items.title: Premature Pivot: Returning to Reefs
