rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for shifting the topic back to the benefits of oyster reefs before fully dismantling the learner's belief in the wall's permanent effectiveness.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is overwhelmed by the sudden introduction of the 4x4x4 calculation and is still conceptually anchored to their belief that they should be using a 3:1 ratio. They do not understand where the '4' comes from for each individual gene, causing a complete breakdown in their ability to follow the math.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should step back from the three-gene calculation and ground the '4 combinations' in a single gene, ideally by prompting the learner to recall the 4 outcomes (or boxes) in a standard monohybrid Punnett square.

rubric_items.title: Ground the '4' in a Single Gene
rubric_items.description: Requires the tutor to break down the '4 combinations' by focusing the learner on just one gene first (e.g., asking how many boxes or outcomes are in a standard Punnett square for two heterozygous parents).

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge and Step Back
rubric_items.description: Rewards the tutor for explicitly acknowledging the learner's confusion and validating the need to step back from the complex 3-gene calculation.

rubric_items.title: Bridge to the 3:1 Misconception
rubric_items.description: Rewards the tutor for connecting the '4 combinations' back to the learner's fixation on the 3:1 ratio (e.g., pointing out that the familiar 3:1 ratio actually comes from the 4 total outcomes of a single-gene Punnett square).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Forcing the Math
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for simply providing the final answer (64) or insisting the learner calculate 4x4x4 without first establishing what the '4' represents biologically.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Penalizes the tutor for asking a vague, open-ended question (like 'What part are you confused about?') that leaves the overwhelmed learner without a concrete conceptual foothold.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on an apparent contradiction in the tutor's previous explanations, conflating the center of gravity's fixed physical location on the forklift with the shifting downward projection of gravity as the forklift tilts. They need a conceptual bridge to visualize how a fixed point on an object can have a changing vertical alignment when the object itself rotates.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the apparent contradiction and introduce a concrete visual analogy or thought experiment (like a plumb line hanging from a tilting ceiling) to help the learner distinguish between the fixed point on the machine and the changing downward path of gravity.

rubric_items.title: Target the 'Fixed vs. Shifting' Contradiction
rubric_items.description: The response must directly address the learner's confusion by distinguishing between the center of gravity's fixed physical location on the forklift and the changing vertical path of gravity pulling straight down from that point.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Visualization Prompt
rubric_items.description: The response should introduce or ask the learner to imagine a concrete physical analogy (such as a string hanging from a tilting object or leaning back in a chair) to make the shifting downward projection intuitive.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the tutor's previous statements ('it doesn't move' vs 'what's shifting') sound contradictory or that this is a tricky concept to visualize.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating Failed Terminology
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely repeat the abstract phrases 'line of action' or 'point on the ground' without offering a new, concrete way to visualize them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that fully explain the analogy and its conclusion without asking a guiding question that requires the learner to apply the visualization themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply ask 'What do you think is moving?' or tell the learner to re-read the previous message, leaving them stranded in their current confusion.

learning_objective: LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the age of a lineage's divergence with the age of the modern species itself, mistakenly believing that because the kangaroo split off earlier, the modern kangaroo is 'older.' They need to realize that both the human and kangaroo lineages have been evolving for the exact same amount of time since that deep split.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a targeted prompt or the previously established family analogy to help the learner deduce that both the kangaroo and the human have been evolving for the same amount of time since their common ancestor.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Elapsed Time to Present
rubric_items.description: The tutor prompts the learner to evaluate the elapsed time from the shared ancestor to the present day for both the kangaroo and human lineages.

rubric_items.title: Distinguish Split Age from Species Age
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly validates the learner's intuition that something is indeed older (the split or the common ancestor) while questioning the assumption that the modern kangaroo itself is older.

rubric_items.title: Leverage the Family Analogy
rubric_items.description: The tutor incorporates the cousin/grandparent analogy to illustrate that an earlier branch point does not mean the modern descendant is older (e.g., asking if a second cousin is inherently older than you just because your shared ancestor lived longer ago).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly states that both species have been evolving for the same amount of time or that modern species are the same age, bypassing the learner's opportunity to reason this out.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unscaffolded Pushback
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a vague question (e.g., 'What makes you say the kangaroo is older?') without anchoring the prompt in the evolutionary timeline, the present day, or the shared ancestor.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is anchored to the physical snapshot of the ecosystem ('more zooplankton'), unable to reconcile how a visibly smaller population of producers can energetically sustain a larger population of consumers. They need to connect their previous realization about rapid phytoplankton reproduction to the fact that these producers are being consumed just as quickly, which keeps their standing biomass low while their cumulative energy contribution remains high.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's observation about the physical snapshot, then use a targeted prompt or concrete analogy (like a small, constantly refilled plate of food) to help the learner deduce that the phytoplankton are being eaten as fast as they reproduce.

rubric_items.title: Reconcile Biomass with Consumption Rate
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to consider what happens to the rapidly reproducing phytoplankton that keeps their visible numbers low, guiding them to realize they are being eaten by the zooplankton almost immediately.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Snapshot Observation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly acknowledges that the learner is correct about the physical reality: at any single moment, there really are more zooplankton than phytoplankton.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Rate Visualization
rubric_items.description: Introduces or asks the learner to imagine a concrete analogy (e.g., a small plate of food that is continuously refilled vs. a large plate that isn't) to distinguish between standing amount and continuous flow.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Mechanism Directly
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner the answer (e.g., 'The phytoplankton are eaten as fast as they reproduce, so their biomass stays low') instead of prompting them to figure out why the numbers stay low despite rapid reproduction.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating 'Over Time' Without Context
rubric_items.description: Merely repeats the rule that energy is measured 'over time' or asks a generic question about energy flow without directly addressing the learner's specific sticking point about the physical presence of 'more zooplankton'.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner just correctly established that gaining electrons results in a negative charge, but they immediately contradict this by guessing that the 'plus side' of the triboelectric chart represents gaining electrons. They need to reconcile their previous realization with the chart's labels before tackling the more complex concept of relative positions on the chart.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted cognitive-conflict prompt that asks the learner to evaluate their guess ('plus side') using their own immediately preceding conclusion that gaining electrons makes an object negative.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Reconciliation with Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner to apply their just-stated conclusion (that gaining electrons makes an object negative) to evaluate their new guess about the 'plus side' of the chart.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Correction
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that the negative side of the chart is the one that gains electrons, bypassing the opportunity for the learner to catch their own contradiction.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's guess with a generic 'Are you sure?' or 'Look at the chart again' without explicitly anchoring them back to their recent realization about negative charges.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Explaining Relative Position
rubric_items.description: Introduces the concept that charge depends on the relative position of two fabrics on the chart, which skips over the immediate bottleneck of mapping 'gaining electrons' to the negative label.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that a duplicate gene can safely mutate, but they lack the mechanistic link between a change in the DNA code and a physical change in the resulting protein's shape. They need to connect DNA instructions to the sequence of building blocks (amino acids) that determine how a protein physically folds.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to recall what physical components DNA actually provides the instructions to build (amino acids or building blocks) so the learner can deduce how changing those components alters the final structure.

rubric_items.title: Focus on DNA as Instructions for Building Blocks
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to recall or consider what physical components DNA provides the instructions to assemble (e.g., amino acids, parts, or building blocks).

rubric_items.title: Connect Components to Physical Shape
rubric_items.description: Guides the learner to think about how changing the sequence or type of those building blocks would physically alter the final 3D structure of the object being built.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Explanation of Protein Folding
rubric_items.description: Penalizes telling the learner directly that DNA codes for amino acids which determine how the protein folds, bypassing their opportunity to make the connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague DNA Questions
rubric_items.description: Penalizes asking overly broad questions about DNA (e.g., 'What does DNA do?' or 'What is a mutation?') that fail to focus the learner specifically on the physical construction of proteins.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Question
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that the learner's question ('Wait, why does the shape change?') is a great question or highlights that this is the crucial missing link in understanding adaptation.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating their experience of cold glasses getting wet with all glasses, leading them to believe that everyday room-temperature glasses also get wet because water leaks through microscopic holes in the glass. They need to be guided to realize that normal glasses do not get wet, or that a leaking glass would lose water over time, before they can understand the actual mechanism of condensation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to critically evaluate their claim that normal glasses get wet, either by asking about the logical consequences of a glass leaking (like the water level dropping) or by contrasting a cold glass with a room-temperature or hot glass.

rubric_items.title: Dismantle the Leaking Hypothesis
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate their belief that normal glasses leak by asking about a logical consequence (e.g., the water level dropping over time) or by questioning if room-temperature/hot glasses actually get wet.

rubric_items.title: Re-anchor to the Colored Liquid Test
rubric_items.description: Bring the learner's attention back to the previously mentioned red juice test as a concrete way to prove whether the moisture on the outside is coming from the inside.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is remembering real instances of glasses getting wet (like cold drinks), validating their everyday experience before challenging their proposed mechanism.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Refutation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply tell the learner that glass lacks holes or that room-temperature glasses do not get wet; allow them to realize this through questioning.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unfocused Pushback
rubric_items.description: Do not merely ask 'Are you sure?' or 'Do they really get wet?' without introducing a concrete physical constraint or comparison to help the learner evaluate their claim.

rubric_items.title: Defer the Condensation Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Do not explain that water comes from the air or address the hidden belief about the cold cup acting like a magnet, as the 'leaking' misconception must be fully resolved first.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confusing the reciprocal trigonometric function (cosecant) with the inverse trigonometric function (arcsine or $\sin^{-1}$) needed to isolate the angle. They need to understand this distinction and be guided toward the correct inverse function notation or concept.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, not the inverse, and provide a concrete hint (such as calculator notation) to help the learner identify arcsine or $\sin^{-1}$.

rubric_items.title: Address Cosecant Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly explain that cosecant is the reciprocal (1/sin) of sine, distinguishing it from the inverse function needed to undo sine.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Inverse Function
rubric_items.description: The response must provide a concrete hint (e.g., referencing calculator buttons like $\sin^{-1}$ or the prefix 'arc') or directly introduce the inverse sine function to help the learner move forward.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response should not apply the inverse function to the equation for the learner (e.g., by writing out $\frac{\pi}{12}t = \arcsin(0.75)$).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply reject 'cosecant' and repeat the question 'What is the inverse?' without offering new scaffolding, as the learner has already exhausted their current knowledge.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Sine Connection
rubric_items.description: The response can acknowledge that the learner was on the right track by picking a function that is indeed related to sine.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is relying on circular reasoning, assuming that the mere physical act of 'clumping' is sufficient to explain the drastic change from a liquid milk protein to a plastic-like solid. They need to realize that physical rearrangement alone cannot account for such fundamentally new material properties, which indicates the formation of a new substance.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should create cognitive conflict by challenging whether physical clumping alone ever changes a material's fundamental properties, prompting the learner to realize that a new substance must have been formed.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the Sufficiency of Clumping
rubric_items.description: The response must challenge the learner's assumption that merely clumping or grouping a substance together can drastically change its fundamental properties.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the 'New Substance' Connection
rubric_items.description: The response should guide the learner to connect the emergence of entirely new properties (like the plastic texture) to the creation of a brand new substance.

rubric_items.title: Use a Contrastive Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response uses an everyday example of physical clumping (e.g., crumpling paper, packing a snowball) to illustrate that physical grouping retains the original material's properties.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly state that a chemical reaction occurred or directly tell the learner that a new substance was formed.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Validating the Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response must not accept 'clumping' as a valid explanation for the plastic-like behavior, nor should it vaguely ask 'what else?' without actively dismantling the clumping hypothesis.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified the core conceptual reason for switching counting units—the remaining tallies do not form a complete group of five—but their hesitant tone ('Because... there's not five?') indicates they need validation to fully dismantle their prior assumption that skip-counting must continue indefinitely.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's correct reasoning and summarize the general rule for counting mixed-unit tally marks to consolidate the concept.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's realization that you cannot count by fives if there isn't a complete group of five.

rubric_items.title: Consolidate the Rule
rubric_items.description: Connect the learner's specific observation ('there's not five') to the general rule for reading tally charts: we count by fives for full groups and switch to ones for the remainders.

rubric_items.title: Address Hesitation
rubric_items.description: Provide positive reinforcement to build confidence, acknowledging that the learner successfully figured out the reasoning despite their hesitant tone.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Redundant Questioning
rubric_items.description: Ask another question probing why we switch counting units, which would undermine the correct answer the learner just provided and cause confusion.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Unacknowledged Transition
rubric_items.description: Move on to a new problem or topic without first validating the learner's correct explanation for why the counting unit changes.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the base and height values but is experiencing cognitive dissonance because the formula ignores the diagonal edge(s) of the triangle. Their immediate need is a conceptual bridge explaining why the area formula only requires base and height, and how the diagonal is implicitly accounted for by the 'divide by 2' step.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should pause the arithmetic calculation and prompt the learner to visualize what shape is created by multiplying just the base and height (a rectangle), so the learner can discover that the diagonal cuts that shape in half.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Bounding Shape Concept
rubric_items.description: Guides the learner to consider the shape or area created by multiplying just the base and the height (a 5x8 rectangle or parallelogram).

rubric_items.title: Connect Diagonal to Halving
rubric_items.description: Helps the learner connect the diagonal edge(s) to the 'divide by 2' step in the formula, illustrating that the diagonal is the line that cuts the bounding shape in half.

rubric_items.title: Inquiry Over Telling
rubric_items.description: Uses a question to prompt the learner's visualization (e.g., 'What shape would we get if we just multiplied the 5 by the 8?') rather than simply explaining the geometric relationship to them.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Good Question
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's intuition by explicitly acknowledging that asking about the diagonal is a great geometric observation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dismissive Rule-Stating
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that simply state the diagonal is 'not needed for area' or 'only used for perimeter' without providing a geometric reason why.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Forcing the Calculation
rubric_items.description: Penalizes responses that ignore or bypass the conceptual question to push the learner to finish the arithmetic (5 * 8 / 2).

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the second group of seeds must also be dried after growing, tentatively moving away from their hidden belief that they could compare wet seedlings to dry seeds. They now need confirmation of this step and guidance on how to mathematically compare the two distinct groups' measurements to find the change in mass.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm the learner's correct intuition to dry the second group, and then prompt them to either articulate why this is necessary (to remove water weight) or how they will mathematically compare the two dry masses.

rubric_items.title: Validate Drying the Second Group
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's correct intuition that the second group of seeds must also be dried after they finish growing.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Mathematical Comparison
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner how they will use the two measurements (Group 1's starting dry mass and Group 2's final dry mass) to figure out the overall change in weight.

rubric_items.title: Elicit the Purpose of Drying
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explain why we must dry the grown plants before weighing them, directly challenging the hidden belief that wet weight could be compared to dry weight.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Math
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner the calculation steps (e.g., 'Yes, then you subtract Group 1 from Group 2'); leave the cognitive work of designing the math to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Mere Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely say 'Yes' or 'Exactly' without prompting the learner to take the next step (either formulating the math or explaining the reasoning behind drying).

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is fixated on the total number of particles lost (4) and is not internalizing the tutor's repeated explanations because they haven't been asked to actively break down those 4 particles themselves. They need to shift from passively receiving the proton/neutron distinction to actively stating it.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that validates the learner's correct assertion (that 4 things are indeed lost) but asks the learner to explicitly identify what specific types of particles make up those '4 things'.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Learner's Premise
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is absolutely correct that exactly 4 things (or particles) are being lost.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Particle Composition
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explicitly state what specific types of particles make up those '4 things'.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeated Explanation
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for simply telling the learner again that the 4 things are 2 protons and 2 neutrons, as this direct explanation has already failed multiple times.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Ignoring the '4'
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for ignoring the learner's focus on the '4 things' by pivoting to a generic question about the definition of atomic number.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the resting heart rate (R) must be added to the 'extra beats' expression, but their phrasing ('So... plus R?') shows hesitation. They need validation of this insight and a prompt to synthesize all the components into a single, final algebraic equation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct addition of R and prompt them to assemble the complete equation for the target heart rate.

rubric_items.title: Validate Addition of R
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that adding the resting heart rate (R) is the correct next step.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Full Equation Assembly
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to combine the previously discussed parts into one complete final equation.

rubric_items.title: Suggest an Output Variable
rubric_items.description: Encourage the learner to set their expression equal to a variable representing the target heart rate (e.g., T = ...) to form a complete equation.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Final Equation
rubric_items.description: Do not write out the fully assembled expression or equation (e.g., `(M - R) * P + R`) for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Dead-End Affirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not merely say 'yes' or 'correct' without prompting the learner to actually construct the final equation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly calculated that the $-9i^2$ term evaluates to $+9$, but they are experiencing cognitive dissonance because the original expression $25 - 9i^2$ looks like a subtraction problem. They need to explicitly visualize the algebraic substitution of $-1$ for $i^2$ to understand how the double negative transforms the operation into addition.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to explicitly write out or visualize the full expression with the substitution in place (e.g., asking 'What does $25 - 9(i^2)$ look like if you replace $i^2$ with $-1$?').

rubric_items.title: Prompt Explicit Substitution
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explicitly substitute $-1$ into the full expression $25 - 9i^2$ so they can visually process the resulting $25 - 9(-1)$.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the source of the learner's confusion by validating that the original expression indeed started with a subtraction sign.

rubric_items.title: Premature Resolution of Sign Change
rubric_items.description: Do not simply tell the learner 'subtracting a negative makes a positive' or give away the final addition step without requiring them to look at the substituted expression first.

rubric_items.title: Vague Sign Rules
rubric_items.description: Do not ask generic questions about negative numbers or subtraction rules without anchoring them to the specific expression $25 - 9(-1)$.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Difference of Squares Distraction
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce or reference the 'difference of squares' formula ($a^2 - b^2$) here, as it will distract from resolving the immediate arithmetic substitution.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is fixated on the pure arithmetic fact that 2+2=4 and is ignoring the units or variables attached to those numbers. They need a concrete demonstration, using the established mystery bag analogy or numerical substitution, of why adding the coefficients and constants together produces a logically flawed result.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's arithmetic fact (2+2=4) and then prompt them to apply that '4' to the concrete analogy (e.g., asking 'Would that give us 4 bags or 4 loose coins?') to create cognitive conflict about the mismatched units.

rubric_items.title: Validate Arithmetic Fact
rubric_items.description: Explicitly acknowledges that the learner's arithmetic is correct (that 2 + 2 is indeed 4) when dealing with plain numbers.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Evaluation of the Sum
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to evaluate the logical consequence of their '4' by either asking what physical item it represents in the analogy (e.g., 'Would that be 4 bags or 4 loose coins?') or by having them calculate the total with a specific number of coins per bag.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Direct Explanation of the Mismatch
rubric_items.description: Explains the punchline of the analogy directly (e.g., 'You can't add them because bags and coins are different things') instead of prompting the learner to discover the absurdity of the combination themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Reverting to Abstract Rules
rubric_items.description: Abandons the concrete analogy to repeat abstract algebraic rules about 'like terms' or 'variables,' which the learner has already shown they do not understand.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a generic prompt (e.g., 'Think about the bags again' or 'Are you sure?') that fails to specifically challenge the learner to evaluate what the '4' represents.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is clinging to the misconception that physical vibration ('shaking') must travel through the blood to transmit information, struggling to map the tutor's electrical analogy onto the biological reality of the spider. They need help distinguishing the external mechanical stimulus (the web shaking) from the internal transmission mechanism (electrical nerve signals).
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that contrasts the external physical shaking with the internal electrical signal, asking the learner to apply the lamp/wire analogy to evaluate whether the blood actually needs to shake to deliver the message.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Shaking Blood' Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to reason about whether the blood needs to shake to carry the message if the nerves are already acting like the fast electrical wire.

rubric_items.title: Extend the Electrical Analogy
rubric_items.description: Utilize the previously introduced lamp/wire analogy (or a similar contrast) to help the learner visualize how information can travel without physical vibration.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Origin of the Shaking
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's intuition about shaking makes sense because the external web and the spider's leg do physically shake at the start of the process.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Direct Correction of the Misconception
rubric_items.description: Do not simply tell the learner 'No, the blood doesn't shake' or directly explain that nerves replace the need for shaking blood without requiring them to do the reasoning.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Blood Question
rubric_items.description: Do not ignore the learner's specific question about the blood to move straight to how the brain controls the legs or muscles.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that the reflex arc bypasses the brain and is expressing surprise at this counterintuitive idea, needing immediate confirmation. At the same time, they hold a hidden belief that physical heat (rather than an electrochemical signal) travels through the nerves, which the tutor must begin to gently challenge now that the routing of the signal has been established.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly confirm that the reflex happens without the brain, and then use this fact to probe what exactly is traveling through the nerves, surfacing the learner's hidden belief about physical heat without directly correcting it.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Brain Bypass
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly confirm the learner's realization that the reflex action occurs without the brain's immediate involvement.

rubric_items.title: Probe the Nature of the Signal
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to consider what exactly is traveling through the nerves (e.g., 'If the brain hasn't felt it yet, what is moving up your arm?'), to begin addressing the hidden belief about physical heat.

rubric_items.title: Establish the Purpose of the Shortcut
rubric_items.description: The response may prompt the learner to think about why bypassing the brain is beneficial (e.g., saving time to prevent a burn).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Correction of Signal Type
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner that nerves use electrical signals or that physical heat doesn't travel through them; it must leave room for the learner to realize this themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The response should not introduce formal anatomical terms like sensory neurons, motor neurons, or interneurons before the learner has resolved what kind of signal is actually traveling.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response should not merely confirm the brain bypass without providing a specific follow-up question that advances the learner's understanding of either the signal's nature or the reflex's purpose.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner holds the misconception that all fractions have terminating decimal representations, which conflicts with the tutor's statement that 355/113 continues forever. They need to recognize that rational numbers can have infinite, repeating decimal expansions before they can understand why the exact difference between their fraction and pi is non-terminating.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to recall or calculate the decimal form of a simple, familiar fraction that repeats (such as 1/3) to guide them to realize on their own that not all fractions terminate.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for a Repeating Fraction Counterexample
rubric_items.description: The response must guide the learner to consider a simple, familiar fraction whose decimal expansion does not terminate (such as 1/3 or 1/9) to create cognitive conflict with their belief that 'fractions stop.'

rubric_items.title: Validate the Partial Truth
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that the learner's intuition is partially correct because many common fractions (like 1/2 or 1/4) do indeed terminate.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Stating the Rule Outright
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner that fractions can repeat forever, rather than guiding them to recall or discover this fact themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Reusing the Complex Fraction
rubric_items.description: The response asks the learner to re-evaluate 355/113 (either via calculator, which truncates and reinforces the misconception, or via long division, which is too tedious), instead of pivoting to a simpler example.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Return to Pi Subtraction
rubric_items.description: The response shifts focus back to pi, the gear ratio, or the subtraction problem before the learner has resolved their confusion about whether fractions can have infinite decimals.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes they only have two explicit side lengths for the kite panels, temporarily blocking them from using SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence. They need to realize that the two panels share a central diagonal, which serves as the third congruent side.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's count of the explicit sides and prompt them to look at how the two panels are physically connected in the kite to discover the shared third side.

rubric_items.title: Direct Attention to the Shared Boundary
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to examine the physical relationship between the two panels in the kite, such as asking where they meet or what part of the shape they share.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Explicit Information
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is correct in noticing that only two outer side lengths are explicitly given or known for each panel.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Shared Side
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the triangles share a third side or that the shared diagonal counts as the third congruent side.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Prompts
rubric_items.description: Do not ask vague questions like 'what else can we find?' or 'look closer' without specifically directing the learner's attention back to the kite diagram or the panels' physical arrangement.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Pivoting to Angles
rubric_items.description: Do not shift the focus to finding angles (e.g., SAS congruence) when the learner is currently one step away from completing the SSS congruence criteria via the shared side.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly calculated and compared the percentages but is fixated on the absolute values (75% > 60%), failing to recognize that a sample size of only 4 shots is highly volatile and unreliable. They need scaffolding to understand why a small sample might not accurately reflect true shooting ability compared to a 50-shot sample.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a concrete hypothetical scenario (such as missing the very next shot from the corner) or ask a targeted question about luck to help the learner discover the fragility of the 4-shot sample's 75% success rate.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Sample Volatility
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider how easily the 75% success rate could change with a few more attempts, or ask how 'luck' might play a bigger role in 4 shots compared to 50.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Mathematical Comparison
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner is mathematically correct that 75% is strictly greater than 60%, validating their calculation before introducing the concept of reliability.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Rule)
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that small sample sizes are less reliable, more volatile, or worse predictors of future success than large sample sizes.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not simply repeat the question (e.g., 'But look at the 4 vs 50 again') or ask vaguely why 50 might be better without offering a concrete scenario or concept to scaffold their thinking.

rubric_items.title: Concrete Hypothetical Next Shot
rubric_items.description: Use the specific mathematical hypothetical of taking one more shot from the corner and missing (which drops the percentage to 3 out of 5, or exactly 60%) to vividly illustrate the fragility of the small sample.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused by the term 'scale factor' and does not realize it simply refers to how much the 3D object is being stretched, shrunk, or kept the same along the z-axis. They need to connect this geometric concept to their original problem context before they can construct the third row of their matrix.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explain 'scale factor' in plain geometric terms (e.g., stretching or shrinking) and prompt the learner to identify what physical change they want to apply to the z-axis based on their original CAD problem.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Concept of Scale Factor
rubric_items.description: Explain that a 'scale factor' is simply the multiplier that determines how much an object stretches, shrinks, or stays the same along a specific axis.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Z-Axis Goal
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to state what their specific goal is for the z-axis (e.g., height or depth) in their CAD model, prompting them to find the number themselves.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Prior X and Y Rows
rubric_items.description: Draw a parallel to the learner's previous work by pointing out that the '1's in their first two rows (1,0,0 and 0,1,0) meant the scale factors for the x and y axes were 1.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Confusion
rubric_items.description: Briefly validate the learner's confusion by acknowledging that 'scale factor' is a new or formal term for a simple concept.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly provide the numerical scale factor or tell the learner the contents of the third row (e.g., 'The third row is 0, 0, 2').

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Abstract Math Without Geometry
rubric_items.description: Do not explain 'scale factor' using purely abstract matrix definitions or formulas without referencing the physical or visual change to the 3D object.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has reverted to superficial guessing ('Webbed feet?') because they are struggling to visualize the foot structure of a hawk or crow, remaining anchored to the current topic word. They need concrete scaffolding to visualize the sharp, curved structures (claws/talons) required for gripping, contrasting them with the flat, slippery webbed feet they just discussed.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted visualization prompt that asks the learner to imagine or describe the specific shape of a hawk's or eagle's foot (e.g., when catching prey or perching) to elicit the concept of claws or sharp toes.

rubric_items.title: Elicit Gripping Structure
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to describe the physical shape or features of a hawk, eagle, or crow's foot (e.g., sharp, pointy, curved) to replace their incorrect guess of 'webbed feet.'

rubric_items.title: Scaffold with Concrete Imagery
rubric_items.description: Provide a familiar, concrete scenario (such as a hawk catching a mouse or a bird perching tightly on a branch) to help the learner visualize the gripping action and the necessary foot shape.

rubric_items.title: Contrast with Flatness
rubric_items.description: Briefly remind the learner that they just agreed webbed feet are flat and slippery, reinforcing why their guess is physically incompatible with gripping before redirecting them.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that hawks or crows have 'claws,' 'talons,' or 'sharp nails.'

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply reject the guess (e.g., 'No, try again' or 'Are you sure?') without providing new descriptive scaffolding to help them visualize the correct bird's foot.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited that multiple water molecules will arrange themselves radially around the central sodium ion, forming a 'circle.' Their immediate bottleneck is translating this conceptual realization into a concrete drawing that correctly orients the oxygen and hydrogen atoms within that circular arrangement.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's 'circle' idea and prompt them to describe or draw exactly how the V-shaped water molecules are positioned to form that circle around the sodium ion.

rubric_items.title: Validate the 'Circle' Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly confirm that the learner's visualization of a circle of water molecules around the central ion is correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Specific Atom Orientation
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to articulate or draw how the specific parts of the water molecule (the oxygen 'point' vs. the hydrogen 'arms') are arranged to form this circle.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge 3D Reality
rubric_items.description: The response briefly notes that while a circle is perfect for a 2D drawing on paper, the actual arrangement in a glass of water is a 3D sphere.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving away the drawing)
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner exactly how to draw the circle (e.g., 'draw the oxygens on the inside and hydrogens on the outside') instead of asking them to deduce the arrangement based on their prior conclusions.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The response merely agrees with the learner (e.g., 'Yes, exactly like a circle') without prompting them to apply this insight to the specific orientation of the atoms in their drawing.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has lost track of the entities in the tutor's hypothetical scenario, answering 'the fish' even though the tutor specified the competition is between algae and coral, and the scenario assumes the fish are absent.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted redirect that reminds the learner of the two actual competitors (algae and coral) and the premise that the fish are gone, prompting them to re-evaluate who wins the space.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Competitors
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner's attention back to the specific competitors (algae and coral) to correct their misconception that the fish are the ones competing for space.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce the Premise
rubric_items.description: Reminds the learner of the premise of the previous question: the parrotfish are currently absent or removed from the scenario.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly states that the algae wins the competition or explains the resulting harm to the coral, rather than prompting the learner to deduce who wins.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Rejection
rubric_items.description: Rejects the learner's answer (e.g., 'Not quite') without providing any scaffolding about the two competitors or the absence of the fish.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Fish's Role
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's focus on the fish by acknowledging their importance (e.g., they eat the algae) before clarifying that they are not the ones competing for space.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully completed the mathematical comparison, recognizing that the surviving generation's average toe pad size is larger. They now need to transition from mathematical observation to biological explanation by connecting this physical shift to the environmental pressure of the invasive brown anole.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe asking the learner to hypothesize why the surviving lizards might have larger toe pads, specifically prompting them to consider the impact of the invasive brown anoles.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Biological Cause
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to explain or hypothesize why the surviving population ended up with a larger average toe pad size.

rubric_items.title: Anchor to Environmental Pressure
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly mention the environmental context, such as the arrival of the invasive brown anoles, to help focus the learner's reasoning on natural selection.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Mathematical Conclusion
rubric_items.description: The tutor should briefly validate the learner's correct observation before pivoting to the biological concept (e.g., 'Exactly, it is bigger.').

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not explicitly state the biological advantage of the larger toe pads (e.g., do not say 'because bigger pads helped them climb higher to escape the brown anoles').

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Interpretation Prompts
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not ask a generic, unanchored question like 'What does this mean?' or 'Why?' without specifically referencing the physical trait (toe pads) or the environment.

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is likely confusing squaring a number with multiplying it by 1 or simply stating the base, leading to the incorrect evaluation that $2^2 = 2$. They need to unpack the arithmetic definition of an exponent before they can correctly compare the squared values and apply them to the kinetic energy relationship.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to define what it means to square a number or to expand $2^2$ into a multiplication problem, isolating the arithmetic error before returning to the physics context.

rubric_items.title: Unpack the Exponent
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to recall the definition of squaring or to expand the exponent into a multiplication expression (e.g., asking what number is multiplied by what).

rubric_items.title: Address the Specific Calculation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly reference the learner's answer of '2' or ask them to apply the definition of squaring specifically to the base number 2.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Arithmetic Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the correct mathematical result for $2^2$ (which is 4) or $1^2$ (which is 1).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not simply tell the learner they are wrong or ask them to 'try again' without specifically directing their attention to how exponents work.

rubric_items.title: Defer Physics Application
rubric_items.description: Do not attempt to connect the math back to kinetic energy, the original equation, or the physical concept of doubling speed until the arithmetic error is resolved.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has overgeneralized the rule for mitochondrial inheritance, concluding that the father contributes no genetic material at all. They need to be guided to distinguish between the specific case of mitochondrial DNA and the general case of nuclear DNA.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the father gives no mitochondrial DNA, but prompt the learner to recall the primary location or type of DNA (nuclear DNA) to realize that the father does contribute genetic material.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Mitochondrial Exception
rubric_items.description: The tutor must validate the learner's statement by confirming that it is true specifically and only for mitochondrial DNA.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Main DNA Location/Type
rubric_items.description: The tutor must ask a question that guides the learner to recall or identify the other type or location of DNA (nuclear DNA) that is inherited from both parents.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Telling
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly state that the father contributes nuclear DNA or that most DNA is in the nucleus, leaving the cognitive work of recalling this distinction to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Correction
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not simply say 'No, he gives half his DNA' without anchoring the correction to the specific biological distinction between mitochondrial and nuclear DNA.

learning_objective: LS4.A Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully discarded the 'sinking' misconception but is now stuck on the mechanics of burial, wondering how the bottom layers became so deep. They need to connect the idea of continuous deposition of new material on top over vast periods of time to the resulting depth of the oldest layers.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to apply the idea of continuous accumulation over a very long time, perhaps by extending the previous analogies of stacking books or pouring sand.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Accumulation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to deduce that continuous addition of new material (dirt, sand, etc.) on top is what causes the older layers to become deeply buried.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Geological Time
rubric_items.description: Incorporate the concept of vast geological time (e.g., thousands or millions of years) to help the learner scale up the accumulation process to explain the extreme depth.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Explanation
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that new layers piling up on top makes the bottom layers deep; the response must require the learner to make this connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Questions
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a generic, unguided question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that fails to provide a conceptual stepping stone like time or adding more material.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Previous Analogies
rubric_items.description: Explicitly reference the previously used analogies of stacking books or pouring sand to help the learner visualize the continuous buildup.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is frustrated and cognitively overloaded, unable to recall or connect the degrees in a half-circle to the current problem. They are stuck at a procedural bottleneck and need direct instruction on the 180-degree adjustment to regain confidence and move forward.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly state that a straight line or half-circle is 180 degrees, validate the learner's frustration, and prompt them to add 180 to -45.

rubric_items.title: Provide the Missing Fact
rubric_items.description: Explicitly state that a half-circle or straight line is 180 degrees, directly answering the tutor's previous question.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Specific Calculation
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to perform the specific arithmetic step of adding 180 to -45 to find the final angle.

rubric_items.title: Validate Frustration
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge the learner's frustration or normalize the difficulty of visualizing these angle adjustments.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Guess-What's-In-My-Head
rubric_items.description: Do not ask further conceptual questions or continue prompting the learner to guess the number of degrees in a line or circle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Doing the Final Arithmetic
rubric_items.description: Do not perform the final calculation (180 - 45 = 135) for the learner; leave the actual addition for them to complete.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that a gamma ray has zero mass and zero charge, but needs confirmation and a final push to assemble all the discussed components into the complete nuclear equation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Confirm the zeros, briefly reinforce why gamma has zero mass and charge (it is energy, not matter), and prompt the learner to write out the final, fully notated equation.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Zero Values
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's correct intuition that the mass and atomic numbers for the gamma ray are both zero.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Final Equation Assembly
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to write out the complete, final nuclear equation using all the components they have identified across the last few turns (symbols, mass numbers, and atomic numbers).

rubric_items.title: Reinforce Gamma Properties
rubric_items.description: Briefly explain or prompt the learner to state why gamma gets zeros (e.g., because it is electromagnetic energy/a photon, not a particle with mass or protons).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Final Equation
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that write out the final assembled equation for the learner instead of requiring them to synthesize the pieces themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Stranding Before Assembly
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely confirm the zeros without prompting the learner to take the final step of writing the complete equation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner successfully used addition to find that two rows of 5 blocks equal 10, overcoming their initial error of adding the dimensions (5+4=9). They now need to continue this additive, row-by-row process to reach the target of 4 rows and complete the bottom layer.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct calculation for two rows and prompt the learner to extend the pattern to three or four rows.

rubric_items.title: Validate Partial Success
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that 10 is the correct number of blocks for two rows.

rubric_items.title: Extend the Additive Pattern
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to determine the number of blocks for the third or fourth row, using their established total of 10 as a stepping stone.

rubric_items.title: Maintain Spatial Context
rubric_items.description: Reinforce the physical arrangement by referring to the blocks as 'rows' or mentioning 'covering the bottom'.

rubric_items.title: Premature Abstraction (Takeover)
rubric_items.description: Do not state the final answer for the bottom layer (20) or explicitly tell the learner to multiply 5 by 4.

rubric_items.title: Premature Volume (Takeover)
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce the vertical dimension (height or stacking layers) before the learner has successfully calculated the total for the bottom layer.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not ask an unguided question (e.g., 'Keep going' or 'What's next?') that fails to specify adding more rows of 5.

learning_objective: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is unable to follow the purely verbal explanation of distributing $(x+5)(x+5)$ and cannot visualize where the four distinct terms come from. They need a more structured, step-by-step, or visual representation to track the multiplication process.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a structured tool like the box method (area model) or split the distribution into two distinct parts (e.g., $x(x+5)$ and $5(x+5)$), prompting the learner to complete just the first step of this new method.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Structured Method
rubric_items.description: Introduce a structured or visual method for binomial multiplication, such as the box method (area model) or splitting the expression into $x(x+5) + 5(x+5)$.

rubric_items.title: Prompt First Step Only
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to perform only the first step of this new method (e.g., 'What is $x$ times $(x+5)$?' or 'What goes in the first box?'), rather than asking them to do the full expansion at once.

rubric_items.title: Validate Confusion
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that keeping track of all the multiplied parts is difficult or confusing, validating their current struggle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating Failed Explanation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply repeat the verbal explanation of 'multiply the first term by the second term' that the learner just stated they are confused by.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Terms
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly list out the four uncombined terms ($x^2 + 5x + 5x + 25$) for the learner.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is ignoring the biological mechanism of inheritance and randomly guessing genotype combinations ('Cc', 'CC'). They have bypassed the tutor's previous guiding question and need to be redirected to recognize that offspring can only inherit alleles that are physically present in the parents' genotypes.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should redirect the learner to answer the previous question by looking at the parents' 'cc' genotype and confirming whether a capital 'C' is available to pass down.

rubric_items.title: Redirect to the Missing 'C'
rubric_items.description: The tutor must redirect the learner to look at the parents' 'cc' genotypes and explicitly answer whether there is a capital 'C' available to give.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Available Allele
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce what specific allele the parents actually have available to pass down if they do not have a capital 'C'.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly tell the learner that the children's genotype is 'cc' or that the parents only have 'c' to give; the learner must deduce this.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not simply reject the learner's guess (e.g., 'No, not CC' or 'Try again') without anchoring the correction in the parents' actual alleles.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the median of the non-owner group (7,000) with its minimum value, despite the tutor's previous clarification. They need to be directed back to the data representation to visually or numerically identify the actual lowest data point.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly state that 7,000 is not the lowest value and prompt the learner to look at the data representation (such as the far left of a dot plot) to find the actual minimum for the non-owner group.

rubric_items.title: Correct the 7,000 Misconception
rubric_items.description: Explicitly state that 7,000 is not the lowest value, reaffirming that it represents the middle.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Minimum
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to look at the data for the non-owner group and identify the actual lowest step count.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Data Reading
rubric_items.description: Provide a concrete hint on where to look for the lowest value, such as checking the far left side of the dot plot or the smallest number in the data list.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the actual lowest or highest step counts for the non-owner group.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not simply say 'no' or 'try again' without directing the learner to the data representation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confusing the operations happening in the dividend/remainder with those happening in the quotient, mistakenly believing that bringing down a zero means appending a zero to the quotient (turning 14 into 140). They need immediate clarification that the zero applies to the remainder (making 30) while a decimal point applies to the quotient (making 14.).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly correct the '140' misconception by distinguishing between the remainder (which gets the zero) and the quotient (which gets the decimal point), and then prompt the learner to calculate the next digit by dividing 30 by 8.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Quotient vs. Remainder
rubric_items.description: Explicitly correct the '140' misunderstanding by clarifying that the zero is added to the remainder (making 30), while a decimal point is placed after the 14 in the quotient (making it 14.).

rubric_items.title: Prompt for the Next Digit
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to find the next digit of the quotient by asking how many times 8 goes into the new remainder of 30.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Source of Confusion
rubric_items.description: Validate the learner's logic by acknowledging that adding a zero next to 14 would indeed make 140, before correcting the placement.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Next Digit
rubric_items.description: Do not calculate 30 divided by 8 for the learner or provide the next digit (3) or the final answer.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Ignoring the Misconception
rubric_items.description: Do not ignore the '140' confusion by merely repeating the prompt to divide 8 into 30 without addressing the quotient's format.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identified 1.03 as the growth factor but mistakenly placed it in a linear algebraic structure ('1.03x'), confusing multiplying by a variable with repeated multiplication. They need to realize that '1.03x' does not represent multiplying the salary by 1.03 year after year.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to test their proposed expression '1.03x' (e.g., by plugging in x=2) or ask them how to mathematically represent multiplying by the same number repeatedly, guiding them toward the need for an exponent.

rubric_items.title: Engage with the Learner's Proposal
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly references the learner's suggested expression '1.03x' as the starting point for the turn, rather than ignoring it to focus on other missing parts of the equation (like the $50,000 starting salary).

rubric_items.title: Guide Toward Exponential Structure
rubric_items.description: The tutor provides a concrete path for the learner to rethink their equation, either by prompting them to test '1.03x' with a specific year (like x=2) or by asking how to mathematically represent multiplying by 1.03 repeatedly.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Correct Multiplier
rubric_items.description: The tutor validates that the learner correctly identified 1.03 as the necessary growth factor before challenging the algebraic structure.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Equation
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly provides the correct exponential equation (e.g., $50,000 * 1.03^x) or explicitly tells the learner to 'use an exponent' without giving them a chance to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: The tutor simply tells the learner 'no' or 'that is linear' without providing a concrete prompt to help them investigate why '1.03x' is mathematically incorrect for this situation.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that specific whales have specialized roles (bubble blower, caller) but assumes the rest of the group is passive. They need to realize that the ultimate goal of the trap is feeding, and the remaining whales actively participate in the final step of the hunt.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to deduce what the rest of the whales must do once the fish are herded and trapped, guiding them to realize the others are actively participating in catching or eating the food.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Waiting' Assumption
rubric_items.description: The response must directly address the learner's specific question by confirming that the other whales do not 'just wait' or are not passive.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Deduction of the Final Role
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to guess or deduce what the remaining whales must do to the trapped fish to complete the hunt.

rubric_items.title: Frame Around the Ultimate Goal
rubric_items.description: The response should remind the learner of the ultimate goal of the bubble net (getting food/eating) to scaffold their deduction of the remaining whales' jobs.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away the Final Step
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly tell the learner that the other whales swim up to eat, lunge at, or engulf the fish, bypassing the learner's chance to deduce this final step.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Stranding the Learner
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply say 'No, they don't wait' or 'They have other jobs' without providing a clue or prompt about the final stage of the hunt.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly calculated the full circumference (~25) and intuitively knows the half-circle curve should be ~12, but is confused because they haven't connected that dividing the full circumference by 2 bridges these two numbers. They need to realize that both numbers are correct steps in their established formula.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate both numbers and prompt the learner to recall their earlier step of dividing by two to connect the full circumference (25) to the half-circle curve (~12.5).

rubric_items.title: Validate Both Numbers
rubric_items.description: Confirm that the learner's multiplication result (~25) is correct and that their intuition about the answer being around 12 is also on the right track.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Connection
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to explain how the 25 relates to the 12, or ask them what the 25 represents in the context of the formula they built.

rubric_items.title: Reference Prior Formula
rubric_items.description: Explicitly refer back to the formula the learner helped build earlier (dividing by 2) to help them anchor their reasoning.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Overhelpful Explanation
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that 25 is the full circle and 12.5 is the half circle; leave the cognitive work of connecting the two numbers to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Total Perimeter
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce the need to add the straight diameter to find the total perimeter before the learner has confidently resolved the calculation for the curved part.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Pedantic Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not penalize or correct the learner for estimating '12' instead of calculating exactly '12.56' at this conceptual stage.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly deduced that a coefficient ('a big 3') is needed to balance the sodium atoms without changing the substance's identity. Their immediate need is to apply this coefficient and recognize that it multiplies every atom in the entire baking soda molecule, not just the sodium.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the learner's correct intuition and prompt them to calculate how placing this 'big 3' in front of the molecule changes the total count of the other elements (H, C, and O) on the left side.

rubric_items.title: Affirmation and Placement
rubric_items.description: Affirms the learner's answer ('a big 3') and clarifies or confirms that it goes in front of the entire baking soda molecule.

rubric_items.title: Prompting Distribution
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to determine the new total number of atoms for at least one of the other elements (H, C, or O) in the molecule now that there is a 3 in front.

rubric_items.title: Formal Terminology
rubric_items.description: Connects the learner's informal phrase ('a big 3') to the formal chemical term 'coefficient'.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Math
rubric_items.description: Explicitly states the new atom counts for Hydrogen, Carbon, or Oxygen (e.g., 'So now we have 9 oxygens') instead of requiring the learner to calculate them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Advancement
rubric_items.description: Moves on to balancing the next element or asks if the whole equation is now balanced before establishing the updated atom counts on the left side.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified that multiplying both the length and width by 2 introduces a '2 times 2' factor into the area calculation. They are tentatively offering this arithmetic insight but need confirmation and a prompt to explicitly connect it back to why the total fabric quadruples.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's '2 times 2' insight and prompt them to synthesize how this arithmetic explains the quadrupling of the banner's area, without making the final connection for them.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Arithmetic Insight
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative '2 times 2?' answer to validate their realization about the multipliers.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to articulate how the '2 times 2' math explains why the total area or fabric quadruples.

rubric_items.title: Generalization Check
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to apply this logic to a new scenario, such as asking what happens to the area if both dimensions are tripled.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Conclusion
rubric_items.description: State the final conceptual link for the learner (e.g., 'Yes, 2 times 2 is 4, which is why the area is 4 times larger') instead of letting them synthesize it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Merely confirm the arithmetic (e.g., 'Yes, 4') and move on without ensuring the connection to the banner's area is explicitly established.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Introduce algebraic variables or formal proofs (e.g., Area = 2L * 2W) before the learner has fully grounded the concept in their own arithmetic terms.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is confused by the tutor's prompt about the side being 'between' the two 'A's, likely because they have only identified one angle (60 degrees) so far and cannot visualize how a side connects two angles on the physical triangle.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that the side must physically connect the two angles used in the ASA proof, and prompt the learner to realize that since they only have one angle so far, they need a second angle to define this 'between' relationship.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Referents
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly state or prompt the learner to recognize that 'between' refers to being between the two angles (the two 'A's).

rubric_items.title: Define Included Side Physically
rubric_items.description: The tutor should guide the learner to understand that a side 'between' two angles is the physical line segment that connects the corners (vertices) of those two angles.

rubric_items.title: Highlight the Missing Angle
rubric_items.description: The tutor should connect this concept to the learner's current progress by pointing out that they currently only have one angle (the 60-degree angle), meaning they need a second angle to establish what the side is between.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Next Step
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for directly telling the learner which specific side to use or instructing them to calculate the next angle without first resolving their conceptual confusion about what 'between' means.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Repetition
rubric_items.description: Penalize the tutor for merely repeating that 'S' is between the 'A's in the acronym without grounding the concept in the physical features of the triangle.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly sees the four vertical lines but views the diagonal slash merely as a grouping symbol or boundary, rather than a countable tally mark representing an individual ant. They need guidance to separate the vertical lines from the diagonal line and recognize the slash as an additional, distinct item.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate that the learner correctly counted the four vertical lines, and then explicitly prompt them to count the diagonal slash as one additional ant.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Partial Count
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges that the learner correctly identified the four vertical lines, validating their observation before expanding on it.

rubric_items.title: Reframe the Diagonal Slash
rubric_items.description: Directs the learner to explicitly treat the diagonal slash as an additional, countable mark representing one more ant.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Total
rubric_items.description: Gives away the final answer by directly stating that the bundle equals five or that there are five ants.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Recounting
rubric_items.description: Simply tells the learner to 'count again' or 'look closer' without specifically addressing the diagonal line's role as a countable item.

learning_objective: PS1.A Structure and Properties of Matter

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly but hesitantly deduces that a shadow has no weight, having just established that it takes up no physical space. They now need validation of this second property so they can synthesize both findings to conclude whether a shadow is matter.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's conclusion about weight and prompt them to combine the two established facts (no space, no weight) to determine if a shadow is matter.

rubric_items.title: Validate Weight Conclusion
rubric_items.description: The tutor should validate the learner's tentative answer by confirming that a shadow indeed has no weight.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Synthesis for Matter
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to conclude whether a shadow is matter based on the two properties they just discussed.

rubric_items.title: Explicitly Recap Both Properties
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly restates both findings together (that a shadow has no weight and takes up no space) to frame the final question.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not explicitly state that a shadow is not matter, as the learner must make this final connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Synthesis Prompt
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not ask a vague follow-up (e.g., 'So what is a shadow?') that fails to focus the learner on the definition of matter.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully visualized that adjacent edges sharing a corner on the 2D net pivot to form a 3D corner, but their phrasing is tentative. However, they hold a hidden belief that only these directly adjacent edges will touch, meaning they are not yet ready to fold the entire box where non-adjacent edges must also meet.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct visualization of the adjacent edges forming a corner, and then direct their attention to two edges that do not share a corner on the flat net to challenge their hidden belief.

rubric_items.title: Validate the 3D Visualization
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge and confirm the learner's tentative realization that the two adjacent edges meet to form a corner of the 3D box.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the 'Only Adjacent' Belief
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to consider what happens to edges that are further apart and do not share a corner on the flat 2D net.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Next Match
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that non-adjacent edges will also meet or point out exactly which distant edges connect.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Progression
