rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has mixed up the shape names despite the tutor's mnemonic, incorrectly concluding that a pentagon has six sides. They are experiencing a momentary cognitive tangle and need to be guided to apply the mnemonic to one shape at a time to resolve the confusion.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted redirect that asks the learner to apply the 'x' mnemonic specifically to 'hexagon' first, establishing its side count before returning to 'pentagon'.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Application of Mnemonic
rubric_items.description: The response should direct the learner to explicitly apply the 'x' mnemonic to the word 'hexagon' to figure out its side count.

rubric_items.title: Isolate One Shape
rubric_items.description: The response should focus the learner on establishing the side count for just one shape (hexagon) before asking them to deduce the other, avoiding asking them to map both simultaneously.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that directly give away the answer by stating that a pentagon has five sides or a hexagon has six sides.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that simply tell the learner they are wrong or ask them to guess again without anchoring them back to the 'x' mnemonic.

rubric_items.title: Normalize the Mix-up
rubric_items.description: The response may gently validate the learner's confusion by acknowledging that mixing up these two shape names is a common or understandable mistake.

learning_objective: LS1.B Growth and Development of Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has made a highly accurate intuitive leap, recognizing that by disabling self-destruction, these damaged cells achieve a form of biological immortality. They need validation of this insight and a prompt to connect this 'immortality' back to the macroscopic consequences for the organism (tumor growth).
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's accurate intuition that these cells are biologically 'immortal' and prompt them to consider the consequences of immortal cells continuously dividing within a finite organism.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Immortality Insight
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly validate the learner's intuition by confirming that 'immortal' is an accurate and commonly used term for cancer cells that evade cell death.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Organism-Level Consequence
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to predict what happens to the organism or tissue when these 'immortal' cells continue to divide indefinitely.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Evasion of Apoptosis
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly link the concept of 'immortality' back to the cells' inability to trigger self-destruction, reinforcing the mechanism discussed in the previous turn.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Introducing Telomeres
rubric_items.description: The response must not introduce advanced molecular mechanisms of biological immortality (such as telomeres or telomerase) that the learner has not raised.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Consequence
rubric_items.description: The response must not explicitly state that this immortality leads to massive tumor growth, organ failure, or death, as the learner should deduce this consequence themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dead-End Validation
rubric_items.description: The response must not merely confirm that the cells are immortal without providing a follow-up question or prompt to advance the dialogue.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is persistently clinging to the '97%' figure (1 minus the p-value), attempting to shoehorn it into the tutor's qualitative language ('convincing evidence'). They need explicit guidance to drop percentages entirely and state the conclusion in purely qualitative terms.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should firmly instruct the learner to drop the '97%' and prompt them to answer the previous question (whether we have convincing evidence) using only words, such as a simple yes or no.

rubric_items.title: Reject Percentages
rubric_items.description: Explicitly instruct the learner to drop the '97%' and remove any percentages or numbers from their conclusion.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Qualitative Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to answer whether there is convincing evidence that the campaign worked using only words (e.g., asking for a simple 'yes' or 'no').

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Partial Adoption
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner correctly tried to use the target word 'convincing' before correcting their use of the number.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final, correct concluding sentence for the learner (e.g., do not say 'Just say: We have convincing evidence that the campaign worked').

rubric_items.title: Avoid Re-explaining Probability
rubric_items.description: Do not launch into another conceptual explanation of why 97% is mathematically incorrect, as the tutor just explained this and the immediate need is to fix the phrasing of the conclusion.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is still trying to find a direct causal link between the soot and the moths' biology, hypothesizing that the soot acted as an environmental trigger to activate the dark gene. They need to shift their focus from how individuals change to how a changed environment (dark trees) affects the survival of pre-existing genetic variations.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should clarify that the dark moths were already fully dark and the soot only changed the trees, then prompt the learner to predict how this environmental change would affect the survival of the light versus dark moths.

rubric_items.title: Address the 'Turned On' Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly correct the idea that the gene was 'turned on' by clarifying that the dark moths were already born fully dark before the soot arrived.

rubric_items.title: Shift Focus to Environmental Change
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly state or remind the learner that the soot changed the environment (the trees) rather than the moths themselves.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Differential Survival
rubric_items.description: The response should ask the learner to predict how the soot-covered trees would affect the pre-existing light and dark moths (e.g., asking which ones would be easier for predators to see).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the answer by explicitly stating that predators ate the light moths or that the dark moths survived and reproduced more; leave this for the learner to deduce.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not merely reject the 'turned on' idea without providing a concrete prompt about how the darkened trees affected the moths.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Tangent into Epigenetics
rubric_items.description: Do not get bogged down explaining the actual biological mechanisms of gene expression or epigenetics, as this distracts from the macro-level concept of natural selection.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has just observed that a fast but light movement produces a quiet sound, disproving their earlier hypothesis that speed equals volume, but they are eager to return to playing. They need to explicitly synthesize this new observation with their earlier 'big swing' observation to conclude that the size of the vibration, not the speed, determines loudness.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's observation, allow them to drum again, but attach a specific condition that requires the learner to physically demonstrate or verbally explain what kind of movement actually makes the sound loud.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Resolution
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to resolve their earlier confusion by asking them to state or show what actually makes a loud sound, now that they have proven 'fast' does not.

rubric_items.title: Channel the Distraction
rubric_items.description: Leverages the learner's request to drum by turning it into a physical demonstration of the concept (e.g., 'Yes, drum again, but show me the exact movement that makes it loud').

rubric_items.title: Validate Observation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirms the learner's correct observation that the fast scratching was indeed quiet.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly states the conclusion that larger movements or bigger vibrations cause louder sounds, robbing the learner of the opportunity to articulate this realization themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Concession
rubric_items.description: Permits the learner to drum again without giving them a specific conceptual focus, question, or demonstration task to complete while doing so.

rubric_items.title: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Introduces formal physics vocabulary like 'amplitude' or 'frequency' before the learner has fully solidified the physical concepts of size versus speed in their own words.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly hypothesized that the carbon returns to the wetland sediment when the plants die and sink, but their question mark indicates they need confirmation. The immediate need is to validate this correct step and prompt them to close the loop by connecting this dead organic matter in the oxygen-free mud back to the production of methane.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the learner's hypothesis about the plants dying and sinking, and then prompt them to explain what happens to that dead material in the oxygen-free mud to produce the methane they discussed at the start.

rubric_items.title: Validate Sinking Hypothesis
rubric_items.description: Confirms that the learner's hypothesis about the plants dying and sinking into the mud is correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt the Final Link to Methane
rubric_items.description: Asks the learner what happens to the dead plant matter once it is buried in the oxygen-free mud to turn it back into methane.

rubric_items.title: Frame as Cycle Completion
rubric_items.description: Explicitly frames this final step as completing the cycle or returning to the starting point of their conversation.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Learner Effort
rubric_items.description: Praises the learner for successfully reasoning through the complex steps of the carbon cycle.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving Away Decomposition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly names the mechanism (decomposition, breaking down) or the agents (bacteria, microbes, methanogens) before the learner has a chance to generate them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: Unanchored Prompt
rubric_items.description: Asks a generic 'What happens next?' without grounding the prompt in the specific environment (oxygen-free mud) or the target product (methane).

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is evaluating the numerator and denominator separately, getting stuck because $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational on its own. They need to realize that by combining the terms under a single radical, the division of 27 by 3 happens before the square root is evaluated, creating a perfect square.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Acknowledge that $\sqrt{3}$ is indeed irrational on its own, then prompt the learner to recall that combining the terms under one radical allows the division to happen first.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's correct observation that $\sqrt{3}$ by itself does not have an integer square root.

rubric_items.title: Redirect to Combined Radical
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner's attention to the combined expression $\sqrt{27/3}$ or prompt them to consider what happens when the division is performed inside the radical first.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Over-Explaining the Resolution
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that dividing 27 by 3 inside the radical resolves the irrationality; leave the cognitive work of connecting the combined fraction to the disappearance of the radical to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Dismissing the Bottleneck
rubric_items.description: Do not ignore the learner's specific concern about $\sqrt{3}$ by simply repeating the question about $\sqrt{9}$ or moving on without addressing their confusion about the denominator.

learning_objective: PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly identifies rain as the physical mechanism that moves water to the mountains, but they have not yet recognized that lifting this water into the sky requires an input of energy. They need to trace the water's path backward to realize that something had to work against gravity to get the water up into the clouds in the first place.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's answer and prompt them to explain how the water gets lifted up into the sky or clouds before it rains, focusing their attention on the upward movement.

rubric_items.title: Trace Water Upward
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to explain how water gets up into the sky or clouds before it can fall as rain.

rubric_items.title: Emphasize Upward Effort
rubric_items.description: Frames the prompt around the physical effort, force, or energy required to move the water upward (e.g., asking what 'lifts' it or how it goes 'against gravity').

rubric_items.title: Validate Rain Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or validates the learner's correct observation that rain is the physical process that delivers water to the mountains.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Evaporation/Sun)
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that the sun provides the energy or that evaporation lifts the water, bypassing the learner's opportunity to deduce it.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness (Generic Weather)
rubric_items.description: Asks a generic question about the water cycle (e.g., 'Where does rain come from?') without specifically directing the learner's attention to the upward movement or the energy required.

rubric_items.title: Premature Pivot to Falling
rubric_items.description: Abandons the discussion of how water gets up the mountain and prematurely returns to discussing the water falling down the dam.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly recognizes that building a nest requires energy, but they are stuck because they haven't compared the effort of building one massive shared roof to the effort of building dozens of individual, separate roofs. They need a prompt that helps them contrast the workload of cooperative construction against solitary construction.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that validates the learner's observation that building requires work, and then asks them to compare the effort or materials needed for 100 birds to build one shared roof versus 100 birds each building their own separate roof.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Shared vs. Individual Comparison
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to compare the effort, time, or materials required to build one shared roof versus each bird or family building its own separate roof.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Observation
rubric_items.description: Acknowledges or validates the learner's correct realization that the birds still have to expend energy to build the structure.

rubric_items.title: Use Concrete Scale
rubric_items.description: Incorporates the previously established scale (e.g., '100 friends' or 'dozens of families') to help the learner visualize the math of the workload difference.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Directly explains that sharing a roof means less work, fewer materials, or less surface area per bird, rather than asking the learner to deduce this.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Asks a vague question about sharing or energy (e.g., 'How does teamwork help?') without providing the specific contrast between individual and group building.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly mapped the concrete calculation (5 times 3) to the real-world concept (the seeds), resolving their earlier confusion. They now need validation for this tentative insight and a prompt to synthesize their understanding into the final algebraic expression.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's correct connection between the calculation and the seeds, and then prompt them to state the final generalized algebraic expression for $c$ cups.

rubric_items.title: Validate Concrete Meaning
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm the learner's tentative statement that the '15' (or 5 times 3) represents the weight of the seeds.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Algebraic Synthesis
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to write or state the complete general expression for $c$ cups, combining the variable term and the constant.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce the Parallel
rubric_items.description: Explicitly point out that multiplying 5 by 3 for the concrete example is exactly why we multiply 5 by $c$ in the general expression.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final combined algebraic expression (e.g., '$5c + \text{feeder}$') for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Non-Guidance
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with only validation or a vague prompt (e.g., 'What's next?'); the response must specifically guide the learner toward constructing the final expression.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Regressing to Prior Concepts
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to explain again why the feeder weight doesn't change, as they have already successfully articulated this.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully grasped the 'T' analogy and realized that a perpendicular line must tilt if the base line tilts, breaking their assumption that right angles must align with the grid. They now need to apply this visualization back to the specific trail ($y=x$) to determine the direction of the shortest path.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Confirm the learner's realization and prompt them to describe the specific direction or slope the stem would point if the top bar tilts like the trail $y=x$.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Insight
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge or validate the learner's realization that the perpendicular line (the stem) must tilt.

rubric_items.title: Apply to the Specific Trail
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to describe the specific direction or slope the stem would have if the top bar is tilted like the trail y=x (which goes up and to the right).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Direction
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state the direction (e.g., 'down and right') or the mathematical slope (e.g., '-1') of the perpendicular line.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Calculation
rubric_items.description: Do not ask the learner to calculate the exact equation of the line or the new distance before they have qualitatively described the direction of the perpendicular path.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Validation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply confirm the learner is correct without prompting them to take the next step of applying the insight to the graph.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is persistently confusing the 4-foot total width of the archway with the radius, despite the tutor repeatedly providing the correct definitions. They are failing to map the geometric concepts of radius and diameter onto the physical reality of the archway and need to actively visualize this relationship rather than just hearing the definitions again.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should ask a targeted question that forces the learner to actively visualize the radius within the physical archway, such as asking where the center of the circle is or what the total width would be if the radius were actually 4 feet.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Radius Visualization
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to actively explain or visualize what a radius is, such as asking where it starts and ends or where the center of the circle is located.

rubric_items.title: Ground in Physical Context
rubric_items.description: Reference the physical features of the archway (e.g., the floor, the doorway opening) to help the learner map the geometric terms to the real-world object.

rubric_items.title: Hypothetical Scenario
rubric_items.description: Pose a hypothetical question to create cognitive conflict, such as asking how wide the total opening would be if the radius were actually 4 feet.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating Failed Explanations
rubric_items.description: Do not simply repeat the definitions of radius and diameter or state again that the radius is half of the 4-foot width, as this approach has already failed.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Calculation
rubric_items.description: Do not mention the circumference formula, pi, or the calculation steps, as the learner must resolve the physical dimension of the radius first.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly computed the mean (17.5) but has immediately become distracted by a shell, requiring a gentle redirection to consolidate what this calculated number actually represents in the context of their data.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the correct calculation, briefly acknowledge the distraction to maintain rapport, and prompt the learner to articulate what the value 17.5 represents about the plastic items.

rubric_items.title: Validate Calculation
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly confirms that 17.5 is the correct answer to the division step.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Contextual Interpretation
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks the learner to explain what the number 17.5 represents in the context of the plastic items or the beach cleanup.

rubric_items.title: Gentle Acknowledgment
rubric_items.description: The tutor briefly acknowledges the shell to maintain rapport before redirecting back to the math.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Meaning
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly tells the learner that 17.5 is the 'mean weight' or 'average weight' of the plastic, rather than prompting the learner to make that connection themselves.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Redirection
rubric_items.description: The tutor tells the learner to focus or get back to work without asking a specific, math-related question about the 17.5 value.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Encouraging Distraction
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a follow-up question about the shell (e.g., 'What color is it?' or 'Where did you find it?') that further derails the conversation away from the math objective.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully calculated both the vertical change (rise = 6) and the horizontal change (run = 4) using subtraction. Their immediate need is to connect these two isolated values to the concept of slope before moving on to constructing the full linear equation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the correct calculation of the run and prompt the learner to combine the rise (6) and run (4) to determine the slope.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Run Calculation
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm that the learner's calculation of the run (4) is correct.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Slope Connection
rubric_items.description: The tutor should prompt the learner to combine the previously calculated rise (6) and run (4) to find the slope, or ask if they recall how rise and run relate to slope.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Subtraction Strategy
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly praises the learner for successfully applying the same subtraction strategy they used for the rise to find the run.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Slope
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not calculate the slope for the learner (e.g., stating 6/4, 3/2, or 1.5) or explicitly tell them to 'divide 6 by 4' before giving them a chance to recall the relationship.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Equation Building
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not ask the learner to find the y-intercept or write the final linear equation before the slope itself has been explicitly established.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not ask a generic question like 'What do we do next?' without specifically anchoring the next step to the concept of slope or the calculated rise and run values.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive dissonance, resisting the fact that cells can burst because they hold a teleological belief that biological structures must possess a conscious self-preservation mechanism. They are struggling to reconcile the cell's 'need' to survive with the physical reality of passive, always-open water channels.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's intuition that bursting is detrimental, but prompt them to recognize that a passive physical structure (like the previously discussed open tunnel) lacks the ability to 'choose' to close, regardless of the cell's needs.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the 'Smart Gate' Belief
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to confront the difference between what the cell 'needs' to survive and whether a simple protein shape has the conscious ability or mechanism to make that happen.

rubric_items.title: Reapply the Passive Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response should direct the learner back to the physical reality of the 'open tunnel' or 'coin slot' analogy to reason about whether such a structure can actively respond to danger.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Intuition
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's logic makes sense from a survival standpoint (e.g., validating that it seems like a cell *should* want to protect itself).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Dismissive Assertion
rubric_items.description: Do not simply assert that cells burst or that they lack the ability to close without prompting the learner to reason about why the channel can't close based on its physical structure.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Introducing Structural Workarounds
rubric_items.description: Do not introduce other biological structures that prevent bursting (such as plant cell walls or contractile vacuoles), as this validates the learner's search for a rescue mechanism rather than addressing the passive nature of the channel.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: Do not respond with a generic prompt like 'Why do you think they have to?' that fails to highlight the specific conflict between the cell's survival needs and the channel's physical limitations.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner believes that because infrared light lacks color, it lacks the physical properties required to reflect off a wall, equating invisibility with being 'like air.' Their immediate need is to decouple the human perception of color from the physical ability of light to bounce off solid surfaces.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to question the causal link between having color and being able to bounce, either by asking why color would matter to a wall or by offering a counter-example of a colorless object that bounces.

rubric_items.title: Challenge the Color-Bounce Link
rubric_items.description: The tutor must prompt the learner to evaluate their proposed causal link, asking why lacking color would prevent something from bouncing off a wall.

rubric_items.title: Distinguish Perception from Physics
rubric_items.description: The tutor guides the learner to consider whether the wall reacts to human visibility (color) or to the physical presence of the light.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Premise
rubric_items.description: The tutor acknowledges that the learner is factually correct in stating that infrared light does not have a color visible to humans.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The tutor directly tells the learner that color does not affect reflection or that invisible things can still bounce, doing the reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: The tutor asks a generic question about color (e.g., 'What is color?') that fails to connect back to the specific mechanism of bouncing or reflecting off the wall.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: The tutor introduces scientific terms like 'wavelength', 'frequency', or 'electromagnetic spectrum' to explain color, bypassing the learner's intuitive block about physical bouncing.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly, though tentatively, predicts that adding mass to the screen will cause the laptop to tip at a smaller angle. They now need to connect this prediction back to the underlying mechanism by explaining how the added mass affects the overall center of mass.
rubric.ideal_next_move: Validate the learner's correct prediction and prompt them to explain why the coin causes the laptop to tip sooner, specifically asking how the coin changes the position of the overall center of mass.

rubric_items.title: Validate Prediction
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that the learner's prediction is correct, building their confidence in the idea that it would tip sooner.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to explain why the coin makes the laptop tip sooner, specifically directing them to think about what happens to the overall center of mass.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Explanation
rubric_items.description: Do not explain that the coin shifts the center of mass further back or closer to the pivot; leave the articulation of this mechanism entirely to the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Follow-ups
rubric_items.description: Do not ask a generic 'Why?' without anchoring the question to the physical concepts already discussed (the center of mass or the pivot point).

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified water and carbon dioxide as the products of the atomic rearrangement, but they now need to connect this microscopic chemical process (bond formation releasing energy) to the macroscopic observation (the compost pile heating up). Furthermore, they need to articulate this connection themselves to overcome their hidden belief that the heat comes from the physical friction of atoms moving, rather than the chemical formation of new bonds.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm 'water' and then prompt the learner to synthesize their understanding by explaining exactly why the compost pile gets hot, requiring them to attribute the heat specifically to the formation of the new CO2 and water bonds.

rubric_items.title: Affirmation of the Product
rubric_items.description: The tutor must explicitly confirm that water is the correct second molecule.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Macro-Micro Synthesis
rubric_items.description: The tutor should ask the learner to connect the microscopic process they just figured out (forming CO2 and water) back to the macroscopic phenomenon of the compost pile heating up.

rubric_items.title: Targeting the Mechanism of Heat
rubric_items.description: The tutor's prompt should specifically ask the learner to explain *how* or *why* the formation of these molecules creates heat, creating an opportunity to surface and correct the hidden belief about physical friction versus chemical bond formation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Synthesis
rubric_items.description: The tutor explicitly states the connection for the learner (e.g., 'So because billions of water and CO2 molecules are forming bonds, the whole pile gets hot') instead of asking the learner to articulate it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Moving On Prematurely
rubric_items.description: The tutor moves on to a new topic (e.g., what happens to the water next, or another step in respiration) without having the learner connect the bond formation back to the heat of the compost pile.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Complete Picture
rubric_items.description: The tutor praises the learner for successfully identifying both of the main products of this process (CO2 and water) before asking the next question.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is applying a physical 'container' schema to electromagnetic energy, failing to realize that the UV light converted into heat does not occupy physical volume and continuously transfers out of the glass. They are stuck because the tutor's previous mention of 'dissipates' was not internalized.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should use a targeted probe or everyday analogy about heat (like a hot road or a warm mug) to help the learner reason that thermal energy continuously transfers to the surrounding air rather than taking up physical space and 'filling' the object.

rubric_items.title: Target the 'Container' Misconception
rubric_items.description: The response must directly challenge the learner's premise that the windshield has a physical capacity or volume that can 'fill up' with light or heat.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Reasoning About Heat Dissipation
rubric_items.description: The response should ask a guiding question that prompts the learner to think about where the heat goes or what happens to an object as it gets warm, rather than just stating that it leaves.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response validates the learner's mental model by acknowledging that it makes sense to think of absorption like a sponge or a cup filling with liquid.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating the Previous Explanation
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply repeat that 'it converts to heat' or 'it dissipates' without introducing a new angle, as the learner already heard this and still asked if it gets full.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner the conclusion (e.g., 'Energy doesn't take up space' or 'The heat goes into the air') without requiring them to do the reasoning.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly identified the minimum voltage (-170V), successfully resolving their confusion about how a 340V peak-to-peak range corresponds to an amplitude of 170. They now need confirmation of this insight and a prompt to return to the deferred task of finding the frequency or period to complete the equation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should confirm the -170V minimum, briefly connect the -170V to 170V range back to the 340V total swing to fully close the loop, and then redirect the learner to finding the frequency or period.

rubric_items.title: Confirm Minimum Voltage
rubric_items.description: Explicitly confirm that the learner's answer of -170 volts is correct.

rubric_items.title: Close the Loop on Peak-to-Peak
rubric_items.description: Connect the range between -170V and 170V back to the 340V total swing to explicitly resolve the learner's earlier question ('But isn't the voltage 340?').

rubric_items.title: Redirect to Frequency/Period
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to return to the deferred task of determining the frequency or period to find the 'B' value in the equation.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Next Step
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the actual value for the frequency, period, or 'B', nor the formula for calculating 'B', before the learner has a chance to attempt it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Lingering on Amplitude
rubric_items.description: Do not ask further probing questions about amplitude or voltage, as the learner has already demonstrated understanding of this component and needs to move on.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck on the idea that the vertical height of the teepee (3 feet) is identical to the length of the fabric on the slanted sides, unable to visualize the difference. They need a concrete mental model or analogy to distinguish the straight-down vertical path from the diagonal path of the fabric.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a concrete visual analogy or thought experiment (like a center pole vs. the outer fabric, or dropping a string straight down vs. pulling it to the edge) and ask the learner to deduce which path is longer.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Vertical Height
rubric_items.description: Explicitly affirm that the learner is correct about the 3-foot measurement applying to the straight-down vertical height (e.g., a center pole).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Visual Deduction
rubric_items.description: Ask a guiding question based on a concrete visual analogy (like a center pole vs. the outer fabric, or a ladder leaning against a wall) to help the learner deduce for themselves why the slanted path is longer than the 3-foot drop.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Repeating the Assertion
rubric_items.description: Do not merely repeat the statement that 'slanted sides are longer' or 'the fabric is tilted,' as this explanation has already proven ineffective for this learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Formalization
rubric_items.description: Do not give away the geometric explanation by explicitly naming right triangles, the hypotenuse, or the Pythagorean theorem before the learner has intuitively grasped the physical difference in lengths.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands the math of the decay equation but lacks the foundational knowledge of what an alpha particle actually is, causing confusion about why a piece of radiation is represented by the element helium. They need to connect the physical composition of an alpha particle (2 protons) to the atomic number of helium on the periodic table.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should state that an alpha particle contains exactly 2 protons (an atomic number of 2) and prompt the learner to check the periodic table to see which element that corresponds to.

rubric_items.title: Establish Alpha Particle Composition
rubric_items.description: Provide the necessary foundational information by stating that an alpha particle consists of 2 protons (or has an atomic number of 2).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Periodic Table Connection
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to use the periodic table to determine which element corresponds to an atomic number of 2.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that explicitly tell the learner that Helium is the element with atomic number 2, doing the matching work for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Non-guidance
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that ask the learner to explain the connection to helium without first establishing that an alpha particle has 2 protons or an atomic number of 2.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Question
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that 'Why helium?' is a great question, validating the counterintuitive nature of a decaying heavy metal emitting a noble gas nucleus.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is incorrectly applying their 'vertical shift = bottom' misconception to the standard y = sin(x) graph, failing to realize that standard sine oscillates between 1 and -1 around a midline of 0. They need concrete scaffolding to see that the standard graph goes below 0, which makes 0 the middle rather than the bottom.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to recall or calculate the maximum and minimum values of standard y = sin(x) to help them discover that the wave goes below 0 and is therefore centered at 0.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold Standard Sine Range
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to recall or calculate the maximum and minimum values of the standard y = sin(x) graph (e.g., 1 and -1) to establish its actual boundaries.

rubric_items.title: Clarify 'Above and Below' vs. 'Bottom'
rubric_items.description: Explicitly clarify the distinction between the central axis a wave oscillates around and its lowest boundary, directly addressing the learner's persistent focus on 'the bottom'.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Giving the Range/Midline)
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that standard sin(x) oscillates between -1 and 1, or that its midline is 0.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Do not simply tell the learner they are wrong or repeat the previous question without providing a concrete mathematical (e.g., evaluating sine) or physical (e.g., resting spring) stepping stone.

rubric_items.title: Physical Equilibrium Analogy
rubric_items.description: Ground the concept of the midline by asking where the physical spring would sit if it were completely still (equilibrium), contrasting this with the momentary pause at the bottom.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has successfully multiplied the coefficients to get 9, but is unsure how to combine the powers of 10 ($10^{-6} \times 10^{-6}$). They need guidance on the algebraic rule for multiplying exponents with the same base.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should affirm the correct coefficient (9) and prompt the learner to apply the rule for multiplying exponents by asking what happens to the exponents when multiplying powers of 10.

rubric_items.title: Affirm Coefficient
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate the learner's correct calculation of the front numbers (9).

rubric_items.title: Prompt Exponent Rule
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to the rule for multiplying terms with the same base, either by asking them to recall the rule or by prompting them to add the specific exponents (-6 and -6).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Give Away the Answer
rubric_items.description: State the final exponent (-12) or the complete scientific notation ($9 \times 10^{-12}$) instead of letting the learner determine it.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Respond with a generic question (e.g., 'What do you think?') that fails to focus the learner on the specific operation of combining exponents.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the mechanical advantage of a lever with their everyday intuition that holding a heavy object far away from their body feels heavier. They have temporarily lost track of their earlier realization that the wheel, not their arms, supports the weight when the load is placed far from the handles.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted prompt that asks the learner to recall their earlier realization about what is physically supporting the load when it is placed over the wheel, prompting them to resolve the contradiction themselves.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Recall of Support
rubric_items.description: The response must prompt the learner to recall or consider what physical object is actually holding the weight up when the load is placed far away from their hands.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Distance Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response should acknowledge why the learner is confused, validating their everyday experience that holding an unsupported object far away from the body normally does feel heavier.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Analogy Scope
rubric_items.description: The response clarifies that the 'long wrench' analogy was specifically about controlling the side-to-side twist, helping to separate that concept from the effort required to lift the load.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Premature Resolution
rubric_items.description: The response must not explicitly tell the learner that the wheel bears the weight or that the distance makes it lighter to lift, as the learner needs to reconnect these dots themselves.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unanchored Questioning
rubric_items.description: The response must not simply ask a generic question like 'Why do you think it would be heavier?' without directing the learner's attention back to the wheelbarrow's structure or their previous insights.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has explicitly chosen the incorrect option from the tutor's previous prompt, doubling down on the misconception that the iron core merely 'squeezes' the existing field. They have forgotten or failed to apply the previously established fact that the domains have their own magnetic fields which previously canceled each other out.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should redirect the learner's attention to the domains' own magnetic fields—reminding them that these fields previously canceled out—and ask what those individual fields do now that they are aligned.

rubric_items.title: Leverage Prior Insight on Domain Fields
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to reconsider their answer by reminding them, or asking them to recall, that the domains have their own individual magnetic fields (which previously canceled out).

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Additive Effect
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to deduce what happens to the overall magnetic strength when these individual domain fields point in the same direction.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Direct Correction
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly tell the learner that they chose the wrong option or directly state that the iron adds its own magnetic field to the mix.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Pushback
rubric_items.description: Do not simply ask 'Are you sure?' or 'Why do you think that?' without grounding the prompt in the physical properties of the domains.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Learner's Stance
rubric_items.description: Neutrally acknowledge that the learner clarified their belief in the 'squeezing' mechanism before pivoting to the domains' properties.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is grappling with the concept of energy transduction, wondering if the physical sound wave simply vanishes since it doesn't travel to the brain. They need to connect their prior realization that the wave bends the hair cells to the idea that the wave's energy is transferred or converted rather than destroyed.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to recall what the sound wave physically did to the hair cells, guiding them to deduce that the wave's energy was transferred into bending the hairs rather than simply disappearing.

rubric_items.title: Redirect to Hair Cell Interaction
rubric_items.description: The tutor's response must direct the learner to consider the physical interaction between the sound wave and the hair cells, such as asking what the wave just did to the hairs.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Energy Transfer or Usage
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to deduce that the wave's movement or energy was transferred, absorbed, or used up in the process of bending the hair cells.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Conservation Instinct
rubric_items.description: The response acknowledges that asking if the wave 'disappears' is a good scientific instinct because energy or movement must go somewhere.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Transduction Concept
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner that the wave's energy is transferred, converted, or absorbed, doing the conceptual reasoning for them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Prematurely Advancing to the Pathway
rubric_items.description: The response ignores the 'disappear' question or immediately re-asks about the pathway or nerve to the brain before resolving the learner's confusion about the sound wave.

learning_objective: LS2.B Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that breaking chemical bonds releases something, but they are currently conflating matter (CO2 gas) and energy (heat) by assuming they are the exact same entity. They need to decouple these concepts and recognize them as two distinct products of the decomposition process.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A targeted probe that prompts the learner to contrast the physical properties of gas (which is matter/atoms) with heat (which is energy), helping them deduce that they are two separate outcomes of breaking the wood's bonds.

rubric_items.title: Decouple Matter and Energy
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to distinguish between the gas (which is matter made of atoms) and the heat (which is energy), rather than treating them as the same thing.

rubric_items.title: Connect to Prior Context (Bonds)
rubric_items.description: Frames the question around the previous turn's concept, reinforcing that breaking the chemical bonds results in both the release of gas and the release of heat as separate outcomes.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge the Source of Confusion
rubric_items.description: Validates the learner's question by acknowledging why it makes sense to link them (e.g., because both are released at the same time from the same wood molecules).

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover (Telling)
rubric_items.description: Directly tells the learner that gas is matter and heat is energy, robbing them of the opportunity to deduce the difference themselves.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness
rubric_items.description: Responds with a simple 'No' or a generic prompt (e.g., 'What do you think?') without providing a conceptual contrast between the properties of gas and heat.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is stuck in a persistent misconception, applying Newtonian mechanical intuition ('more force/energy equals more speed') to light waves. Because previous analogies (flashlight, sound) failed to break this intuition, the learner needs a shift in perspective to decouple a wave's energy from its propagation speed.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should explicitly contrast how physical objects behave (where force changes speed) with how waves behave, or prompt the learner to consider the medium (the air) as the actual 'speed limit' for the wave.

rubric_items.title: Decouple Force from Wave Speed
rubric_items.description: The response must directly challenge the learner's application of mechanical 'force' to light waves, prompting them to separate the energy/intensity of the wave from its travel speed.

rubric_items.title: Pivot to the Medium
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to consider what actually determines the speed of light (the medium it travels through, like air), shifting focus away from the properties of the light pulse itself.

rubric_items.title: Acknowledge Mechanical Intuition
rubric_items.description: The response validates the learner's logic by acknowledging that for everyday physical objects (like throwing a ball), less force does mean less speed, before contrasting this behavior with waves.

rubric_items.title: Prematurely Stating the Rule
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner that the speed of light is constant or that the medium determines the speed, giving away the conceptual leap rather than guiding the learner to it.

rubric_items.title: Looping on Failed Analogies
rubric_items.description: The response asks another generic question about energy or repeats the flashlight/sound analogies, which have already proven ineffective at breaking this specific misconception.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands that converting pounds to kilograms requires division to produce a smaller number, but they are experiencing a procedural execution bottleneck regarding the correct order of division (140 / 2.2 vs. 2.2 / 140). They need a concrete strategy to evaluate which setup is correct rather than just guessing.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should prompt the learner to evaluate the two options by estimating the outcome of '2.2 divided by 140' and checking if that result makes sense as a person's weight, or by conceptualizing what is being divided into groups.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Evaluation of Options
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to evaluate the two division options by either estimating the numerical outcome (e.g., 'What roughly is 2 divided by 140?') or conceptualizing the division (e.g., 'Are you splitting 140 into groups of 2.2?').

rubric_items.title: Ground in Real-World Context
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to use the real-world context of a person's weight as the criterion for evaluating the division options (e.g., 'Would that result make sense for someone's weight?').

rubric_items.title: Validate the Operation
rubric_items.description: Explicitly validate that the learner has successfully identified the correct operation (division) and the correct numbers to use before addressing the order.

rubric_items.title: Overhelpful Takeover: Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: Do not directly state that '140 divided by 2.2' is the correct setup or do the math for them.

rubric_items.title: Underhelpful Vagueness: No Evaluation Strategy
rubric_items.description: Do not leave the learner stranded by asking a generic question (e.g., 'Which one makes more sense?') without offering a concrete way to test or conceptualize the two options.

rubric_items.title: Premature Shift to Formal Rules
rubric_items.description: Do not abandon the current intuitive 'reasonableness' strategy by introducing formal dimensional analysis, unit cancellation rules, or memorized formulas at this exact moment.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner understands they need to multiply the new base (4) by the ratio (1.5), but they are stuck on the mechanics of performing this specific arithmetic operation. They need scaffolding to break down the multiplication of a whole number by a decimal.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should offer a concrete strategy or first step for calculating 4 times 1.5, such as breaking it into 4 times 1 and 4 times 0.5, without giving away the final answer.

rubric_items.title: Scaffold the Calculation
rubric_items.description: Prompt the learner to take a concrete first step in calculating 4 times 1.5, such as asking them to multiply 4 by 1 first, or asking how they usually handle decimals.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Answer-Giving
rubric_items.description: Do not provide the final calculated height (6) or complete the arithmetic steps for the learner.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: Do not leave the learner stranded by merely repeating the instruction to multiply 4 by 1.5 without offering a strategy to execute it.

rubric_items.title: Validate the Difficulty
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that multiplying by a decimal can be tricky, validating their hesitation before guiding them.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has tentatively grasped the tutor's analogy, realizing that offspring from the same parents can inherit different traits and look different. They now need validation of this insight and a prompt to apply it back to the original context to resolve their misconception about the smooth and bumpy pumpkins.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should enthusiastically confirm the learner's realization about sibling variation and prompt them to apply this new understanding to conclude whether the smooth and bumpy pumpkins could share a parent.

rubric_items.title: Validate Sibling Variation
rubric_items.description: Confirm the learner's tentative realization that offspring from the same parents can indeed inherit different traits and look different.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Application to Pumpkins
rubric_items.description: Ask the learner to apply their new understanding of variation back to the original problem of whether the smooth and bumpy pumpkins could have the same parent.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Conclusion
rubric_items.description: Do not explicitly state that the smooth and bumpy pumpkins can or do share a parent; leave this final connection for the learner to articulate.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Confirmation
rubric_items.description: Do not simply say 'Yes' or 'Exactly' without directing the learner's attention back to the specific pumpkins they were discussing.

rubric_items.title: Reinforce 'Instructions' Terminology
rubric_items.description: Reincorporate the previously established term 'instructions' to remind the learner of the mechanism behind the variation.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is experiencing cognitive conflict upon realizing that individual foxes do not physically adapt to their environment during their lifetimes (the Lamarckian misconception). They need a conceptual stepping stone—specifically the idea of natural variation within a population—to understand how average traits change over generations without individual transformation.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's surprise that individuals cannot change their traits, and then prompt them to consider natural variation (e.g., asking what happens if foxes in a group are naturally born with different ear sizes).

rubric_items.title: Confirm Fixed Individual Traits
rubric_items.description: The tutor should explicitly validate the learner's surprise by affirming that an individual fox is stuck with the ear size it is born with.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Natural Variation
rubric_items.description: The tutor should introduce or prompt the learner to consider natural variation, such as asking what it means for the group if foxes are naturally born with a mix of different ear sizes.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining Natural Selection
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not give away the full mechanism by explicitly stating that foxes born with smaller ears survive longer and pass on that trait.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Underhelpful Repetition
rubric_items.description: The tutor must not simply repeat the previous question about how the group changes without offering a new conceptual stepping stone like natural variation.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Reverting to Ear Function
rubric_items.description: The tutor should not regress to discussing why small ears are beneficial (such as preventing heat loss or keeping out cold wind and snow), because the immediate bottleneck is the mechanism of generational change, not the function of the trait.

learning_objective: LS2.D Social Interactions and Group Behavior

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is conflating the peaceful activity that builds trust (grooming) with the urgent cooperative actions that rely on that trust (predator defense), guessing that chimps would groom each other during an attack. They need to realize that while grooming builds the friendship, trusted friends will take different actions to protect each other when immediate danger appears.
rubric.ideal_next_move: A cognitive-conflict prompt that gently challenges the practicality of grooming during a predator attack and asks what trusted friends would do instead to survive.

rubric_items.title: Challenge Grooming During Danger
rubric_items.description: The response should explicitly question or gently challenge the learner's suggestion that chimps would sit and groom each other while a dangerous predator is actively threatening them.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Defensive Action
rubric_items.description: The response should prompt the learner to think of a specific, urgent action trusted friends would take to protect each other from the predator instead of grooming.

rubric_items.title: Validate Prior Insight
rubric_items.description: Acknowledge that grooming is indeed the activity that made them trusted friends in the first place, before the danger arrived.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving the Answer
rubric_items.description: The response should not explicitly tell the learner the defensive actions chimps take (e.g., making warning calls, fighting the predator together, or helping each other escape).

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Repetition
rubric_items.description: The response should not simply repeat the previous question without addressing the learner's specific, impractical guess about grooming during an attack.

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is fixated on glucose as the ultimate goal of all plant processes and missed the implication that glucose's chemical makeup (C, H, O) excludes nitrogen. They need to realize that plants must build other macromolecules besides carbohydrates to survive and grow.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should firmly clarify that nitrogen is not part of glucose, and prompt the learner to think about other structural materials or nutrients living things need to build their bodies.

rubric_items.title: Clarify Glucose Composition
rubric_items.description: Explicitly state or guide the learner to conclude that nitrogen is not a building block of glucose, reinforcing that glucose is strictly made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.

rubric_items.title: Prompt for Alternative Macromolecules
rubric_items.description: Ask a guiding question that shifts the learner's focus away from glucose and toward other structural components or molecules living things need to build (e.g., asking what else bodies or cells are made of).

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Target Molecules
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner that nitrogen is used to make proteins, amino acids, or nucleic acids/DNA.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Validating the Enzyme Connection
rubric_items.description: Do not validate the learner's guess by explaining that nitrogen makes enzymes which then help synthesize glucose; while technically true, this pedantic detail would reinforce their core misconception that the bug's ultimate purpose is energy production.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Rejection
rubric_items.description: Do not simply say 'No' or 'Try again' without reminding the learner of glucose's chemical makeup or providing a hint about other biological structures.

rubric_items.title: Bridge to Familiar Nutrition
rubric_items.description: Use a familiar analogy, such as human nutrition (e.g., eating carbohydrates for energy vs. eating protein for building muscle), to help the learner conceptualize non-energy building blocks.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly, though tentatively, identified that the ramp's base aligns with the right-side zero. Their immediate bottleneck is connecting this specific zero to the correct scale on the protractor to understand why 50 is the right measurement and 130 is not.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's choice of the right-side zero and prompt them to follow the sequence of numbers starting from that zero to see which scale counts up toward their angle.

rubric_items.title: Validate Learner's Answer
rubric_items.description: Confirm that the learner correctly identified the right-side zero, addressing the uncertainty indicated by their question mark.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Scale Tracing
rubric_items.description: Direct the learner to follow the sequence of numbers starting from that right-side zero to see which scale counts up (e.g., 0, 10, 20) toward their angle.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Explaining the Scale
rubric_items.description: Do not directly tell the learner which scale (inner or outer) to use or explicitly state that counting from the right zero leads to 50.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Unscaffolded Questions
rubric_items.description: Do not merely confirm the right side and ask a broad question (like 'So why does it say 130?' or 'Which number is correct?') without providing the concrete step of tracing the numbers from zero.

learning_objective: PS2.C Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner has correctly intuited the practical effect of a staggered stance (the front foot 'catches' the forward momentum), but they have not yet connected this physical action to the geometric concept of the upper body staying within the widened base of support. They need to bridge their tactile understanding of 'catching' with the spatial relationship between their moving upper body and the boundaries of their feet.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's practical intuition about the front foot 'catching' them and prompt them to explain how the position of that front foot relates to how far their upper body can travel forward before tipping.

rubric_items.title: Relate Front Foot to Upper Body Travel
rubric_items.description: Prompts the learner to articulate how the position of the front foot changes how far their upper body can move forward before leaving the 'space' between their feet.

rubric_items.title: Validate 'Catching' Intuition
rubric_items.description: Incorporates the learner's specific phrasing about the front foot 'catching' them to validate their practical intuition.

rubric_items.title: Reintroduce Center of Gravity
rubric_items.description: Encourages the learner to map their practical understanding of the front foot 'catching' them back to the formal concept of 'center of gravity' they mentioned earlier in the dialogue.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Giving Away the Mechanism
rubric_items.description: Explicitly tells the learner the physics mechanism, such as stating that the front foot extends the base of support so the center of gravity remains over it.

rubric_items.title: Avoid Vague Probing
rubric_items.description: Asks a generic follow-up (e.g., 'How does it catch you?' or 'Why?') without providing spatial scaffolding like referencing the upper body, the space, or the center of gravity.

learning_objective: LS1.C Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner is persistently conflating chemical rearrangement (forming new molecules) with elemental transmutation (changing one type of atom into another), misunderstanding the tutor's previous explanations. They are stuck on the word 'rearrange' and need a concrete way to visualize that rearranging pieces does not change the fundamental nature of the pieces themselves.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should introduce a concrete, non-chemical analogy (like Lego bricks or letters in a word) to redefine 'rearrange' and prompt the learner to explain why rearranging the pieces cannot create a fundamentally new type of piece.

rubric_items.title: Clarify the Concept of 'Rearranging'
rubric_items.description: The response must explicitly address the learner's misuse of the word 'rearrange' by distinguishing between changing how atoms are connected together versus changing the identity of the atoms themselves.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Learner Application
rubric_items.description: The response must end with a question that requires the learner to actively explain why rearranging carbon/hydrogen/oxygen cannot produce nitrogen, rather than just telling them it is impossible.

rubric_items.title: Introduce Concrete Analogy
rubric_items.description: The response should use a familiar, non-chemical analogy (such as Lego bricks, building blocks, or letters in an anagram) to help the learner visualize the physical limits of rearranging.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Repeating Abstract Rules
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that merely restate the abstract rule that 'atoms cannot change type' or 'enzymes cannot create elements,' as the tutor has already stated this twice without success.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Premature Biological Advance
rubric_items.description: Penalize responses that return to discussing chitin synthesis, amino acids, or the caterpillar's digestion, as the fundamental chemistry misconception must be resolved first.

rubric.learner_state_analysis: The learner correctly spotted the '-1' in the expression but likely views it as an isolated operation (taking a block off the end of the stem) rather than understanding that the entire (n - 1) term represents the stem's blocks excluding the shared intersection.
rubric.ideal_next_move: The tutor should validate the learner's identification of the '-1' and prompt them to explain what the entire (n - 1) grouping represents physically in the T-shape.

rubric_items.title: Shift Focus to the Grouping
rubric_items.description: The response should validate the learner's focus on the '-1' but direct their attention to the entire (n - 1) term as a single unit in the expression.

rubric_items.title: Prompt Physical Mapping
rubric_items.description: The response must ask the learner to identify which specific physical blocks in the T-shape correspond to the (n - 1) part of the expression.

rubric_items.title: Probe the Subtraction Location
rubric_items.description: The response should ask the learner to specify exactly where the subtracted block is located in the physical shape, targeting the hidden belief that it is taken from the bottom of the stem rather than the intersection.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Giving Away the Mapping
rubric_items.description: The response explicitly tells the learner that (n - 1) represents the stem without the shared middle block, doing the structural mapping for them.

rubric_items.title: Pitfall: Vague Acceptance
rubric_items.description: The response simply accepts 'the minus one' and moves on, or asks a generic question (like 'Why is it there?') without anchoring the prompt to the physical T-shape or the (n - 1) grouping.
